events.title: Anduril lands $2.9 billion Navy submarine shipyard contract days after Luckey joins Pentagon weapons group
events.summary: Anduril landed a $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy to support submarine production. The company said it will build components for the Virginia-class submarine. Co-founder Palmer Luckey, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk were named to the Pentagon's Project Meridian. Anduril won an up to $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy on Tuesday to boost submarine production, days after co-founder Palmer Luckey was named to a Pentagon future weapons task force. The company is also investing $3.7 billion to scale a new shipyard at Sparrows Point, outside Baltimore, Maryland, slated to start operations in 2030 and create about 3,100 jobs. Anduril said the 2 million-square-foot facility will build components for the Virginia-class submarine. Some parts, including torpedo tubes, will be manufactured at a 160,000-square-foot facility in Orange County, California. "This is about putting more food on the table and being able to meet the requirements that our country has to produce more submarines," said Anduril President and Chief Strategy Officer Chris Brose in a press briefing. The deal comes days after the Department of Defense tapped Luckey to join a new initiative called Project Meridian to identify and develop capabilities for future U.S. conflicts, raising questions over defense tech's growing sway in Washington as the companies compete for government contracts. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk are also part of the project. Both SpaceX and Anduril are actively working with the U.S. government. Department of Defense Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael addressed Luckey's involvement with the Pentagon in comments to CNBC on Tuesday, dismissing any concerns about a potential conflict of interest. "There's really nothing to see here," he said. Michael said the collection of academics, former military and industry leaders in Project Meridian is "exactly the right kind of mix that you want" to prepare for any future conflict. Defense tech companies and their leaders have seen their influence grow in Washington in recent months as President Donald Trump seeks to bolster U.S. military capabilities, including shipbuilding. Marc Andreessen , whose venture firm Andreessen Horowitz pours billions into defense tech firms, including Anduril, was named to the Pentagon's defense policy board this summer, alongside Thiel Capital's Blake Masters. Google unveils latest AI model, but Wall Street wants a breakout personal agent Former LinkedIn chief Roslansky to leave Microsoft, following other exec departures SpaceX launches Google AI chips into orbit in push toward space-based data centers Trump's AI lunch included every major tech company. Except Apple Anduril is widely known for building autonomous drones and crafts. Over the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was reportedly in talks to build drone boats on the site. Brose said the facility will focus on the Virginia-class submarine program, illustrating a push into conventional shipbuilding by the growing defense contractor. "Our goal here is to be a critical, and hopefully, over time, much larger and growing part of the supply chain for our lead shipbuilders," He said. "And over time, we hope that'll grow up to very large sections of the ship." The massive vessels are built by General Dynamics Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries. This summer, General Dynamics won a $76.6 billion Navy award to build submarines. "This is an opportunity to really reimagine how a shipyard is built and how this work is done, and that's just not something that our current industrial base has the luxury of doing," Brose said. CORRECTION: This headline has been updated to reflect that co-founder Palmer Luckey was named to the Pentagon's Project Meridian. An earlier version misstated his title.

events.title: Trump hedges on paying back government for ads that already aired
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he and his political action committee will pay for controversial television ads that praised him and had been funded by the U.S. government. The White House later clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service ads moving forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. Trump's announcement came after continued backlash to the ads, which had run in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election. A new Trump ad began airing on Tuesday. President Donald Trump hedged Tuesday when asked whether he would reimburse the U.S. government for previously aired television advertisements that praised him, saying, "We'll decide." The ads cost the federal government nearly $10 million before Trump on Monday announced that he and his political action committee will pay for the segments in the face of criticism that they are propoganda and aimed at helping Republican political candidates. The White House later Monday clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service announcements going forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. The prior airings reportedly were funded from a pool of up to $20 million set aside by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security . Asked whether he would reimburse the government for the costs of ads already aired, Trump told reporters, "The ads were really good." "They were promotion for the country, done by many presidents before," he said. "So we'll decide." Trump's latest comments on the furor came hours after a new ad aired. That ad was labeled as paid for by the U.S. government. The ad features video clips of Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussing the U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year. "Nicolás Maduro had his chance ... until he didn't," Hegseth says in the ad. "He effed around and he found out." Another clip in the ad shows Rubio warning, "Don't play games with [President Trump] in office." The ads have been running in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election . Those contests will determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans will maintain their majorities in both chambers of Congress. The White House and MAGA Inc. did not immediately reply when asked whether the super PAC would cover the cost of the new ad or whether the buy had already been placed before Trump's announcement and would remain taxpayer-funded. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.," Trump said. AdImpact has tracked roughly $9.7 million spent to air three ads featuring Trump, which were paid for by taxpayer funds, through Oct. 5. Trump's announcement that he would pay for the ads came three days after The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that "Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency." Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' The Times said federal money to pay for the ads became available on Sept. 19, "when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events." Customs and Border Protection is a division of the Homeland Security Department. Sen. Maggie Hassan , D-N.H., in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, wrote, "The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates.'" In a statement on Monday night, Hassan said, "These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer's dime to begin with." "They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the President should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads," Hassan said. "There's a lesson here: We can't underestimate the difference that citizens can make in our country when they speak out and hold their leaders to account," she said. On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., called for the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate the ads. events.title: Boomers' dividend stocks take beating from bond yields, with retirement income on the line
events.summary: The rapid rise in bond yields led by the 10-Year U.S. Treasury has made dividend stocks less attractive as income investments. This market dynamic has hit stock prices hard in sectors that income-seeking investors such as seniors rely on, from real estate to utilities and materials. Giving up on dividend stocks is not a strategy, experts say, but neither is a desperate chase for higher yields. Dividend stocks like utilities are being pummeled amid bond market chaos and the rise of the 10-year U.S. treasury , raising questions for seniors about how to continue meeting their income needs. While dividend stocks are only part of a diversified portfolio for older investors, many boomers often depend on dividend stocks and funds for at least some of their income. When returns are rocky, it can, understandably, cause some consternation. Many dividend funds are giving back some of their gains from earlier in the year when bond rates were lower, said Timothy Chubb, chief investment officer at Girard, a Univest Wealth Division, in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania. Sectors including real estate, utilities, and materials have seen stock prices plummet as bond yields become more attractive and dividend stock yields less attractive on a relative risk-reward basis. For all the concern about bonds, inflows into bond ETFs have been rising. Consider the iShares 20+ Year Treasury ETF ( TLT ): it has taken in over $3.2 billion in net inflows from investors over the past month, according to ETFAction.com. To be sure, there is a split in the market between investors who continue to pile into ultrashort bond funds, which had record inflows near $20 billion in September, according to Morningstar. And those investors making a bet that the worst in the bond market is over and the yields are too attractive to pass up. TLT's inflows were its largest monthly inflows on record as its yield hit the highest since 2002, according to Dow Jones data. Boomers, however, shouldn't necessarily give up on dividend-paying stocks. Instead, they should consider several strategies that can blunt the impact of rising bond yields on their income-stock portfolios. Here are a few. While it can be tempting, financial advisors and strategists caution older investors that before doing anything else, the most important thing is what not to do: simply chase yield. "The worst thing that a retiree could do is sell a high-quality dividend payer at depressed prices to chase income somewhere else in the stock market just to get higher yield," said Chubb. Instead, investors should focus more on fundamental earnings growth. In the short term, dividend yields of these companies may look less attractive, but that can change over time as dividends rise and the stock price is likely to be steadier as well. "I'd much rather get a company going up 4% to 5% with another 3% in dividend yield than chasing an 8% dividend yield for a business that's in decline," he said. Be selective about stocks, sectors that can beat inflation Boomers who are buying individual dividend-paying stocks should look at the quality of the company by asking several questions, according to Chubb. Are they able to increase their dividend, and in a way that beats inflation? Is the company growing? Are they borrowing debt to fund the dividend, or are they funding it through the cash flows of the business? The higher-yielding the company, the more debt it has or the more risk that a dividend could get cut in the future, he said. And the more interest rates rise, the more highly levered companies face greater financing risk. "It really comes down to the underlying business," he said. With dividend ETFs, consider the strategy fund managers employ. ETFs that focus on the highest-yielding dividends in slow-growth sectors such as utilities and consumer staples can be hit harder when rates move higher. So investors might want to look more closely at funds that seek dividend growth versus those that are more focused on high yield. One example of a high-yield dividend fund is the Invesco S&P 500 High Dividend Low Volatility ETF ( SPHD ), which tracks an index that selects S&P 500 stocks that offer the largest dividends while seeking to minimize volatility. This fund had a one-month negative return of 7.59%. It's up around 4% year-to-date. Consumer staples (18.5%) and utilities (14%) are the No. 2 and No. 3 sectors in the ETF by weight after real estate (20%), according to Invesco data through Sept. 30. Other high-dividend yield funds haven't been hit quite as hard. Vanguard High Dividend Yield Index ETF ( VYM ), for example, chooses securities based on current yield, with only the highest-yielding companies selected, according to ETF Database. That fund has a negative one-month return of 3.85%, though it's up about 11% for the year to date. Its top sectors are financials, industrials and technology, according to Vanguard data as of Aug. 31 (it has not provided a more recent portfolio disclosure).

events.title: Meta Muse popularity lifts AMD stock to fresh highs as AI agents juice CPU sales
events.summary: The personal agent boom is lifting the fortunes of AMD and Intel, which have outperformed their megacap tech peers this year and over the past month. As leading developers of central processing units, the longtime rivals are finding a major role in the AI market, which had been dominated by Nvidia. "As more agents are created and developed, and more people start to use them for more tasks, it's going to start to shift the workload away from GPUs and onto CPUs," said Ryan Shrout, president of Signal65. The personal AI agent boom is giving Advanced Micro Devices and Intel new life after the companies spent years watching Nvidia and its GPUs dominate the artificial intelligence market. The central processing unit, or CPU, was once the primary workhorse of a computer server before Nvidia's graphics processing units took center stage with the launch of ChatGPT and the start of the generative AI era. Now CPUs are back, lifting the fortunes of market leaders AMD and Intel, whose chips specialize in powering long-running agents that can work for hours on their own. Last week OpenAI released its AI agent Dots, following the lead of Meta , which debuted Muse in early September. Muse caught on so quickly that it topped the Apple App Store in less than two weeks . Well before that, AMD and Intel were already huge winners in the stock market this year due largely to surging demand for CPUs, but they've picked up steam in the past month, jumping 32% and 21%, respectively, as of Monday's close beating all of tech's megacaps. The rally continued on Tuesday, with AMD jumping almost 3% to a fresh high of $649.42. AMD's growing strength in both CPUs and GPUs has pushed the company into the trillion-dollar market cap club. "As more agents are created and developed, and more people start to use them for more tasks, it's going to start to shift the workload away from GPUs and onto CPUs," said Ryan Shrout, president of Signal65, which consults on AI hardware and costs. Users learned about the power behind the new agents by asking them. Muse tells users that it runs on an AMD-powered computer, while Dots said it runs on a virtual computer powered by AMD's EPYC-branded CPU. A Meta spokesperson told CNBC that the company designed its system to use whatever kind of CPU is available. "We take a diverse approach to our hardware and are largely CPU-agnostic by design, which gives us the most flexibility in acquiring capacity," the Meta spokesperson said in a statement. OpenAI similarly uses multiple CPU providers, meaning AMD isn't the only game in town. Most servers at hyperscalers — Amazon , Google , Meta and Microsoft — use CPUs made by Intel or AMD. But nearly every major cloud provider is also developing custom chips of their own, typically based on Arm technology. Arm announced its own CPU for agents in March, with Meta as the debut customer, and its stock price has more than doubled since. Earlier this year, Nvidia released Vera — a fully redesigned central processor — along with an entire rack filled only with the CPUs . The chip giant says it built the new Vera CPUs specifically for agents and expects CPUs to be a $200 billion market by 2030. But it's one part of the chip industry where Nvidia isn't currently the favorite, analysts say. "It's just a new product and they're going to be competing against a lot of different players," Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview, adding that he believes AMD currently has the "best product." CPUs are driving a healthy portion of AMD's growth. Revenue in the company's data center business more than doubled to $6.7 billion in the quarter ended in June, accounting for almost 60% of total sales. " The conversation has changed quite a bit over the last eight to 10 months in terms of agentic usage," said Dan McNamara, AMD's senior vice president and general manager of compute and enterprise AI. McNamara added that CPU sales are going to "really ramp." Muse, Dots and even coding software like OpenAI's Codex use AI models to plan tasks that can run autonomously. The agents need their own computer that can run for hours or even days in the background, explained Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman. GPUs are still needed for inference, or processing an AI model, but an agent also needs a CPU. "CPUs are actually performing the workflows while GPUs are doing the thinking," Newman said. Meta and OpenAI use virtual machines, which partition a server into several lighter virtual computers, so one server can support scores of users. Some AMD EPYC processors have up to 192 CPU cores. According to benchmarks and the agents themselves, Muse's virtual computer uses two cores and Dots uses nine. Benchmarks and queries show Dots using an AMD EPYC 9V74 CPU, which is available from resellers for under $3,000. The EPYC 9D25 reportedly used by Meta for Muse costs even less on the secondary market.

events.title: Treasury yields slide as surge to multiyear highs cools
events.summary: U.S. Treasury yields were lower on Tuesday as a surge easing to multi-decade highs took a pause. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was last down more than 2 basis points at 5.286% after reaching its highest level since April 2002 on Monday. The 30-year Treasury yield was down less than 1 basis point at 5.659% following its rise to levels not seen since May 2002. The 2-Year Treasury note yield was down more than 3 basis points at 4.80%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. Treasury yields soared on Monday. The 10-year and 30-year recorded 24-year highs after fresh data from the Institute for Supply Management showed cooling services growth. The PMI reading rose to 54.9 in September, virtually in line with expectations but just below August's growth, while the prices index was up 1.4 points to 74. Traders are now pricing in a roughly 80% chance that the Fed will keep rates unchanged at its next meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool . The event of the week will be the release of the FOMC minutes from its September meeting on Wednesday, which investors will parse closely for clues about future monetary policy. "The bond market is sending a more important signal right now than the stock market. The Fed controls the short end, but it has far less control over the long end," said David Miller, CIO at Catalyst Funds. Bonds have been volatile over the past six weeks, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management investment chief Lisa Shalett said in a note to clients. She cited a potentially new Fed policy framework, economic growth and high oil prices while the Middle East conflict stretches on as factors. "Nevertheless, while intraday implied volatility has risen, the six-week stretch has not reached the extremes that catalyzed the 2022 equity bear market," Shalett wrote.

events.title: A week alone in Europe taught me 9 lessons about solo travel in other countries
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter traveled solo during a train trip through Europe. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I had plenty of experience traveling alone before I went to Germany and Austria. But solo travel in Europe was a different beast. I learned how to tame it. I thought I knew what I was in for. I thought I had it all figured out. I'd taken 30-hour train trips up and down the East Coast, spent seven nights sailing the Caribbean on one of the world's largest cruise ships , and traveled by rail to Niagara Falls , Montreal, and Quebec City — all by myself. So I was pretty used to traveling alone by October 2022, when I went backpacking through Europe . I took a two-week train trip through Germany, Austria, Italy, and Switzerland. I spent the first half of the trip by myself, and a friend joined me for the second half. That first week alone in Europe made me realize that I'm still learning about the art of solo travel in foreign countries. When planning my trip, I learned that some countries are safer for solo travelers — particularly females. Brandenburg Gate in Berlin. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When I travel alone, nothing is more important to me than safety. In my research ahead of my trip, I found that some countries are generally safer than others for solo travelers. The migration firm Global Citizens Solutions releases an annual study about the safest destinations for women traveling alone, based on gender equality, crime rates, and community security initiatives. Both of my solo destinations, Austria and Germany, made the 2025 list, though only Austria made the 2026 list, which included 14 countries. When I visited Austria, I stayed in the heart of Vienna, which allowed me to explore the city streets into the night. In my experience, people kept to themselves, and I didn't doubt my safety while exploring after dark. When I visited Germany, I stayed in an Airbnb in Neustrelitz, a quaint town outside Berlin. I found it relatively easy to figure out the local train system and get to and from Berlin each day. I felt safe walking around on my own in both places. If you're traveling solo, researching your destination beforehand is a must, but your safety is never guaranteed. So stay aware of your surroundings along the way, and use your best judgment throughout your trip. Taking public transit immediately made each destination feel less intimidating. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I live in New York, where I take the subway pretty much everywhere. Still, I was nervous about using public transit in foreign countries where I didn't speak the primary language or have a good sense of where things were. I didn't have to be. I may have felt uneasy stepping into the underground world of Berlin's subway system, but it was no different from my home city. The platform looked the same, with signage identifying the coming trains. I thought both Berlin and Vienna had great transportation systems, and taking trains and trams helped me get a better sense of each place. Public transit apps made it easier to get tickets and plan trips. When I was riddled with self-doubt about navigating these cities, taking public transit gave me a real sense of competence as I stood among local commuters. Booking a stay within city limits made exploring alone easier. The street where the author found a hotel in Vienna one morning. Joey Hadden/Business Insider On solo trips , being intentional about where you stay is important. For this trip, I booked a combination of Airbnbs inside and outside the cities to give me a chance to see what life is like in the heart of the metropolis and the surrounding areas. Commuting to small villages with a travel companion later in the trip felt like a little adventure each time, where we could plan and recap our days. But when I was alone, these treks felt more mundane, like I was wasting time and energy I could have spent exploring the city. In Germany, I booked a stay at a tiny home hotel in Neustrelitz and commuted to and from Berlin by train, about an hour and a half each way. While I was glad I got to experience Neustrelitz, staying far from the city center made my days in Berlin shorter. When I got to Vienna, I stayed in an Airstream trailer in the heart of the city. This made it much easier to explore from morning to night. Though it wasn't as quiet as Neustrelitz, I left Vienna feeling like I had a better sense of the city than I did in Berlin. While staying outside the city can be an adventure, I recommend that first-time solo travelers stay in the center to make their trip easier. I spent one week alone in Europe before a friend joined me, but I surprised myself by wishing I'd booked a longer solo trip. The author prepares to board a train in Europe. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My first week in Europe was tough. Getting used to navigating and exploring on my own took some time. Without someone else to share the process with, I found the first few days difficult to fully enjoy. But by the end of the first week, I felt settled into the nomadic lifestyle and confident in my abilities to navigate cities independently. In fact, I left Europe wishing I had given myself more time alone to truly immerse myself in these new places. Each challenging moment I faced allowed me to grow. To those planning a solo trip to another country, I recommend giving yourself at least two weeks to explore — especially if it's your first visit. After finding your footing that first week, the second week will feel even better. When I'm alone, my headspace can make or break a trip. So, I learned to stay in the moment, celebrate small wins, and not dwell on mistakes. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My trip wasn't perfect. There were times when I went to the wrong train station, got caught in the rain, and struggled to sleep. Dwelling on these mishaps made it harder to overcome them and get back to enjoying myself. Early in my travels, I made a conscious choice to push through and focus on what I could control, like buying an umbrella, arriving at stations early, and taking extra time to sleep. These small wins boosted my spirits. When I arrived in Vienna on an overnight train from Berlin, I was exhausted and hadn't slept. I knew I needed rest, but I couldn't check into my Airbnb until 3 p.m. I started going into random hotels to book a room. By the third hotel, I had booked a safe, comfortable place to doze. I framed this as a small win to celebrate. I got out of my head by focusing on positive problem-solving and found exactly what I needed. My trip was full of little victories like this, from finally getting to my Airbnb in Neustrelitz on the day I arrived in Berlin to finding a delicious food cart next to a park while exploring Vienna. Being dehydrated and tired made it harder for me to stay positive. I learned that it's important to prioritize health when traveling solo. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Sleep makes everything better. events.title: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
events.summary: British Airways is building what it says is the world's largest business class on its Airbus A380 jets, the world's largest passenger plane. A high-end travel boom has airlines from budget carriers to large, international icons introducing new first-class cabins and other pricier seat options. British Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business-class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers. The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub. British Airways will outfit its Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger plane, with a monster 106-seat business-class cabin, up from the current configuration of 97 business-class seats. First class will also be refreshed and will include 12 suites, down from the current A380 configuration of 14. Premium economy class will grow to 84 seats from 55. Standard economy seats will shrink to just 215 from 303. British Airways said the 106 business-class suites, with sliding doors, will take up the entirety of the A380's upper deck. Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers' appetite for more luxurious trips. British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines , last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in a recent interview that customers are seeking high-end options on long flights, like its Perth-London nonstop. "There is absolutely a customer who wants this and is prepared to pay a premium for it," she said. Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase. The prices can be even higher if they're selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights. Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification. British Airways' overhaul of the cabins on its 12 A380s is also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane's largest user, Emirates, in late 2021. events.title: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Cloud provider Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation, marking what could be its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. Coatue Management and Blackstone are leading the round. A letter to investors reviewed by the Journal shows Lambda’s backlog grew from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September. While that might look like a hearty increase in demand, much of that increase appears to be driven by a $35 billion commitment from one company: Anthropic, which signed a deal with Lambda in late August. That means Lambda’s valuation, which has climbed significantly since its 2025 funding round , could be leaning heavily on Anthropic’s ability to keep paying. Still, with reliable GPU capacity so scarce, investors are clearly still willing to bet on companies that provide it, especially ones with large contracts with a major AI lab. For neoclouds like Lambda, demand isn’t so much the problem as is the cost of meeting it. Data center buildouts are largely funded by debt — of which Lambda just raised an additional $1 billion last week — and lenders are getting choosier about who they offer cash to and under what circumstances. Lambda’s decision to raise more now not only sets the tone for its IPO pricing, but also gives it access to more capital before the scrutiny of public markets arrives. If and when Lambda does IPO — the company was reportedly meant to debut this year, but has pushed that back amid market uncertainty — it will join other Nvidia-backed neoclouds, like CoreWeave and Nebius , that now depend on the health of their stock to fund their data center buildouts. British neocloud Nscale filed for an IPO last month and is expected to begin trading soon. Lambda, Coatue, and Blackstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment. events.title: Tourists must pay and book ahead to see iconic Twelve Apostles
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts From April, visitors will begin paying a fee to visit the Twelve Apostles. ( Supplied ) A booking system has gone live for tourists to visit the Twelve Apostles on the Great Ocean Road. Visiting the Twelve Apostles remains free until April 2027. A new $126 million visitor centre will open on October 16. Tourists wanting to visit one of Australia's iconic natural wonders, the Twelve Apostles, will now have to book ahead and pay an entry fee . Each year, more than 2 million people travel down the Great Ocean Road to visit the remaining seven limestone rock stacks that rise out of the Southern Ocean, about four hours' drive west of Melbourne. The Victorian government has revealed from October 16, visitors will need to book ahead to enter a newly constructed $126 million visitor centre and see the sights. In April, the government will start charging tourists an entry fee. Local residents and traditional owners will be exempt from paying. Acting Regional Development, Local Government and Territories Minister Catherine King said the new visitor centre would support sustainable tourism along Victoria's south-west coastline. "The redevelopment is already playing an important part in the local economy and will encourage even more visitors to spend time in the region, boosting local jobs and businesses," Ms King said. The government said the new booking system would help manage overcrowding at peak times, with money collected from the entry fees used to help fund visitor infrastructure and environmental projects. events.title: Singles struggle to afford housing as cost of living rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Singles struggle to afford housing as cost-of-living rises Louise Taylor, 71, says she has had to accept a small duplex north of Brisbane is all she can afford to live in. ( ABC News: Lottie Twyford ) Single-income households can struggle to meet housing costs, and older women are one group at risk of housing insecurity. The singles tax refers to extra costs people pay when they can't split expenses like couples can. Housing experts say Australia also has a lack of affordable, suitable dwellings for singles. By her 70s, Louise Taylor had hoped her house would be more than a roof over her head, but somewhere she could happily call home. But after "knockback after knockback" when she was trying to find a rental on the private market five years ago, she has been forced to accept her small duplex, north of Brisbane, is all she can afford. "I was at desperate times and I went, 'you know what, I don't care, I just have to do it,'" she recollected. "I was so grateful … then I'm looking around thinking, 'how in the hell am I going to … where am I going to put my lounge room?'" Ms Taylor is the first to acknowledge she is one of the lucky ones and says she's on the housing waitlist and has contacted other housing organisations to see if they could help. Ms Taylor says she has modest hopes for a home – somewhere she could fit a lounge. ( ABC News ) But on the pension, she is fearful about what the next rent rise will mean, and says if it gets any more expensive, she believes she will have no choice but to move in with her adult daughter. She is also scared that if she cannot afford to rent a house on her own, she may have no choice but to move into a share house. Ms Taylor believes she would have had more success finding a rental and more power on the private rental market if she was applying in a couple. Singles tax costing people hundreds of dollars a month That concept is known as the singles tax – the idea that single-income households do not benefit from the same cost-sharing benefits when it comes to things like rent and bills as a couple does. Australian Bureau of Statistics data suggests a single person spends more than $770 extra on living costs a month compared to a person in a couple . Better Financial Planning's Michael Khouri says a single person also has to take on more of the mental load when it comes to managing finances. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Brisbane-based financial advisor Michael Khouri said there was also the time and effort factor to take into account, as well as that inability to share resources. "If somebody's single and they're trying to do everything themselves, they're usually a bit more time poor," he said. He said he also saw people who had just come out of a separation struggling to fund separate homes – either renting or buying – especially as the cost of housing continued to rise. "Fifteen years ago, I'd find that probably half or maybe say 30 to 40 per cent of their expenses was housing — and now it's just getting higher and higher." Ms Taylor says her two bedroom duplex is really one bedroom. ( ABC News ) More than half of Australians living alone are women, and around half of those women are aged 65 or older. Older women are also a growing group at risk of experiencing housing distress or homelessness. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare reports that women and girls make up 60 per cent of the people seeking assistance from homelessness services. And the number of homeless women aged over 55 has surged, with earlier census data pointing to an approximately 40 per cent increase over the decade from 2011 . Single, older women at risk of housing insecurity The Housing Older Women's Network Maggie Shambrook says many older women are reluctant to describe themselves as homeless. ( ABC News: Elizabeth Pickering ) The Housing Older Women's Network's Maggie Shambrook said many women who fell into that cohort were living invisibly — couch-surfing or living in vans as they searched for an affordable, suitable home. Some empty nesters want to move into smaller homes but say the cost of doing so keeps them in their large properties. Ms Shambrook said systemic issues including having worked in lower-paid professions or participated in caring unpaid caring work, along with the difficulty of building an asset base, contributed to this. And as Ms Taylor had experienced, there was also the issue of finding something suitable and affordable for a single person, especially as they aged. "Your mobility does change as you get older … your ability to navigate obstacles becomes less and less," Ms Shambrook explained.

events.title: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer. But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job. Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog. However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity. What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction. For instance, TechCrunch has seen a handful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. ( NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.) But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences. The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out. It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into. To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post. This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0 In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds. Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology. For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests. Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.” “While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s General Manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained. United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.) Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp , eBay , Zillow , Pizza Hut , Adidas , and various airlines .

events.title: Ronaldo apologizes for Portugal walkout; says Jesus broke promise
events.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promises, but leaves international return open. Cristiano Ronaldo has accused Portugal ‌coach Jorge Jesus of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly ⁠explain his omission ⁠against Norway drove him out of the camp, but insisting he remained available after any punishment. In a lengthy statement, the 41-year-old gave his account of the dispute ⁠that prompted his departure from Copenhagen before Portugal’s Nations League match versus Denmark last week. list 1 of 4 FIFA chief Infantino’s ‘abuse of power’ questioned by Norway in complaints list 2 of 4 Qatar and India among seven countries bidding for 2036 Olympics, IOC says list 3 of 4 UEFA to investigate spitting incident at Ireland-Israel football match list 4 of 4 What happened between Ireland and Israel in their Nations League match? Ronaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark ⁠matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 minutes. “Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from halftime onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager had broken his word to me.” Portugal’s ‌captain and all-time leading scorer said a subsequent meeting with Jesus, attended by his club side Al Nassr’s sporting director Simao Coutinho, produced an agreement for the coach to clarify events at his next news conference. According to Ronaldo, an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus’s decisions and that the coach asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Ronaldo said the agreed notes did ⁠not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach’s ⁠public remarks bore no resemblance to their private discussion. “It was the second time he had broken his word to me,” Ronaldo said. “I decided to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises.” The statement provided Ronaldo’s account⁠, but on Sunday, after Portugal’s win over Norway , Jesus denied he had made any agreement with the player, nevertheless leaving the door open ⁠for his return. The Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) did not immediately respond ⁠to a request for comment about Ronaldo’s statement. Ronaldo apologised for failing to greet supporters after the Norway match and for leaving his teammates , accepting that his captaincy made his conduct more serious. “The consequences of my actions must be assessed ‌and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation,” he said. Despite the rupture, Ronaldo said he was not limiting his international ambitions to a farewell appearance. “If I’m physically fit, playing for my club – scoring ‌goals, ‌I hope – after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I’ll be available, as I’ve always been until now, to compete and win for our national team,” he added.

events.title: I take about 15 solo trips a year. These 6 must-have products make traveling alone easier.
events.summary: There are a few products I swear by when traveling alone. oatawa/Shutterstock I swear by a few items to help make my solo trips more convenient. My portable tripod allows me to capture photos of myself without relying on help from strangers. My other must-haves include a lotion applicator for my back, a first-aid kit, and a portable charger. As a travel writer , I'm often taking off by myself — as often as 15 times a year. Because I typically travel without a partner, I make sure to pack a few essential items to make my trips easier, safer, and more enjoyable. Here are seven things I never leave for a solo trip without. Having a tripod means I don't have to rely on strangers to take pictures for me. Kelly Magyarics I like to take pictures of myself traveling, whether to post on social media or send to my boyfriend. I'm not into selfie sticks, and unfortunately, I can't always rely on strangers to take photos for me. So, having a cell phone tripod is a good compromise. I love my Toneof universal cell phone tripod because it easily slips into my carry-on luggage and expands when I need to snap a picture. It also includes a rechargeable remote control for the shutter. A first-aid kit is a must-have when traveling alone. I supplement my first-aid kit with over-the-counter medicine. Carol Yepes/Getty Images When I get injured or start to come down with something while traveling alone, there's no one to run out to the drugstore to get medicine or first-aid supplies for me. Sometimes, I'm not even in an area with a drugstore nearby, so I make sure to bring along any items I may need. My first-aid kit is stocked with bandages, cleansing wipes, gauze, tick removers, nosebleed plugs, sting relief, burn ointment, and a thermometer. I also pack some over-the-counter medicine for pain, gastrointestinal issues, motion sickness, and congestion. My portable speaker doubles as a white-noise machine. Kelly Magyarics When I'm traveling by myself, I always carry my LectroFan Bluetooth speaker with me. The sound is incredible considering its tiny size, and it has several white-noise settings to drown out noisy neighbors or street sounds. When I'm feeling lonely, I also like to use it to have a solo dance party in my room. A portable charger is always good to have on hand. Kelly Magyarics One of my biggest concerns when traveling alone is my cell phone battery running low. After all, I need my phone to navigate cities, book Uber rides, make restaurant reservations, and research tourist attractions . That's why I always carry a USB portable charger with me. This lotion applicator helps me avoid getting sunburn in the areas I can't reach. Kelly Magyarics Since I often travel to tropical places , I prefer to pack bottles of sunscreen lotion since the coverage is heavier than spray. But it's tricky to apply the lotion to my own back and shoulders. Foam-brush applicators are clunky to pack, but luckily, I found a cloth applicator from Steugo that folds up and doesn't take up much room in my suitcase. I pour some lotion onto the fabric and then use the handles to rub it onto my back as if I'm drying myself with a towel. I rinse or hand-wash it between uses and throw it in the washing machine once I return home. Having a portable wash bag allows me to do my laundry. Kelly Magyarics I never check my luggage, and being a single traveler means I can bring only one carry-on with me. Even though I can fit a lot in my bag, I sometimes need to re-wear and freshen up my clothes. Because hotel laundry service is often expensive, I bring my own Scrubba portable wash bag with me. To use it, I fill the packable bag with socks, underwear, and T-shirts and then add water and a laundry sheet. Then, I deflate the bag and rub my clothes along the inner washboard before rinsing, wringing, and hanging my garments to dry. events.title: Yemen’s government is on the attack against the Houthis. What has changed?
events.summary: Yemeni forces are trying to reverse Houthi gains, aided by heavier air power and renewed international support. Yemen’s internationally recognised government wants to show that it has finally taken the initiative against the Houthis in the country’s long-running war. The announcement of Operation Dawn of Yemen on Monday to restore state authority across the country was quickly followed by a military offensive on the southern Red Sea coast. list 1 of 3 What would it take for the Yemen offensive to succeed? list 2 of 3 Saudi Arabia says East-West pipeline pumping 5.8 million bpd list 3 of 3 Pakistan, Turkiye join Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means The initial aim is to reverse gains made by the Houthis last month, when the Iranian-backed group took control of one of the world’s most important waterways, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait . But the ultimate goal of the operation is to retake the areas of the country held by the Houthis for more than a decade, including the capital, Sanaa, which they seized by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. It is a lofty ambition, and the achievements so far have been modest – most notably a limited advance into areas near Bab al-Mandeb. Still, the attacks indicate that the Saudi-backed Yemeni government operation is being conducted in a more organised manner – particularly notable after last month’s capitulation and loss of the Red Sea coast to the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God). The main issues faced by government forces in early September included a lack of cohesiveness among the groups fighting against the Houthis and a lack of military preparedness, as well as what analysts have described as Houthi infiltration of government forces’ communications. It is too early to say whether those problems have been resolved, but the inability of the Houthis to secure the highlands overlooking the areas they conquered in the southern Red Sea has left them vulnerable to a counteroffensive. There are a number of other factors that, when taken together, suggest the government’s shift to the attack may bring about more success than it has enjoyed since fighting resumed in Yemen in July, ending a fragile truce that had been in place since 2022. Most notable has been the involvement of Saudi Arabia, which is providing heavy aerial support. On Monday, the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government said that 100 fighter jets had participated in the offensive, its first acknowledgment in four years – since a 2022 truce – that it had resumed air attacks against the Houthis, despite reports of strikes in September. The air strikes have aided government forces attacking the Houthis on multiple fronts aside from the Red Sea coast, including Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf. Maged al-Madhaji, chairman of the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the “rate and accuracy of the air strikes” was higher than it had previously been, even compared with the start of the Saudi-led coalition’s anti-Houthi bombing campaign in 2015. Coupled with intelligence from the United States, the strikes were more efficient and coordinated with ground forces. A US official told Al Jazeera on Monday that 200 US advisers were stationed in Saudi Arabia in support of the campaign. Elias Hanna, a retired Lebanese general, said the coordination revealed a unified command structure that was vital to military success. “[There is] a central leadership managing operations and coordination between the ground forces and the air forces,” he told Al Jazeera on Monday. “The air force attacks, but ground forces then have to occupy the territory, remain there, and control it.” The US expertise, Hanna added, essentially provided an “intelligence bank” of targets that would be able to repeatedly attack Houthi positions. Another factor that has so far set the government offensive apart from the fighting in early September has been the prominent role taken by the Giants Brigades. Previously trained by the United Arab Emirates and now backed by Saudi Arabia, the force had been present during the losses to the Houthis in the Red Sea, but in smaller numbers. This time it has been leading the battle in the area and in Taiz’s al-Waziyah district, which overlooks the port city of Mocha. The Giants Brigades previously defeated the Houthis in Shabwah in 2022 and drove them out of the southeastern coastal governorate, as well as parts of Marib and al-Bayda east of Sanaa. “They are the most experienced with the Houthis’ fighting methods,” said al-Madhaji, “because they are the force that has engaged them the most across different theatres of operations – some on flat terrain and some mountainous .” “In practice, this is the first time we have seen Saudi operational management, together with forces that had been under Emirati management, produce effective results,” added al-Madhaji.

events.title: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video in 2027 under six-year deal
events.summary: Amazon's Prime Video will become the exclusive global home of the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal beginning in 2027. The Emmys will stream live and free in more than 240 countries and territories, with no Prime subscription required. The agreement ends the Emmys' long-running broadcast network rotation among ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. The Emmy Awards will leave its long-running broadcast network rotation for Amazon Prime Video in 2027 under a six-year exclusive global streaming deal, the e-commerce giant and the Television Academy announced on Tuesday. Under the agreement, Prime Video will stream the annual awards honoring the best in TV for free to all audiences, including nonsubscribers, in more than 240 countries and territories. Prime Video's rights to the Emmys will begin with the 2027 ceremony. NBC, owned by Comcast , aired the 2026 ceremony on Sept. 14. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. In the release, Prime Video was named as the "permanent home" for the Emmys, in contrast to the rotating agreement in place years prior. The switch ends the traditional "wheel-deal" setup to broadcast the awards, where ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox took turns hosting the Emmys each year. The system has been in place since at least 1994 , with the most recent eight-year contract expiring this year. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement. "Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year," he said. The decision to move the 70-plus-year-old awards show to streaming reflects a broader trend in a shifting media landscape as Americans continue to ditch broadcast and cable TV for streaming service subscriptions. Streaming services have pushed further into live events in recent years, securing entertainment and sports rights alongside broadcast networks, and even winning rights that were previously exclusive to networks. In December 2025, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal with Alphabet's YouTube and YouTube TV for media rights to the Oscars, taking over from ABC in 2029. Netflix has exclusively aired the SAG Awards since 2024.

events.title: Trump's PAC won't pay taxpayers back for his ads
events.summary: President Trump's super PAC will not reimburse the government for taxpayer money spent on campaign-style ads promoting the administration. Why it matters: Taxpayers have footed a multimillion-dollar bill for the advertisements, which some critics of the president have called " government propaganda ." What they're saying: "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday evening. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," he wrote, referring to a super PAC affiliated with the president. Worth noting: Federal law generally bars federal officeholders from directing spending decisions for super PACs. Zoom in: When reached for comment, a White House spokesperson told Axios that Trump's announcement "was not referring to reimbursement." Catch up quick: The White House previously defended the ads as "public service announcements" that are "clearly not political." The White House says the ads are instead meant to be patriotic, noting that Trump isn't on the ballot this year. Nonetheless, one such ad repurposes a nearly identical ad from Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, cutting it shorter and adding "Paid for by the U.S. government." events.title: Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills
events.summary: Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers John Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households at this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed at forecasts which show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January. The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits. Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether. Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills. If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living. The chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and to rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs. He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular. Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year. But they have become increasingly concerned by forecasts showing that the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut. As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months. The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits. Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is. Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies. Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead. She told the Guardian last week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it? “That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.” Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future. Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or ones that use less energy. Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours. “This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.” A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones. Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks. An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs which energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income. The idea, which was proposed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level. Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.” He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform.

events.title: Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death
events.summary: Russia denies plague cases after laboratory technician’s death; US demands ‘transparency’ as WHO monitors situation. What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case Russian authorities have denied that they imposed anti-plague measures after a laboratory technician died of suspected pneumonic plague in a case which has drawn international scrutiny. Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova , who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague on Friday. list 1 of 3 Bubonic plague in China not a high risk: WHO list 2 of 3 China plague claims third victim list 3 of 3 Madagascar has the plague: What you should know Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among staff who had come ⁠into contact with the laboratory worker for the past 10 days. “This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests,” the watchdog said. The institute said in a statement that extensive testing during an autopsy on the woman’s body found no microorganisms linked to her work at the anti-plague institute. It said results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing other infectious diseases had been detected. Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said no “dangerous diagnosis” had been confirmed. She added that 60 percent of ⁠those placed under quarantine as a precaution had already been released. Local media said about 200 people ⁠had previously been quarantined. US Secretary ⁠of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information on Friday. “Anytime you hear there is a disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago in 2020 and 2021 when we saw that happen. That said, it would be irresponsible for me to sit here and speculate,” Rubio said. The World Health Organization in Geneva said on Tuesday that Russia had told it there were no ⁠cases of plague in the city of Irkutsk. It was unclear if this meant that the laboratory technician’s death was unrelated to plague infection. Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas. Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the WHO.

events.title: I had 5 kids headed to college. I took a demotion so they could go tuition-free.
events.summary: The author took a demotion for the tuition benefit. Courtesy of Melania Murphy My husband and I blended a family of six kids. Five of them were nearing college at the same time. To make tuition affordable, I took a lower-paying job at a college with tuition benefits. I spent years questioning whether I had given up too much, but the decision changed all our futures. I recently took a career demotion , but not because I lacked ambition. I made this choice because five of our kids were headed to college, and the math was impossible to ignore. When my husband and I married, we blended a family of six children in a western suburb of Chicago. Five were in high school at the same time — two seniors, a junior, a sophomore, and a freshman. We were thrilled to have a big family . We were also staring at the possibility of five college tuition bills arriving almost at once. We found a solution that seemed too good to be true My husband and I both believed college had changed our lives. We wanted our children to have that same chance, but we also knew we could not simply write checks and hope for the best. We expected them to work, apply for aid , and have skin in the game. Still, we did not want them starting adulthood buried in debt. Then I heard about a benefit that seemed too good to be true. Some colleges offer free or deeply discounted tuition to employees and their children. It was the first practical solution we had found. At the time, my marketing career was still young. I had gone back to school after years at home raising kids and was trying to build momentum. My husband had already spent two decades building his career in the office supply industry, so if one of us was going to chase a college job for the tuition benefit, it made sense that it would be me. I found a job that offered a tuition benefit, but it was a step back in my career After months of searching, I was offered an entry-level, data-entry job at a small liberal arts college about eight miles from our house. The tuition benefit was fantastic — my kids would get free tuition if they attended the school where I worked or one on a list of small liberal arts colleges across the country — and it would start right away. The salary, though, was hard to swallow. Taking the job meant accepting a salary that would cut my pay in half and a title that felt like I was taking three steps backwards. On paper, the decision made sense. One year of tuition for one child could cost more than the pay cut. Multiply that by five kids, and the financial logic was obvious. Emotionally, it was not that simple. I had worked hard to create a professional identity after years of being known mainly as someone's mom. Now I was choosing lower pay, a lower title, and work that did not reflect where I wanted my career to go. I told myself I was doing it for the kids, and I was. But that did not erase the sting. For years, I wondered whether I had given up too much. I thought about the salary I had walked away from, the career momentum I had slowed, and the ego I had to set aside every time I explained why I had taken the job. Still, parenting often requires a kind of math no spreadsheet can capture. You add up income, debt, opportunity, pride, fear, and hope. Then you make the choice you believe will give your children more options, even if it costs you something no one else can see. The author earned her master's degree while working at the college. Courtesy of Melania Murphy The decision to take a demotion changed our lives In the end, the decision changed all of our futures. Over the years, the tuition benefit covered 17 years of college for our kids. I earned my master's degree while working at the college, too. Eventually, I moved into an assistant director of marketing role, and one year, my total rewards statement showed my tuition benefit was worth 350% of my salary. Our kids took different paths. One was not ready for college right after high school, but later returned to work on his degree. Two went on to earn master's degrees. Two built careers outside the fields they studied, but their degrees still opened doors. Our youngest, who was not yet in grade school when we married, is now finishing her degree. Parents make quiet sacrifices all the time. Some look dramatic from the outside, but many do not. Mine looked like a smaller paycheck , an entry-level title, and years of wondering whether I had set aside too much of myself. But now looking back, I don't regret it. When I eventually left the college, one of our sons said, "We had a good run. Thank you for all you've done for us." That was when I understood the tradeoff differently. The demotion had not made my life smaller. It had helped make all of our futures bigger. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: What can I do to protect myself after 'Asos hacked' message?
events.summary: The message, which Asos says people should not engage with, popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on Tuesday If a strange-looking message from Asos popped up on your phone today, you may be worrying what it could mean and whether you need to do anything. The online retailer has emailed customers apologising for the "unauthorised push notification" containing an external link, adding that they should disregard the message and not click on it. Here's what has happened, and what those who may have been affected are being advised to do. On Tuesday morning, Asos users across the UK were sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company. "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message read. Later that day, Asos said it took immediate action to restrict the apparent hackers' access, was investigating and working with advisers and relevant authorities on "next steps". Data storage company Snowflake told the BBC its investigations had "found no compromise" of its platform. At this stage it isn't clear what information, if any, has been accessed. On Tuesday evening, Asos told customers it may include "basic personal information including name and contact details". "However, we don't believe that any payment-card information or account passwords have been impacted," it added. While those who received the pop-up message will undoubtedly be concerned, it does not mean your phone has been hacked. Don't click the link: The hack notification included a link to a Telegram account - Asos and cyber security experts say not to click on it Change passwords: It's worth updating your password, including across other sites that use the same one as your Asos account. The advice for a strong password is to mix numbers, symbols and upper and lower case characters, and avoid using the same password across multiple accounts Turn on two-step verification for important apps like banking and email: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls this "one of the most effective ways to protect your online accounts from cyber criminals". You can usually turn it on by going into the security settings in your account Monitor transactions: Keep an eye on your online transactions for anything unusual According to Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at global cyber-security firm Check Point, "the biggest immediate risk may be what happens next". She says criminals know people will be searching for information online and expects there to be "attempts to exploit that confusion". Her advice to Asos customers is not to be "scared and frightened". But she says they should be "extremely suspicious" of emails, texts or messages claiming their account has been compromised, offering a refund or asking them to click a link to reset their password. People should hang up the phone if they receive any calls from someone they think might be posing as Asos or another organisation, says Which? spokesperson Kat Cereda. The consumer rights expert says they should contact the organisation themselves afterwards through separate means. It's been less than 24 hours since the notification popped up on people's phones, and there are a number of unanswered questions. It isn't yet clear who is behind the message, what their motivation is, how many people received the notification or how many may be impacted Wilson, from the cyber-security firm Check Point, says there's still "an awful lot" we don't know. Asos said its website and app were operating "as normal, and customers can continue to shop with confidence on ASOS as normal" as of Tuesday night. It said protecting customers "is our priority", and it will provide a further update "as soon as we have confirmed more information". People should visit Asos's official website directly for updates.
