events.title: Amazon wins global rights to stream Emmys in six-year deal
events.summary: Theagreement replaces the "Wheel Deal" system, which rotated the gala among major networks like ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. Published 6 October 2026, 18:51 BST Amazon Prime Video has secured exclusive global rights to stream the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal, ending the ceremony's run on traditional US broadcast television. Starting in 2027, the agreement replaces a rotation of the gala among major networks like ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. The ceremony will instead stream live for free worldwide each September, with no Prime Video subscription needed. Official terms were not disclosed. The BBC has contacted Amazon and the Emmys for comment. The move is another indication of how live events are shifting to digital platforms as viewing habits evolve. The Oscars, for example, are moving to YouTube live globally starting in 2029. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, said the existing setup had become out of sync with modern television. "The shows driving the industry forward largely originate on streaming platforms, yet the awards themselves were tethered to broadcast television," Proulx said. "That's why a leading streaming service like Prime Video makes sense for the Emmy's next act." Cris Abrego, chair of the Television Academy, said the deal gives the ceremony "unprecedented global reach", allowing audiences in more than 200 countries to watch live. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Abrego said in a statement issued by Amazon. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said the platform is honoured to serve as the "global home" for the ceremony, adding that streaming the show for free delivers " the best entertainment to our customers worldwide." The agreement marks a milestone for Amazon, giving Prime Video its first marquee entertainment broadcast after building a live profile centred on sports, including the NFL's Thursday Night Football, NBA, and UEFA Champions League fixtures. Amazon's latest earnings highlighted strong gains in live viewership , external , including record ratings for its inaugural NBA season, which peaked at 6.5 million viewers for Game 7 of the Eastern Conference Semifinals. The Emmys deal positions Amazon directly alongside Google, whose video platform YouTube holds the upcoming Oscar rights. YouTube relies primarily on an ad-supported model, whereas Amazon is leveraging free live access to draw massive global audiences into its wider ecosystem. Like its live sporting events, the free broadcast will allow Amazon to build a substantial global advertising footprint. Moving exclusively to Prime Video is significant for the Emmys, ending a rotation across the major legacy broadcast networks that has been in place since 1955 and marking the first time the gala will leave traditional broadcast television entirely. First held in 1949, the Emmys honor achievements in acting, writing, and production, serving as a primary showcase for the global television industry. events.title: President Trump ranks 12th among the country's richest real estate moguls. Meet the other billionaires in his industry.
events.summary: Donald Trump owns the Mar-a-Lago Club. Win McNamee/Getty Images; Joe Raedle/Getty Images Forbes estimates that several US real estate moguls are worth billions more than Donald Trump. You may have shopped, worked, or even lived in a building owned by one of these magnates. Their portfolios range from office buildings and malls to student housing and rental properties. Real estate has been the source of some of America’s biggest fortunes, including that of US President Donald Trump . However, despite his extensive property portfolio, Trump ranks 12th among the country’s richest real estate moguls. These magnates rarely own only residential properties . Their portfolios often span some of the country’s biggest office buildings, malls, hotels, and logistics hubs. In several cases, they also hold stakes in sports teams and other assets. This ranking was compiled from the Forbes 400 list for 2026, which provides an estimated snapshot of the net worth of the 400 richest people in America as of September 4. Forbes estimated each person’s net worth using sources including interviews and asset valuations, while accounting for debt and charitable giving. In some cases, Forbes lists individuals as “and family” to indicate that some of the wealth is held by immediate family members. Here are America’s richest real estate moguls, ranked by net worth. 15. Robert Faith — $6 billion Bloomberg/Getty Images State: South Carolina Robert Faith founded Greystar in 1993. He is the chair and CEO of the real estate company, which specializes in rental housing properties, including senior housing and student housing. 14. Annette Lerner & family — $6.1 billion Annette Lerner. The Washington Post/Getty Images State: Maryland Annette Lerner's husband, Ted Lerner, built a real estate company in 1952 after she gave him a $250 loan. The firm, Lerner Enterprises, is one of the largest real estate owners in Washington, DC. After Ted Lerner died in 2023, she and her children inherited his estate. 13. Mitchell Morgan & family — $6.7 billion Hilarie and Mitchell Morgan Sean Zanni/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images State: Pennsylvania Mitchell Morgan is the founder and chair of Morgan Properties, which specializes in apartment complexes. The firm owns over 97,000 units across the US. 12. His portfolio includes golf clubs, resorts, and commercial skyscrapers. 11. The firm developed shopping and mixed-use destinations such as The Grove and The Americana at Brand. 10. H. Ross Perot Jr. — $7.4 billion Bloomberg/Getty Images State: Texas Ross Perot Jr. founded Hillwood, a real estate development firm, after borrowing against his billionaire father's fortune. The company's portfolio includes residential and commercial developments, as well as logistics hubs. 9. events.title: Some public transport trips are more expensive in Adelaide than anywhere else
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ABC NEWS analysis found that train journeys are generally cheaper in Adelaide than Sydney, except for trips shorter than 10km. ( ABC News ) Cost of living pressures and recent price increases to Adelaide's public transport fares poses a budget challenge to people living on low incomes. ABC News analysis has found that Adelaide Metro fares are currently among the nation's most expensive, and are the most expensive for short journeys. Amid a cost-of-living crisis, some Australians have turned to public transport in an effort to curb the pinch at the petrol pump. But for many, public transport is a necessity that enables them to undertake the basics of everyday life. "Public transport is the only way that I can access things like engagement with employment opportunities, education, culture, public events and health appointments," Ann-Maree Anderson told ABC News. She rents in Mount Barker, an Adelaide Hills town about 30km south-east of the CBD. Ms Anderson has recently graduated from university, volunteers for poverty outreach groups and is associated with the Anti-Poverty Network, and has recently shifted from Austudy to the Jobseeker support payment. Analysis shows high expenses in Adelaide Governments across Australia have introduced a range of measures to reduce public transport fares. Tasmania offers free public bus travel, as did Victoria before introducing a half-price fare until the end of the year. The NT government has offered free buses for several years and Queensland's LNP government recently legislated the universal 50c fare introduced by Labor in 2024. Other states and territories have introduced various measures to trim fares, such as age-based free travel and other fare discounts. The SA government pointed to three measures introduced this year to address cost-of-living pressures. "By slashing the cost of 28-day student passes and expanding the Seniors Card, millions of more dollars have stayed in the pockets of South Australians," a government spokesperson said. "The government also put a three-month pause on annual increases for MetroCARD public transport fares to provide cost-of-living respite for commuters during the early impacts of the conflict in the Middle East." An analysis of single fares by ABC News showed Adelaide commuters, including those like Ms Anderson, were currently paying the second-highest fares in the country, behind Sydney. For short trips, Adelaide's fare prices were comparatively the most expensive in Australia. That's because Adelaide Metro uses a network-wide fare system, charging commuters with a single tap of a metroCARD or payment card. In Sydney — which has the most expensive public transport fares in Australia — those short trips of fewer than 8km on a bus or tram, or 10km on a train, are charged at rates lower than Adelaide's standard fares. The SA government's delay to its annual fare rise meant prices grew roughly 3.3 per cent in line with CPI on October 1. Certain fares, including regular and concession metroCARD single trips were raised above CPI though, as were regular 14-day MetroCards, and both 14 and 28 day concession MetroCards. Adelaide's public transport system uses a single tap fare structure applied across its whole network. ( ABC Radio Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton ) Fare reductions can get people on board, sometimes Transport strategist Elliot Fishman, who is the director of the Institute for Sensible Transport, said public transport provided practical means to reduce household spending and the need for more than one car. But when it came to reducing fares, there have been varying results for boosting use of public transport. Dr Fishman's group analysed the fare reductions taken by the Victorian and Queensland governments. Dr Elliot Fishman believes that fare reductions in Adelaide may not have the same impact as fare-cutting initiatives in Melbourne. ( ABC News: Wayne Hammond ) In Queensland, he said "there was a small increase in usage, but a lot of the increasing usage came from existing public transport users". In Melbourne, the program had seen a "13 to 20 per cent increase in public transport [usage] compared to before those fare reductions". "For the increase in patronage, it was more effective for the government to reduce and eliminate the fares than it would have been to provide an increase in the quality of the service to try and get the same boost," he said. Dr Fishman said Brisbane's Bus Rapid Transit system and Melbourne's rail-heavy network moved large numbers of people each day, were primed to benefit from fare subsidies.

events.title: Anduril and the US Navy are planning a $6.6 billion shipyard to produce critical submarine parts
events.summary: Virginia-class submarine production has run into various problems with the supply chain and industrial base. US Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Nicholas A. Russell Anduril and the US Navy are building a new shipyard for producing parts for Virginia-class submarines. The shipyard is expected to open in 2030 in Maryland. Supply chain and industrial base problems have caused delays in deliveries of the vessels. The US Navy and Anduril Industries are teaming up to build a new shipyard to produce critical parts for Virginia-class submarines. Both the defense company, co-founded by Palmer Luckey, and the Navy will invest billions of dollars to construct the facility in Maryland, with plans to launch initial operations in 2030. The shipyard is the latest step to address gaps in the Navy's submarine industrial base and supply chain, which have contributed to delays in the delivery of Virginia-class submarines and other vessels. On Tuesday, Anduril and the White House announced the new facility, named Arsenal-2, in Baltimore County, Maryland. It comes with a $6.6 billion investment, $3.7 billion of which is private capital. The remaining $2.9 billion will come from the Navy. Anduril expects the shipyard will create over 3,000 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 jobs. "The facility will manufacture critical components for the Virginia-class submarine, adding significant new capacity to America's submarine industrial base in support of the Navy's effort to increase attack submarine production," Anduril said in a statement. The Virginia-class submarine is built by General Dynamics Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries' Newport News Shipbuilding. Anduril's Arsenal 2 facility will build "complex components and large scale assemblies" for the vessels, according to the company. A graphic rendering of the new facility. Photo courtesy of Anduril When the facility opens, it'll start by producing smaller parts like torpedo tubes before expanding into more complex designs like full sections of the vessel. Anduril said that adding another source for this work will help boost submarine construction. "We need to grow the maritime industrial base, the submarine industrial base, so that we can produce more submarines. So the goal here for Anduril is to contribute to that. This is not about taking food off the plate of anybody," Chris Brose, Anduril's president and chief strategy officer, told reporters on Tuesday, according to a transcript. "This is about putting more food on the table and being able to meet the requirements that our country has to produce more submarines." The Navy has been navigating issues with the production of Virginia-class submarines for years now, with the program and other shipbuilding projects facing delays and cost overruns . US officials and experts have raised concerns over an atrophied industrial base and a shortage of skilled workers to build vessels. In July, a report from the US Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog, noted that late material deliveries and a limited skilled workforce have driven the trend of lower deliveries of Virginia-class submarines. The Navy and industry's priorities for fixing these issues have included investing in rebuilding the US shipbuilding industry, paying workers more , upgrading shipyards, and solidifying supply chains. Earlier this year, Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, told the House Appropriations Committee that he anticipates industry will start delivering two Virginia-class submarines a year by 2032. events.title: Chinese company to face Australian privacy probe over 'pervert' glasses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australian regulator launches probe into Chinese smart glasses company amid privacy fears Carly Kind says her office has a "range of concerns" about Shenzhen Qingcheng. ( ABC News: Scott Kyle ) Chinese software company Shenzhen Qingcheng is being investigated by the Australian privacy commissioner following an ABC investigation. It revealed last month more than a dozen serious security flaws in the company's app and website used in the glasses for sale in Kmart, Big W Marketplace and Amazon. The privacy commissioner is urging retailers to reconsider selling the product for now. The Australian privacy commissioner has launched a formal investigation into the Chinese software company behind an influx of cheap smart glasses to Australia. It is the most significant action authorities have taken so far to address mounting community concern over the devices nicknamed "pervert glasses" by their detractors. In August, Attorney-General Michelle Rowland took the unusual step of asking the regulator to prioritise the issue amid calls for an import ban . A recent ABC investigation found more than a dozen serious security flaws in the HeyCyan phone app used in smart glasses sold by Kmart, as well as online platforms such as Big W Marketplace and Amazon, among others. Cheap smart glasses leaving Australians' data exposed Independent testing finds a hacker can access cheap smart glasses without a password. Independent testing of the low-cost glasses found Australians' sensitive data, including email addresses, dates of birth, images and videos, were left exposed to hackers. It also found the devices could be hijacked by nearby attackers without a password using only a Bluetooth connection, and that data was in some cases being sent to Chinese servers. "The ABC's reporting … raised the prospect that there haven't been reasonable steps taken to secure [user] information," Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind said. She said her office had "a range of concerns" about the practices of the company, Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology Co (Shenzhen Qingcheng), including about the possible use of facial recognition technology. Smart glasses, which look like ordinary glasses, allow the wearer to capture images, video and audio with the press of a button or verbal command. It is not always clear when they are in use. The regulator also made preliminary inquiries with Meta, Google, Kmart, and an importer called BDI Technology over their supply of similar tech in Australia, but none of the other companies is the subject of a formal investigation. Shenzhen Qingcheng was the only company which opted to ignore the regulator completely, Ms Kind said. "The company did not respond at all to our multiple attempts to obtain information … [and] did not even acknowledge receipt of our communications," she said. "It does suggest that some of the fundamentals may not be in place, for example, compliance teams that are appropriately staffed. "We would normally expect pretty prompt attention [to] be given to any outreach from the regulator". An influx of cheap smart glasses have made their way into Australia. ( ABC News: Scott Preston ) A formal investigation means the privacy commissioner will now have the power to compel Shenzhen Qingcheng to provide information about how it is complying with Australian laws. If the company continues to ignore the regulator, she can seek a court injunction to limit the supply of its products. Shenzhen Qingcheng could theoretically face fines of hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars if ultimately found to have interfered with the privacy of Australians. "The Australian Privacy Act provides for really, really considerable monetary penalties in the form of $50 million per contravention … and that can be applied per individual," Ms Kind said. "That would be what we would be shooting for, should our concerns be borne out". In the meantime, the regulator has urged retailers such as Kmart to reconsider selling the product at all. "We have written to the Australian Retail Council and to other retailers, putting them on notice that this company is under investigation," Ms Kind said. The governments said new and improved rest stops and pull-over bays would also be added as part of the project. A road corridor used to transport wind turbines between Newcastle and Dubbo will be among the regional routes to share in more than $1.2 billion of new funding for vital upgrades. Other projects include the corridor between Muswellbrook and Armidale, and the route between Euston and Tocumwal in the state's south-west. The Albanese government is tipping in $674 million, while the Minns government is investing $610 million. When added to previously announced contributions, it takes the investment from both governments to $1.74 billion. Federal Transport Minister Catherine King said the upgrades would ensure the state's supply chains were not disrupted. "Our export industries and freight operators are the backbone of the Australian economy, and they rely on safe and reliable roads," she said. NSW Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said the corridor between Newcastle and Dubbo was especially important in light of the Great Western Highway's closure due to a structural failure at Victoria Pass. "[The Golden Highway] is quite important because it doesn't have that more fragile geological infrastructure that we see across the Great Dividing Range," she said. "Also it connects Dubbo and the broader Central West with the second largest city in New South Wales." Jenny Aitchison says the upgrades will support the movement of all kinds of freight. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) It has also been an important route for transporting massive wind turbines and generators to the Central West Orana Renewable Energy Zone (REZ). Pauline Hanson's One Nation party has been critical of the REZs, citing the impact on regional roads, among other concerns. However, Ms Aitchison said the upgrades were not solely focused on supporting the renewable energy industry. "It is important for freight of all kinds, whether it's agriculture, mining or anything else," she said. Ms Aitchison said the upgrade, helped by a new cash injection of $294 million, would also include improvements to John Renshaw Drive and the Hunter Expressway. The state and federal governments said the regional road upgrades would include wider shoulders and intersections, as well as new turning and overtaking lanes. New and improved rest stops and pull-over bays would also be added as part of the project, along with additional heavy vehicle facilities, they said. More than $680 million of new money will be invested in the Muswellbrook to Armidale corridor, taking the total investment in the project to $849 million. Ms Aitchison said the upgrades would include key sections of the New England Highway. "People are looking for better productivity. That requires the roads to be wider and to allow more opportunities for passing from general traffic," she said. In the state's south-west, the corridor between Euston and Tocumwal will receive $310 million in new funding for upgrades along the Sturt and Newell Highways, as well as Kidman Way. Premier Chris Minns said better roads would lead to a stronger economy. "This investment will make roads safer for local families, improve travel times and make it easier for businesses and freight operators to get their goods where they need to go," he said. events.title: Finding value from AI in big companies comes down to people, not technology
events.summary: Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition: Highlights from the Fortune AIQ Summit . Trump names Clayton AI czar and appoints ‘Superintelligence Task Force.’ OpenAI, Anthropic and their insurers face mounting legal claims over ‘rogue AI’ agents. A Tencent AI agent swarm? A better business simulator for AI agents. How much tolerance for AI causing “bad things” should we tolerate? I spent last week in New York, where I was helping to host and moderate Fortune’s inaugural AIQ Summit, held at the New York Stock Exchange. The event was focused on how Fortune 500 companies are implementing AI successfully at scale and there was a lot of insightful conversation, both on stage and off. Today, I’ll talk about a few of the highlights. (You can check out more of our coverage of the Fortune AIQ Summit, check out the AIQ 75 list, and read some case studies from the companies on that list here . You can also see my on-stage session on “Building the Company of the Future” on this week’s Fortune AI Weekly vodcast. You can view the vodcast here .) One of the themes that came across strongly was the extent to which people are the X-factor in determining AI success. The methodology behind Fortune’s AIQ List is based, in part, on the five pillars of ServiceNow’s Enterprise AI Maturity Index, and ServiceNow’s Diana David (who has the amazing title “forward-deployed futurist), told me that the most striking gap between the companies that are AI “Pacesetters”—scoring in the top fifth of all companies on the Maturity Index—and everyone else, is that 57% of those Pacesetter companies are investing in upskilling their employees on AI, compared to just 4% for those not in that top bracket. The gap between these Pacesetters and the rest of the pack is big across other people-oriented dimensions too: 68% of Pacesetters have plans to attract, hire, and retain AI talent; just 10% of the rest do. The Pacesetters also stand out for having developed a long-term HR strategy specifically to support their AI strategy and for having conducted a comprehensive assessment of AI skills across their organizations. This focus on people was echoed throughout the day. Futurist Amy Webb (yes, futurists are a bit like London buses—I go months without encountering one and then I get to interview two in a single afternoon!) said that one reason so many large companies complain that they aren’t seeing enterprise-wise returns on investment for AI is because they are not investing in training people in how to use the technology well. She said there’s a lot of “learned helplessness” in large organizations when it comes to technology. (She compared this to taxi drivers who have become completely reliant on GPS, and in many cases, can’t even type the address into the phone themselves.) Drew Holler, the chief human resources officer at homebuilder Lennar , agreed, but told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell that employees have to take some responsibility too. “We’re going to give you all the tools, but it’s your responsibility to upskill yourself as well,” he said. “We’re going to give you trainings, but you, as an individual, have to upskill.” Adaptability may matter more than expertise Many of the speakers said that the most important human—and organizational—skills for the AI era are flexibility and adaptability. “It’s not about being AI native,” Webb said. “It’s about being flexible, and it is entirely possible for any company to be more flexible, but they have to put together the mechanisms to effectuate that.” Danielle Gonzalez, the chief people officer at cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks , also emphasized the need to be adaptable. “We’re looking for agency, and we’re looking for those people who can not only learn something at a fast rate…but also unlearn what they thought to be true, so that they can make space to move forward,” she said. She said Palo Alto Networks now uses “observable interviews” and hackathons to assess job candidates, using these to see firsthand how a person solves problems, rather than doing more static interviews where a candidate simply tells stories about their accomplishments. Interestingly, given all the news of “rogue AI” incidents lately, executives at the AIQ Summit were much more focused on how to deploy AI successfully than they were on governance concerns. If anything, there was a view that an over-emphasis on risks, especially from chief information security officers and corporate general counsel, was often what prevented large companies from implementing AI in ways that generated big returns. “There’s a pretty big disconnect between the CEO, oftentimes, and their board of directors, and the CISO or the chief risk officer and their desires to make sure that things are safe and stable,” Webb said. She said that chief risk officers and CISOs deserve “a seat at the table” when it comes to formulating AI strategy but that they need to learn to “stop saying ‘no’ before they say ‘tell me more.’” She said these executives needed the right incentives to ensure they are not blockers to AI implementation. Forget the SaaSpocalypse Another observation that came out of my discussions at both AIQ and elsewhere recently: the SaaSpocalypse fears of earlier this year were clearly overblown. Michelle Kwon, the chief operating officer at AI startup Runway, told me on stage at AIQ that while the company is as AI-native as it gets and uses AI to do a lot of work within the company, especially when it comes to coding, it still buys plenty of off-the-shelf software from traditional SaaS vendors. “We are not going to build our own payment system. That probably is not the best use of our time. There are some fantastic payment processors and fintech companies we work with on that side,” she said. “I am also not thinking about building out our own HR compliance system. That also doesn’t seem the best use of our time and investment.” Instead, she said Runway is focused on building software with AI that has clear topline impact: it recently debuted an AI agent that can plan, execute, and measure an online video advertising campaign. Meanwhile, another frontier AI company I spoke to a few weeks ago mentioned that they had just implemented Workday. If that company isn’t looking to replace its HR software with something it coded in-house, believe me, no Fortune 500 company is looking to do that either. So it’s not exactly end times for the big SaaS vendors. With that, here’s more AI news. Jeremy Kahn jeremy.kahn@fortune.com @jeremyakahn This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain after warrant lifted
events.summary: Spain’s Constitutional Court ruled an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applied to the politician. EU Parliament lifts immunity of 3 Catalans, including Puigdemont Self-exiled Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont could be set to return to Spain after the country’s Constitutional Court ruled that an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applies to embezzlement charges against Puigdemont. A Supreme Court judge then lifted a warrant for Puigdemont’s arrest on Tuesday, clearing the way for his return without fear of arrest. list 1 of 3 Catalonia’s former leader denounces Madrid’s ‘threats’ list 2 of 3 German prosecutors request Puigdemont’s extradition to Spain list 3 of 3 Spain withdraws request for Puigdemont’s extradition Puigdemont, then president of Catalonia, fled to Belgium in 2017 after holding an independence referendum for his self-governing region to break away from Spain. Madrid said the vote was illegal. Catalonia unilaterally declared independence from Spain that year after the referendum, with 90 percent of voters backing independence. He has since avoided several extradition attempts by Spain to face trial over the vote, while many of his confidants and supporters spent time in prison. Members of Puigdemont’s political party Junts welcomed his potential return. “It’s a great victory for President Puigdemont and the two other exiled ‌[leaders in Belgium]”, Jordi Turull, secretary-general of Junts, told reporters. “They held firm, they resisted, they prevailed in Europe, and today they have prevailed against the Spanish state.” Junts’ role in Spain’s snap election Puigdemont appears set to return to Spain just as the country is preparing for a snap election in November, although an official from his Junts party said he is unlikely to take part. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was only able to remain in power in 2023 when Puigdemont’s Junts party, along with another Catalan party, backed his new government in exchange for the amnesties. A year ago, Junts withdrew its support for the minority central government, and the party was decisive in Spain’s progressive government losing two key votes in parliament this week when it tried to push through emergency housing measures amid street protests . Sanchez responded by calling a November snap election, hoping anger over housing will mobilise his voters. The prime minister told ⁠reporters on Tuesday he did not regret launching the amnesty and welcomed the court ruling. “I believe the important message is that of coexistence among Catalans,” he said. Although separatism has lost ground and Junts is trailing in opinion polls, Puigdemont’s return could prompt renewed political drama. events.title: I’ve Covered Death Row Cases for Nearly a Decade. What Happened to Christa Pike Wasn’t an Anomaly.
events.summary: The death chamber in Huntsville, Texas Joe Raedle/Getty Images Over the course of two hours, witnesses watched and listened as Christa Pike cried, whimpered and snored through Tennessee’s attempt to execute her. By the end of it, executioners had given her two doses of the state’s lethal injection drugs. Her arms were swollen and blistered, and one had turned purple, her attorneys said. And she was still alive, marking what legal experts say is the first time a prisoner in the U.S. has survived one dose — let alone two — of lethal injection drugs.  Even if the outcome was unprecedented, what went wrong was not. Pike’s was the third Tennessee execution in 14 months to go awry. But as a reporter who has covered death row for nearly a decade and witnessed several executions, I know the state is not alone. The factors behind the breakdowns in Tennessee have popped up again and again across the country — and show how easily another botched execution could occur, even as soon as the ones planned Wednesday in Texas and next week in Florida. Here’s what we know about Tennessee’s attempt to execute Pike: The procedure started more than nine hours late, delayed by last-minute legal fights. Then, inside the death house, executioners struggled to find a vein, jabbing Pike with at least seven needles, according to her lawyers, one of whom watched in dismay. As the caustic barbiturate finally started flowing into the IV lines, Pike did not fall into sedation quickly. Instead, witnesses said, she sang with her spiritual adviser. Then she said her arm felt like it was about to burst open. “Does this happen like that?” she asked.  Like Pike, many aging death row prisoners have medical problems that can complicate efforts to kill them, potentially turning what are supposed to be relatively quick deaths into agonizing, drawn-out procedures. Even when prisoners are healthy, several states have faced questions about the competence of their execution teams, as both the American Medical Association and American Nurses Association have strongly opposed their members taking part in death penalty procedures. And death penalty states across the country shroud their executions in such secrecy that it is often difficult or impossible to confirm the age, source or sterility of the drugs. “The types of failures that went into this botch happen all the time,” said Robert Dunham, director of the Death Penalty Policy Project. “There is nothing in the execution process that states are incapable of getting wrong.” The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment, though hours after the attempted execution the agency said in a statement that it had “followed every step” of the state’s established protocol, which “has been consistently effective.” On Saturday, the head of the agency resigned . Meanwhile, Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement that he had ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the execution previously scheduled for December would no longer take place this year. His office didn’t respond to a request for comment. On Friday, Pike’s lawyers filed a motion asking a court to order the agency to preserve any evidence related to the state’s failed effort to kill their client. In a statement, they said the filing “details the serious complications that occurred during the execution attempt, many of which Christa and her attorneys had warned the State and the courts about months earlier.” Pike remains critically ill in the hospital, they said, where she is on a ventilator, intubated and unconscious. Unhealthy Prisoners By the time the Tennessee Department of Correction strapped her to the gurney last week, Pike had been on death row for 30 years. She had been sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer , a fellow Job Corps student in Knoxville. Pike was 18 at the time and, like many people on death row , had a history of mental illness and childhood sexual abuse .  Now 50 years old, Pike has faced an array of health problems, which her legal team had repeatedly warned could lead to a bungled execution. During a three-day hearing in August , Pike’s attorneys argued that her small veins and a blood disorder would make it harder and more painful to put in the IV lines to administer the lethal dose. The Tennessee Supreme Court did not agree , calling their arguments “speculative” and rejecting their request for a stay. Tennessee’s execution protocol relies on pentobarbital, a caustic barbiturate that slows down breathing and has been used to treat seizures, sedate people before surgery and euthanize animals. But its use in putting to death humans has drawn scrutiny. After relying on the drug for all 13 federal executions during the first Trump administration, the Justice Department under President Joe Biden said there was too much uncertainty about whether it would cause “ unnecessary pain and suffering ” and decided to stop using it “unless and until that uncertainty is resolved.” This year, President Donald Trump’s DOJ reversed course and readopted its use. Despite supply difficulties and repeated lawsuits from death row prisoners arguing that using pentobarbital is cruel and unusual, several states still use it, including Georgia, Missouri, South Carolina and Texas, where I witnessed five executions in the late 2010s as a reporter for the Houston Chronicle. Four of the condemned prisoners said the drug burned. Two said they could taste it. One said he could “hear it going through the vein.” But all of them stopped moving within minutes and were declared dead in under an hour.  Tennessee prison officials have not offered an explanation as to why Pike’s attempted execution was so drastically different. Initially, Pike’s attorneys and several death penalty experts raised the possibility that the drugs may have been too old or degraded to work as intended. Yet in Friday’s legal filings, Pike’s lawyers focused on the way the drug was administered, saying it was “abundantly clear” that Tennessee prison officials either didn’t know that the IV lines were out of place or didn’t realize her veins had been so badly damaged that the highly alkaline liquid started leaking out into the surrounding tissue of her arm. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology in Atlanta and one of Pike’s medical experts , said that meant there wasn’t enough of the drug in her bloodstream at once to kill her. “It just got into her arms, and most of it stopped there,” he said.   Like Pike, many people on death rows nationwide have significant health problems often compounded by old age. As the appeals process has drawn out, condemned prisoners are spending longer awaiting execution. People put to death in 1988 had spent an average of less than seven years on death row, federal data shows . By 2023, the most recent year with data, that figure had ballooned to more than 23 years. events.title: Salmon company to inject fish with antibiotics ahead of expected marine heatwave
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Salmon company Tassal will inject fish with antibiotics ahead of expected marine heatwave summer Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The salmon industry's preferred method to combat the disease Piscirickettsia salmonis, the antibiotic florfenicol, cannot be used. ( Huon ) Seafood giant Tassal will begin injecting salmon in a Tasmanian pen with the antibiotic oxytetracycline. The industry has been grappling with how to prevent mass fish deaths during the past two summers. The federal regulator is assessing the industry's request for a florfenicol permit after its use was suspended. A salmon company will begin individually injecting diseased fish in Tasmanian waters with an antibiotic this week, in what it says is a new practice for the state. Tassal, the Canadian-owned seafood giant, said it will use oxytetracycline (OTC) to treat a bacterial outbreak in fish at a lease in Tasmania's south, in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel, on Thursday. The announcement follows the salmon industry's controversial use of the antibiotic florfenicol last summer , which was dispersed in the water with salmon food. Both antibiotics treat disease in farmed salmon caused by the bacteria Piscirickettsia salmonis, which has led to mass fish deaths when waters warm during the summer months in recent years. Tasmania's salmon producers have been hit hard over recent years by a bacterial disease in waterways, resulting in large amounts of dead fish. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) The resultant dead fish and the proliferation of antibiotics in the marine environment have made the industry the subject of the ire of environmentalists, swimmers, recreational fishers and the wild fisheries sector . Tassal waiting for approval to use banned antibiotic again Ahead of last summer, the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) approved the industry's use of florfenicol in southern Tasmanian waters. The APVMA retracted the licence in March, citing an "unacceptable risk of residue exposure to non-target species". In the first three months of this year, the industry used more than five tonnes of florfenicol trying to control a disease outbreak that killed 9,000 tonnes of farmed fish. The fallout from the bacterial outbreak has emboldened opponents of the industry. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) In a statement today, a Tassal spokesperson said the company was waiting for approval to once again use florfenicol to treat disease outbreaks. "Florfenicol in feed is the most effective option, and while we await a permit for it, we're using OTC where required," they said. OTC has been used by the industry in the past, but the spokesperson said this would be the first time it is used to treat fish at sea. They said about 10 kilograms of OTC would be used in the first pen on Thursday, with fish individually anaesthetised, injected and then monitored for recovery. 'Huge amount' of antibiotics at fish farm concerning, say Greens, expert Almost 3 tonnes of the antibiotic florfenicol were used at one Tasmanian salmon farm lease in just two months, with information on its use across eight other sites yet to be released to the public by authorities. Despite the preference for florfenicol, Tassal said direct injection of OTC uses "a fraction of the medicine needed for medicated feed and is expected to deliver a more targeted treatment". Tassal rival Huon Aquaculture tried to use OTC to overcome disease outbreaks in coastal pens last year, but ruled it "largely ineffective" before the first florfenicol approval. At the time, the industry argued florfenicol had a range of advantages over oxytetracycline because it required lower dosages, lower levels were excreted by fish, and it had lower toxicity for aquatic organisms. Before the use of florfenicol was approved last November, salmon company Huon trialled oxytetracycline, but found it "largely ineffective". ( Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan ) Animal welfare a top priority, industry says John Whittington, the chief executive of industry body Salmon Tasmania, said he was bracing for a marine heatwave this summer. He said across the industry, fish were being bred and fed for resilience to warmer waters, and would be vaccinated against disease before being released into pens. But, he said, florfenicol remains the best treatment option for disease outbreaks, and the industry planned to use it as soon as possible, if approval is granted by the APVMA. "We are doing everything we can to ensure the welfare of our animals over summer is maintained," Dr Whittington said.

events.title: Meta joins with group of companies to tame ‘chaos’ of doing business with AI bots
events.summary: Walmart, Meta and OpenAI Chairman Bret Taylor’s startup Sierra are building a set of tech standards to make it easier to do business with AI bots. As Meta’s Muse and other buzzy AI agents like Instinct see a boom in popularity, some companies have struggled to figure out what's happening inside their walls. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists,” said Taylor. A month after Meta's launch of Muse, the personal agent that quickly turned into a viral sensation, a group of companies is coming together to try to simplify the process of bringing the technology into the business world. Meta, Walmart , Stripe and a handful of other companies are publishing what they're calling a "personal agent protocol." It's an open standard meant to dictate how artificial intelligence agents can interact with businesses. Enterprise AI startup Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, is part of the group. Taylor, who's also chairman of OpenAI and is leading the initiative, told CNBC in an interview that companies have a lot of work to do to figure out how and when personal agents are able to access information. "Companies will know when it's a personal agent versus an actual person. For a lot of companies there's a risk: you don't want just a random bot that isn't acting on behalf of a person to have access to this service," Taylor said. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists." Meta's Muse has become the most popular and buzzy version of personal AI agents since hitting the market in early September. It soared to the top of Apple's App Store and remains there, ahead of ChatGPT. However, Amazon is among the companies that have blocked Meta's agents, citing worries of website scraping. Amazon also blocked Perplexity's AI agent and sued the startup in November, alleging the company took steps to "conceal" its AI agents so they could continue to scrape Amazon's website without approval. Perplexity called the lawsuit a "bully tactic." For the new standard, Taylor compared it with the experience of logging into other websites with Google or Facebook credentials, technology he worked on when he was tech chief at Facebook. He said the practice will help with authentication so that businesses know if they're dealing with a bot, and will provide visibility into what personal agents are actually doing through these websites. David Singleton, vice president of engineering and consumer products at Meta Superintelligence Labs and former technology chief at Stripe, highlighted security. In order for agents to work well, he said, customers need to share credit card and personal information, and the new standard creates some level of visibility and control. "We're defining rails that we hope personal agents and business agents can run over for the future," Singleton said, comparing it to email. "If you think about email, it works great because it is a standard that everyone can use to talk to each other, and we think this is going to be quite similar." Singleton said Muse already has millions of users in the U..S and it's "growing rapidly." "What we're finding is that people love using Muse for all kinds of things, things like signing their kids up for classes, finding and buying the best gifts, scheduling that dentist appointment that you have been putting off for six months," he said. "We need a mechanism to have it go faster and smoother." While OpenAI and Anthropic aren't on board now, Taylor said he expects the AI giants to participate, and indicated he will be "really disappointed" if it's not being used by competitors. "The whole point of this is to be an open standard," Taylor said.

events.title: How event contract bundles are boosting volume on prediction markets
events.summary: Combo contracts, similar to parlays on traditional sportsbooks, are increasingly making up a large share of prediction markets' notional volume as traders seek potential high payouts. But those contracts are a very small portion of transactions on prediction market platforms, putting into question if notional volume is still an accurate reflection of where trader activity is on event contract exchanges. The way combo contracts are counted follows federal regulatory guidance governing how exchanges measure volume activity. The growing popularity of a combo contracts on prediction markets is leading to soaring volumes, even as they makes up only a small amount of total activity on the platforms. Combos, or multiple contracts stacked together that only pay out if all of them win — similar to parlays on traditional sportsbooks — have exploded in popularity. Last month, combos accounted for more than 50% of notional volume on Kalshi , driven by the start of the NFL season . Combos are overwhelmingly made up of combinations of multiple sports contracts. As rival Polymarket worked to expand its U.S. exchange this year, combos were a priority following the domestic platform's official launch in May . Combos are now nearly 50% of daily volume on Polymarket U.S., helped by growth during the NFL season. But while combos hold a large share of volume, they actually aren't where most speculators on prediction markets execute their trades. That's because of how the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal regulator overseeing prediction markets, requires exchanges to report volume. The multi-leg contracts are "helping [Polymarket and Kalshi] claim a higher number with lower realistic cash output," said Chris Park, a researcher and founder of MSR Decode, a research firm analyzing prediction market data. When a trader places a trade on a prediction market, no matter the cash they put down, platforms measure it as $1 of notional volume. All event contracts have binary outcomes between $0 to $1, and no matter what price a speculator pays to place a trade, someone has to take the other side of that order and make $1 in total volume. But combos can have payouts that are much greater than $1, meaning someone can put very little money down, pennies in some cases, and it will be measured as potentially thousands of dollars in volume thanks to the market makers who take the other side of these high-payout trades. A CNBC analysis for trades on Kalshi on Sept. 27 showed this in practice. On single contracts, the average amount of cash placed on a trade was less than 47 cents. But on combo contracts, that average per contract was about 9 cents. Similarly, while combos comprised 58% of Kalshi's trading volume in September, they made up less than 13% of the total transactions on the platform, according to data on Dune. Other than sports, combos trump other categories for notional volume on Kalshi, with over 35% total volume share. Details on how combos are measured is not always clear to the public, but their effect on total headline volume numbers can make platforms look as though they're growing faster than they are. The rising popularity of prediction markets' sports-related event contracts has hurt traditional online sportsbooks — including FanDuel parent Flutter Entertainment, and DraftKings — whose stocks have plunged 70% and 45%, respectively, over the past year. But some note that investors may be confusing activity numbers that aren't exactly comparable. "I have spoken to investors who see the notional number and compare it to [the] handle in sports betting, and then make the argument that. you know, these prediction markets have already exceeded [the] scale of sports betting," said Ian Moore, an analyst at Bernstein. A "handle" in a sportsbook measures the total dollar amount wagered, while prediction markets count both sides of a trade. "When a client buys a deep out-of-the-money contract or a combo, prediction markets may have dollar volumes anywhere between 20 to 100 times greater than sportsbooks because CFTC reporting requires one thing and sportsbooks report the same activity differently," said Rich Jaycobs, an independent advisor to prediction markets seeking regulatory approval from the CFTC. "Same basic bet, same basic idea, but you're getting a completely different perception of activity." Kalshi said its notional volume doesn't overstate activity. "If people are more interested in other measurements, they can look at other metrics," said spokesperson Jack Such. While notional volume is the standard metric for prediction markets, some have suggested looking instead at taker volume as a better measurement. That's because "takers" scoop up liquidity from market makers, rather than provide it, and thus can be a better yardstick of where activity is on exchanges. Polymarket agrees with that approach.

events.title: All 27 James Bond movies ranked, according to critics
events.summary: Sean Connery posed as James Bond on the set of "Goldfinger." Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images The first " James Bond " film, "Dr. No," turned 64 this month. To commemorate this anniversary, all 27 "Bond" films are streaming at their new home, Amazon Prime. "Bond 28," whenever it comes, will be the first without longtime producers, the Broccoli family. 007 fans, rejoice: Every film starring the world's most famous spy is finally streaming in one place, the franchise's new home, Amazon. Longtime "James Bond" producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli ceded creative control of Bond , James Bond, to Amazon MGM Studios in February 2025, so it makes sense that Bond's films would live there. Wilson had been involved with Eon Productions, the original studio behind "Bond," since 1972, and Broccoli's family had cinematic stewardship of the franchise since it began in 1962. Amazon officially acquired MGM in 2022, but the studio hasn't produced any 007 content since then; it hasn't even picked a successor to Daniel Craig after his 2021 exit. The Broccoli family's fierce protectiveness of the character was widely believed to have stalled franchise development, but that could change now that Amazon MGM Studios has full creative control. Announcements have been slow, though — all we know is that "Bond 28" will be directed by Denis Villeneuve . In honor of the new James Bond, who's hopefully coming our way soon, we used Rotten Tomatoes to see how all 27 films in this storied franchise stack up, according to critics. 27. "Casino Royale" (1967) "Casino Royale." Columbia Pictures Rotten Tomatoes score:   26% The lowest-rated Bond movie by critics is 1967's "Casino Royale," starring David Niven as the titular spy. This version of "Casino Royale" is a parody of spy films, rather than a straightforward Bond caper. It's also one of two films about James Bond that wasn't produced by Eon Productions. "Casino Royale" also starred Peter Sellers, Ursula Andress, Joanna Pettet, Daliah Lavi, Barbara Bouchet, and Terence Coop in double roles — all of them play different versions of Bond. Woody Allen also appeared as Bond's nephew, Jimmy. "Unfortunately, after the introductory sequences, 'Casino Royale' begins a downhill slide. It gets progressively sillier and more incoherent until it's impossible to keep any of the plot elements straight. Worse, with only occasional exceptions, the humor ceases to be funny, and the whole production degenerates into absurdity," wrote James Berardinelli of ReelViews. 26. "A View to a Kill" (1985) A matte shot of English actor Roger Moore as 007, clinging to a fire engine ladder in a publicity still for the James Bond film 'A View To A Kill', 1984. Keith Hamshere/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   36% Roger Moore's seventh and final outing as 007 was also his worst, according to critics. The film sees Bond travel to San Francisco to save Silicon Valley from a former KGB agent played by Christopher Walken. His bodyguard and lover, May Day, was notably played by Grace Jones. The classic "Bond girl" was played by Tanya Roberts, of future "That '70s Show" fame. "It's not double-oh-seven anymore, but double-oh-seventy, the best argument yet for the mandatory retirement age," wrote The Washington Post's Paul Attanasio. 25. "The Man with the Golden Gun" (1974) Actors Roger Moore and Christopher Lee on the set of "The Man With The Golden Gun". Sunset Boulevard/Corbis/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   40% "The Man with the Golden Gun" starred Moore as Bond and legendary actor Christopher Lee as the titular man with the golden gun, Francisco Scaramanga. Meanwhile, Bond's love interest, Mary Goodnight, was played by Britt Ekland. Bond and Scaramanga engage in a game of cat-and-mouse for much of the movie, as no one knows what Scaramanga looks like, outside the fact that he has a third nipple. "If you enjoyed the early Bond films as much as I did, you'd better skip this one," wrote Nora Sayre of The New York Times. 24. "Octopussy" (1983) Actor Roger Moore, left, and Actress Maud Adams, stars of the latest James Bond film 'Octopussy' pose for a photograph during filming on set at the Nene Valley Railway (NVR) Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, U.K, on Monday, September 6, 1982. Bryn Colton/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   41% Let's get it out of the way: Yes, this movie is really called "Octopussy." Its titular character, a successful businesswoman and jewel smuggler, was played by Maud Adams. Bond and Octopussy have personal business: Years earlier, Bond arrested her father for treason. The two form an uneasy alliance to defeat an exiled Afghan prince, Kamal Khan, played by Louis Jourdan. "It's an easy film to hate (and often paints a big target on its back encouraging you to do so), but it works perfectly as a piece of entertainment, where the good ultimately outweighs the bad," wrote Jake Tropila of Film Inquiry. 23. "The World Is Not Enough" (1999) Irish actor Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 in the James Bond film 'The World Is Not Enough', 1999. Here he visits the offices of a Swiss banker in the opening sequence. Keith Hamshere/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score: 51% Critics think the worst Bond film starring Pierce Brosnan is 1999's "The World Is Not Enough," Brosnan's third. Bond shares the screen with an American nuclear physicist named Dr. Christmas Jones. Equally improbable, she's played by Denise Richards. His  other  female costar is Elektra King, an oil heiress played by Sophie Marceau. The classic Bond villain, Renard, an ex-KGB agent who became a terrorist, was played by Robert Carlyle. "What do the James Bond series, the Chicago Cubs, and Master P's No Limit empire have in common? All owe their considerable commercial success more to loyalty, marketing, and tradition than to quality," wrote Nathan Rabin for the AV Club. 22. "Die Another Day" (2002) "Die Another Day." MGM Distribution Co. Rotten Tomatoes score:   55% Brosnan's fourth and final appearance as Bond, 2002's "Die Another Day," saw him get overshadowed by Halle Berry. "Die Another Day" plays as a classic early 2000s film: heavy on the CGI and the product placement. But it's notable for its casting of Berry as Jinx Johnson, an NSA agent, whose entrance in an orange bikini remains iconic over 20 years later. "Die Another Day" was also the first Bond movie in 39 years to not feature Desmond Llewelyn's Q as the head of the British Secret Service's fictional research and development division — in other words, he provided Bond with all of his nifty gadgets. Llewelyn died in 1999, just a few weeks after the premiere of "The World Is Not Enough." events.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
events.summary: Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance Published 6 October 2026, 14:00 BST It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance. Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom. Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch. HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS. Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time. While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability . The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings. Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come. While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes". As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger , Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years. For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year. That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas. The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year. If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein. Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date. "Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said. "Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift". Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema. As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas. Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year. Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground. Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods. Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken". "It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts." A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years. The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022. Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities". She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network." Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts. "Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added. CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount. The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

events.title: ASOS customers got an ominous notification this morning. Here's what the retailer is telling users.
events.summary: ASOS and Snowflake both confirmed to Business Insider that they're investigating the Tuesday morning incident that led to a rogue app notification. Gonzalo Marroquin/Getty Images for Nordstrom and ASOS ASOS app users posted screenshots of a troubling notification they received on Tuesday: "Engage with us, or we will leak it." The retailer confirmed that some personal information was hacked. It's the latest in a string of cyberattacks on major UK retailers. Some ASOS shoppers opened their phones Tuesday morning to find a troubling notification declaring "ASOS HACKED." "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance," a notification from the fast-fashion retailer said, according to several screenshots posted to social media. "Engage with us, or we will leak it." The notification, which arrived on phones at around 10 a.m. in London, ASOS confirmed to Business Insider, included a link to a Telegram chat. ASOS hacked, never deleted my payment methods so quick looool https://t.co/ZLnkMRoieU — Air-Rio (@vxleri0) October 6, 2026 "We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers," ASOS said in a statement. "We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities." The company said basic personal information of ASOS shoppers, including names and contact details, may have been accessed. The retailer said that it does not believe payment-card information or account passwords were affected. Snowflake, the cloud-data company named in the message, said it had started an investigation after learning of the notification. "At this time, we can report that we have found no compromise of the Snowflake platform," a company spokesperson said. ASOS said its website and app were operating normally in the meantime. The Tuesday incident appears to be the latest in a string of cybersecurity attacks on UK-based companies. Last year, automaker Jaguar-Land Rover shut down production for five weeks after a ransomware attack, while retailer Marks & Spencer had to shut down its online store after a hack. events.title: Kalshi launches transparency features on its election contracts ahead of midterms
events.summary: Kalshi is launching three features on its election contracts to provide traders with more transparency on how active its markets are. Kalshi's election markets will have a Brier score, which will measure the accuracy of its market's probabilities versus actual outcomes. The platform is also launching an activity feeds feature, where it shows individual trades happening on election contracts live. Kalshi decided to provide these additional features after noting election traders were participating on markets covering local races over national ones. With less than a month until midterms, Kalshi is launching three features on its election contracts to ensure traders have more transparency on how active and accurate its markets are. First, the platform will provide tags that indicate which election markets are low volume, which Kalshi defines as those with less than $10,000. Prediction markets experts have warned prices in low-volume markets can fluctuate widely, while spreads between buying and selling can stretch. Second, Kalshi's own election markets will have Brier scores, which will measure the accuracy of the market's probabilities versus actual outcomes. Finally, the platform is launching an activity feeds feature, where it shows individual trades happening on election contracts live. Kalshi decided to provide these transparency features after noting election traders were participating on markets covering local races over national ones. Kalshi's co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour called the midterms the "first meaningful prediction market election," noting the platform's election markets have grown six times faster than football markets this year, compared to the year before. Kalshi's internal data also indicates that more people are viewing their midterm markets than those who are trading by a ratio of five to one. In July, the prediction markets platform released a "Midterms Hub," which allows anyone to view traders' odds on markets tied to U.S. Senate and House of Representatives races. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: The 10 safest states in the US — and the 10 least safe
events.summary: Maine ranked as one of the safest US states to live in. : Dukas/Universal Images Group via Getty Images WalletHub released a report ranking the safest states in the US. States were ranked based on 52 safety indicators, including work safety and emergency preparedness. Vermont and Massachusetts scored the highest. Mississippi and Louisiana scored the lowest. Safe to say , safety comes in many forms beyond crime. The ability to prepare well for an emergency situation is a form of security, as is the number of emergency responders available nearby. One's financial well-being amid fear of job loss and inflation is also relative to one's sense of safety. A report released by the personal finance website WalletHub on Monday evaluated all 50 US states, ranking them from the most to least safe. For each state, WalletHub examined 52 indicators across five categories: personal and residential safety, financial safety, road safety, workplace safety, and emergency preparedness. The personal and residential safety category included factors such as crime rates, emergency responders per capita, and neighborhood watch groups per capita. To evaluate financial safety , WalletHub looked at factors such as unemployment rates, median credit scores, identity-theft complaints per capita, and poverty rates. The road safety ranking was determined by each state's rates of traffic fatalities and DUIs, road quality, and share of uninsured drivers, among other factors. WalletHub's workplace safety ranking included examining the number of fatal occupational injuries per 100,000 full-time workers and the presence of Occupational Safety and Health Act plans. Finally, the emergency preparedness ranking looked at states' histories of climate disasters. WalletHub used data from sources such as the US Census Bureau, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Department of Labor, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Crime Victims Center, among others. Here are the 10 safest states in the US, and the 10 least safe states. 1. Vermont Montpelier, Vermont. Erika Mitchell/Getty Images WalletHub ranked Vermont as the safest state in the US. Vermont's unemployment rate is 2.7% — one of the lowest in the country — which helped it place fourth in the financial safety ranking. It's also the state with the second-fewest reported identity theft complaints per capita. The state's road safety ranking was the third-highest in the US, with the second-best road quality and the fifth-fewest traffic fatalities of any state. Its workplace safety ranking also made the top 10, placing sixth overall. Vermont placed 16th in the personal and residential safety ranking and 11th in emergency preparedness. 2. Massachusetts Boston, Massachusetts. Thomas Roell/Getty Images As the second-safest state in the US, Massachusetts ranked in the top 10 of nearly every category of WalletHub's analysis. The state placed second in the personal and residential safety ranking, with low crime rates, including the eighth-fewest thefts and fourth-fewest murders of any state, according to the WalletHub report. Massachusetts also placed second in WalletHub's road safety ranking, eighth in financial safety, and ninth in emergency preparedness. Its workplace safety ranking was the lowest, coming in at 23rd overall. 3. Maine Portland, Maine. Sean Pavone/Getty Images Maine's low crime rate propelled it into the top three safest states in the US. With the fewest mass shootings between 2024 and September 2026, the third-fewest murders per capita, and the fewest aggravated assaults per capita, it ranked fourth in personal and residential safety. Maine ranked 16th in financial safety with an unemployment rate of 3.4% and the 12th-lowest poverty rate in the US. It ranked 8th in road safety, 21st in workplace safety, and second in emergency preparedness. 4. New Hampshire Portsmouth, New Hampshire. travelview/Getty Images New Hampshire was ranked the fourth-safest state in the US, but it had the highest financial safety ranking of any state. It placed third in personal and residential safety and fourth in emergency preparedness. New Hampshire's road safety and workplace safety rankings were lower, at 12th and 41st, respectively. 5. Connecticut Hartford, Connecticut. SeanPavonePhoto/Getty Images/iStockphoto Connecticut's personal and residential safety ranking was the highest of any state. It placed 21st in both the financial safety and the road safety rankings, 25th in workplace safety, and 15th in emergency preparedness. 6. Utah Salt Lake City, Utah. Sean Pavone/Getty Images Utah was ranked No. 1 in road safety, No. 3 in emergency preparedness, and No. 4 in workplace safety. It placed 26th in financial safety and 35th in personal and residential safety. 7. Minnesota Minneapolis, Minnesota. Sean Pavone/Getty Images Minnesota's workplace safety ranked second, road safety ranked sixth, and financial safety ranked seventh. The state's personal and residential safety and emergency preparedness both ranked 23rd. 8. Indiana Indianapolis, Indiana. Nicholas Klein/Getty Images WalletHub ranked Indiana 7th in personal and residential safety, 25th in financial safety, 11th in road safety, 10th in workplace safety, and 28th in emergency preparedness. 9. Rhode Island Providence, Rhode Island. tupungato/Getty Images/iStockphoto In Rhode Island, the state's personal and residential safety and emergency preparedness were both ranked eighth-best in the US. It placed 20th in financial safety, 16th in road safety, and 39th in workplace safety. 10. Hawaii Honolulu, Hawaii. rebelml/Getty Images/iStockphoto Hawaii rounded out WalletHub's list of the top 10 safest states in the US, placing 10th. Hawaii performed well in financial safety, with the second-highest ranking of any state. Personal and residential safety ranked 20th, road safety 26th, workplace safety 22nd, and emergency preparedness 13th. Keep reading for the bottom 10 states, which were ranked the least safe in the US. 41. Georgia Atlanta, Georgia. Alex Slitz - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images Georgia ranked 34th and 35th in personal and residential safety and road safety, respectively. It placed 47th in financial safety and has the second-highest share of uninsured people. 42. Alabama Birmingham, Alabama. : Joe Sohm/Visions of America/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Alabama ranked 36th in personal and residential safety, 34th in financial safety, and 31st in road safety. It ranked 40th in emergency preparedness. The state tied in the lowest unemployment rate with Vermont, North Dakota, Hawaii, and South Dakota. 43. Colorado Denver, Colorado. Justin Edmonds/Getty Images In Colorado, personal and residential safety ranked 46th among US states. The state placed 19th in financial safety, 41st in road safety, and 38th in workplace safety.
