events.title: Why deep-red Kansas has become an unexpected Senate battleground
events.summary: Kansas has emerged as an unexpected Senate battleground, forcing national Republicans to spend millions defending GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in a state Donald Trump carried by 16 points in 2024. Trump administration policies on trade, beef imports and immigration have created political headaches across Kansas' agriculture, cattle and aerospace industries, giving Democrat Adam Hamilton an opening in the deep-red state. Marshall retains a sizable cash advantage, and Kansas' long Republican Senate history gives the GOP reason for confidence. In a state that hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1932, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall suddenly finds himself in a competitive race with weeks to go until the 2026 midterm elections . Stubborn inflation, blowback from White House trade policies, and a formidable Democratic challenger in megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton have combined to turn ruby-red Kansas into an unexpected Senate battleground. The tightening contest has forced Marshall into a balancing act confronting a growing number of vulnerable Republicans: creating space from President Donald Trump on issues that pose risks at home without alienating his base. "When a sitting Republican senator in Kansas starts running away from their leader in the White House, the five-alarm bell is ringing for the entire party," said Bob Beatty , a political scientist at Washburn University. "Loyalty to Washington is becoming a liability when voters are feeling the squeeze at home." The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted the race from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican" on Sept. 23. A September Emerson College/Nexstar survey of 750 Kansas likely voters put Hamilton at 45% and Marshall at 43%, a dead heat within the poll's 3.6% margin of error. In the same poll, Trump's approval in Kansas stood at 40%, with 53% disapproving and nearly half of likely voters naming the economy their top issue. National Republican groups have taken note. Outside groups are now pouring millions into Kansas to defend the seat that once sat safely outside the Senate battlefield. At stake is the GOP's Senate majority. Marshall has been a stalwart Trump ally for years. Though Trump carried Kansas by 16 points in 2024, the senator has recently shown a willingness to distance himself. In September, Trump threatened to ban U.S. sales of aircraft built by Canadian manufacturer Bombardier, potentially putting the future of many of the company's roughly 1,500 Wichita-based jobs in limbo. While Marshall offered little resistance to the broader trade dispute that spurred the threat, he insisted he had taken the fight for local aerospace jobs "inside the Oval Office." Meanwhile, farmers are being squeezed from both ends. Trade disputes and retaliatory tariffs have weighed on grain and soybean markets just as the Iran war has driven up fuel costs. Diesel — essential for combines, tractors and transport trucks — jumped nearly a dollar a gallon during one 30-day stretch this harvest season, according to AAA . Ranchers have been hit, too. In a bid to tamp down ground beef prices, Trump in August moved to lower tariffs on an additional 300,000 metric tons of imports for lean beef trimmings. "The interference in Washington is causing more harm than good," said Matt Teagarden , chief executive of the Kansas Livestock Association. "Many of our members would prefer policymakers to let the market work." The association endorsed Marshall in both his 2016 House race and his 2020 Senate campaign. This year, it has declined to endorse either Marshall or Hamilton. Marshall, meanwhile, has offered calibrated pushback against several Trump administration policies, calling for "targeted relief" on fuel costs and arguing the administration took the wrong approach to food prices. Immigration enforcement further complicated Marshall's balancing act. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids have swept across southwestern Kansas, home to some of the nation's largest meatpacking plants and feedlots, stoking fear among immigrant workers. "Workers stayed home, causing plants to shorten shifts, slow production lines or cancel shifts altogether," Teagarden told CNBC. "Canceled processing left feedlots holding cattle longer, driving up costs in an industry already facing labor shortages." Marshall responded with measured critique: "When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement," he posted on X on Sept. 23. "Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone." Adding to Marshall's troubles are controversies all his own. The New York Times reported on Sept. 8 that Marshall, a physician, sued more than 700 patients of his medical clinic over unpaid bills. The Times found that patients were arrested in 81 cases after missing court dates; lawyers also garnished patients' wages and bank accounts, and patients were routinely charged 18% annual interest.

events.title: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates
events.summary: The new system will be 25% faster than having to show your passport, officials said Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced. On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said. The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically. Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials. If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer. Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said. East Midlands Airport said they expected a 'smoother, swifter and simpler' passenger experience Phil Douglas, director general of Border Force, said: "This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country. "By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK's robust border security. "Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families." Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, the trade body for the country's airports, said the move was "excellent news for the passenger". She added: "It is vital that we have the fast, efficient borders that arrivals into the UK now expect, and we will work closely with our members and government officials to ensure a smooth rollout." Steve Griffiths, managing director of East Midlands Airport, in Castle Donington, Leicestershire, said: "We're delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force. "As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers' journeys smoother, swifter and simpler. "This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area." Standard e-gates are currently available at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted. Criminals called BYOD claim to have broken into the Trump-branded mobile biz and leaked data belonging to 3,615 people, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, and order details. BYOD is a new ransomware-as-a-service operation, and Trump Mobile is only the third organization posted on its data-leak site. According to the group’s posted claim, after telling Trump Mobile that it had been breached, the wireless provider replied: “We have no team to handle this" and “Anyone who hacks them are a terrorist.” “Well unfortunately for them, all 3615 customers and their PII, alongside telecom details are now up for grabs,” the leak site says. “Feel free to take a gander at it yourself, don't be shy, we (and them) certainly aren't stopping you.” The hackers reportedly told International Cyber Digest that they first infected a Liberty Mobile employee with an infostealer, and then accessed Trump Mobile via the MVNO. BYOD claims to still have access to Trump Mobile’s systems, and told the publication that neither wireless provider used any form of multi-factor authentication. Neither the Trump Organization nor Liberty Mobile responded to The Register ’s questions about the breach. The data dump doesn’t include any details about US President Donald Trump or his family members, according to Straight Arrow News, which first reported the breach and verified some customers’ information. This could mean that the Trump family doesn’t eat its own dogfood. The leak does, however, include personal information about Eric Brunnett , vice president and chief information officer for the Trump Organization. Brunnett’s LinkedIn profile says he oversees “all Information Technology and Information Security for all aspects of the Trump Organization.” Additionally, one customer contacted by Straight Arrow said he paid a $100 pre-order deposit last year for Trump Mobile’s flagship smartphone, the T1, but never received a gold-colored device. Another criminal group, EndZone, also claimed to have breached Trump Mobile and leaked a stolen dataset a week before BYOD’s post in what “appears to be the same original breach,” according to security sleuth Dominic Alvieri. These aren’t the fledgling mobile phone company's only security snafus. Before these two apparent breaches, a security researcher in May claimed he discovered a now-plugged website vulnerability that leaked Trump Mobile customers’ details . events.title: OpenAI Is Pissing Off a Bunch of Mathematicians—Again
events.summary: In August, OpenAI convened around 40 mathematicians to discuss what to do if AI outpaces human capabilities in the field. The company hinted that its powerful models had solved hundreds of long-standing math problems, say people who were in attendance, but company representatives assured attendees it would not release the solutions all at once—an assurance OpenAI spokesperson Lindsay McCallum says the company is “not aware of”—and, worried by how the community might react, sought advice on how to publish the findings. Attendees responded with “a mixture of excitement and dread,” but the meeting was a promising first step, recalls Northwestern University mathematician Bryna Kra. The group, she tells WIRED, asked the firm not to just publish them in a blog or tweet, like they had done with 10 problems earlier that month . Instead, it would be important for OpenAI to publish papers explaining the work so that mathematicians could absorb, digest, and use the results, according to Kra. “Apparently, that input was ignored,” she says. OpenAI has told people it plans to dump hundreds of results to unsolved problems on GitHub on Tuesday, people familiar with the plans tell WIRED. The release would be the latest of tens of thousands of mathematical solutions generated by AI this year, as frontier models become increasingly capable. “On August 28, we began training a new internal model. In addition to resolving the Navier—Stokes Millennium Prize problem⁠, this model has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics,” says McCallum. “We are working to responsibly release the next math results from our model, drawing on advice and public recommendations from the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study to inform how we release these results. We have not set a release time.” But for several leading mathematicians, the impending output is also a sign that the company has learned little from the controversies over previous releases. In conversations with WIRED, the academics say they feel the field has become a playground for OpenAI and its rival Anthropic to show off their models as both prepare for blockbuster initial public offerings. In their rush to outdo each other, mathematicians say, traditional scientific processes for releasing and attributing results have been cast aside. The most striking case so far came in September. OpenAI deployed thousands of agents to solve a legendary million-dollar Millennium Prize problem after hearing “rumors” that others were closing in on solutions. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician and professor at New York University, accused the company of front-running the work he had done toward solving an element of the problem in a personal collaboration with Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge. The pair hadn’t published their work but had been using OpenAI’s tools to help them. During an attempt to negotiate credit, Buckmaster claims, OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck seemed to imply that Alpöge should be excluded from any paper, since that would make things complicated. (In response to a request for comment, Bubeck pointed to a previous public statement in which he denied asking for Alpöge to not be listed as an author.) Buckmaster said he refused. In a call, Bubeck claimed that there is some worry about what Anthropic is doing, according to meeting notes seen by WIRED. Levent must be talking to his leadership right now letting them know fucking OpenAI can get a Millennium Prize problem, he said, per the notes. What’s to stop Anthropic from giving all their compute to get a Millennium Prize problem? According to the notes, Bubeck also seemed to suggest that Buckmaster would be ruining his career when Buckmaster threatened to tell the press about his belief that OpenAI had stolen his work. If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice , Bubeck said, according to the meeting notes. Nestor Guillen, a visiting math professor at NYU, tells WIRED that “there's a perception of mobster behavior” from the AI companies among mathematicians. “We disagree with that characterization,” says McCallum. “I feel a lot of angst, and I see this more and more in my colleagues in mathematics, not over AI, but over the AI companies,” Guillen says. “I think a lot of the angst is about the accumulation of power in one place.” OpenAI assembled an advisory group in mid September to help determine how the company assesses and communicates new results, upholds academic and professional standards, and builds tools that support mathematical research and learning. But the company doesn’t seem to have made much progress, mathematicians say. Many are frustrated that OpenAI and Anthropic continue to release results through blog posts, rather than scientific papers, which makes them harder to verify and often excludes prior work from other mathematicians.

events.title: Patagonia’s CEO is worried about political apathy—so the company offered 112,000 people $100 to help 3 friends plan to vote
events.summary: Patagonia has spent decades getting young people off their screens and into the outdoors, sporting the Fitz Roy mountain logo on their fleeces. Its next bet: getting them to the polls for the midterms. The outdoor apparel company set aside $11.2 million for its 11.2 Million Vote Project , which launched Sept. 26. Anyone who sent a voting plan to at least three friends or family members could choose $100 in Patagonia credit or a $100 donation to the League of Conservation Voters.   The money was gone in four days. By Sept. 30, more than 112,000 people had signed up, and nearly 500,000 people, counting participants and the friends they had reached, had plans to vote in this year’s midterms, the company told Fortune.  Behind the giveaway is a gap between caring about the environment and actually showing up to vote—and a bet that friends can help close it. Patagonia partnered with non-profit organization Environmental Voter Project , whose polling suggests Americans often think about tackling climate change through recycling and shopping choices rather than politics. Researchers who study turnout say personal outreach is a promising way to turn that concern into votes, particularly during midterm elections.  “Offering a meaningful incentive was a game changer,” Corley Kenna, Patagonia’s chief communications and impact officer, told Fortune . Without it, the company might still have reached its goals, she said, but doing so probably would have taken longer than four days—or it might not have reached them at all. The campaign also reflects Patagonia’s concerns surrounding the future of public lands. “There are 90 million acres of public lands at threat,” Kenna said, while saying Patagonia would continue explaining to its community which lands are threatened and what people can do through Election Day and beyond. That push comes as Patagonia renews its fight with President Donald Trump over public lands . In July, Trump sharply reduced Utah’s Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments; Patagonia announced in September it was joining a coalition challenging the Bears Ears reduction in court, reviving a battle it fought during his first term. Caring about climate doesn’t always mean voting CEO Ryan Gellert told Axios apathy is “probably the single biggest thing that concerns me right now.” The campaign’s name and budget draw on EVP research finding that 11.2 million registered voters identified as environmentalists skipped the 2024 presidential election.  Nathaniel Stinnett, EVP’s founder, told Fortune that when his organization asked respondents open-ended questions about addressing immigration, gun violence, and education, they overwhelmingly suggested political solutions. But for climate change, personal solutions outnumbered political ones, about four to one, with the most common answer being recycling, followed by changing consumer behavior. “We’re not going to recycle our way out of the climate crisis,” Stinnett said. Stinnett suspects that framing helps explain why people who care deeply about the environment can still fail to vote. They think about changing what they eat or how they commute, he said, without necessarily thinking about casting a ballot. That absence has consequences.  “When we talk about apathy, we need to recognize that politicians know who votes and who doesn’t vote,” Stinnett said, arguing non-voters risk having their priorities ignored. EVP identifies people who already care about the environment and encourages them to become consistent voters. The nonprofit’s approach relies on social influence rather than another argument about why climate matters, Stinnett said. “Your friends carry much more of a social impact on what your behavior is or ought to be than a stranger does,” he said. A $100 nudge from a friend Patagonia said participants signed up for the 11.2 Million Vote Project through its voting-plan app, where they could take an optional training and add friends to generate personalized voting plans. Registered contacts could be matched to public voter files to provide accurate voting information. Those who weren’t registered could still receive information about registering or updating their registration as part of making a plan.  Participants then shared the app-generated plans however they preferred and logged their outreach. After repeating the process for three friends, they qualified for the incentive.  Their friends did not have to register or vote for participants to receive the reward. Donald Green, a Columbia University political scientist known for pioneering field experiments on voter mobilization, said that differs from paying people to register or vote, which is illegal in federal elections.  He compared the arrangement to a TaskRabbit gig: Patagonia was “essentially hiring people as temp workers, as temp political workers,” he told Fortune . Green said the midterms offer a promising opportunity. People who ordinarily vote in presidential elections may be less inclined to participate in midterms, leaving room for outreach to influence their behavior. “If anything, this is the right venue for this kind of campaign,” he said. Reaching people through friends also makes sense as contacting strangers through phone calls or social media becomes increasingly difficult, Green said. Outreach from friends may help cut through the flood of messages competing for people’s attention online. David Nickerson, a political scientist at Temple University who studies voter mobilization, agreed. Messages from friends are more likely to get noticed and carry more credibility than outreach from strangers, he told Fortune . Making a voting plan also helps recipients picture themselves following through. A voting plan isn’t a ballot Still, reaching nearly 500,000 people does not mean producing nearly 500,000 additional voters. One limitation of outreach through friends is that volunteers often belong to social circles where people already vote, Nickerson said. “You can’t mobilize your friends who will already vote,” he said. The $100 credit could help attract younger Patagonia customers with less disposable income, he suggested—a group with lower turnout and more room for outreach to make a difference. To establish whether the campaign increased turnout, Nickerson said researchers would need a randomized experiment comparing people selected to receive outreach with a control group. Public voting records could then show whether the groups voted at different rates. Simply finding that recipients voted would not separate the campaign’s influence from their existing likelihood of voting. For Stinnett, the broader goal is to make voting part of how environmentally minded people act on their concerns. Seeing friends vote can help establish that habit, he said. “People vote because at some point they come to realize that they want to be the type of person who votes,” he said. This story was or

events.title: ‘AI Snake Oil’ author sees chatbots evolving into a ‘truth oracle’—and journalism heading somewhere it hasn’t been in 200 years
events.summary: Arvind Narayanan thinks AI will come to feel more trustworthy—and it will remove the tells that let readers know they’re encountering AI slop in the wild. The Princeton computer scientist even predicts that these more accurate chatbots to come could become what many people treat as a “truth oracle.” Pew’s survey this year found that 10% of Americans are already doing this. Narayanan addressed the Computation + Journalism Symposium at Northwestern’s McCormick Foundation Center, where Fortune attended. The agenda included the challenges facing media and proliferation of AI slop. His keynote was titled “AI and Journalism: Skating Where the Puck is Going.” He urged the audience to prepare for AI “not as it is today, but as it will be five or 10 years from now.” He said his computer science background is helpful in delineating which of today’s limits are fixable engineering problems and which are inherent. He has never worked in a newsroom, he noted. “It’s possible I don’t know what I’m talking about,” he cautioned, before laying out a compelling argument. He broke his argument intwo two parts: If chatbots become the default place to settle factual questions—Narayanan said “virtually all” questions about, say, who is running for political office are headed there—the newsroom loses one more piece of its bundle, and arguably the most basic one. What’s left is the work a machine can’t settle: contested questions, narrative, storytelling and being explicit about what he called “positionality,” a challenge for an industry that strives for objectivity. Narayanan directs Princeton’s Center for Information Technology Policy but he has emerged of late as a thought leader on AI, the future of work and the media industry; he co-wrote AI Snake Oil with Sayash Kapoor and his newsletter AI as Normal Technology has over 87,000 subscribers. Narayanan talked to Fortune in August about the AI backlash, which he sees as a complicated thing, and expanded on his insight into why productivity and return on investment has been so hard to measure or even nonexistent. He calls this a “ skinny hamburger, fat bun ” problem, where the meat of execution shrinks down to almost nothing with the use of AI, while the decision and deliberation “buns” swell, with a great deal of anxiety and uncertainty. The oracle and the slop Narayanan said the common picture of chatbots as simple next-word predictors is outdated. Today’s chatbots are “neurosymbolic systems,” he said: a language model plus tools that search the web, retrieve documents and write code to analyze data. Errors that were common a year ago, such as miscounting the letters in “strawberry” or Google’s AI Overviews suggesting glue on pizza, now rarely occur. He called the remaining problems “gradually getting solved.” He then asked what happens when expectations catch up. His elementary-school-age children, he said, may never experience hallucination the way adults do, much as Wikipedia once went from an untrusted reference to a “much more authoritative” source. “I’m not saying it’s inevitable. I’m not saying it’s a good thing,” he said. On X, he noted, users already settle arguments by asking Grok, mostly conservatives with low trust in legacy media. He estimated the wider shift at about a decade out. A member of the audience ventured that chatbots can suffer from what press critic Jay Rosen famously called the “view from nowhere” for the false neutrality expressed by journalists reluctant to use their own judgment and properly inform the audience. Daniel Trielli of the University of Maryland asked about this danger, and Narayanan agreed, and said he sees that as a challenge for journalism to continue defining going forward. One of Narayanan’s most contrarian claims was that agenda-setting by the media has backfired. The Washington Post ‘s role in Watergate was “an unalloyed good,” he said, but cited research from “many communication scholars and economists” showing that efforts to do the same in the Trump era, with audiences already splintered, have fed polarization and hastened the collapse of trust. AI writing, he said, is similarly “largely a solvable technical problem.” A model could be trained to mimic one writer almost perfectly, mainly a question of cost, and detectors “might not work that well.” The unbundling Narayanan said his talk was “as much about the continuing effects of social media on newsrooms as it is about AI.” The newsroom is now thought of as a single institution bundling reporting, analysis, fact-checking and distribution, Narayanan noted, but he argued that this was a “historically contingent” development and not a given going forward. The ad-supported penny papers of the 1830s broadened what counted as news because earlier papers lived on subscriptions and political patronage. Objectivity arose in response to World War I propaganda, and paid reporters and interviews also “had to be invented.” Calling someone a “hired reporter,” he noted, was once an insult, “like a hired gun.” Narayanan’s framework draws on earlier debates. He quoted Clay Shirky’s line that “society doesn’t need newspapers. What we need is journalism,” and said Paul Starr had warned, from the same era, that the loss of newspapers’ economics would leave public goods like accountability unfunded. Starr has been proven right “in many ways,” Narayanan said, “but it’s maybe not been as apocalyptic” as feared, because philanthropy has stepped in. His claim is that, piece by piece, specialists now do each job more cheaply than a newsroom can, and AI is hastening the process along. “For each of these components, there is kind of a competitor that produces this component in a more standalone way that is better structurally equipped just based on the economics of production,” he said. Trade reporting, for instance, went to outlets like Politico , Punchbowl and Stat News . Civic and local journalism has largely moved to a “philanthropy-funded model,” he said, and investigations increasingly run on nonprofit money—”a reversion to historical patterns.” Analysis, he stressed, has moved to independent journalists, social media creators and “people like me.” Returning to what he called “the overarching point” of his talk, he said that the idea of packaging everything together in a single newsroom “is no longer the most economically viable way of producing news.” One of Narayanan’s most contrarian claims was that agenda-setting by the media has backfired

events.title: Paramount completes Warner Bros takeover to form media giant Skydance
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Skydance brings together some of the biggest names in US media. ( AP: Yuki Iwamura ) Paramount's takeover of Warner Bros Discovery is now complete, creating a new Hollywood juggernaut under the name Skydance. CEO David Ellison, whose ultra-wealthy family has ties to US President Donald Trump, called it a "historic day" for the media industry. It follows Paramount winning a bidding war with the streaming service Netflix earlier this year. Paramount has completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, uniting two of Hollywood's most storied studios in a media empire spanning television, news and cinema under the control of David Ellison. The combined company, renamed Skydance, brings together Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures, the CBS News and CNN networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Mr Ellison plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services over time. "Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Mr Ellison, whose ultra-wealthy family has ties to US President Donald Trump. Paramount clears way for Warner Bros merger Opponents say Paramount's multi-billion-dollar merger with Warner Bros will slash Hollywood jobs, reduce the number of films produced, and threaten CNN's independence. Skydance shares began trading Tuesday, local time, on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker "SKYD," while Warner Bros Discovery shareholders will receive about $US31 ($44) per share in cash. The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds. Paramount won a bidding war against Netflix in February for Warner Bros Discovery, and the Trump administration approved the deal, one of the largest-ever media mergers, in June without demanding a change to its business. Skydance, which will have nearly $US70 billion ($100.8 billion) in annual revenue, said it was targeting more than $US6 billion ($8.6 billion) in cost savings within three years. Mr Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO, with former Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations and integrating the two businesses. David Ellison is the chairman and chief executive officer of the newly formed Skydance Corp. ( AP: Alberto Pezzali ) The deal was backed by $US47 billion ($67.3 billion) in new equity led by the Ellison family, private equity firm RedBird Capital and the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. David Ellison's father, billionaire Oracle founder Larry Ellison, provided major funding and a guarantee to lenders backing the deal. The Ellison family holds the largest equity stake in Skydance. Opponents in the movie industry said the combined company would slash jobs in a Hollywood already under pressure and reduce the number of films produced every year, while news media groups feared CNN's independence could be compromised. The decree includes several safeguards on these issues, including a board meant to protect CNN's editorial independence. events.title: Salesforce shares sit at the epicenter of AI confusion. Here's how to trade it
events.summary: If ever there was a stock that personified the promise and peril of the AI trade, it's Salesforce . Salesforce shares have been in a tug of war throughout 2026, and it may present an opportunity for options traders. The stock bottomed in late June, down more than 40% from the start of the year on fears that AI agents would make traditional software subscriptions obsolete. Fear collided with reality when the company released Q2 earnings in August that blew away Street expectations and put to rest, at least temporarily, that the so-called SasSpocalypse was upon us. The stock responded by jumping from $205 to a share price of $252 by the end of the following session, a rally of over 22% and the second biggest single day gain in the company's history. Now, just one month later, the stock has faded much of that post-earnings momentum and sits near a share price of $230, significantly above yearly lows but still down nearly 10% YTD. Like many other legacy SaaS names, Salesforce has reported strong financials, but many investors remain unconvinced the business can grow through an AI driven overhaul of enterprise software. That unresolved debate may be part of why the stock has stayed stuck between its highs and lows rather than settling into a clear trend. With the next earnings announcement estimated in December, this gives options traders several weeks to potentially play this choppy range before the next major catalyst. Implied volatility on Salesforce currently sits around 39%, somewhat elevated relative to its annual range but fairly in line with levels for the past month. For context, that volatility spiked into the mid 50s back in August around the earnings reaction. Current volatility levels in Salesforce are more consistent with sustained, moderately elevated investor uncertainty as opposed to the market gearing up for another violent move. That kind of grinding, directionless uncertainty makes Salesforce an interesting candidate for a neutral, short premium trade. I'm selling the Nov 20 210/200 put spread (short 210P, long 200P) and the Nov 20 260/270 call spread (short 260C, long 270C) for a total credit of $3.54 This trade set-up is a short iron condor, which assumes that the standoff described above continues a while longer. This is a neutral strategy which reaches the maximum profit of $354 if Salesforce's stock remains above the $210 strike put and below the $260 strike call by November 20th. The structure brackets the range that Salesforce has occupied since the rally stalled out in August. The $210 put sits just above where the stock was trading pre-earnings, while the $260 call sits just under the post-earnings peak of $264. With breakeven stock prices of $263.54 to the upside and $206.46 to the downside, the real danger of the trade is a decisive move beyond either long strike before expiration. The maximum loss of $646 is reached if Salesforce moves above $270 (+17%) or below $200 (-13%) within the next six weeks. The upside for assuming this risk is a theoretical probability of profit of 61%. Additionally, the position's P50, the probability of capturing half the max profit before expiration, sits at 72%. Traders may look to close or roll the position once it hits that halfway point rather than holding all the way to November 20th for the remaining decay. If assigned, the trader ends up owning shares below where Salesforce traded even before its blowout quarter, a level some may be comfortable owning at given the stock's demonstrated ability to rally hard from similar territory. One wrinkle worth watching: ServiceNow reports earnings October 27, squarely inside this trade's window. Salesforce has a documented history of moving in sympathy with ServiceNow, and a sharp move in ServiceNow's shares could pull Salesforce along with it. Disclosures: Spina owns this trade. events.title: High diesel prices may put 'another squeeze' on the consumer, economist says
events.summary: Diesel prices are up about 68% since the start of the Iran war, to $6.32 per gallon as of Tuesday, according to AAA. The conflict has curbed oil supply flowing in the Middle East and damaged the region's refining infrastructure. Russia's war in Ukraine has also contributed. High diesel prices raise costs to transport goods and food to market. Diesel is also a key input cost for farmers, manufacturers and other businesses. They pass those costs on to consumers slowly over time, economists said. Consumers are feeling the pinch of higher gasoline prices. But another type of fuel — diesel — also threatens to push up prices at the store in a less visible way, economists said. Diesel prices have soared 68% since the start of the Iran war, a larger increase than for gasoline prices, according to data from AAA. That dynamic threatens to push up costs for consumers across store shelves, from food to physical goods, at a time when inflation is already persistently high , economists said. "It's going to be another squeeze on the consumer," said Michael Reid, head of U.S. economics at the Royal Bank of Canada. "And it's really the lower- and middle-income consumers who feel it disproportionately." How much have diesel prices increased? Average diesel prices rose to $6.32 per gallon on Tuesday from $3.76 per gallon on Feb. 27, the day before the U.S. and Israel bombed Iran, according to AAA. September marked the first time national average diesel prices ever breached $6 a gallon. The Group of Seven nations — France, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States — on Friday agreed to a "substantial release" of diesel stocks to combat rising fuel prices. The Trump administration had been pressuring Europe to release diesel stocks as an alternative to the U.S. imposing an export ban to lower prices. The Iran war is the primary cause for the run-up in prices, economists said. The conflict has curbed oil supply flowing through the Middle East, thereby raising prices, and damaged refining infrastructure in the region that turns oil into products like diesel, gasoline and jet fuel. Russia's war in Ukraine has also contributed to higher diesel prices , economists said. Kyiv has bombed Russian refineries, leading Moscow to ban diesel exports. Meanwhile, average gas prices were $4.37 per gallon as of Tuesday, up about 47% from $2.98 per gallon on Feb. 27, according to AAA. Gasoline price movements are more apparent to consumers than those of diesel, since drivers feel them immediately when filling up, economists said. But diesel's impact is more under the radar. "Gas is direct: It's coming right out of my pocket into the gas tank," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's. "Diesel is indirect." Diesel is a fuel used by trucks, trains and ships to transport goods to stores. It has many uses beyond transportation fuel, such as in farming and manufacturing, as well as residential and industrial heating, according to a Goldman Sachs Research note on Sept. 21. Businesses pass those higher diesel costs on to consumers via higher prices at the store, economists said. "Anything that's on a truck will be impacted by the higher diesel costs, everything from groceries to whatever you'd get delivered to your front door by UPS or Amazon," Zandi said. There's a common saying that sums it up nicely, he said: "Cars run on gas, the economy runs on diesel." Freight costs are accelerating at a rapid pace, comparable to the post-Covid reopening of the economy — and many of those transport methods rely on diesel, Reid said. Trade routes are largely fixed — meaning businesses can't reduce distance to save on fuel — so higher diesel input costs will likely be passed along the supply chain, ultimately to the consumer, he said. Those price impacts take time to filter through to consumers, perhaps anywhere from six months to a year for the full effects to pass through, Zandi said. As a general rule of thumb, for each $1 increase in the cost of a gallon of diesel, consumers can expect overall inflation to rise by 0.1 percentage points, assuming higher prices are sustained, he said.

events.title: Developers are burned out, disengaged, and facing an AI-powered reset, a survey of 30,000 workers found
events.summary: Developers are embracing AI coding, but many feel exhausted, obsolete, and unable to trust it. Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images AI coding tools are speeding up work but leaving engineers anxious and depleted, Stack Overflow found. Nearly half the 30,000 developers surveyed said they are complacent, with burnout a major driver. "Keeping up with AI is virtually impossible," one software engineer told Business Insider. The people building the AI boom are running on empty. According to Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey, released Tuesday, nearly half of 30,903 developers surveyed in 169 countries reported being complacent in their current jobs, while a third were unhappy, and just over 22% were happy. Among the complacent group, burnout or tech fatigue was the leading reason, cited by 21% of respondents. The findings come amid an environment where software engineers' jobs are changing at breakneck speed . AI coding has taken over a greater share of their daily work — reducing some developers to button-pushers and human meat proxies , contributing to an identity crisis among some engineers, and fueling "off-the-charts" anxiety among tech workers. The malaise comes alongside a major shift in how software gets made. Stack Overflow found that almost two-thirds of respondents use AI coding assistants or agents, while 62% use general-purpose AI chat tools. Among daily AI users, 31% said they use them for four hours or more. The findings echo what Annie Wright, a Bay Area psychotherapist and executive coach whose practice is dominated by tech workers, told Business Insider in August. Her clients had moved beyond ordinary burnout, she said, to questioning their identity and future as automation reshapes the work they have built their careers around. "Three years ago, people would walk in saying, 'I'm exhausted, burned out beyond belief,'" Wright said at the time. "Now they walk in saying, 'I'm exhausted. I'm burned out beyond belief. I don't know who I am if my work gets automated.'" A faster way to work — and more pressure to keep up Marc Backes, a senior software engineer at Directus, said AI has made his work less fulfilling. He used to enjoy working through a feature or tracing a technical problem to its source; now, he spends far more time asking AI agents to do it. "It's definitely less fulfilling," Backes told Business Insider. "I always enjoyed drafting out the best ways to implement a new feature and really think about it." The pressure is not coming directly from his manager, he said, but from an industry moving faster and treating writing — or even reading — code by hand as "the old way." "If I don't 'keep up,' I will be 'left behind,'" Backes said. "And keeping up with AI is virtually impossible." Not everyone feels diminished by the shift, though. Simon Willison, founder of the Datasette open-source project, said AI coding tools have made his work "a lot more fulfilling" by allowing him to take on projects that once might have required a small team. Willison said that being his own manager shields him from many of the pressures facing employed developers, though he still finds the pace of AI releases exhausting. "As an entrepreneur and product developer, I know that any space I operate in will be significantly more competitive now because the cost of developing software has dropped so much," he said. Still, Willison said he was optimistic about his career. "Using coding agents well is a deep skill," he said, one that requires both software-engineering knowledge and experience with the agents, "and I have both." Developers are using AI but want control Despite many using AI coding tools extensively, developers don't necessarily trust their output. The survey found that under 10% of respondents said they were prepared to trust AI for important decisions, while almost 80% said source attribution was important or very important when evaluating AI-generated code or technical answers. Prashanth Chandrasekar, Stack Overflow's CEO, said developers' skepticism was becoming a "critical safeguard" as agents took on more work. "Trust is not a given when it comes to developers," he said. "It is earned through transparency, source attribution, and rich technical context." Read the original article on Business Insider

JioHotstar , the streaming platform with more than 500 million monthly active users backed by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries, is expanding into the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) through Starzplay, one of the region’s largest streaming services. The new overseas push comes after its debut in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore. Under the partnership announced Tuesday, JioHotstar will have a dedicated section in Starzplay’s app and on its website, offering Indian films, TV shows, originals, and reality franchises across multiple languages. This is different from JioHotstar’s September launch in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore, where it replaced Hotstar and debuted as a stand-alone streaming service. The expansion is part of Reliance’s push to build JioHotstar into a global streaming platform after establishing a massive audience in India. MENA has one of the world’s largest South Asian diaspora communities, giving JioHotstar a sizable potential audience for its Indian films, television shows, and original programming. As with its earlier debut in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore, JioHotstar’s own sports offering in India will not be available in MENA. However, a plan bundling JioHotstar with Starzplay’s sports offering, including cricket, is priced at AED 49.99 (about $13.60) a month. JioHotstar is also available through Starzplay’s Plus monthly plan at AED 34.99 (around $9.50). With MENA’s large Indian diaspora in focus, new JioHotstar originals will premiere in the region simultaneously with their release in India, with audio available in up to 10 languages. The catalog spans Hindi, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, and Bangla, among other languages, and includes shows such as “Bigg Boss” and “Koffee with Karan.” Additionally, JioHotstar is putting particular emphasis on Malayalam programming, given the large Malayali population in the region. JioHotstar was created after Reliance and Disney merged their Indian media businesses into an $8.5 billion joint venture in 2024. The service, which combined JioCinema and Disney+ Hotstar , launched in India in February last year. Before JioHotstar’s launch, Hotstar was available in MENA. Disney Star expanded its distribution deal with evision, e&’s media and entertainment arm, in 2024, making it the regional home of Hotstar Specials. Evision is also a major shareholder in Starzplay, where JioHotstar will now have its first dedicated streaming presence in the region. Starzplay counts more than 2.3 million subscribers and has built a sizable South Asian audience in part through its cricket offering. Financial terms of the partnership were not disclosed. events.title: French riot police fire tear gas as more than 250,000 rally nationwide for school funding
events.summary: More than a quarter of a million people have marched in cities across France in support of school pupils demanding more education funding, increasing pressure on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron PARIS -- Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support school pupils demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron . As pupils again blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron’s nearly decade-long tenure. “We need to listen to them,” said Léa Monimart, a demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. “They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It’s important to show that there are adults who support them.” The Interior Ministry estimated that 256,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square during a largely peaceful march through the city. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students’ concerns and find solutions. Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced “ultra violence” threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any “accidents” would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a “lie.” More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,100 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign . Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make “any sense to hit minors.” “Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas,” said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests. The violence is “absolutely unbearable,” Le Coq said. Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers’ riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured. The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties , such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war , to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term. At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade. Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry. Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see. events.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return
events.summary: More than 4,000 people have died in the worst outbreak in the DR Congo’s history, with confirmed cases surpassing 8,300. Kenya has confirmed its ‌‌first Ebola case after the death of a Kenyan national in Nairobi, who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The patient, who had lived in the DRC for seven years, had been ill for about a month before travelling by road from the DRC to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, and then flying to ⁠⁠Nairobi on Saturday, Aden Duale, Kenya’s health secretary, told a news conference on Tuesday. list 1 of 3 Ebola cases surpass 8,000 as DRC struggles to control outbreak list 2 of 3 Mourners bury DR Congo official killed after defending Ebola response list 3 of 3 DR Congo begins Ebola vaccination trials for frontline health workers Seeking to halt local transmission, Kenya’s President William Ruto said at least eight family members of the victim and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined, as he ordered an enhanced response to contain the virus in the country. Earlier, Health Secretary Duale said 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight from Uganda were being traced. Patrick Amoth, director-general of the Kenyan Ministry of Health, said the contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released if they test negative for the virus. Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but was declared Ebola-free in August. The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15. The outbreak has claimed more than 4,000 lives, according to figures released by the government on Friday, and confirmed cases have ⁠⁠reached 8,300 across seven provinces, making it the worst Ebola epidemic in the country’s history . The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “ far from over ” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. At the same time, the United Nations organisation has advised against imposing travel and trade restrictions on Kenya, DRC and Uganda following the Ebola-related death in Kenya.

events.title: Djokovic wins China Open after de Minaur retires, Alcaraz wins Japan Open
events.summary: Novac Djokovic won 102nd match of his career, while ATP 500 tournament victory was Carlos Alcaraz’s third of the year. Novak Djokovic won the China Open after his opponent Alex de Minaur retired from the final with injury, while Spaniard Carlos Alcaraz retained his Japan Open crown to continue his resurgence after a lengthy wrist injury layoff. The 39-year-old Serbian won the first set in the tie-break 7-6 (7-3) and was down a game in the second set when the Australian ended the match with retirement on Tuesday. list 1 of 4 Gauff hits back at ‘insane’ racist abuse after replayed point at China Open list 2 of 4 Tennis: World number one Sinner will not play in 2026 due to knee injury list 3 of 4 Sabalenka, Rybakina handed shock defeats at China Open tennis list 4 of 4 Asian Games: Alex Eala out of gold medal contention after semifinal loss Djokovic extended an astonishing unbeaten streak in Beijing and winning the 102nd title of his career. De Minaur left the court for a medical timeout after losing the first-set tie break but played on with his left thigh heavily bandaged. However, he had to stop after winning the first game of the second set, leaving him trailing 7-6(3) 0-1. “I don’t feel great … I want to say sorry to all the amazing fans,” de Minaur said at the trophy presentation. “I didn’t want to finish like this … hopefully see you next year,” added the 27-year-old fifth seed. Alcaraz made another slow start before cruising past unseeded Czech Jiri Lehecka 7-6(4) 6-4 in the Japan Open final on Tuesday. The ATP 500 tournament victory is Alcaraz’s third of the year after the Australian Open and Qatar Open, before the 23-year-old was sidelined by an injury for nearly five months and returned at the US Open in late August. “I’m really happy to be able to lift a trophy again,” Alcaraz said. “It’s been a while and obviously it’s extra special after my injury and my comeback, in the second tournament that I’m playing. “It was a really tough week and I didn’t play my best tennis and my best level but I did find good solutions and that’s what matters in the end.” Alcaraz became the first man to go back-to-back in Tokyo since American Pete Sampras won the men’s title in both 1993 and 1994. The world number three started shakily, dropping serve in the first game, but soon recovered and dialled up the intensity to break world number 19 Lehecka’s serve with a scorching backhand to level at 3-3. More uncharacteristic errors from Alcaraz gave Lehecka hope in the tiebreak, but the Spaniard unleashed a sublime drop-shot en route to clinching the opening set to lay the platform for his 27th title overall. The seven-time Grand Slam champion took control midway through the second set, breaking to claim a 4-3 lead before sealing victory by forcing an error on match point and then celebrating wildly with his team courtside. Alcaraz said his triumph helped erase the doubts that he faced during his injury break. “A lot of negative thoughts come to your mind,” Alcaraz added: “If you’re going to come back healthy, if you’re going to come back the same as you were before, if I will be able to hit the ball normally without pain. I trusted myself and it worked out.” Alcaraz will return to action at the Shanghai Masters where he will take on Argentina’s Juan Manuel Cerundolo or a qualifier first. The main draw of the ATP 1000 event begins on Wednesday.

events.title: What would it take for the Yemen offensive to succeed?
events.summary: Territorial gains alone will not be enough to change the trajectory of the war. Two days after the announced counter-offensive by the internationally recognised Yemeni government, the operation named Dawn of Yemen has already made significant advances. Its forces recaptured territory from the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, along the Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. The Saudi-led coalition backing the government has deployed 100 fighter jets, flying round-the-clock to help secure the strait. In response, the Houthis have claimed attacks on Saudi territory. This is the most consequential escalation in the Yemen war since the UN-brokered truce of 2022. For four years, the war was managed as a frozen conflict. Now, both sides are trying to redraw the map. In the coming days, the success of the offensive will be determined not only by gains along three different fronts, but also by the ability of the forces loyal to the Yemeni government to maintain cohesion and force the Houthis to change their cost of conflict calculus. The western coast is where the campaign will be won or lost, and the reason lies beyond Yemen. With Iran disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea has become the Gulf’s strategic lifeline. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline to Yanbu is its main route around Hormuz, yet crude shipped from Yanbu to Asian markets must still pass through Bab al-Mandeb. A Houthi grip on the strait’s Yemeni shore turns that bypass into a hostage. The Arabian Peninsula would then be squeezed at both ends simultaneously, a scenario that no Gulf capital, and few oil importing economies, can tolerate for long. There is also a counterintuitive point here. The Houthis’ greatest gain of the year – the territories near Bab al-Mandeb – may also be their most exposed position. Their traditional strength lies in the mountains of the north, where terrain, tribal networks and short supply lines favour defence. The Tihama coast is the opposite: a flat plain, far from their highland base, with long and vulnerable supply routes and little cover from sustained airpower. If the government can win decisively anywhere, it is here. The immediate aim need not be to defeat the Houthis outright, but to push them back from the strait, retake the islands and deny them the ability to convert geography into regional leverage. The second decisive front is Taiz. The city is the hinge between the Houthi-held north, the government-held south and the western coastal theatre. If the Houthis keep the Aden road severed, any broader offensive is split in two. If government forces reopen it, they gain territorial continuity between Aden, Taiz and the coast. The third is Marib governorate, where fighting has escalated on the Raghwan front, and potentially al-Jawf. Despite sweeping rhetoric from the Yemeni government, an early march on Sanaa remains unlikely. The more plausible strategy is cumulative pressure: if the coast, Taiz and Marib are pressed at the same time, the Houthis will struggle to concentrate manpower, missiles, drones and logistics on any single axis. The government does not need breakthroughs everywhere; it needs to keep the Houthis overstretched. Support is not the problem, cohesion is The government has rarely lacked external backers. Its recurring failure has been converting that support into coherent Yemeni military power. Saudi Arabia remains decisive, and its incentives are now direct rather than abstract: Aramco facilities are under fire, Saudi-linked shipping has been declared a target and the main route circumventing the Strait of Hormuz is exposed. The commitment of 100 aircraft signals that Riyadh is willing to invest heavily. Airpower can destroy positions, cut supply lines and break concentrations of force, but it cannot hold territory. That requires Yemeni forces to fight under a unified chain of command, support functioning local administration and maintain political agreement that prevents infighting between factions. Here the anti-Houthi camp is arguably weaker than at any point in the war. The Southern Transitional Council, which launched its own offensive across the south in December 2025, was dissolved in January after a Saudi-backed counteroffensive, and its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, left the country. The southern units that fought under its banner remain armed and capable, but without a political roof, and their loyalty to the Yemeni government is conditional. Alongside them, Tareq Saleh’s National Resistance on the coast, the Southern Giants Brigades, and units aligned with the Islah Party in Taiz and Marib each answer to different leaderships, regional priorities and external patrons. The Houthis, by contrast, possess a centralised political and military command. This asymmetry is the offensive’s greatest vulnerability.

events.title: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
events.summary: Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also melt away the years. Drug giants Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their drugs age less quickly, according to readouts from molecular “aging clocks.” Such clocks assess a person’s biological age by looking at changes to DNA that accumulate with time, or, in newer versions, by tracking levels of key proteins. Both companies found that overweight or diabetic patients taking the drugs, called GLP-1s, had reduced biological age compared to those taking a placebo, although the difference varied widely, depending on which type of clock was used, and what organ was tested.  Overall, the difference was around “two to three years,” according to Nikolaj Roed, a global project leader at Novo, who says the company has been seeing “improved biological age in our patients across trials and across different tissues.”  The findings add to wide speculation among scientists that GLP-1 drugs, as they are known, are acting on basic causes of aging and might be a true longevity treatment. “Two years is a pretty strong effect, in my book,” says Steve Horvath, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who’s credited with inventing aging clocks . Horvath says the emerging data could provide “evidence that these GLP-1 drugs are actually what is known as geroprotectors, medications that slow or possibly even reverse biologic aging.” The companies shared their findings over the weekend during Aging Research & Drug Discovery, a conference devoted to seeking scientific remedies for old age. While that quest has not yet produced any clear-cut success, some scientists now think Novo’s drug semaglutide (sold under the names Ozempic and Wegovy) is coming close. “In an unhealthy population, I do think it’s an anti-aging drug,” says Vadim Gladyshev, a Harvard biologist who assisted Novo with its molecular measurements. “But in a healthy population, no one knows.” The drugs cause weight loss by stimulating a receptor, GLP-1, that tells your brain you’re not hungry. Yet real-world studies have shown much wider benefit. The drugs improve kidney function, reduce blood pressure, and even sharply cut the overall chance of death. “If the question is,‘Can semaglutide reach several diseases relevant to health span and aging?’ we know we can say the answer is yes,” said Alejandro Aguayo-Orozco, a senior scientific director at Novo, the Danish drug giant, during the meeting. The next question to answer, he said, is whether such effects are accompanied by changes to molecular measures of biological aging: “When you intervene with semaglutide, does it actually move the clocks in any direction? And the answer is yes.”  The company found that, over time, the drugs cause a wide slowdown in aging clocks—as much as 4 years in the case of a clock that looks at heart proteins. “I think it’s pretty clear that the organ age is shifting,” said Aguayo-Orozco. The studies are also a huge boost for the science of aging clocks. Although these measures reflect a person’s age, it’s been uncertain if they are useful as true biomarkers. Now clock makers have evidence  that their readouts show a drop in age when people take drugs with broad, well-demonstrated benefits.   “The clock people have been pushing for a decade to get this kind of study done,” says Yuge Ji, a biologist who previously worked in the field and now runs a startup, Reflector Bio. “It’s huge for them.” As part of its study, Novo took blood draws from 10,052 people, half on the drug and half on a placebo. Their blood, collected at the start of the study as well as months later, was then measured with “proteomic clocks,” which use levels of key proteins to predict a person’s age and risk of dying .  Scientists at Eli Lilly performed similar research on their GLP-1 drug, tirzepatide, using so-called “epigenetic” clocks that assess age by counting accumulated changes to DNA. Lilly’s study was smaller, but also found that for the most part, molecular time moved more slowly for people on the drug.   “All the clocks are telling a consistent story that we’re seeing a reduction in age,” Kevin Duffin, vice president for aging research at Lilly, said during the conference. “It’s not like we’re going to reverse age by 30 years or something, but it’s a significant reduction.” The molecules have become the best selling drugs in the world,, with Lilly’s tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for obesity, topping the list with more than $36 billion in revenue to the company last year . Novo’s semaglutide, also sold under more than one name, was a close second. Alex Zhavoronkov, the founder of Insilico Medicine, and the organizer of the Boston meeting, says that extending lives by even one year across the world’s population would be equal to tens of millions of lifetimes.   Last month Zhavoronkov showed that one of his company’s drugs, for a lung disease, also reversed the signals from aging clocks . That drug is experimental, but Zhavoronkov has sought to promote the idea that humanity is entering a new era of longevity medicines. He also disclosed during the event that he has been “microdosing” the available weight-loss drugs, even though he is not overweight. “I am on tirzepatide and I am an equal-opportunity injector of semaglutide as well,” Zhavoronkov said. It was part of an effort to directly raise the question of whether the first mass-market anti-aging remedy is already here. “Do you think a reasonable person should start taking semaglutide?” he asked Aguayo-Orozco, the Novo scientist, in front of a crowded audience. “I am not a physician. I cannot answer that question,” Aguayo-Orozco replied. Several people cautioned that GLP-1 drugs do have side effects, including muscle loss. That is one reason they might not help most people, says Horvath, who says he isn’t ready to take the drugs himself, although he’s thought about it. “Clearly, the drugs have many benefits in obese people, but I did not yet see sufficient evidence that they will benefit skinny people,” he said. “I guess we will have to wait.” Answers could start to emerge in a year or two. This past January, a US agency, ARPA-H, put $38 million toward a study in Texas that will attempt to determine whether semaglutide has anti-aging effects in healthy people over 60. That research will look at changes in cognition, mobility, and acuity of the senses. That project also seeks to help define a regulatory pathway for anti-aging drugs and to “build a new therapeutic industry” around longevity.

events.title: Norway proposes temporary ban on Meta glasses in public spaces
events.summary: The latest styles of Meta Ray-Bans won't be so popular in Norway if a temporary ban in certain public spaces goes into effect. Bloomberg/Getty Images Norway is proposing a temporary ban on camera glasses in certain public spaces. The proposed ban would be for places like beaches, daycares, and parks. The government plans on making a decision about regulation after more investigation. Correction, October 6, 2026 — This story has been corrected to reflect that Norway's legislation is in the proposal stage, and has yet to be passed. Bad news if you planned on capturing photos of the majestic fjords in your Meta Ray-Bans. Norway is proposing a temporary ban on camera glasses in public spaces like parks, schools, and beaches. The proposed ban wouldn't prohibit the sale of Meta glasses, and it only applies to their use in certain areas, like changing rooms or beaches. It also points to the need for extra privacy around places for children, like schools and daycares. Norway's Minister of Digitalization, Torgeir Micaelsen, expressed concern that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio recorded without their knowledge, according to a translated press release . Micaelsen just started as Minister of Digitalization in September, but his predecessor had started floating the idea of looking into regulation on Meta glasses in August. Representatives for Minister Micaelsen did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The proposed ban would need to be approved by Norway's legislative body. Meta's CTO, Andrew Bosworth, has said that only a few "bad actors" are responsible for disabling the glasses' LED indicator lights, which has given the glasses a bad reputation as "pervert glasses ". Meta recently rolled out a software update in which the camera won't work if the light is covered or  tampered with . The government also said it will form an expert group to investigate the challenges posed by wearable technology and provide advice on permanent regulation. Norway's move follows unease about camera glasses in other European countries. In the last few weeks, a debate about smart glasses has  been brewing in the Netherlands , following media reports and advocacy group concerns. An official from the country's data privacy group told Parliament they want to wait for findings from a broader European Union report on the matter before taking any action. Meanwhile, Hans Anders, a large eyewear retailer in the Netherlands and Belgium, has paused selling Meta glasses in its stores. "We're excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we're continuing to expand styles and features around the world," a Meta spokesperson told Business Insider in response to the Norway ban. "Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video," they said. " It can't be turned off, and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other cameras don't have." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: These 6 current US senators were born outside the country
events.summary: Ted Cruz (R-TX) is one of six US senators currently in office who were born outside the US. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images The US Senate comprises 100 senators, two from each state. US senators do not need to be natural-born citizens in order to take office. Six senators currently holding office were born outside the US. Unlike the president and vice president , US senators do not need to be natural-born citizens in order to take office. The US Senate , alongside the House of Representatives, is one of the two chambers of Congress. It comprises 100 senators, two from each state, who serve six-year terms with no term limits. To qualify as a US senator, a person must be: At least 30 years old A US citizen for at least nine years Live in the state they want to represent when they are elected Six current senators were born outside the US, bringing the total number throughout history to 74 , according to the US Senate Historical Office. Many were US citizens at birth despite being born in another country — for instance, because they were born to American parents working in government positions abroad. One of the best-known foreign-born senators who became a naturalized US citizen was former New York Sen. Robert Wagner. He was born in Germany and introduced and championed the Wagner Act, a landmark 1935 labor law that protects many private-sector workers' right to organize and bargain collectively. Here's a closer look at the six active senators born outside the US. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.) Sen. Michael Bennet, a Democrat representing Colorado, was born in New Delhi, India. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sen. Michael Bennet, a Democrat representing Colorado, was born in New Delhi while his father, Douglas Bennet, was working for the US State Department. He got US citizenship at birth. The family later moved back to the US, settling in Washington, DC, where Bennet would eventually graduate from Wesleyan University in Connecticut in 1987 and from Yale Law School in 1993. In the late '90s, Sen. Bennet moved to Denver to become a director of Anschutz Investment Company, where he guided businesses as they reorganized under bankruptcy orders and restructured debt. After working his way through Colorado's political sphere — he once was superintendent of Denver Public Schools — Bennet was appointed to the Senate in 2009 and won a special election for the seat in 2010. Sen. Bennet ran for president in 2020 and is known for writing legislation to train veterans in energy and cybersecurity fields, helping craft the 2014 and 2018 Farm Bills — the latter removed federal restrictions on hemp cultivation — and helping overhaul the No Child Left Behind law. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) Sen. Ted Cruz was born in Calgary, Canada. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Sen. Cruz was born in Calgary to a father from Cuba and a mother from Wilmington, Delaware, and grew up in Houston. He had Canadian and US citizenship at birth. He later earned his Bachelor of Arts from Princeton University in 1992 and his Juris Doctor from Harvard University in 1995. He advised George W. Bush's 2000 presidential campaign, held positions at the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department, and became Texas solicitor general in 2003. Sen. Cruz was elected to the Senate in 2012 and took office the following year. In 2014, he formally renounced his Canadian citizenship amid speculation about his eligibility to run for president , a race he lost in 2016. "Nothing against Canada," Sen. Cruz wrote in a statement at the time, "but I'm an American by birth, and as a US Senator, I believe I should be only an American." In 2018, Sen. Cruz helped pass a bipartisan bill that requires the review, declassification, and release of government records related to unsolved criminal civil rights cases. He also authored a measure in 2023 requiring the State Department to report on efforts by the Venezuelan government to detain US citizens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) Sen. Tammy Duckworth was born in Thailand, but graduated from high school in Hawaii. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Born in Bangkok to an American father and a Thai mother, Sen. Duckworth had US citizenship at birth. Her father served in the US military and later worked for the United Nations, so the family moved frequently throughout Southeast Asia before settling in Hawaii. Sen. Duckworth graduated from the University of Hawaii in 1989 and earned a master's degree from George Washington University in 1992. While serving in Iraq for the Army National Guard, Sen. Duckworth 's Black Hawk helicopter was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade, which resulted in her losing both legs and partial use of one arm. She received a Purple Heart and continued serving in the Guard until 2014, ultimately reaching the rank of lieutenant colonel. She was elected to the House in 2012 and to the Senate in 2016. Sen. Duckworth is known for her work on veterans' issues, disability access, and family policy. Her Friendly Airports for Mothers Act, which requires certain airports to provide private lactation rooms, became law in 2018. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) Sen. Mazie Hirono was born in Japan. Like Sen. Duckworth, she also graduated from high school in Hawaii. Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Student Borrower Protection Center Sen. Hirono was born in Fukushima, Japan, and moved to the US when she was nearly 8, knowing no English. Sen. Hirono is a naturalized citizen. She grew up in Hawaii and graduated from the University of Hawaii in 1970. She graduated from Georgetown University in 1978, moved back to Hawaii, and worked in the state attorney general's antitrust division afterward. During her time in the Hawaii House of Representatives, she focused on consumer and worker protections. She unsuccessfully ran for governor in 2002, but was elected to the US House in 2006 and won her Senate seat in 2012. In Congress, Sen. Hirono has focused especially on advocacy for civil rights, veterans, education, environmental protection, and Hawaii's tourism economy. In 2022, she authored acts to protect coral reefs, help reunite Korean War-separated families, and establish a Veterans Affairs advisory committee for veterans in US territories and freely associated states. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) Sen. Bernie Moreno was born in Colombia and graduated from the University of Michigan in 1989. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sen. Bernie Moreno, born in Bogotá, Colombia, moved to the US at age 5. He is a naturalized citizen. He earned a business degree from the University of Michigan in 1989. After graduating, he worked at General Motors and, by his mid-20s, became a general manager at an automotive dealership group. In 2005, Sen. Moreno bought a car dealership near Cleveland and expanded it into the Collection Auto Group, a network of luxury dealerships. He later turned to technology, cofounding Champ Titles, a company that digitizes vehicle-title transfers. He assumed office in 2025, becoming the first Latino to represent Ohio in the chamber.
