events.title: Birzeit University memorial destruction aims to crush Palestinian memory
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Israeli soldiers removed the monument to students and alumni killed by Israel and replaced it with a fig sapling. After Israeli soldiers stormed Birzeit University near Ramallah to demolish a stone memorial dedicated to dead students, Rania Washaha, 47, felt the pain of bereavement again. Her brother, Fadi, 34, was shot in the head by an Israeli soldier near the northern entrance to el-Bireh in the central West Bank in May 2021. list 1 of 4 How reconstruction became Israel’s new weapon of ‘silent transfer’ in Gaza list 2 of 4 Birzeit University raid seen as warning against Palestinian defiance list 3 of 4 Israeli assault on Palestinian university wounds dozens in West Bank raid list 4 of 4 Israeli forces raid Birzeit University in the occupied West Bank His name was among the 38 students from the university killed by Israel and listed on the stone pillar known as the Martyrs’ Monument. Israeli soldiers raided the university campus at dawn on Monday, accompanied by 10 military vehicles. A bulldozer demolished the pillar, and soldiers took away the marble stone. In its place, the Israelis left a planter containing a fig sapling, bearing the inscription: “Water it twice.” This raid marks the fifth Israeli incursion into the campus since the beginning of 2026 and the 28th since 2002. Birzeit University’s administration condemned the recent raid, describing the destruction of the Martyrs’ Monument as a violation of international law and an attack on education and national memory. “Bulldozers won’t erase the memory of the martyrs, military vehicles won’t extinguish the light of knowledge, and these assaults won’t break the university’s resolve to pursue its academic and national mission,” a statement by the university pledged. It came 10 days after another incursion by Israeli forces during the daytime, a day before the start of the new fall semester. Nardeen al-Memi, the university’s public relations and media officer, told Al Jazeera in the brief minutes of their incursion, Israeli soldiers approached the monument for the first time and photographed it. The Martyrs’ Monument was erected between 1994 and 1996, bearing the names of students and alumni at Birzeit killed by Israeli forces. The list starts with Sharaf al-Tayyibi, who was shot dead by Israeli forces on the campus in 1984. The names of other students and alumni were added during the years that followed. “The last name inscribed on the monument was that of student Omar al-Naasan, whom soldiers killed in al-Mughayyir east of Ramallah on September 2 while he was confronting settler incursions,” said Nardeen. “Days after his death, his father came and personally wrote his son’s name on the monument.” University students organised a protest at the site of the destroyed memorial on Tuesday afternoon, most viewing it as an Israeli attempt to intimidate them. Sami Adel, a Birzeit student who wanted to use a pseudonym due to his fear of being detained, told Al Jazeera the memorial holds a place in the heart of everyone who has attended the university since the 1990s. In recent years, Israel has tried to suppress any student activity dedicated to commemorating the martyrs, he said. “Soldiers detained me for several hours three weeks ago and threatened that if I participated in any political student activity on campus, I would face a long and harsh detention,” he added. The removal of the memorial is part of a broader Israeli policy targeting memorials dedicated to Palestinians killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank. The Israeli far-right has made the issue part of its campaign to erase markers of Palestinian identity. Zvi Sukkot, a member of the Knesset from the Religious Zionism Party, destroyed one such memorial in the village of Madama, south of Nablus, with a sledgehammer in August. The Israeli military later said that it routinely removes “symbols of incitement”. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich submitted a list of approximately 40 Palestinian memorials, proposing their destruction, to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. There has been a wider targeting of civic and cultural symbols across the West Bank, particularly in Jenin, by Israeli authorities. “Jenin Horse”, a monument constructed from the wreckage left behind by an Israeli incursion into the city, was removed. A memorial dedicated to Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh in Jenin was also targeted in 2023. A cemetery containing the bodies of Iraqi soldiers killed during the 1948 war, also located in Jenin, has been raided by Israelis from illegal settlements. Other landmarks embedded in the city’s collective memory, including the “Watermelon Roundabout”, have also been targeted. Israel’s targeting of Palestine’s collective memory has coincided with a wider campaign of suppression in the occupied West Bank.

events.title: Paramount completes Warner Bros merger in historic media deal to create Skydance
events.summary: Paramount Skydance closed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery on Tuesday, completing one of the biggest media mergers of all time after engaging in a bruising battle for control with Netflix and fending off antitrust lawsuits. The new company, which is to be called Skydance, combines two of the five largest Hollywood film studios, covering major franchises such as Harry Potter and Mission Impossible. It will be home to dozens of TV networks, from CBS to TNT, and two major subscription streaming services, Paramount+ and HBO Max. David Ellison, who completed the merger of his Skydance Media film production company with Paramount in 2025, has become one of Hollywood’s biggest moguls. He appointed Ynon Kreiz, formerly chief executive of Mattel, to share oversight of Skydance as co-chief executive. Mr Kreiz will manage day-to-day operations, while Mr Ellison maintains the creative vision and handles relationships with talent. “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Mr Ellison said in a statement. After pulling off two mega-mergers of century-old Hollywood companies in little more than a year, he now faces the significant challenge of making it all work . That means eliminating overlapping businesses and jobs without fanning the ire of Hollywood, which is suffering through a downturn and has opposed the consolidation from the start. Skydance also will need to manage nearly $80 billion in debt while adhering to a strict calendar of theatrical releases as stipulated by the lawsuit settlement. The path to closing the merger was often rocky and at times seemed likely to derail the endeavour. But Mr Ellison deemed the deal to be essential if he was to compete with the likes of Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Apple. “They’re starting off at a great place,” Michael Wolf, chief executive of management consulting firm Activate Strategy, told Bloomberg TV on Monday. “The logic makes sense. Scale puts them in the right position. Now they have to deliver against scale.” Paramount agreed to acquire Warner Bros in February after a months-long bidding war against Netflix, which had previously committed to purchasing Warner Bros’ studios and streaming business, but not its cable channels. Mr Ellison clinched the deal by sweetening the offer price and bringing his father, Larry Ellison, in to personally guarantee funding. Paramount paid a $2.8 billion break-up fee to Netflix on behalf of Warner Bros and said it would be able to close its own deal quickly, promising to pay fees to Warner Bros' shareholders of $7 million a day if the deal was not finalised by September 30. While Paramount managed to secure antitrust approval from the US Department of Justice, the EU and other jurisdictions, it was delayed by a pair of lawsuits brought by 12 states and the Writers Guild of America, which were concerned about the threat of higher prices for consumers and fewer jobs. Thousands of actors, directors, writers and producers signed a letter protesting against the deal. Much of that fear stemmed from Paramount’s pledge to extract more than $6 billion in annual synergies within three years of closing the merger. Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners, a Paramount investor, said there were other ways to cut costs and operate more efficiently than reducing jobs. A company would not spend billions of dollars a year making movies “and figure your entire premise of your business plan is to fire everybody in Hollywood", he said at the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last week. “It’s just the opposite.” Heavy debts Skydance’s debt load will continue to weigh on the company, however. Its interest bills are much higher now than if it had issued debt just a few months earlier, since inflation concerns have lifted global borrowing costs. Paramount sold $52 billion of loans and bonds in only a week, a tight timeline for any debt deal – particularly for one of the largest financings in recent history. As part of a negotiated settlement with the states, whose case was led by California's attorney general Rob Bonta, Paramount vowed to release at least 30 films a year in theatres and keep them there for 45 days, before making them available for viewing at home. The company also agreed to create an editorial independence board for its news organisations, CBS and CNN, an effort to address concerns that the Ellison family’s close ties with US President Donald Trump would cause them to try to influence coverage. Mr Ellison has so far agreed to keep CBS and CNN separate and under different leadership. In announcing a new executive team on Monday, he said CNN chief executive Mark Thompson would remain in his role and Bari Weiss would keep her title as editor-in-chief of CBS News. While acknowledging “trepidations about this moment", Mr Thompson said in a letter to staff that he had “real confidence” that the Skydance leadership understood “and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for". Dana Goldberg, a long-time Skydance Media executive who developed and produced films including Top Gun: Maverick , and Josh Greenstein, a former president of Sony Pictures’ Motion Picture Group, will jointly oversee the new Skydance Motion Picture Group. James Gunn and Peter Safran, the co-chiefs of DC Studios, will continue in their roles at Skydance. Casey Bloys, who has ushered in hits for HBO including Game of Thrones spin-off House of the Dragon , will be in charge of Skydance’s streaming division, overseeing HBO Max and Paramount+ programming. George Cheeks, who joined Paramount in 2020, is to manage a newly formed TV division, encompassing a mix of Paramount and Warner Bros studios, networks, sports and cable brands. JB Perrette, who led the global introduction of the HBO Max streaming service at Warner Bros, will work as co-chairman and chief business officer of Skydance TV and Skydance streaming. While Mr Kreiz’s appointment came as a surprise to many on Wall Street, his experience complements Mr Ellison’s, bringing years of oversight of a large public company and more than three decades in entertainment. During his tenure at Mattel, Mr Kreiz was instrumental in pushing the toy company to capitalise on its beloved brands, such as Barbie and Hot Wheels, turning them into franchises that could span movies, TV and games. One executive who will not be part of the new team at Skydance is David Zaslav. The president and chief executive of Warner Bros is to take his leave along with potentially more than $667 million in cash severance and stock awards triggered by the sale.

The file types are .msix and .msixbundle , used for Windows application packages and bundles. The change affects New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the Web in Exchange Online . By default, users of the affected clients will no longer be able to download or open attachments with these extensions, which is no bad thing because blindly installing a malicious .msix package could compromise a device. That said, although Microsoft noted that the file types were "infrequently used," there are legitimate reasons for their presence in emails. Administrators who need to permit these attachments can add the extensions to the AllowedFileTypes property of the relevant OwaMailboxPolicy before the rollout, scheduled for early to mid-November 2026. "This update is part of our ongoing efforts to strengthen security and help protect organizations from potentially unsafe file attachments," Microsoft said. The Windows giant's application packaging system has come under fire over the years. Microsoft disabled the ms-appinstaller protocol handler by default in December 2023 after attackers abused it to distribute malware. The attachment block adds another layer of protection, unless administrators explicitly allow these file types. Other file types blocked by Outlook on the Web include .py Python files, .ps1 PowerShell files, and .cab files. It's a little surprising that it has taken until now for .msix and .msixbundle to be added to the list, considering the havoc malicious packages can wreak on a system. Renaming an attachment's extension or sending a download link may get around the attachment restriction, but neither makes the package safe. events.title: As a Florida native, I skip Tampa's crowded beaches for this beautiful, lesser-visited spot
events.summary: In my experience, Tarpon Springs is often more peaceful and less crowded than hot spots like Tampa. Ruth Peterkin/Getty Images As a Florida local, I like to ditch the crowded, popular beaches and head to Tarpon Springs . This town is a Greek enclave with tons of culture, charm, and a European feel — and amazing food. Fred Howard Park has gorgeous beaches and tons of space to sprawl out with loved ones. Growing up in Tampa, I learned early that getting to my area's most famous beaches isn't always as easy as it looks. Clearwater and St. Pete Beach are undeniably gorgeous, but by mid-morning on a weekend, the parking lots are full, and the sand is packed with umbrellas — and then, the traffic getting home takes hours. So these days, when I want salt air and sunshine without the shoulder-to-shoulder crowds, I drive my car to a place that feels like a well-kept secret hiding in plain sight. Tarpon Springs is a Greek enclave on the Gulf Coast Tarpon Springs is known as the sponge capital of the world. ©fitopardo/Getty Images Known as the "sponge capital of the world," Tarpon Springs sits about 30 minutes north of Clearwater on Florida's Gulf Coast , or 20 minutes from my family's home in northern Tampa. The beach is special, but so are the layers of history and culture wrapped around it. In the early 1900s, Greek immigrants arrived to work in the sponge-diving industry, and their legacy still shapes the town's food, architecture, and rhythm today. Walking around feels less like you're in Florida, and more like you're stepping into a little corner of the Mediterranean. I always start at the sponge docks. The working waterfront is lined with boats, and vendors still sell natural sponges pulled straight from the Gulf. It's part market, part living museum. From there, I wander into the Greektown Historic District, filled with delicious food options. This is where I've eaten some of the most authentic Greek cooking I've found anywhere in the state: flaky spanakopita, thick Greek coffee, and fresh, crunchy Greek salad. The beaches can feel calm, beautiful, and relatively uncrowded I head to Fred Howard Park every time I visit Tarpon Springs. baluzek/Getty Images When I'm ready to jump in some cool water, I head to Fred Howard Park. This is my favorite part of visiting. The park connects the mainland to a small barrier island, and the water here is calm, clear, and blissfully uncrowded compared to the bigger-name beaches down the coast. I like to rent a kayak or paddleboard to explore the inlet coves, drifting past mangroves and spotting the occasional dolphin or heron in the water. Whenever I'm paddling, it's easy to forget how close I am to a major metro area. On the island, I love the scenic, mile-long Fred Howard Causeway, which links the mainland to the beach. You can walk it, bike it, or drive it slowly with the windows down, and the water stretches out on both sides the entire way. The park is the perfect place to unwind My family always tries to stay late enough to catch the sunset. Anika Nayak Fred Howard Park is family-friendly and the perfect place to spend some quality time with loved ones. On the mainland side, kids can play at the two playgrounds or spread out on the open softball and ball field. When I go with my family, we usually claim a shady picnic spot, unpack a spread of food, and settle in for the afternoon. My favorite tradition is staying late enough to watch the sunset. There's a stretch where the sky turns orange and pink over the Gulf, the temperature gets a little cooler, and the whole place feels like it belongs to just us. Tampa's headline beaches will always draw in crowds, and I understand the appeal. But when I want beauty, history, great food, and room to breathe all in one trip, Tarpon Springs wins every time. events.title: Retired Warren Buffett now spends his evenings glued to YouTube—watching Glenn Close clips, 1950s commercials, and Uzbekistani talent shows
events.summary: After stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway last month, 96-year-old Warren Buffett has officially entered his retirement years. But instead of spending his evenings at the beach or traveling the world, Buffett’s nights can look surprisingly familiar: sitting in front of the television, watching YouTube. “Warren’s range is broad,” Sharon Osberg, one of Buffett’s closest friends who often visits and watches with him, told the Wall Street Journal . “It can be the silliest things.” But Buffett isn’t spending his nights scrolling through AI slop on YouTube Shorts or watching clips of CNBC, either. His viewing tastes are decidedly more eclectic: clips featuring Glenn Close, a documentary about attorney Roy Cohn, commercials from the 1950s, and Uzbekistan’s version of America’s Got Talent . It’s a hobby Buffett, who has a net worth of $143 billion, appears to have embraced even before stepping away from Berkshire. He handed the CEO reins to Greg Abel in January and chairmanship to his son Howard in September. But even while he was still running the over $1 trillion conglomerate, his evenings were largely his own.  Buffett has long made time for hobbies—he used to spend 8 hours a week playing bridge, including with Bill Gates Buffett’s YouTube habits are especially notable considering he has long been known for his reluctance to embrace technology. Even as a longtime Apple investor, he waited until his late eighties to swap his flip phone for an iPhone . But what isn’t unusual about Buffett is his reluctance to spend every waking hour thinking about business. Reading books and newspapers, for example, has long been one of his favorite pastimes. At one point, he said he spent as much as 80% of his working day reading. “Read 500 pages like this every day,” he said . “That’s how knowledge works. It builds up, like compound interest. All of you can do it, but I guarantee not many of you will do it.” And when he wanted to put business aside completely, he’d often pick up a deck of cards and play bridge —including with his former longtime friend Bill Gates . Buffett played as many as eight hours a week. Buffett played bridge with Bill Gates in 2015 at Berkshire Hathaway’s annual shareholders meeting. Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images “I play a lot,” Buffett told the Washington Post in a 2017 interview. “At least four sessions a week, about two hours a session.” The card game, he said at the time, kept him on his toes. “You can play a hand every six or seven minutes every day for the rest of your life, and you will never see the same hand,” Buffett said. “It’s a game you can enjoy when you are in your nineties, and you are seeing a different intellectual challenge every seven minutes.” Buffett found work-life balance later in life. Gen Z want it now The desire to step away from work from time to time—but still be successful—is a balance many young people are trying to figure out much earlier in their careers. For Gen Z, that means putting work-life balance ahead of the traditional markers of career success. According to a 2025 report from Randstad , Gen Z workers ranked work-life balance as a higher consideration than salary when evaluating their current or future jobs. Buffett became a millionaire at 32 . And his advice to young people who want to emulate his success is simple: Find a career that feels less like a chore, and more like a hobby that you’re working on every day. “I tell the students, look for the job that you would take if you didn’t need a job,” Buffett told PBS in 2017. “I mean, it’s that simple.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Photos: School blockades, street protests grip France
events.summary: Protesters increased pressure on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron demanding more education funding. Tens of thousands have taken to the streets across France as unions and teachers joined high school students who, for days, have been demanding better learning conditions in protests punctuated by violent confrontations. The French Ministry of the Interior said 86,000 people had already joined demonstrations across the country early on Tuesday, while the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) union put the figure at 260,000. Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings unable to cope with rising temperatures. While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police. Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds. The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement. Unions, rights groups and students have accused the authorities of using disproportionate force. A 15-year-old lost a hand to a stun grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Monday. Police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests began, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late on Monday. Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the Ministry of Education. More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been arrested. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said 85 members of teaching staff have also been injured. The government is also pushing legislation to make those responsible for damaging public property pay for repairs themselves, instead of using public funds.

events.title: Bulgaria searches for missing crew after drones hit two ships in Black Sea
events.summary: Bulgaria launches search operation after Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sinks at scene of attack. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev says drones have hit two commercial vessels, sinking one ship and wounding several people, in what he denounced as an “absolutely unacceptable” attack. Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Radev said the ships were attacked by sea drones and aerial drones at about 3am (00:00 GMT), about 70 nautical miles (130km) off Bulgaria’s coast, amid a rise in attacks on Black Sea shipping due to expanding drone attacks related to the Russia-Ukraine war. list 1 of 4 Why has Putin added 15,000 new soldiers to Russia’s army? list 2 of 4 Ukraine calls for tighter sanctions as Russian attacks spark Kyiv gridlock list 3 of 4 Russia’s ‘new doctrine’ targets civilian sites in Ukraine, Zelenskyy says list 4 of 4 Ukraine says Russian drone attack sinks ship in Romanian waters “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law,” Radev said. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan suffered critical structural damage and sank at the scene. There was no immediate word on the crew’s fate, he said, as Bulgarian authorities launched a major search for the missing crew. Radev did not specify how many people were missing. The second vessel, the Palau-flagged Able, caught fire after the attack. A Bulgarian ferry and a naval fast boat evacuated all 18 crew members. Two sailors suffered serious injuries and were flown to a hospital in the port city of Varna, Radev said. The Able was reportedly carrying wheat and sailing south, while the Alfa Watan was heading north. The Alfa Watan’s cargo was unknown, Radev said, adding that authorities were monitoring for possible oil spills and other signs of environmental pollution. The origin of the drones was not immediately established, but the dual strike came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one and leaving one missing, in what Ukraine said was a drone attack launched by Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described that attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters. “What is happening is seriously disrupting shipping in the Black Sea, driving up insurance costs even further and making shipping extremely difficult,” Radev said after an emergency meeting on Tuesday. Black Sea shipping has been heavily affected by the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months, and Radev warned that the war was expanding geographically and increasing the risk of global conflict. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said Budapest “stands in full solidarity with Bulgaria” after the attack on the two ships.

events.title: El Niño comes to Ukraine’s aid
events.summary: Tim’s view As Russia again ramps up its attacks on Ukraine’s electricity grid ahead of the winter heating season, this time Kyiv has a new ally in its corner: El Niño. Last week, 8,000 households around Ukraine temporarily went dark after the Kremlin’s first large-scale grid attack since last winter. It was a disheartening preview of things to come: Just seven months ago, Ukrainians emerged from their harshest winter since the full-scale invasion, when relentless bombardment of energy plants and substations left many with no heat and few hours of daily power access for weeks at a time. This week, Russia’s Defense Ministry made clear that more of the same is coming following a record campaign of strikes by Ukraine’s long-distance drones against Russian oil refineries in the past two months, which according to Kyiv have now taken out more than half of Russia’s refining capacity . Ukraine has good reason to be worried: Moscow’s offensive position in the air war has improved since this time last year , with the deployment of jet-powered drones and a gaping deficit in Ukraine’s missile defense supplies. But a number of factors are working in Ukraine’s favor. Western aid for rebuilding the energy sector continues to flow in; some $250 million in energy hardware is expected for delivery between now and February, according to European officials. Ukraine is entering the winter with a natural gas surplus it didn’t have a year ago, and with a much higher share of its critical energy assets ensconced behind protective concrete barriers that are surprisingly effective at blunting damage from all but direct missile hits. More utility-scale renewables are online, and people and businesses across Ukrainian society have learned from successive bleak winters how to muddle through with batteries, generators, blankets, and candles. Finally, and perhaps decisively, there’s the weather. Last year’s winter in Ukraine was the coldest in decades. That’s the factor that turns a blackout from an inconvenience to a deadly threat. This year, however, an exceptionally strong and possibly even record-breaking El Niño weather pattern — driven by warm ocean surface temperatures in the Pacific — is expected to make for a warm and wet winter in Europe. That’s good news for the EU, which is staring down a gas shortage. It could be problematic for Russia, which will also likely be warm but will be exposed to above-average food and fuel import prices . For Ukraine, it’s an asset. But I’m still looking for an apartment with a working fireplace. Notable German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced another €1 billion in military aid to Ukraine during a visit to Kyiv, and €350 million for repairs for the energy sector .

events.title: Bluesky wants to give you your own domain on the open web
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider teased long-term plans on Monday when he shared that the company has applied to make “.bsky” an internet domain suffix, like .com or .org. If approved, users will be able to turn their longer social handles into shorter, cleaner domain names. For instance, instead of @sarahp.bsky.social , my handle could one day become just “sarahp.bsky.” That could leave Bluesky room to innovate around user profiles, turning them from a simple page that houses someone’s bio and their posts into a more comprehensive personal home page that establishes someone’s online presence. Bluesky’s application hasn’t been approved yet. Schneider said that ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers), the nonprofit that oversees domain names for the internet, will publish the applications for the new domains on October 7, 2026, and Bluesky’s request will be among them. It’ll take 18 to 24 months for the process to be completed. Reached for comment, Bluesky said it hasn’t finalized how .bsky domains would be requested, registered, or distributed, but the company did say it had no plans to either sell or monetize the domains. That’s a notable decision given that domain registration can be a profitable business that could serve as a potential revenue stream for a startup that has raised significant funds but isn’t ( yet? ) generating ad revenue. However, Bluesky says selling domains goes against its belief in an open web. “Domains are a big part of the open web, as they allow users to control their own online identity,” said Rose Wang, Bluesky’s COO, in a comment shared with TechCrunch. “Bluesky was built on the belief that you should own your presence online, not rent it from a platform that can take it away.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon announced on Tuesday that Prime Video will be the new home for the Emmy Awards, marking another major Hollywood awards show’s move from broadcast television to streaming. This will also be the first time that the ceremony has had a dedicated home, as the show rotated across broadcasters like ABC, CBS, Fox, and NBC over the past seven decades. Prime Video will stream the awards show worldwide for six years for free, starting in 2027, where it will go live in over 240 countries and territories. Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will also be able to watch the awards show on the Prime Video platform. The terms of the deal were not disclosed. The move comes as the Emmys face potential viewership declines, as more of its audience moves to streaming services. This year’s ratings for the 78th primetime Emmy Awards on NBC were down nearly 10% from the year prior, after a couple of years of growth, the AP reported . However, the telecast’s 6.87 million viewers this year were higher than its all-time low of 4.3 million in January 2024. The Emmys aren’t the only major awards show making the shift to streaming. Last year, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal giving YouTube the rights to stream the Oscars beginning in 2029, while Netflix has streamed the Screen Actors Guild Awards since 2024. events.title: 'We did it!': Read David Ellison's memo to employees after Paramount's WBD deal closed
events.summary: David Ellison is CEO of Skydance after Paramount merged with Warner Bros. Discovery. Paul Morigi/Getty Images; David Becker/Getty Images for CinemaCon Skydance CEO David Ellison sent employees a memo after closing Paramount's WBD deal. "We did it!" Ellison told staffers, before adding his four top priorities for the new company. Read Ellison's full memo to Skydance employees below. David Ellison is taking a victory lap after completing Paramount's merger with Warner Bros. Discovery , a $110 billion deal that formed the new-look Skydance and will transform Hollywood. "It has taken hard work, perseverance and commitment with many challenges along the way — but we did it!" Ellison said in a memo to employees on Tuesday morning, which was obtained by Business Insider. Ellison expressed thanks to staffers across Paramount and WBD for "your patience, your resilience and, above all, your belief in what we could accomplish together." Skydance will be "powered by creativity and technology," Ellison said, adding that the company has four top priorities: Win in storytelling. Become the most technologically capable media company. Lead in a crowded market. Earn Trust Every Day. Skydance is now a Hollywood behemoth that owns assets including Paramount Pictures, the Warner Bros. studio, Paramount+, HBO Max, Pluto TV, Discovery+, HBO, CBS, CNN, TruTV, TLC, and Comedy Central. However, the combined company faces fierce competition from Hollywood rivals like Disney and tech giants, including Google's YouTube. Paramount and WBD's streaming viewership share on US TVs was 3.6% in July, according to Nielsen — lower than Disney's 4.7%, Netflix's 7.8%, and YouTube's 14.2%. "Audiences have more choices than ever, technology is reshaping how stories are created, distributed and experienced, and competition for people's time and attention has never been greater," Ellison said in his memo. "We don't just want to succeed in this environment — we want to win and help shape the future of the industry." The Skydance CEO also had a section on "financial strength," which he said will give the company "the freedom to take creative risks, invest in our people and our technology, and pursue the kind of opportunities that set us apart." Ellison said the combined company will generate close to $70 billion in revenue and will save $6 billion from this merger. It will also have about $80 billion in debt. Ellison has brought in Ynon Kreiz as Skydance's co-CEO to oversee the merger integration and run day-to-day operations. The former Mattel top exec is known for cutting costs, as Business Insider's Peter Kafka noted. The Paramount-WBD merger followed a monthslong saga in which Ellison's company started a hostile bid for WBD , outbid Netflix , faced lawsuits from 12 states and the Writers Guild of America, and settled those suits by agreeing to concessions. events.title: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The race between open and closed AI is on, and Europe is still in the mix. On Tuesday, French AI lab Mistral AI released Mistral Large 4 (ML4), a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals — following what French president Macron described as “a third way in AI.” Amid a growing divide between closed models that can be unplugged and open models that are often made in China, Mistral is positioning ML4 as an alternative to both. Nicknamed Le Chonk in reference to its 1 trillion parameters, ML4 is definitely not small; but is not an open-weight model yet. For the time being, it can only be accessed via a public guardrail endpoint, but Mistral plans to make its weights available in just three weeks, after safety testing is complete. “In the meantime, we’ll work with trusted partners and governments to make sure that the open source weights can be used to defend, but not to [perform] malicious attacks,” Mistral VP Science Pierre Stock told TechCrunch. Security concerns have been mounting in recent months, particularly among Mistral’s core audience — enterprises and institutions. At the same time, an open-weight model is easier to audit, Stock said. Another important behind-the-scenes aspect is that ML4 was trained entirely on Mistral’s compute; using only 4,000 Nvidia GPUs “which is two to three times less than our Chinese competitors, and significantly less than the closed source competitors,” Stock said. With benchmark results still pending, Mistral hopes ML4 will be best in class among open-weight models, especially outside of China, but not only, Stock said. Thanks to focused training, it could also outperform closed models in specific areas that are key to its customers, and where multimodal capabilities can add value. According to Stock, ML4’s optimized use cases include cybersecurity and finance, but also chip design, which is core to two of Mistral’s main backers — Dutch giant ASML, which led its Series C , and Samsung, which led its Series D last month at a €21 billion valuation (about $24.39 billion). At the time, the company tried to convey that its decision to host Chinese models wasn’t a pivot into becoming a mere inference provider . events.title: I've always taught my children to respect their elders. I also needed to teach them to speak up for themselves.
events.summary: The author (top right) said she is rethinking how she teaches her kids to respect their elders. Courtesy of Sana Sheraz. When I was growing up, I thought staying quiet was part of respecting elders and being polite. Now that I have my own kids, I'm starting to see things differently. I want my kids to respectfully speak up when others make them feel a certain way. Growing up, I was taught that respecting elders meant listening without arguing, staying quiet when an adult was speaking, and accepting criticism because the person was older. As a mother, I have always wanted to pass that value on to my children. But recently, I realized there was another part of that lesson I needed to teach them. Their feelings matter, too. I had always thought teaching children to compromise was part of teaching them to be considerate. I hadn't thought enough about what happens when that compromise starts coming at the expense of their feelings. It started with a family visit This summer, my aunt came to stay with us for a few days with my sister and her children. With the whole family staying together, everyone had to make some compromises. My daughter and son had to share a room , and my daughter also had to share her space with my aunt. She gave up some of her usual privacy and comfort without complaining. I was proud of how she handled it. She understood that having family together sometimes means making room for one another. We were all adjusting in different ways, and I thought she was learning an important lesson about being flexible and considerate. Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. But over the next few days, I began noticing something that made me look at the interactions she was having with my family differently. My aunt would sometimes compare my daughter with my sister's daughter, who is four years older. At first, I didn't think much of it. But as it happened again, I noticed my daughter becoming quieter. That was the moment I started questioning what I was teaching her. She had been taught that when an elder speaks, you listen. You don't argue. You don't question. You certainly don't tell them that what they said hurt you. I suddenly wondered whether the lesson I had always considered a sign of good manners was also making it harder for her to speak for herself. I don't believe children should be rude to their elders. I don't want my children to respond with anger, judgment, or disrespect. But I also don't want them to believe that someone's age automatically makes every comment acceptable. I stepped in When the comparison came up again, I politely responded. I explained that the girls were different children and were also four years apart, so comparing them was not fair. I didn't raise my voice. I didn't criticize my aunt or try to make her feel bad. I simply put my point across respectfully. Then I looked at my daughter and gave her an encouraging smile. That small moment stayed with me. I realized that this was something I needed to teach my children by example: You can stand up for yourself without being rude. You can disagree without being angry. You can explain your point without judging someone. You can tell someone that something is uncomfortable or unfair without trying to hurt them in return. And sometimes, children learn these things better by watching us than by listening to us explain them. I'm teaching boundaries When my daughter saw me respond calmly and respectfully, I hoped she understood that she could do the same if someone ever tried to make her feel small. She didn't have to shout or argue. She could remain respectful while still knowing that her feelings and perspective mattered. That is the kind of boundary I want to teach both of my children. I still want them to greet their elders, listen to them, speak politely, and treat family with kindness. Those values matter to me. But I also want them to understand that respect goes both ways. Being older does not mean someone should be allowed to make a child feel inferior. And teaching children to respect adults should not mean teaching them to silence themselves. Perhaps the biggest lesson was for me. My daughter had quietly compromised her space for our family, and I had failed to acknowledge it. I apologized to her for that. I am learning that raising respectful children doesn't mean raising children who never speak up. It means teaching them how to speak up with kindness , confidence, and without anger. That is the balance I want my children to carry with them: be respectful, be kind, but never believe that respect requires you to accept emotional harm. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: British Airways to launch world’s biggest business class cabin
events.summary: British Airways will introduce what it describes as the world’s biggest business class on its upgraded double-decker Airbus SE A380 jets , targeting premium passengers as airlines rush to cash in on upscale travel . The IAG SA-owned airline will update its fleet of a dozen A380s with a 106-seat business class cabin spanning the entire upper deck of the aircraft, the airline said at an event in London. The first upgraded A380 is due to enter service in the coming months. The carrier said it would also upgrade its first-class seating with dividers that fold away , enabling the conversion of middle seats into larger cabins for passengers travelling together. The changes will reduce the number of seats on the A380 by 11 per cent, from 469 seats to 417, with the bulk of the reduction coming from the economy-class cabin. Economy berths will be reduced by about 30 per cent to 215 seats. “This is the largest single investment that any airline has ever made in reconfiguring an aircraft stretching from nose to tail and touching every single aspect of the experience on board,” British Airways chief executive Sean Doyle said on Monday. Retrofitting one aircraft takes about 100 days, he said. British Airways' decision to spend millions on transforming its fleet of A380s makes the carrier an industry outlier while rivals around the world are phasing out the four-engine behemoth for smaller, more fuel-efficient twin-engined jets. Slot constraints at London’s Heathrow airport mean it cannot easily replace the super jumbo with smaller aircraft. US and European carriers have been pouring money into first and business-class seating to target well-heeled passengers who are a resilient source of income at a time when the Iran war has caused jet fuel prices to soar, driving up costs. Air France-KLM’s La Premiere recently won an award for the world’s best first-class in Skytrax’s annual airline rankings and has plans to expand the service to more US cities. Emirates, which operates the world’s biggest A380 fleet, has as many as 76 berths in business class. However, it will still have a party trick that British Airways’ upgraded jets will lack – a shower for first-class flyers . The airline is also spending heavily to upgrade its fleet, including reconfigured premium-economy cabins and new business-class cabins. Across the Atlantic, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines Holdings have generated most of the industry’s profitability by catering to premium customers. British Airways unveiled its plans for the new A380 first-class seating in November 2024, and had planned to launch the product in the middle of this year.

events.title: Paramount completes $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form new media empire Skydance
events.summary: David Ellison and ex-Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to oversee both film studios, HBO Max, CNN and CBS News as co-executives Paramount completed its $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery on Tuesday, consolidating some of the world’s most recognizable studios and news outlets after a bidding war with Netflix and months of legal turmoil. The new company, now called Skydance, will have David Ellison, the son of a billionaire tech mogul, at its helm, with the former CEO of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-executive. They will oversee Paramount and Warner Bros’ movie studios, HBO Max, CBS News and CNN. “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement. “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality.” The consolidation of Paramount and Warner Bros combines two of the last five legacy studios in Hollywood, which includes Disney, Universal Pictures and Sony Pictures. Though the merger was approved in June, California, New York and 10 other states sued Paramount over concerns that the move would “extinguish” competition and lead to fewer movie theaters in theaters and at home. As part of the settlement agreement reached last month, Skydance is required to release a minimum of 30 films each year and more than 180 television shows. CBS News and CNN will also be required to maintain independent editorial boards. A trustee will monitor Skydance’s compliance with the terms of the settlement. Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, said he would be prepared to go to court if the company ever fails to comply. “This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger; it’s not a blessing of the broader merger,” he said on 21 September, when the settlement was announced. “Broadly speaking, we believe further consolidation in markets that are essential to American economic life doesn’t serve the American economy, consumers or competition well.” The merger has also raised concerns about Ellison’s influence over CNN after his overhaul of CBS News. Ellison is the son of Larry Ellison, the co-founder of Oracle who was a Trump megadonor in the 2024 presidential election. The elder Ellison’s net worth is $193bn, according to Bloomberg . Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning When David Ellison’s Skydance Corporation acquired Paramount last year, he appointed Bari Weiss , a former New York Times opinion writer who launched an “anti-woke” media outlet, as the head of CBS News, despite her lack of television experience. Since then, the television network has faced accusations of bias toward the Trump administration, though Ellison has defended his stewardship of both CBS and now, CNN. On Monday, CNN’s CEO, Mark Thompson, announced that he would remain in his role under its new parent company, saying that he had spoken with Ellison and Skydance leadership and that he has “real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for”.

events.title: Trump remarks that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles, San Diego draw backlash
events.summary: California leaders blasted President Trump after he said during a Monday rally about Iran , "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." The big picture: The backlash — and the White House's insistence that Trump was misunderstood — underscored the ambiguity of his meandering speech: An argument that the war was worth enduring to protect Americans came out sounding like an invitation to attack two U.S. cities. An administration account posted on X that Trump meant that the U.S. was fighting Iran to "STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego." Driving the news: Faced with an unpopular war and stubbornly high gas prices, Trump seemingly argued that the current economic pain is "a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe" during his Nebraska rally. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe," he said. "They can take out a city. Let them take, let it — let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That's — this is a very small price to pay, and it's gonna be over very soon." Friction point: The comment received swift backlash from Golden State leaders: California Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote , "After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous." San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria also admonished the president, writing, "San Diego is not collateral damage. We are not expendable." And LA Mayor Karen Bass responded , "His statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety. The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives." Between the lines: Analysts online perceived his comments in various ways, with some noting his circuitous language could have masked his true intent. But others reeled at the plain text of the comments from the president, who in the past has suggested using "dangerous" U.S. cities as military "training grounds." The White House pointed Axios to a post from Communications Director Steven Cheung, who argued the president "was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. Context: Military bases across San Diego employ more than 136,000 active duty members and civilians, according to a 2025 report from the San Diego Military Advisory Council. Rep. Scott Peters (D), who represents the city, noted those deep military roots in his statement condemning the president's words, writing, "San Diego is a proud military town, home to 115,000 courageous active duty servicemembers and their families. Military service is at the root of our community and culture." Go deeper: After nixing Iran proposal, Trump tells Axios he expects talks this week

Skydance will also gain control of major franchises such as “The Lord of the Rings,” “Game of Thrones,” the DC Universe, and “Yellowstone.” The merger puts one of the world’s largest entertainment studios under the control of David Ellison. events.title: IMF warns cost-of-living shocks cause ‘lasting deterioration’ in affordability
events.summary: The Iran war has led to a spike in oil prices and has pushed up global inflation. The IMF warns that price rises for essentials like food and energy, driven by wars in Iran and Ukraine, are more persistent, causing lasting affordability issues worldwide. Global inflation is elevated, with forecasts rising to 4.7% in 2026, as supply shocks and conflicts disrupt markets and strain household budgets. The IMF urges targeted, temporary aid over broad subsidies to support vulnerable groups, but notes many low-income countries lack fiscal capacity amid ongoing global debt and shocks. WASHINGTON – The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned on Oct 6 that price increases for necessities like food and energy , fuelled by the wars in Iran and Ukraine, are more persistent than previously expected. Global prices for many commodities have remained elevated for several years, fuelled first by pandemic supply chain shortages and then by the wars in Ukraine and Iran. The war in Ukraine snarled supply chains for many food-related goods as well as energy, and the US-Israel war on Iran has seen energy and fertilizer prices skyrocket due to the closure of a key Gulf supply route. “We find that the prices of necessities relative to other goods continue rising for more than a year after the start of a typical episode, and remain persistently elevated,” the IMF said in a blog post accompanying its new report. “As a result, people face not only a temporary spike in food and energy costs, but a lasting deterioration in the affordability of essentials relative to other items,” it said. Households worldwide have struggled with cost-of-living increases due to the wars and the pandemic, with wages struggling to keep up with persistent price pressures. The Iran war, launched in February 2026 , has pushed global inflation and saw the IMF upgrade its forecast for the metric to 4.7% worldwide in 2026, compared to 4.1% the year before. The IMF is due to release the main portion of its World Economic Outlook update next week, with new figures for global growth and inflation forecasts. The latest report is part of that release, focusing on lessons learned from the cost-of-living crises of the last five years. The IMF warned that the consequences of so-called supply shocks extended far beyond “a few months of higher inflation”. Central banks across the world have begun raising interest rates to combat inflation. Raising the key rate of an economy can help fight higher prices, but also tends to slow economic activity, a difficult balancing act in developing countries that may not be able to afford the slowdown. The report said the persistent inflationary pressures were a threat to macroeconomic stability for many countries. “Inflation remains elevated long after the initial surge in food and energy prices,” it said. “Inflation expectations also rise and stay above pre-crisis levels for years, suggesting that these episodes may complicate efforts by central banks to control inflation.” The burden of those price increases falls disproportionately on working-class families, for whom spending on necessities is both non-negotiable and forms a larger share of their monthly spending. As a result, such inflation has a “substantial” impact on increasing poverty and income inequality. The IMF called on countries to avoid broad-based subsidies to combat such crises, and to instead issue “targeted and temporary transfers” to those who need them most. With global debt levels at elevated levels, however, many low-income and developing countries lack the fiscal space to do so, especially given the repeated shocks since the pandemic. AFP

events.title: NHS supply lorry drivers to strike in pay dispute
events.summary: Lorry drivers are set to host a series of walkouts in October and November Published 6 October 2026, 12:51 BST NHS supply lorry drivers are set for a series of strikes in a dispute over pay. Drivers employed by GXO in Tyne and Wear, Derbyshire, Yorkshire, Kent, Warwickshire and Suffolk will stage five walkouts from October 13-15, 20-22, 27-29 and November 3-5 and 10-12, Unite said. Union members have rejected a 4% pay offer from GXO, which runs the NHS supply chain contract for Supply Chain Coordination Limited (SCCL), and is wholly owned by NHS England. Unite regional officer Phil Silkstone said: "There is still time for strike action to be avoided but that will require a deal our members can accept." NHS Supply Chain and GXO said they had "robust contingency plans" in place to minimise disruption. Drivers deliver general equipment such as bandages, dressings, gowns, gloves and needles to hospitals across England. Silkstone described them as "dedicated workers" and said GXO had refused to put forward a reasonable offer. NHS Supply Chain and GXO said they were aware Unite members had voted in favour of industrial action. GXO said it believed the 4% pay offer was fair. A spokesperson for GXO said: "Patient care remains of paramount importance, and we remain focused on providing a safe and effective operation throughout this period." Depots where strike action is due to take place are in Alfreton in Derbyshire, Bridgwater in Somerset, Normanton in West Yorkshire, Maidstone in Kent, Rugby in Warwickshire, Bury St Edmonds in Suffolk and Washington in Tyne and Wear. events.title: AI turns Wall Street into a herd
events.summary: Liz’s view The keys to succeeding on Wall Street are to a) make money and b) make money differently than others. Performance is table stakes; outperformance gets you the glory. AI is messing with that logic. Nvidia’s $500 billion consortium includes the four largest alternative-asset managers in the world and six of the top eight. Blackstone and Apollo are jointly providing billions of dollars for Anthropic to buy compute. Anthropic’s AI-for-the-real-world consultancy offshoot raised $1.5 billion from Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, Goldman Sachs, General Atlantic, Leonard Green, and Apollo. Nearly every big private-equity firm not on that list is backing OpenAI’s competing version. (Goldman, being Goldman, is in both.) Here is a handy chart. This is not how things usually work on Wall Street, where the goal is to snake investments away from rivals, not share them. The last time private equity clubbed up on deals too big for any one of them to handle solo, we got some of the worst buyouts in history . Some of the crowding can be explained by the sheer amount of money needed. “Why can you get five or six of the leading players at one table? Because there’s enough to go around, ” Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey told me last week. He thinks there will still be winners and losers in the AI trade as investors stake out corners within it; Brookfield has made bets on sovereign AI in Europe, Blue Owl is an AI landlord, Apollo is a lender willing to take on chip risk. But whether those are different bets or marketing gloss for the same big bet is less clear to me. AI is starting to look like an “IBGYBG” trade, a Wall Street phrase that made it into the US government’s postmortem report on the 2008 subprime crash: “I’ll be gone, you’ll be gone.” Everyone wins if it works, even if nobody looks like a standout genius. Everyone loses if it doesn’t, but nobody looks like a standout moron. The irony is that the investing world wasjust returning to a place where outperformance seemed possible again when AI arrived. Two decades of easy money had made everyone look like undifferentiated geniuses. A more fractured, risky, and dynamic world of wars, inflation, and tariffs might have encouraged investors to zig where others zagged. “I think we’ll start to see the pull of groupthink become a little weaker, and contrarianism start to pay off,” I wrote in early 2024 . Oops. Notable A recent PwC study estimates global spending on data centers alone could top $30 trillion through 2050, a buildout the firm says would surpass infrastructure booms such as railroads, the internet and electrification.

events.title: Mary Chia to issue $1m in discounted shares, including to founder to strengthen finances
events.summary: The new shares will be subscribed for by company founder Mary Chia Ah Tow and three other businesswomen, Ng Yen Ying, Lin Yan and Maggie Lim Min Er. SINGAPORE – Mary Chia Holdings has proposed issuing 100 million new shares at one cent each to four investors, which would allow it to raise $1 million to strengthen its financial position and fund overseas expansion plans. The move, announced on Oct 6 after the market closed, will bring in new investors but significantly dilute the shareholdings of Mary Chia’s existing investors. The subscription price represents a discount of about 27% to the volume-weighted average price of 1.37 cents between Sept 30 and Oct 5, the day the company called a trading halt. It is also about 35.1% and 36.3% below the volume-weighted average prices of its shares over the preceding one-month and three-month periods respectively. The beauty and wellness group said the proposed share issue is necessary to strengthen the group’s capital base and liquidity, and give it greater financial flexibility to meet its operating and business development requirements. The company’s net current liabilities stood at about $12.58 million on March 31, while net liabilities were about $11.82 million. Its cash and bank balances stood at about $310,000. Net current liabilities measure the shortfall between assets and obligations due within a year, while net liabilities mean the group’s total liabilities exceeded its total assets. For the financial year ended March 31, the group recorded a net loss of about $2.64 million and net operating cash outflows of approximately $2.97 million. Its independent auditors had also said they could not obtain enough reliable evidence to form an opinion on whether the financial statements were accurate. Mary Chia expects to receive net proceeds of about $946,570 from the proposed share issue, after estimated expenses of about $53,430. Of the amount raised, $750,000, or 79.2%, will be used for working capital, including manpower costs, professional fees, compliance and continuing listing expenses, and administrative and head-office costs, the company said. The remaining $196,570, or 20.8 per cent, will fund the expansion of its operations in China and Thailand, including the establishment of offices and other operating expenses. The new shares will be subscribed for by company founder Mary Chia Ah Tow and three other businesswomen, Ng Yen Ying, Lin Yan and Maggie Lim Min Er. Chia and Ng will each subscribe for 20 million shares for $200,0 00 , while Lin and Lim will each invest $300,000 for 30 million shares. The company said Ng, Lin and Lim were identified through business networking and are independent of the company, its directors, chief executive, controlling shareholders and their associates. They are investing for their own accounts and are not acting in concert with other parties, according to the announcement. Upon completion, Mary Chia’s issued share capital will increase from about 333.84 million shares to 433.84 million shares. The 100 million subscription shares represent about 29.95% of its existing share capital and 23.05% of the enlarged share base. Chia, who is 76, currently owns about 4.23% of the company, and will hold about 7.86% after the transaction, making her a substantial shareholder of the company. She is the mother of Ho Yow Ping, Mary Chia’s executive chairman, chief executive, director and controlling shareholder. Ho’s husband, Lee Boon Leng, is a controlling shareholder of the company. According to its announcement, Chia had approached the company on Sept 21 to express her interest in subscribing for new shares to demonstrate her support for the group. However, as she is an associate and immediate family member of a director and controlling shareholder, Chia’s subscription requires specific shareholder approval. Ng will own about 4.61% of the enlarged company, while Lin and Lim will each hold about 6.91%. After the share issue, the family behind Mary Chia – comprising Ho, Lee, Chia and Suki Sushi, an investment vehicle owned by Ho – will own a combined stake of about 61.5% in the company, compared with 73.93% currently. Mary Chia said it will seek confirmation from the Securities Industry Council that the allotment of shares to Chia will not require her or the family concert-party group to make a mandatory offer for the company. The transaction is also subject to shareholder approval at an extraordinary general meeting. Kang Wan Chern is deputy business editor at The Straits Times.

events.title: Paramount and Warner Bros are now one Hollywood giant: Skydance
events.summary: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros CHICAGO -- It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. The companies completed the deal on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood giant with the now shorter “Skydance” nametag. The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together. And HBO Max, titles ranging from “Harry Potter” to “Sinners” and even networks like CNN find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of “Top Gun” and “The Godfather.” All of them will come under the helm of billionaire David Ellison, and his new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz . That further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. Ellison’s Skydance bought out Paramount for $8 billion just last year , and set its sights on Warner — an even bigger fish — very soon after. What followed erupted into a tumultuous, roughly year-long fight over Warner’s fate. Skydance Corp. emerges from one of the biggest tie-ups ever in the media and entertainment industry. Including billions of dollars in debt, the Warner acquisition amounted to nearly $111 billion. “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a statement Tuesday. "We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.” Here’s a look at some of the key moments that got us here. The early days of Paramount's quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war. Months after disclosing it was open to selling parts or even all of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix back in December. But Skydance-owned Paramount, which claimed Warner management “never engaged meaningfully” with its previous proposals, soon launched a hostile counterbid aimed at taking over the entire company — including networks like CNN and Discovery. The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer on the table, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share, and Netflix opted to bow out of the race . Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement by late February. Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner's future. And from awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known. In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors and other professionals announced their “unequivocal opposition” to the Paramount-Warner merger. The open letter — which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams — warned of fewer jobs and “less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.” Meanwhile, some other stars lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon this past spring , the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise — who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower, with the words “the future is paramount and the future looks pretty great from here." Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison. The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season this year, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, “Remarkably Bright Creatures” actor Sally Field — who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal — stressed that “unique storytelling matters” and “we can’t let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged.” Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix's studio and streaming deal was on the table, with particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters. Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). And over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration wasn't afraid to chime in about hopes for a new owner. At the time, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.

events.title: Brands are fleeing TV for social. The agency that landed more than 50B views for brands like Perplexity and Universal Music sold for at least $100M
events.summary: One of the most viral ads of the last Super Bowl didn’t run on national television. 50 Cent’s “Beef 101” campaign for DoorDash this year was built for social media. The Atlanta-based social-first marketing agency that worked on both campaigns, Get Engaged , has entered a partnership with SAMY , a global social-first marketing company, in what cofounder Cam Fordham told Fortune exclusively is a “low nine-figure deal,” with a stock and cash component and an “injection of resources to scale even further.” That means the deal is valued at at least $100 million. The deal closed Sept. 30, and all three cofounders (Fordham, Alex Dermer, and Ben Hiott) are staying. Dermer will take the CEO title. “Fundamentally, it’s an acquisition, but the founders, all of us here today, will remain,” Fordham said.  From Facebook side hustle to virality Get Engaged started in 2016 as what Hiott calls “essentially a side hustle.” He was monetizing a handful of celebrities’ Facebook pages while working a full-time job, with one foot still in the music business. Fordham, a former LSU football player with a deep roster of talent relationships, heard what Hiott was doing and proposed going into business together. Dermer, who was wrapping up a previous venture and working out of the same office building, became the third partner. Early clients were Atlanta hip-hop artists like Waka Flocka Flame and T.I., whom the trio helped with meet-and-greets and tour merchandise.  “They kept coming to us: What else can you do for us?” Fordham says. The founders decided to build an agency around the question Dermer put this way: “What does a marketing agency look like in 15 years, and how can we start to be that answer today?” The answer came at an unexpected time, when many other businesses were struggling. During the pandemic, brands started moving money from radio and billboard spots into digital spots, Fordham said.  “This is when TikTok started to really emerge,” he added. Get Engaged pushed clients onto the platform, he said, and their company started picking up Fortune 500 brands. Get Engaged’s growth has tracked a broader shift in advertising. Social media overtook paid search to become the world’s largest advertising channel by spend , according to WARC Media. WARC forecasts global ad spend will grow 9.1% to $1.3 trillion in 2026 , with nearly 80% concentrated in retail media, paid search, and social platforms. Linear TV, meanwhile, accounted for 41.3% of global ad spend in 2013 but was on track to fall to just 12.4% in 2025 .  That growth has meant more hiring. Today, Get Engaged has more than 100 employees across Atlanta, New York, Nashville, and Los Angeles, and a client list that includes DoorDash, Perplexity, Raising Cane’s, Universal Music Group, EA, and Sazerac. Fordham says revenue has grown 40% year over year. No layoffs will result from the partnership, the founders said. “There’s this point of inflection when you flip that model and people start to come to you because they’ve heard of a campaign you’ve run or a big moment you’ve been a part of,” Dermer said. This February, DoorDash’s 50 Cent campaign—a social-first push in which the rapper pulled items out of a delivery bag in thinly veiled jabs at Sean “Diddy” Combs and others—launched ahead of Super Bowl LX without a national in-game buy and became one of the most dissected ads of the game.  “To really impact culture, you have to understand how to drive content around the internet,” Dermer said. “You have to understand where conversations start on the internet.” Why SAMY The founders say inbound interest had been building, but SAMY stood out. The Madrid-founded company has roughly 1,200 employees across North America, Europe, Asia, and Latin America, and is majority-owned by private equity firm Bridgepoint. The Raine Group advised Get Engaged. “We weren’t looking for someone to come in and fix what we had built,” Hiott said. “It’s not about correction—it’s about connection.” The Get Engaged brand will still exist and operate as SAMY’s U.S. arm. Dermer credits a kinship with SAMY cofounders Patricia Ratia Garcia-Oliveros and Marta Nicolas: “There’s a human component to this. At the end of the day, as you build to impact and to truly market, you have to get down to the fundamental human level of connection.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Emmy Awards to move to Prime Video in 2027 in 6-year deal between Amazon and the Television Academy
events.summary: The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video starting in 2027 LOS ANGELES -- The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video starting in 2027 in a six-year deal struck between Amazon and the Television Academy that ends a seven-decade run of broadcast networks airing the ceremony honoring the best in TV. The agreement announced Tuesday means a shift to the streaming services that have come to utterly dominate the prestige categories at the Emmys . The show has aired on one of the four broadcast networks every year since 1955. NBC was first to air it nationally, and was the last to host it last month. For the past three decades it has been in a yearly rotation between ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC in what was known as the “Wheel Deal.” Having a single, long-term home starting with next September's 79th Primetime Emmy Awards may be the biggest change. “Continuity is a big part of what we're looking for because the rotating part of it basically meant in many ways that we were starting over every year,” Cris Abrego, chairman of the Television Academy, told The Associated Press. “With one partner over six years, we can really learn together and build from year to year together.” The Emmys will continue to air free of charge as it always has, a demand the Academy made from the start to its suitors. No Prime Video subscription will be required to watch. The move echoes the Oscars’ deal announced in December sending them to YouTube and ending their own, just-as-long relationship with broadcast networks. But unlike that agreement, announced in 2025 and starting in 2029, this one is effective immediately. “We’re on the clock, we gotta get rolling,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, told the AP. Nearly all awards shows have seen steep drops in viewership in a more segmented culture, and the Emmys have consistently lagged behind the Oscars, Grammys and Golden Globes even as the acclaim for the shows they honor has grown. At its peak, the show drew more than 20 million viewers. The figure now hovers around 7 million. Both the Academy and Amazon said Prime Video might be in a position to change that as a place where so much of the Emmys programming can be viewed, whether it's a Prime production or a streaming partnership. The biggest winners at the last two Emmys, “Widow's Bay” and “The Studio,” can both be watched on Prime Video through its partnership with Apple TV. “I think we’re going to be able to increase the viewership over time on this show, age it down, actually bring in a younger audience, which I think is a catalyst to growing,” Hopkins said. “We will have the opportunity throughout the year to be promoting Emmy nominees to our customers as a way of saying ‘Hey, watch these shows, but also watch the Emmys.’” Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Abrego said this approach, and Prime Video's role as a television hub, was a major consideration in taking the show there. “They really support all television,” he said. “We want reach, we want access, and we felt Amazon was in line with that.” And while Abrego acknowledged the significance of the move to streaming and its implications, he said the content is far more important than how it's delivered. “The Academy has never defined television by how it reaches your screen or even which screen it reaches,” he said. “The goal is to consistently want to recognize excellence wherever it comes from.” Live events on Amazon have not been a novelty for a long time. It's been nearly a decade since it first aired an NFL game and many other major sports and other events have followed. “We look at our service as something that’s a hybrid between live and on-demand, and we’ve made live a real priority,” Hopkins said. Football has always been a problem for the Emmys. Its time slots on Sunday or Monday nights in September nearly always lead to a clash with the rating monolith of the NFL. This year’s show was trounced by the first Monday Night Football game of the year between the Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos on ESPN. The ceremony will stay in September in 2027, but that doesn't mean it is set for the run of the agreement. “We had conversations with Amazon, if we wanted to change that date moving forward with time, we could explore it and we would be open to it,” Abrego said, acknowledging that it would have repercussions with deadlines and voting.
