"I was worried… about how I needed to be grateful… and being defiant is not being grateful and making a scene is not being grateful," he said. The complainant said the next morning he saw Mr Jones who had the "same smirk" and that he "wanted to be as far from there as possible". The court heard the boy later said goodbye to Mr Jones before his butler drove the schoolboy home. He said he did not tell his mother about what happened until several days later when she noticed that he was not sleeping at night. Complainant A said he then wrote his mother a letter saying that "something happened at Fitzroy Falls and that "someone did something they shouldn't have" but did not go into explicit detail. "To other people, it's probably not that bad and I should just get over it," he said. The court heard the boy went to police with his allegation a year after the incident. After the boy's letter to Mr Jones four years earlier, the pair began to correspond by email and text message, with the schoolboy explaining in more detail that his father had left the home and was paying "intermittent" child support, and that the house he and his mother were living in was unfinished after the builder walked off the job. "You sound a special sort of young man," Mr Jones responded, and asked the then-teenager for some more information.

events.title: UAE's e& returns to its original Etisalat name as it focuses on AI growth
events.summary: UAE telecoms group e& is to return to its original Etisalat name, four years after it changed the company's name, as it looks to boost growth in the artificial intelligence era. “Etisalat is the name we are taking forward – a name that reflects our heritage, our strategy and our ambition for the AI era,” the company said on Tuesday in a filing to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. The move was announced in the presence of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court. It was revealed as the Abu Dhabi-based company marks 50 years since its formation. Today, I witnessed a new milestone in the journey of “Etisalat” as it celebrated 50 years of achievement and launched its vision for the next chapter. A national institution that has accompanied the UAE's development and helped build its digital capabilities. Etisalat continues… pic.twitter.com/rzHR7uYSJW — منصور بن زايد (@MansourBinZayed) October 5, 2026 Etisalat was rebranded as e& in 2022 amid plans for the company to transform into a global technology investment conglomerate. “Etisalat means connection. For 50 years, that purpose has guided what we build and the role we play,” the company said. “Today, it carries even greater significance as we bring connectivity, digital capabilities and infrastructure together to enable new opportunities.” The telecoms company is pushing for AI-led growth, with the launch of a strategic project to develop and expand digital infrastructure capacity within the UAE and abroad. The project includes plans to expand international connectivity capacity to more than 500 terabits per second by 2030 – more than 25 times the current capacity – in addition to developing diverse routes to enhance connectivity efficiency and reliability, delivering advanced, low-latency performance, it said in a statement. The move comes after the company reported a 9 per cent increase in its second-quarter revenue, as it expanded its customer base across international markets despite uncertainty caused by the Iran war. Revenue in the quarter rose to Dh19.2 billion ($5.2 billion) year-on-year, with its overall customer base increasing by nearly a third to hit 251.5 million. In July, the company also agreed to sell its entire stake in Vodafone Group for $5.95 billion as it refocuses on its core businesses.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters No, this is not GRUB of the meatball variety Sweden is the home of bork, and what better way to mark it than with a huge example of digital signage that shows a GRUB message instead of an ad? Spotted by eagle-eyed Register reader Alexander, the GRUB in question is sadly not the delicious meatballs for which a well-known Swedish furniture maker is famed, but rather the bootloader familiar to Linux fans, usually when something is working as it should (since we can't imagine much call for selecting from multiple operating systems in the world of digital signage). GNU GRUB (the GRUB is short for Grand Unified Bootloader), according to GNU, "is responsible for loading and transferring control to the operating system kernel software." In this case, the user has some options. UEFI firmware is one. Some options for DMS are another. DMS might mean Dank Material Shell, unless you know better. It's an attractive enough desktop, but it seems like overkill for something that slings ads for the few seconds Stockholm commuters raise their gaze from their devices. Some enticing possibilities are on offer. Hitting "e" will edit the commands while "c" will drop the user into the command line. That's assuming, of course, that the user is carrying a keyboard to attach to the stricken screen, something we're sure every Register reader has in their backpack, but not something civilians would necessarily keep on their person. GRUB has featured in this column before , appearing on a UK bus after a filesystem became a bit poorly (motion sickness can clearly affect computers as well as commuters), but this is a wall-sized example of the breed. Judging by the passengers on the escalators opposite, it appears that nobody is rushing to the aid of the stricken signage. That's probably for the best – leave it for a few seconds (by the looks of things), and it'll have another go at booting. Still, it's always good to see GRUB putting in an appearance in a section often dominated by Windows and Android whoopsies. events.title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
events.summary: Published 6 October 2026, 08:03 BST A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters. The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said. Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents. The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said. There were £1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the £1.18bn detected the previous year. At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024. Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters are targeting much bigger payouts. "As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them." Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers." He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg". Macbooks, fishing equipment and Lego sets One of the most notable fraudsters identified by the ABI last year was a man found by IFED to have fabricated reports of stolen high-value Lego sets , external . The man's scam claims to Axa Insurance during 2021 and 2022 also included other high-value items such as MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles and fishing equipment, IFED said. In 2023, IFED said it found collectible Lego sets matching the ones claimed to have been stolen displayed in the man's living room during a search. Alongside his prison sentence handed down last year, he was also ordered to repay the £14,000 he had claimed. Other cases highlighted by the ABI included a man jailed for 20 months for manipulating women he met on dating sites into participating in staged car crashes, and a man sentenced to four and a half years for submitting over £300,000 worth of fraudulent travel medical emergency claims. In general, the ABI said motor insurance remained the area where insurers identified the most fraudulent cases, accounting for 55% of all scam claims. Meanwhile, the ABI's figures found that exaggerated loss remains the most common type of insurance fraud, with 26,900 cases identified. This is when someone deliberately attempts to increase the cost of a claim beyond its true value, the ABI said. events.title: Advancing The CFET-Based Device Roadmap: Novel Integration Modules And Standard Cell Configurations
events.summary: Key takeaways: From the A7 logic technology node onwards, industry may likely transition to CFET-based transistor architectures which enable 4.5-track (4.5T) and below standard cells. Progress in CFET enablement is backed by two complementary R&D tracks, with imec pioneering many of the underlying innovations: the development of CFET-specific process modules, and a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) exploration of scalable standard cell configurations. Part 1 of this two-part article presents two optimized CFET-specific modules: (1) a backside contact module; and (2) a gate-stack integration module that enables multiple threshold voltages in nanosheet and CFET devices. Part 2 covers imec’s latest CFET DTCO studies. A novel scalable architecture for sequential CFET is presented that enables split-gate and common-gate device options, key in advancing both the logic and SRAM scaling roadmaps. Another DTCO study presents improved routability at the back-end-of-line (BEOL) level to support the scaling of CFET standard cells. CFET technology moving forward, backed by integration efforts and DTCO studies The semiconductor industry is going through a major architectural transition, with gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors replacing FinFETs in advanced logic nodes of 3nm and beyond. GAA nanosheet transistor technology offers scalability down to the A10 logic generation, where it enables 5.5-track (T) standard cells – the track being a measure for the standard cell height. For the A7 node, options are becoming increasingly diverse to meet the growing diversification of application needs, driven by the AI revolution. According to imec’s latest roadmap, one option is to design systems around imec’s CMOS 2.0 scaling paradigm. With CMOS 2.0, a system-on-chip (SoC) is partitioned into heterogeneous, functional tiers each optimized using the most suitable technology, and reconnected using 3D interconnect technologies. For other use cases, GAA nanosheet technology may be pushed to its ultimate scaling limits, with power delivered from either the frontside or the backside. But industry may as well transition to complementary FET (CFET) device architectures. By stacking p and nMOS transistors on top of each other, standard cells can be further scaled down to 3T, thereby extending the classical CMOS logic roadmap to at least the A3 technology node. Fig. 1: Imec’s logic technology roadmap. Imec and its industrial partners are working to make CFET-based devices manufacturable. In recent years, they laid the groundwork for key integration approaches, categorized as monolithic CFET (mCFET) and sequential CFET (sCFET) [1,2]. Both approaches start from the vertical stacking of Si/SiGe layers from which the n and pFETs are fabricated. With mCFET, the vertical device structure with common top and bottom gates is patterned and processed in a single sequence of process steps. The patterning, deposition and selective removal of materials around and in between the high-aspect ratio device structure requires considerable effort in terms of module development. sCFET, on the contrary, patterns the top and bottom devices independently using dedicated masks. With sCFET, the individual process steps are simpler compared to mCFET but some critical steps need to be executed twice – for top and bottom separately. sCFET additionally involves two wafer flips, distorting the wafer and challenging the precise alignment of front-to-back device connections. Pending further progress in alignment accuracy, mCFET is believed to offer the fastest path to industrial adoption. Progress in CFET integration is complemented with design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) studies that examine CFET device architectures from a circuit level perspective [2]. These studies aim to identify scalable standard cell configurations and performance boosters that offer the best tradeoff in terms of power, performance, area and cost. In this 2-part article, we report major progress in CFET device integration, and we discuss CFET scalability using DTCO studies. In part 1 [link], two process modules were presented that are essential for both mCFET and sCFET device flavors: (1) a backside contact module, and (2) a gate stack integration approach that enables multiple threshold voltages (V t ) in nanosheet and CFET devices. In part 2, a scalable architecture for sCFET is introduced, allowing both split-gate and common-gate configurations. Besides progressing the logic roadmap, DTCO work shows how this split-gate architecture also benefits CFET-based SRAM scaling. Finally, improved back-end-of-line (BEOL) routability is demonstrated, supporting the scaling of CFET standard cells. The reported results are achieved in the framework of the imec-hosted European NanoIC pilot line, which is targeting the development of beyond-2nm systems-on-chip. CFET development, which is centered on CFET-specific designs, process steps, modules and baseline flows, has been selected as one of the key enabling technologies for extending the logic roadmap into the ångström era. This will help Europe to remain at the forefront of next-generation semiconductor innovation and manufacturing. A novel architecture for sCFET: Split-gate device architecture enlarges CFET’s scaling potential Earlier DTCO studies have already demonstrated the scaling potential of CFET technology across subsequent logic nodes – a prerequisite for the semiconductor industry to adopt the new device architecture. For mCFET, for example, imec previously identified the double-row (DR) CFET architecture as the most optimal way to integrate mCFETs into an A7 standard cell [3]. A double-row CFET standard cell contains two rows of stacked devices with a shared vertical signal via in between, and power walls at the cell boundary (see Figure 2). Later, layout inefficiencies were addressed, resulting in an optimized version of the double-row CFET: the half-height double-row (hDR) architecture. At IEDM 2025, additional scaling boosters such as the integration of hybrid channels were introduced to support aggressive area scaling targets towards A3 [2]. Common-gate and split-gate devices: The challenge of offering both flavors with one device architecture The process flow for fabricating mCFET devices inherently offers common-gate devices: the gates of n and pFETs are structurally connected to one another. This works well for 90-95% of all basic logic gates – think about an inverter circuit (or NOT gate) that performs the logical operation of negation. But for other logic circuits, such as flipflops and multiplex gates, independent control of n and pFET metal gates is desired. One way to address this need is to leave one polarity of the stacked CFET device unused (for example, only using the nFETs, and removing the pFETs). events.title: Why Oura really pulled its IPO: Wall Street experts suspect valuation concerns, an insider cash-out, and an Apple-size threat
events.summary: Hours before Oura, the smart-ring maker behind one of the season’s most closely watched IPOs, was expected to price its shares, CEO Tom Hale delivered a stunning announcement: The company was calling off its public debut, at least for now. The explanation Oura gave was simple: “uncertainty in the IPO market.” But the timing of the Sept. 29 announcement invited more questions than it answered. After all, the buzzy health-tech company had already completed a high-profile roadshow; told investors it was profitable and growing quickly; and was preparing to price an offering that could have raised as much as $2.2 billion. At the top of its proposed $40 to $44 per share range, the deal would have implied a fully diluted valuation of more than $15 billion. A source familiar with the matter told Fortune that the offering was around five times oversubscribed. Yes, IPOs can be postponed at any point before shares are sold. But shelving one this late in the game was unusual. Did investors balk at the offering price or the company’s growth outlook? Or were market conditions like elevated bond yields and higher interest rates actually too risky?  Oura was just one of several IPOs that have been delayed over the past month. Holtec Nuclear postponed its public debut earlier in September. It cited adverse market conditions such as “rising energy costs, elevated global trade tensions, ongoing military conflicts, and mounting inflation fears.” Bamboo Insurance and Amaero shelved theirs around the same time. But Oura hasn’t offered up many details on these “conditions,” which has left Wall Street to wonder whether those conditions were the cause of the delay or a catchall for more company-specific issues. “What else are you gonna say? ‘We aren’t meeting our expectations.’ I mean, that’s just not a thing to say to the public,” Kat Liu, vice president of financial services firm IPOX, told Fortune . IPOX creates specialized indexes that track new IPOs. Jay Ritter, director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business, shared similar sentiments. “They always blame it on market conditions,” he added. “They never say, ‘Uh, the reason we’re pulling the IPO is we had unrealistic expectations about how much we’re worth.’” Management’s reasoning didn’t align with the macro backdrop either, according to D.A. Davidson’s Gil Luria. “The market has actually been remarkably stable,” he told Fortune , pointing to what he described as a healthy consumer and a resilient economy. “To say that market conditions were the reason for the IPO postponement seems like a little bit of a stretch.” The S&P 500 is up more than 13% in 2026, and less than 1% off record highs. Instead, Oura’s IPO delay raised big questions on the Street like whether investors would support its valuation; whether the deal’s structure had become untenable; and how the company stacks up against a growing field of competitors in the wearables market. Is Oura stock too expensive? Some prospective buyers decided not to take part in the deal because of concerns over Oura’s target valuation, Bloomberg reported last week, citing sources familiar with the matter.  Oura had proposed selling 50 million shares at $40 to $44 apiece. At the $42 midpoint, the deal would have raised roughly $2.1 billion in gross proceeds. At the top end of the range, Oura would have had a fully diluted valuation of $15.6 billion. That might be too pricey for a company whose core product is an electronic ring.  But the argument for Oura’s valuation depends on whether or not investors are seeing it as a single-product hardware maker or something bigger with more expansion potential. “If you are viewing Oura as an AI-enabled digital-health platform … then whatever multiple they are looking for can kind of be justified,” Liu added. “But if you are just looking at them as a pure ring manufacturer, just consumer hardware, then that valuation is pretty hefty.” The distinction matters because Oura’s sales still lean heavily toward hardware, according to Liu. Meanwhile, Luria said investors have seen versions of this story before and aren’t buying it. Think back to the Peloton and GoPro debuts in the 2010s. Peloton priced its shares at $29 apiece in 2019. It has since dropped over 82%. GoPro went public at $24 per share five years before that, and has plunged over 94%, as of Monday.  “Investors have a long memory,” said Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson. “It really was a similar type of story about the secular trend for health and the importance of tracking and promoting it. Those ideas in the end did not work out.” Oura IPO terms and competition  The offering’s structure may also have given investors pause. Of the 50 million shares proposed, only 13.5 million, or 27%, were to be newly issued by Oura.  The other 36.5 million shares, or 73% of the deal, were to be sold by existing shareholders, meaning the bulk of the cash raised would have gone to early investors and insiders rather than to the company. At the $42 midpoint, that works out to roughly $567 million in gross proceeds for Oura and approximately $1.53 billion for selling shareholders.  This means there could be a ton of initial selling, which can make an IPO look less like a fundraise and more like a liquidity event for existing investors. “That’s a flag for the market,” Liu said. “It’s signaling that this IPO is not meant for growth.” Then, there’s the competition.  Although Oura may dominate the smart-ring market, it’s only one segment of a massive wearables industry. That space is controlled by big companies with far more resources and larger customer bases. Just look at Apple . The company already offers sleep monitoring and heart-rate tracking with the Apple Watch . Alphabet’s Google, Garmin, Fitbit, and Whoop compete for many of the same users looking for their own health data, as well. “All Apple has to decide to do is come up with a ring, and Oura’s business, for most intents and purposes, doesn’t need to exist,” Luria said. Whether Apple is actually preparing that product is beside the point, Luria added. Just the possibility shows how limited Oura’s competitive position could be against a company that controls the entire iPhone ecosystem. Ritter agreed. “It’s a great product from a company that has been growing rapidly and is profitable,” he said. “But just how big a market is this?” Consumers can already track their health metrics through an Apple Watch and other devices, he said, making it unclear whether the category can expand to millions of more buyers. What’s next Oura has seemingly dismissed all these concerns.  CEO Hale said that Oura has the “luxury of choosing our moment” when it comes to going public. events.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
events.summary: OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney Published 6 October 2026, 05:39 BST OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments. The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox. "We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said. Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation. Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present. An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind. When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake. "In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said. "The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough." Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents. "Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party." OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia. The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said. Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to. This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours. The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations". "We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well." Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI. "We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee. The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models. An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard. "In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association. Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws. events.title: DeepSeek set to raise at least $15 billion in Tencent-backed funding
events.summary: DeepSeek’s funding sets the stage for one of the most highly anticipated Chinese market debuts in years. DeepSeek is set to raise at least 80 billion yuan (S$15 billion) in Tencent-backed funding, exceeding its initial target ahead of a planned IPO in early 2027. The company plans to build a massive AI data centre in Inner Mongolia using 160,000 Huawei AI chips, aiming to advance its large language model technology. DeepSeek's founder prioritises pushing AI technology boundaries over monetisation, reflecting China's ambition to compete globally in artificial intelligence. DeepSeek is close to securing at least 80 billion yuan (S$15 billion) in its latest round of funding, blowing past its own capital-raising target ahead of a landmark initial public offering in early 2027 . Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) and WeChat-operator Tencent Holdings have committed among the largest amounts in the current financing, which closes soon, sources familiar with the matter said. DeepSeek initially sought about 50 billion yuan, but interest outstripped expectations after the successful release of its latest AI model, the sources said, asking not to be named as the details are not public. Based on term sheets signed, the final tally could approach 100 billion yuan, they added. The company is riding high after the release of the V4 Flash large language model, which reset expectations for cost versus performance against leaders Anthropic and OpenAI. That caps a strong run for founder Liang Wenfeng , whose start-up has forged a reputation for technical breakthroughs since a 2025 model that matched the capabilities of Silicon Valley offerings at a fraction of the cost. As with other artificial intelligence players, DeepSeek requires huge amounts of capital to bankroll its ambitions in a potentially revolutionary technology. The company plans to deploy at least 160,000 of Huawei Technologies’ top accelerators at a massive data centre it is building in Inner Mongolia, which may create one of the largest known clusters of Huawei AI chips. It has publicly released software created with Huawei to program AI chips, a foray into a new arena in close partnership with the hardware leader . Rival Moonshot, meanwhile, is also targeting an early 2027 IPO after closing funding at a US$50 billion (S$64 billion) valuation. Liang pledged in at least one meeting with investors in 2026 that he will keep developing open AI models while pursuing a broader goal of achieving artificial general intelligence. The hedge fund manager made it clear his main goal was to push the boundaries of the technology rather than monetisation, Bloomberg News has reported. While discussions around the current deal are near an end, details may still change in final talks, the sources said. DeepSeek had originally targeted a valuation of about 500 billion yuan in its financing. A CATL representative declined to comment, while Tencent had no immediate comment. DeepSeek did not respond to an e-mailed request for comment during a Chinese public holiday. DeepSeek has drawn enormous interest from would-be investors because it is one of a clutch of companies that sit at the heart of China’s effort to compete globally on AI. Once the round closes, the next step should be to restructure the company to prepare for an IPO, the sources said. Tencent, which also landed the biggest investment in the start-up at 10 billion yuan in a previous round of financing, aims to integrate AI into its platforms. CATL may be eyeing an increasingly lucrative business of supplying components to the industry, including for data centres. The AI lab’s capital-raising had attracted its share of controversy. DeepSeek briefly suspended the deal after comments widely attributed to Liang about US-Chinese AI competition went viral on social media. Chinese media outlet Yicai reported in July that the billionaire entrepreneur had talked about a reliance on Nvidia chips and China’s persistent lag in AI sophistication relative to the US. Liang’s net worth more than doubled to around US$36 billion when DeepSeek closed its first round of external fund raising this summer. The AI start-up grew as an offshoot from his hedge fund High-Flyer, which provided much of the initial support. Liang contributed again in the previous 50 billion yuan round, which valued DeepSeek at roughly 350 billion yuan at the time. BLOOMBERG

The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what 1 day ago OpenAI alerts 100+ orgs that its 'misaligned models' attempted to break in - or worse 4 days ago OpenAI's wandering AI agents earn it a California subpoena 4 days ago OpenAI is now offering API customers the option to watermark the output of certain models in order to comply with the letter of Europe's AI Act. And within a few weeks, the biz plans to apply a form of digital watermarking – like it or not – to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union. But unlike rival Anthropic, it isn't applying its watermarking technique to content generated outside of Europe, though API customers can choose to have the marks applied to content made anywhere. Moreover, OpenAI is using technology that misses a fair number of instances of AI-generated text and can easily be tricked. The EU AI Act requires generative AI service providers to make model output identifiable in a way that's readable by machines. Anthropic was the first major AI company to announce its approach to AI Act compliance, which involves the application of Google's SynthID-Text algorithm. It's doing so globally. Microsoft and Meta have been working on similar technology for image-based AI because the EU is not the only market in which people have raised concerns about content provenance and the potential to use AI-generated content to produce misinformation. OpenAI already applies other content provenance signals to AI-generated images, audio, and video. In keeping with the letter of the AI Act, OpenAI is now offering a text watermarking approach called textGrain [PDF] that "adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark." Large language models predict word tokens one at a time from a probability distribution of potential words. By picking a different word to emit periodically – ideally a synonym – the resulting text deviates from the statistical pattern produced by an unbiased model. A watermark detector, which OpenAI is making available only to approved researchers and organizations, should flag that vocabulary divergence. That's the theory, but in practice results vary. The target error rate is one percent, but in short passages of 200 words, the detector may only flag 80 percent of the watermarks, compared to 95 percent in a 400-word passage. The results are also worse in texts that are functional, like passages about math or code, as substitutions are more likely to introduce errors. The textGrain paper does not address the likelihood that a statistically altered word choice might alter the meaning of a given passage. That's a possibility if the algorithm were to alter some salient fact or figure. Anthropic's approach, which also replaces certain output words though using a different algorithm, brings similar risks. In any event, OpenAI's watermark is easily defeated by word substitution. In tests on 400-token passages, swapping out 10 percent of the words with synonyms reduced watermark detection from 92 percent to 66 percent. And when replacing 25 percent of words, the watermark signal could only be detected in 17 percent of cases. events.title: Nvidia-backed start-up Reflection unveils open AI model to rival China offerings
events.summary: The AI model is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks. Reflection AI, founded by ex-Google DeepMind researchers, launched Beam, an open-weight AI model rivaling leading US and Chinese options for business and coding tasks. Beam matches China's GLM-5.2 in reasoning benchmarks and is cost-effective, with more technical details due in October. Backed by Nvidia, Reflection secured major deals with SpaceX and Nebius, supporting US efforts to promote AI exports and counter Chinese tech influence. SAN FRANCISCO – Reflection AI, an artificial intelligence start-up from two former Google DeepMind researchers, has unveiled a new open-weight model that it says rivals leading options in the US and China. The model, called Beam, is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks while costing less than many competitors, the company said on Oct 5. It said Beam scores comparably on advanced reasoning benchmarks to GLM-5.2, a flagship open model from China’s Z.AI. Reflection intends to release more technical details about the model later in October. While China is still widely viewed as behind the US in AI, Chinese developers like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI have gained ground by offering cheaper and customisable open model. Top US firms, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have primarily focused on closed or proprietary offerings as they work to build up their enterprise businesses. Reflection emerged from stealth in 2025 with a focus on developing open AI models. The firm is backed by Nvidia and other investors. It has held talks to raise US$2.5 billion (S$3.2 billion) at a valuation of US$25 billion, the Wall Street Journal previously reported. The start-up has also struck billion-dollar deals with Elon Musk’s SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group to secure computing power to develop its models. The model release stands to boost the American government’s efforts to export the US and its allies’ AI abroad. Earlier in 2026, Reflection was part of a US-brokered deal to build sovereign AI in Korea. Officials are planning to cobble together more of these deals promoting exports of US tech, which are designed to prevent the spread of Chinese alternatives. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Australian consumer confidence plunges to worst level since 1990s after RBA rate rise
events.summary: Key indicator dropped about 20% after the Reserve Bank last month announced the highest interest rates since 2011 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian households are the most persistently pessimistic they have been since the early-1990s recession, after a fourth rate rise this year. Confidence among Australian consumers has plunged about 20% since the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted interest rates to the highest levels since 2011, according to the Westpac–Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index. The survey, conducted between 28 September and 1 October, showed the confidence index dropped by 4.7% to 80.4% in October – the worst level since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict in early April. But for respondents surveyed after the RBA call on 29 September, the index dropped to 67.2% – the lowest level since the late 1990s. That was broadly in line with the weekly ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer survey, which fell about 5% to 67.1 points. Westpac’s head of Australian macro-forecasting, Matthew Hassan, said sentiment had been extremely weak for the longest period since the “disastrous” recession of the early 1990s. “Australian consumers remain stuck in a cost-of-living nightmare that seems to have no end in sight,” Hassan said. “The latest RBA move looks to have badly rattled consumers. Responses over the course of the survey week show a very sharp deterioration after the decision was announced.” Assessments of family finances and buyer sentiment were the biggest categories affected. Expectations about the economic outlook fell less sharply, but assessments about the economy in the next five years were back to lows not seen since August 2020, shortly after Melbourne’s second lockdown and before jobkeeper subsidies were expanded. AMP economist My Bui said the decline was unsurprising given the September rate hike and rising fuel prices. “On our calculation the weekly petrol bill for a typical Australian household has gone up by $20 versus the beginning of the year,” Bui said. “The worry with declining confidence is that it tends to correlate with household spending on a per capita basis: the downtrend in confidence over the past 12 months suggests consumption per person will likely fall further into contraction this year.” Mortgage holders were the most pessimistic home ownership subgroup given rising borrowing costs at 77 index points. Those who own their home outright experienced the largest decline in sentiment in the month, as the housing market downturn extended for a sixth month. Renters were the most optimistic, unchanged at 84.8 points. Hassan said fears of job losses were rising, with unemployment expectations ticking up 1.9% higher. But there are still signs the labour market is holding strong. Citi analysts Josh Williamson and Faraz Syed said “job vacancies have increased to a two-year high of 122 points, which accords with business sentiment expectations of positive employment growth”.

events.title: Irish budget tackles childcare and energy costs
events.summary: Childcare subsidies will be increased in new budget Published 6 October 2026, 06:30 BST The Irish government has used its budget to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs. Taxes on heating oil and gas will be cut and then frozen for the lifetime of the government. Temporary tax cuts on petrol and diesel, which were introduced earlier this year , will be extended. Childcare subsidies will be increased which will be worth up €2,220 (£1,882) per child per year. Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers and Minister for Finance Simon Harris Finance Minister Simon Harris and Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers announced a budget package worth a total of €8.65bn (£7.33bn), €7bn (£5.93bn) on spending and €1.65bn (£1.40bn) in tax changes. Harris raised the threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax from €44,000 to €46,500 (£37,307 to £39,418.05). He said that, alongside other changes, a single person earning €50,000 (£42,395) a year will pay €700 (£593.25) less in personal taxes. Harris added that the government had heard "loud and clear" the importance of an income tax package for middle earners. "People are working hard and doing their best. They need the government to work with them and we get that." Ireland collects more taxes than it spends on services Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services. Harris said the government expects to run a surplus of €6.7bn (£5.7bn) this year and a surplus of €9.5bn (£8.1bn) in 2027. Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments. A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has previously criticised the government for not saving more. Harris said an extra €1bn (£847m) of the surplus would be invested in 2027 on top of the already planned transfer of €4.8bn (£4.1bn). €11m to support cross community projects in NI Other new measures announced on Tuesday include a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK's stock and shares ISA. It will allow people to invest up to €50,000 (£42,395) tax free, with sums above that taxed at a flat rate of 1% a year. There will be a new €15m (£12.7m) fund to help keep rural pubs open, with the details of grants and eligibility to be developed in coming weeks. Chambers restated the government's commitment to fund a range of cross-Irish border projects through the Shared Island Scheme. These include the Narrow Water Bridge and a teaching block at Ulster University in Londonderry. He said there would also be €11m (£9.3m) for the Reconciliation Fund, which supports cross community projects in Northern Ireland and additional money for next year's Belfast Fleadh. events.title: Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
events.summary: Keith Ely remembers the Brunel Centre's heyday but is looking to the future Published 6 October 2026, 06:28 BST The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide. "It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973. Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw. Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling. Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left. That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year . But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space. "It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me." The Debenhams store in the Grafton Centre in Cambridge closed in 2021 In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema. There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre. This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country. So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls? "There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre. "The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet." Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, Before the Brunel Shopping Centre was built in the 1970s, people in Bletchley would travel to Aylesbury or Bedford to shop Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, The centre initially had little natural light, before the roof was replaced with glass Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, In 2021 Milton Keynes City Council was awarded £22.7m from the government's Town Deal Fund to redevelop the site Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, Boots Opticians, the last remaining store in the centre, is already closed on Wednesdays Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE , external found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres. Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres. Dr Kardi Somerfield says centres that have leisure businesses can "extend the day" and attract customers into the evening "It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton. Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds. Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops. "The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open." The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses. Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing. Characters from TV show The Flintstones were at the opening of the Weston Favell Shopping Centre in 1974 But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down. Market Walk in Northampton is t o become a leisure and entertainment space . "Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use. This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton. Footfall – the number of customers entering the building – has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg. "We are still relevant today," he says. "Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got." What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities. Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible. Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store. Silhouette Youth Theatre currently holds sessions in the Emmanuel Church, inside Weston Favell Shopping Centre George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Death of a star may not be game over for the inner solar system after all Google launches first datacenter satellite and research that finds orbiting bit barns can work 4 days ago Boeing's Calamity Capsule gets another shot at the ISS taxi business 7 days ago Starship finally makes orbit but engine trouble cuts the victory lap short 7 days ago Astronomer watches Starlink satellites sinking to build a ‘planetary barometer’ 11 days ago Google's TPUs to catch some rays in orbit next week 11 days ago When yellow dwarf stars like our sun die, they swell to an enormous size and destroy their inner planets by either crushing them with massive gravity or evaporating them with astounding heat. While these suns later settle down to become a white dwarf, the process is nearly always game over for planets in an inner solar system. Or maybe not, according to a paper published on Monday titled “Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf.” As explained by NASA’s Hubble Mission team, the paper’s authors pored over Hubble Space Telescope observations of white dwarf star HS 0209+0832 from 1999. According to the paper, data from those scans “revealed the presence of carbon, aluminum, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere, as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified.” The authors of this paper used new techniques to identify the mystery matter, and concluded that there’s plenty of the element niobium present in what looks like a gas giant orbiting HS 0209+0832. In NASA’s post, co-author Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin, pointed out that “Niobium and other elements heavier than iron are astronomically special because, unlike many common elements, they are not formed in the cores of stars by thermonuclear fusion.” “Instead, these heavy elements can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars. The presence of niobium is a signpost of these ‘death’ throes, and the expulsion of the dying star's innards into space.” Finding niobium is also notable because, as the paper explains, “the canonical rock-forming elements [are] silicon and iron.” The paper explains that its authors compared the material observed at HS 0209+0832 with all known examples of rocky material around white dwarfs, and to all meteorites in our Solar System, but could find “no compositional matches.” That finding suggests that the niobium-rich gas giant at HS 0209+0832 represents both a secondary planet – which are rare – and a body composed of material we’ve not previously seen becoming a planet. It also shows that planets can form close to a star after the hellish red giant phase. Oh, and let’s not forget that HS 0209+0832 is also an exoplanet, a class of body humanity first spotted in only 1992. The paper suggests the niobium gas giant is about the size of Jupiter, but that the white dwarf is blasting away its atmosphere and perhaps creating “a comet-like tail of material that would form a disk around the white dwarf star and fall back on to its surface, leading to Hubble detecting the niobium when studying the star” Co-author Jamie Williams, from the Department of Physics at the University of Warwick, told NASA he thinks the niobium world will stick around. “If the second-generation planet is there, I think it is likely to survive. Eventually the white dwarf will cool and then maintain a consistent temperature, with the planet in its stable habitable zone for millions of years,” Williams said. ® European AI flag bearer Mistral's new open weights model is 'Le Chonk' Oh lawd it is coming ...

events.title: Banks still refusing credit cards, watchdog says
events.summary: The Government of Jersey said whether credit cards were offered to islanders "remains a commercial decision" Published 6 October 2026, 06:23 BST Islanders are still struggling to get credit cards despite personal data changes to make it easier to apply for one, a consumer council has said. The changes which came into force on 30 July meant the government could securely share personal data with UK credit reference agencies, which had been seen as the main barrier to successful applications . However, the Jersey Consumer Council said several providers had still refused applications and called for the government to work closer with businesses and banks. A spokesperson for Jersey's government said it had "engaged with providers throughout this process" and whether products were offered in the island "remains a commercial decision". Carl Walker from the Jersey Consumer Council said credit card companies may need convincing to bring their business back Carl Walker, from Jersey Consumer Council, said credit card companies would need to be reminded of the change which had allowed more information to be shared. "The last time they were involved... Jersey was slamming the door shut, so they have switched off and turned their attention elsewhere," he said. "We're pushing the government to write them an official letter to say this piece of legislation has now changed, Jersey's now open for business... and then leave it up to them whether they decide they to come back or not." Listen to the latest news for Jersey A spokesperson said the government had "successfully delivered a project to share islanders' data with credit reference agencies". "This was a key issue identified by the industry as an obstacle to providing credit cards in Jersey," they said. "It remains a commercial decision for providers to decide whether to offer their products or services, including credit cards, in Jersey. "The government has engaged with providers throughout this process... and will continue to do so." Follow BBC Jersey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: ‘It really hammers people’: Scottish islanders hit by highest diesel prices in UK
events.summary: Inhabitants of the Hebrides and Shetland tell of how fuel costs are putting the squeeze on commuting, services, food and more A s fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas. In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise. While European governments appear to have staved off a US export ban that could have sent prices even higher, in Shetland the lack of competition and the cost of shipping to remote areas have made it the most expensive place in the UK for fuel. The ramifications for island life have been immediate. Adam, 43, who lives in North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, said diesel had reached £2.28 a litre on the island, making his 45-mile round commute particularly expensive. He and his wife have diesel cars that they need for work and transporting their three children. “You accept that things are more expensive, especially food because there’s more distance to travel and we are further from distribution centres. Same with getting things delivered here because you have to drive more miles. But when something like the price of diesel skyrockets, it really hammers people here more than other places around the country,’” he says. In between work and dropping children off with his wife, Adam says they really rack up the miles. To cut costs, Adam says the family is having to buy the cheapest food they can, given that food prices are also dependent on the price of diesel that haulage companies pay. “It’s come down a bit in the last week or so. I never thought I’d look up at a £2.18 diesel price and think: ‘Oh, quick, I better fill up now.’ It’s really bad. Although people think of this place as really tiny, you’re in your car all the time. I average 15,000 miles a year, and my wife does even more because she’s a health visitor. She gets the same mileage as someone who’s a health visitor in the central belt, yet we pay a lot more,” he says. About 26,000 people live in the Outer Hebrides, most on the largest island, Lewis and Harris. Adam says rising prices have also hit accessibility to public services, which are already difficult to reach for islanders. “The Scottish government say they want to help repopulate places like this but in reality, they are not offering much practical support. For example, my daughter had a referral to a paediatrician for a hearing test so I had to take her to Stornoway for that. It involved booking ferries, driving more than 100 miles and staying in a hotel. We can claim some money back from the patient travel scheme but they only offer you £40-£50 for a hotel. Because of the costs getting there, the NHS stops being free at the point of use because we can’t be treated locally,” he says. Bob, a postman who lives in Shetland, said that people in the North Sea archipelago were frustrated by rising fuel prices while also being a hub for the oil and gas industry. “You are resigned to it. It’s always been slightly more expensive than everywhere else, so you have to pay the prices. What can you do? Fuel poverty has always been an issue up here. It’s ironic in a sense given we are near where a lot of the oil and gas arrives from the North Sea. Yet, we are paying higher prices than anyone else. It’s the same with the windfarms,” he says. Bob says that islanders often have no other choice but to drive, especially when getting to work. “Most jobs are in Lerwick so unless you live in town, you need to drive. There is a bus service but people who work don’t use it much because it’s difficult to make their hours,” he says. “I only ever drive small cars. I have a Fiat 500 so it’s not too bad. But an awful lot of people have big 4x4s up here because of the weather. Diesel prices will be having a big impact on them.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ryan, 25, from the Isle of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, says the soaring costs mean many islanders are having to cut back. “A lot of family and friends up here are taking fewer journeys than they would normally outside work. For a lot of people, it’s a case of just going to work and going to the shops. Even those journeys are not short. The Western Isles span 130 miles. South Uist itself is about an hour top to bottom. A lot of us easily get through a few tanks a month on fuel. It’s a lot of the money that’s getting spent up here,” he says. Ryan works in a nearby hotel and is paid close to the minimum wage.

events.title: UK regulator FCA to investigate how it handled Epstein whistleblower who took his own life
events.summary: British banker Simon Andriesz helped to expose alleged ties between late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick A top UK regulator has launched an investigation into how it handled a whistleblower – who highlighted alleged ties between the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick – after he took his own life. The British banker Simon Andriesz died late last month aged 57, the campaign group Transparency Task Force, of which he was a member, confirmed over the weekend. Andriesz had formerly worked as a managing director at BGC Group, the financial brokerage where Lutnick had been chief executive. He had accused the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) of failing to hold his former employer to account for alleged wrongdoing, and had been wrongly told he did not qualify for whistleblower protection. The banker had spent years raising concerns about his former employer: first in regards to accounting irregularities – which he raised internally at BGC in 2016, a year before he was sacked – and then in 2020-21, when he reportedly told the FBI that Lutnick had undeclared business ties with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Lutnick has since said he had no “personal or professional relationship” with Epstein. He was named Donald Trump’s commerce secretary in late 2024. Andriesz, who had been living in Cornwall, later unearthed an email chain in the Epstein files that suggested Lutnick and Epstein had discussed the prospects of a startup business they were both involved in, in 2018. Epstein died in jail in August 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. However, Andriesz told the BBC’s File on 4 Investigates this summer that authorities in the US and UK had failed to hold BGC and its parent company, Cantor Fitzgerald, properly to account, or protect him from potential retaliation. He also later accused the FCA of mistreating whistleblowers, and raised concerns about the toll that whistleblowing had taken on his family, career and health. The FCA had also given Andriesz misleading information, saying he would not qualify for whistleblower protection because his identity had become known. The regulator apologised to him and said that further guidance and training would be provided to its whistleblowing team. The FCA confirmed it had now tasked a new board member to investigate how staff handled Andriesz’s concerns. “We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz’s death,” an FCA spokesperson said. “Our thoughts are with his family and friends. Since expressing our condolences, we’d asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future.” However, the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on investment fraud and fairer financial services is concerned that the FCA is being allowed to “mark its own homework” and called on the regulator to pay an independent party to “forensically and objectively evaluate its handling of whistleblowers”. The APPG’s chair, the Labour MP John McDonnell, said: “It is vital that this time a truly independent and non-conflicted organisation carries out the work needed. If the FCA refuses to respond positively, the APPG will consider all alternatives, including conducting its own call for evidence from whistleblowers who have interacted with the regulator.” Lutnick has not been accused of any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, and has previously said: “I unequivocally condemn the conduct attributed to Jeffrey Epstein and everyone who participated in his illegal activities. The survivors of his crimes deserve our respect and support.” A BGC spokesperson said: “BGC has long disputed Mr Andriesz’s allegations but does not intend to relitigate these matters at this sad time. BGC is sorry to hear this tragic news and expresses our condolences to Mr Andriesz’s family.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org , or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

events.title: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff
events.summary: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it T here’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor Richard E Grant became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, it’s him! Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil. And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, in the Makerfield byelection , without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly last week in Liverpool , and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised much of his own cabinet , an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too. Nigel Farage has been the only one to react with unfettered glee . Reform’s next manifesto is basically now written for him: save Brexit, stop the boats and don’t vote for Restore because it can’t win. Things are more complicated for the Lib Dems and Greens, who, having pitched themselves as the only real pro-Europeans on the left, are now stuck with trying to take credit for pushing Labour into doing the right thing. But it’s the party currently holding its conference in Birmingham that faces the most interesting dilemma. Kemi Badenoch doesn’t mention Brexit much these days – only elected after the referendum, she seems to regard the generational Conservative trauma of that period as history now – and it gets only brief mentions in The Right Way , the 95-page personal essay she says would form the bedrock of a Tory government. In his platform speech on Monday, the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, chose to focus on accusing Burnham of supposedly dragging Britain back to the 1970s, rather than back to 2015. On this they echo much of what’s left of the Tory vote, who are more interested in tax, the costs of doing business, small boats and what exactly Labour has against labradors in pubs than in relitigating the Brexit deal. Yet the Conservatives are still promising to reverse any Labour unravelling of Brexit, regardless of how that affects the economic growth Badenoch simultaneously insists is everything to her. It makes no intellectual sense, which arguably didn’t bother previous Tory leaders. But it’s a mistake for one pitching herself as a rigorous thinker, approaching power with the same robustly worked-through theory of the world as Thatcher in the 1970s. Growth is now Badenoch’s rationale for everything, from scrapping the Environment Agency – accused of being a drag on developers, although that’s precisely what some rural Tory voters like about it – to giving parents earning over £100,000 free childcare (on the grounds that, currently, high earners will cut their working hours rather than lose that nursery place). It’s her defence for some potentially unpopular choices, her alpha and omega. Yet by ignoring the ongoing damage Brexit is doing to trade and GDP, Badenoch is chopping her self-professed growth mission off at the knees. In her 1976 essay The Right Approach , which Badenoch’s treatise consciously echoes, Margaret Thatcher declared that her party “has always been outward-looking, while concerned with the security, the economic interests and the honour of Britain”, and lambasted Labour’s lack of enthusiasm for the then European Community. The context now is obviously different, but Thatcher in 1976 was still a pragmatist arguing for Europe “to concentrate on what is practical and what is attainable”, where Badenoch in 2026 is an ideologue. The Tory brand remains toxic despite its leader’s relative popularity mostly because voters got sick of endless Brexit-related drama consuming Westminster, while none of the practical benefits materialised. There’s no point dangling policies such as free childcare for bankers over the remain-voting former Tory shires without acknowledging all that. But if she can’t bring herself to do so, then Badenoch’s next best bet is to let Burnham rescue her party from a dead end of its own making. Though they would never have opened this door, in truth it suits the Tories to let Burnham walk through it, while blaming him for whatever goes wrong.

events.title: World Bank says Middle East economy to contract 2.1% in 2026 due to Iran war
events.summary: The World Bank on Tuesday lowered its 2026 forecast for the economies in the Middle East , saying the region's overall GDP will contract by 2.1 per cent for this year. The revision was the latest downgrade the World Bank has forecast for the region as the Iran war continues to constrain energy supplies. Economists had previously lowered their 2026 forecasts from 3.6 per cent in January to 2.1 per cent in April. Global growth, meanwhile, is projected to slow to 2.5 per cent this year, the World Bank had said in June. The seven-month conflict has affected a wide variety of sectors as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz initially choked off much of the region's energy supplies. This also led to setbacks in tourism, aviation and logistics, with uncertainty in financial markets, the World Bank said in its latest Economic Update for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Menaap). “This conflict is very painful and it has concentrated the losses of the conflict in our region while the global economy and other regions are upgrading their forecasts, and we are downgrading significantly,” Roberta Gatti, Menaap chief economist at the World Bank, said in an interview. Economies in the Gulf Co-operation Council are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue. Economies in the UAE and Saudi Arabia are set to slow from 6.2 and 4.6 per cent in 2025 to minus 1.6 and minus 2 per cent in 2026, respectively, the World Bank said. Qatar is forecast to have its weakest economic performance in five decades, slowing from 1.8 per cent growth in 2025 to minus 20.9 per cent this year after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites. Kuwait's economy is forecast to contract by 14.6 per cent, a downwards revision of 8.2 percentage points from April. The war has hit oil exporters particularly hard, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks across the region. Oil production in the Gulf dropped from its prewar average of 26 million barrels a day to about 16 million in March, the World Bank said. The IMF's PortWatch monitor showed just three tankers moved through the strait in the seven-day moving average ending September 27. “It's a volume story. It's a quantity story for us. It's a price story for the world,” Ms Gatti said. Oman, which is less reliant on the Strait of Hormuz, is the only GCC member projected to experience positive growth this year, at 3.1 per cent. Iraq 's growth prospects also faced a downwards revision of 3.8 percentage points since April with a negative growth rate of 12.4 per cent. Iraq, which is Opec's second-largest producer, depends on oil for about 90 per cent of its government revenue. Iran's economy also expected to shrink by 7.7 per cent in 2026. The World Bank report works on the assumption that the Strait of Hormuz will gradually reopen beginning on December 31. Under this scenario, economic activity in 2027 for the UAE will rebound to 8 per cent, Saudi Arabia by 6.1 per cent, Qatar by 25 per cent, Kuwait by 20.5 per cent and the GCC as a whole by 8.6 per cent. The UAE has embarked on a “ Zero Hormuz ” strategy to diversify its supply chains, while Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West Pipeline to move oil to Yanbu Port on the Red Sea. Oil prices have swung wildly since the onset of the war on February 28, with global benchmark Brent crude trading at about $118 a barrel in March and in May. Saudi Aramco chief Amin Nasser credited the East-West Pipeline for keeping oil prices at about $100 a barrel. Mr Nasser also warned it could take up to two years to refill global inventories that were reduced under emergency measures. He was speaking at an energy conference in London on Monday. Oil importers, by contrast, are expected to fare better in what Ms Gatti described as a “reversal of fortunes” compared to the 2022 energy shock after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The World Bank anticipates Egypt's economic activity to pick up at a 5.1 per cent pace after growing by 4.4 per cent last year. It also raised its 2026 forecast for Morocco by 0.2 percentage points to 4.4 per cent, and 0.7 percentage points for Pakistan at 3.7 per cent. Its projection for Jordan remained unchanged at 2.7 per cent, while Tunisia received a slight downgrade of 2.3 per cent growth, 0.2 percentage points lower than its April forecast. Compounding effect Ms Gatti said the Iran war is placing a compounding effect on economies already mired in conflict, harming recovery prospects and contributing to long-term economic pain. Renewed hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah are reversing Lebanon's economic recovery of 4.2 per cent growth in 2025 to a contraction of 6.4 per cent this year. Forecasts for growth in Afghanistan and Yemen were also lowered to 3 per cent and 1 per cent respectively, while the World Bank anticipates Syria's economy to pick up between 8 and 10 per cent this year. The World Bank estimates GDP growth in the West Bank and Gaza will slow from 4.3 per cent in 2025 to 1.5 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 3 percentage points compared to April. The poverty rate in the area remains an estimated 41.9 per cent. It also said Gaza's economy is still in a state of “near-total collapse” despite the October 2025 ceasefire, owing to flare-ups in tensions, continued restrictions and stalled reconstruction preventing recovery efforts. “There were ongoing fragilities and now we see less humanitarian aid. We see a need to keep the attention,” Ms Gatti said. She said the economic costs of fragility were being compounded by the conflict, with reduced humanitarian aid making it important to maintain attention and investment in affected countries to prevent the consequences from being felt by future generations. AI productivity gains The report also said that, despite the conflict, artificial intelligence remains a key avenue for opportunity in the region. Economists said it could boost the productivity of up to 20 per cent of the region's jobs. The World Bank has previously urged developing countries to quickly adopt AI or risk falling behind on the economic gains it can deliver. It said developing economies can avoid mistakes by adopting available tools, adapting them to local conditions and advancing towards frontier AI development. “Some of the complements that are needed to fit the benefits of AI might not require money, but they require political will and vision. You need regulation and ethical regulation for AI to operate well,” Ms Gatti said.

events.title: Community supermarket opens in shopping centre
events.summary: Gina English from the SEK Community Food Shop in Chatham says the store is open to everyone Published 6 October 2026, 05:54 BST A new community supermarket offering access to affordable and healthy food has opened in a Kent shopping centre. The store run by SEK Community Food Shop welcomed the public to its home on the first floor of The Pentagon Centre in Chatham. Gina English from SEK says the shop is open to all as "in addition to supporting people with food insecurity, people will also be able get wraparound support from us, help with employment, looking at CVs and interview skills. We're also going to help people with budgeting and money management and signposting to other local services". Initial funding to set up the supermarket was provided by Medway Council through the Crisis and Resilience Fund. Shoppers can walk straight into the social supermarket, with no prior booking required, to access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries, including a £1 fruit and vegetable bag. Cost are kept low as the store redistributes surplus food to reduce waste, helping to protect the environment at the same time. SEK already operates two similar stores in Kent. English said: "We've had Ramsgate for about three years, Ashford just for just over a year and across the two shops in the last year alone we saw 55,500 transactions and we were able to save 170 tonnes of perfectly good food from going to waste, so they do work." Rod Taffs and Shirley Graves from Chatham were among the first customers into the newly opened community supermarket Some of the first to experienced the store were Shirley Graves and her partner Rod Taffs who have already filled their basket with bargains. "People want to come down and see what they've got, it's amazing," says Graves. "I've got a box of 20 samosas for £1.50 and a big huge bag of chicken for £6. Times are quite tight at the moment, being pensioners, it's cheap and the chicken is amazing." "That's going to do us three or four meals," adds Taffs. Medway Council leader, Vince Maple, said: "I think most people across Kent and Medway would want to see food not going to waste, so the ability to have good quality food at a reasonable price, helping not just our families and individuals on low incomes but helping all families has got to be a good thing." The shop also has a confidential, soundproofed office pod at the back of the store where customers can seek personal advice and guidance. The SEK Community Food Shop in The Pentagon Centre, Chatham, is open Monday to Saturday between 10:00 and 18:00.
