AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Tells users ‘action required’ – but maybe don’t make that action a Jira ticket, because it has this bug ServiceNow under siege as Atlassian adds to ITSM take-outs May 1, 2026 Atlassian’s new data collection policy protects rich customers while AI eats the rest April 18, 2026 Atlassian gussies up Confluence for the AI era April 9, 2026 OpenAI now gets to decide which type of product assassin it will become March 25, 2026 Atlassian to shed ten percent of staff, because AI March 12, 2026 Atlassian has told its users to patch its datacenter products, pronto, to prevent attackers accessing their files. The Australian collaborationware company on Monday sent users an email that opens with the words “Action required” and points to a security bulletin that explains CVE-2026-21589 . The 9.3-rated arbitrary file access vulnerability is present in the datacenter versions of its Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye products. Atlassian says the vulnerability “allows an unauthenticated attacker to access specific files within the web application root directory in affected versions.” That’s scary because Atlassian warns “In some configurations, there may be sensitive files present that increase your risk.” There’s also some good news in that attackers must know the exact filename and path to exploit the vulnerability, and the mess doesn’t allow anyone to see the contents of a directory. Another piece of good news is that Atlassian has updated its products – so users only need to find a change window in which to upgrade to a safe version of their software. Atlassian advised those who can’t patch ASAP to remove their instances from the internet, if possible. “Instances accessible to the public internet, including those with user authentication, should be restricted from external network access until you can take action,” the company warned. Its advisory also includes mitigations and advice on how to determine if your instances need the fix. Users who made the move from datacenter products to the Atlassian cloud have nothing to do, as Atlassian fixed the flaws in its own SaaS. That state of affairs rather vindicates Atlassian’s 2020 decision to stop developing its low-end server products and require users to shift into its cloud , and last year’s sequel in which it decided to discontinue its datacenter software , too. Atlassian admitted it hasn’t made that migration easy, because it somehow released a lift and shift tool that was worse than an earlier version . In March 2026, Atlassian axed ten percent of staff . The company’s share price was on a year-long slide at the time, as pundits suggested it might fall victim to the SaaSPocalypse, a theory that AI would replace business software. events.title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
events.summary: It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff? T emperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.” I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues. Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan. Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh. And while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”. For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come. Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this “little treat” economy , eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.” While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque. It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs. It was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer. Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.

events.title: Arizona welcomes new Taiwan representative office, rejecting warning from China
events.summary: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an office in Phoenix to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region PHOENIX -- Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an economic and cultural office Monday to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region, despite pressure from the Chinese government to block it. Taiwanese authorities have said the new Phoenix office — their 14th in the United States — will promote collaboration in technology, especially in semiconductor manufacturing, and better serve a growing number of Taiwanese migrants in the city. After the plans for the office were announced in July, Hobbs received two letters from China’s consulate general in Los Angeles asking her to object to the proposal, according to documents the governor’s office shared with The Associated Press. In a July 3 letter, the Chinese authority called the governor to “refute such an attempt by the Taiwan authorities and stop any political gimmicks to harm the friendship and cooperation between China and the State of Arizona.” The stance was reiterated in an Aug. 21 letter. The letters were first reported by Phoenix radio station KJZZ. Hobbs highlighted Arizona’s ties with Taiwan at Monday’s opening. “Every Arizona elected official should show the courage necessary to support the partnership between Arizona and Taiwan,” Hobbs said. “As our economic partnership grows, we are mobilizing every available resource to support Taiwanese companies expanding here in Arizona.” Beijing claims the island as a breakaway province inseparable from China, while Taiwan considers itself separate from the Chinese mainland and has its own government. Scholars say that local-level collaborations with the Chinese government and Taiwan have become more politicized as U.S.-China relations have deteriorated over the years. Taiwan has been increasing its economic footprint in Arizona, with advanced chipmaker Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, pledging $100 billion to expand its operation in northern Phoenix. That brings its total investment in the city to $265 billion, the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history. Around 500 Taiwanese engineers are working to ramp up production at TSMC in Arizona, according to Jason Hsu, a former lawmaker in Taiwan and a senior fellow at the public policy think tank Hudson Institute. Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego also said the city is seeing a sort of “baby boom” in its Taiwanese communities, with several labor and delivery rooms even launching Mandarin language programs. events.title: Moonshot said to be heading for Hong Kong IPO in early 2027 after value hits US$50 billion
events.summary: Moonshot is one of the biggest stars of China’s AI scene, bursting onto the global stage in July with the debut of Kimi K3. HONG KONG – Moonshot AI has closed the final round of private fund raising at a valuation of about US$50 billion (S$64 billion) and is heading towards an initial public offering in Hong Kong in the first quarter of 2027, according to sources familiar with the matter. The Chinese artificial intelligence champion has also begun laying the groundwork to start gauging investor sentiment through early look meetings starting as early as October, some of the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Moonshot is one of the biggest stars of China’s AI scene, bursting onto the global stage in July with the debut of Kimi K3 , an open model that goes nearly toe to toe with leading platforms from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic on some metrics. Its planned IPO is one of the most hotly anticipated deals in Hong Kong , where fund raising driven by the industry is setting fresh records. The company is considering raising up to US$5 billion in the deal, sources have said. It is unclear how the valuation or the IPO timeline may be affected by tighter oversight of China’s AI industry after regulators opened a data security probe into DeepSeek and Moonshot, according to The Information, adding to broader concerns over governance and safety. Deliberations are ongoing and the timing of the IPO might still change, the sources said. Moonshot representatives did not respond to requests for comment during a Chinese public holiday. The company’s valuation has risen steadily through a series of fund-raising efforts. A previous round this summer valued it at US$31.5 billion. Moonshot’s annual recurring revenue (ARR), a gauge of future sales, is expected to rise to US$2 billion by December from US$1 billion now, sources have said. The firm achieved US$300 million of ARR in June, Bloomberg News reported earlier. The Beijing-based AI lab previously added Bank of America as overall coordinator for the transaction alongside sponsor banks China International Capital, Deutsche Bank and Goldman Sachs Group, sources said previously. The company has filed confidentially for the IPO , they said. Founded in early 2023 by Yang Zhilin, a former Tsinghua University professor who previously worked at Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google, Moonshot counts Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and 5Y Capital as its backers. events.title: Oprah-backed True Food Kitchen files for bankruptcy after expansion
events.summary: Oprah Winfrey had decided to invest in True Food Kitchen and joined the board after dining in its Palo Alto, California, location. True Food Kitchen, backed by Oprah Winfrey, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy due to management turnover, Covid-19 impacts, and a cyclospora outbreak, closing a dozen locations. The chain plans to recapitalise or sell, has secured a US$20 million bankruptcy loan, and ended its ghost kitchen delivery strategy. Founded in 2008 with a wellness focus, remaining locations continue serving health-conscious food with natural ingredients amid restructuring efforts. True Food Kitchen, a health food focused restaurant chain that counts American media mogul Oprah Winfrey among its investors, has filed for bankruptcy after struggling with management turnover and lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic. The company said in court papers that it had closed a dozen locations after filing for Chapter 11 protection on Oct 4 and will seek to either recapitalise or sell the business. The chain said it grappled with “significant management turnover, which resulted in frequent changes to expansion strategy, brand direction and menu offering”. The chain has sought permission to end leases in Miami, New Jersey, Southern California, Columbus, Ohio, New Orleans, Chicago, Bethesda, Maryland, Reston, Virginia, Scottsdale, Arizona and Long Island, New York. True Food Kitchen’s advisers have already entered into separate transactions for certain unexpired leases, chief restructuring officer Nathan Cook said in a court filing on Oct 5. Winfrey decided to invest in the restaurant and joined the board after dining in its Palo Alto, California, location, former True Food Kitchen chief executive Christine Barone said in a 2018 interview with Bloomberg. Barone now leads the Dutch Bros Coffee chain; Jeff Chandler was appointed CEO of True Food Kitchen in July. In 2022, True Food Kitchen announced a US$100 million (S$127.9 million) investment round led by new investors HumanCo and Manna Tree and support from Centerbridge Partners. A True Food Kitchen spokeswoman said on Oct 5 that Winfrey remains a minority investor and that Centerbridge is no longer a shareholder in the company. Like most restaurants, Covid-19 era lockdowns significantly impacted True Food Kitchen at a time it was expanding. To offset the loss of in-person dining, the chain used some of its locations as “ghost kitchens” and opened one off-site kitchen for delivery service, only, Cook said in the filing. The strategy, which has since ended, impaired staffing and the dining experience at its restaurants, he said. A True Food Kitchen lawyer told a bankruptcy judge on Oct 5 that the cyclospora outbreak in July “also didn’t help”. True Food Kitchen has lined-up a US$20 million Chapter 11 loan to help fund operations during the bankruptcy. The financing is being provided by an affiliate of HumanCo. The brand was founded in 2008 by wellness author Andrew Weil, who has appeared on Oprah’s talk-show, and restaurateur Sam Fox. True Food Kitchen’s remaining locations are open and serve items that are cooked without seed oil, grass-fed beef, pasture-raised eggs and antibiotic-free chicken, according to court papers. events.title: 'Can I be in the UAE after overstaying my visit visa?'
events.summary: Question : Can a telecoms company impose a travel ban over an unpaid bill? I owe a telecoms company money and haven't paid it for months. I have been sent a message saying that I owe Dh2,930 and that my account is now 190 days overdue. It also said: “We hereby inform you that legal proceedings may be initiated to recover the outstanding amount.” The message was from a credit management company. Can they make a case against me and put a travel ban on me for this? Is there any other action they can take? JC, Abu Dhabi Answer : For an unpaid telecom debt of Dh2,930, a full court case is unlikely, but JC can still face consequences. The account has probably already been cut off, and the company will follow up as he owes it money. Companies can pursue debts in court but, for in this case litigation costs would be disproportionate relative to the amount owed. A travel ban will not happen. Under Article 324 of the UAE Civil Procedure Law (Federal Decree Law No 42 of 2022), a creditor – a person or company that is owed money – can only apply for a travel ban against a debtor if the debt is Dh10,000 or more. Below that threshold, a civil travel ban cannot be issued, regardless of the risk of a person leaving the country without settling their debts. It is common for UAE companies to hand over small debts to collection agencies. That will lead to regular telephone calls, emails and even WhatsApp messages. These companies are licensed and regulated, and there are rules that they must follow. The agency must not overstep by making repeated calls designed to intimidate rather than to communicate, as that constitutes harassment under UAE law. They are only allowed to make contact between 9am and 8pm, and must not disclose information to any third party. That includes calling a place of work and telling anyone the call is about a debt. If the collection agency breaks these guidelines, a complaint can be made, first to the telecoms company, but if that doesn’t stop it, then to the Central Bank of the UAE. JC needs to start making repayments in order to stop follow-up calls and messages. Non-payment of any debt will affect a person’s UAE credit record . This will affect a person's ability to borrow and open financial accounts. Since the change in legislation this year, landlords can now ask for confirmation of a credit score, which can also affect a person's ability to rent a home. Q : I have overstayed my visit visa after my employer failed to arrange a work permit. What can I do? I have a question about overstaying a visit visa. I came to work for a company, and although the team promised me a visa, it never happened. I don’t have a contract, and they have now said they do not want me to work for them any more. What can I do about this? I want to find another job and stay in the UAE. Will I get in trouble or have to pay a fine? MP, Dubai A : The important point here is that MP has been working illegally since arriving in the UAE. From the outset, the employer should have given MP a proper offer of employment and a labour contract, and applied for a residence visa and a work permit. As this did not happen, the company has been employing MP illegally, so she has been working illegally. Sadly, this means that she has no protection under UAE law. This means that MP is unable to make a legal complaint against the company, even if it has broken the law. No doubt the employer will know that this is not permitted, but the company can be reported for breaking the law. Any company that takes on staff without a visa can be fined up to Dh50,000 and may have difficulty obtaining visas in the future. As MP has been in the UAE without a valid visa, MP will have overstay fines. Since February 2026, the UAE has unified overstay fines across all visa types and emirates. They are now the same for all visas, whether tourist, visit or residence visas, and there is no variation by emirate. The fine is Dh50 per day. If an overstay exceeds 30 days, an additional exit permit, known as an “outpass”, at a cost of Dh250 to Dh300, including base and service fees, is required before leaving the country. It is possible to pay the overstay fines and stay in the UAE without leaving the country, provided a new employer initiates the visa process immediately. If not, MP will need to leave and return on an employment entry permit from a new employer. MP should visit an Amer centre, a division of the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs, for advice and to find out how much MP owes. Once the overstay fine has been settled, MP can find a new job and be employed with a visa in order to stay legally in the UAE. events.title: Ukraine claims to have taken out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity
events.summary: Ukraine said long-range strikes have put more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity out of action KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine says its long-range strikes have neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces during its 4 1/2-year-old invasion. The Defense Ministry said late Sunday that recent strikes on refineries in cities, including Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran, had disabled 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified. Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their aerial assaults as progress along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line has largely ground to a halt. Ukraine has launched repeated attacks on refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict gasoline sales. Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact, President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” Putin told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said analysts from Ukraine’s intelligence services, the General Staff and the Defense Ministry had assessed the strikes' effects. “Fifty-one percent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings. Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory,” he said. Russia has historically been the world’s third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude, after the U.S. and China. Some of Russia’s 32 refineries have been hit as many as 15 times since the start of the war, and one refinery has been hit every three days in recent months, creating a cycle of damage and emergency repairs that could degrade units long term, according to the International Energy Agency. Ukrainian strikes have also increasingly targeted the more complex equipment that removes impurities from fuel, which takes months to repair. The IEA says diesel output has fallen by about 30%, and drivers have had to wait up to 40 hours to fill up at gasoline stations. Russian refiners have tried to compensate by delaying scheduled maintenance and bringing mothballed units back online. Another response has been to lower fuel quality standards to maintain gasoline supplies, which risks damage to engines and pollution control equipment. The Kremlin has also banned diesel exports, pushing global prices higher and prompting U.S. President Donald Trump on Sept. 13 to urge Ukraine to stop hitting refineries. A Russian attack with a guided aerial bomb killed at least three people and wounded 39 others, including three children, in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv on Monday, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said. “There may be people under the rubble of the residential building that was hit. A search and rescue operation is underway,” Terekhov wrote on his Telegram channel. An earlier Russian drone attack on the city's Industrialnyi district also killed one person, Terekhov said late Sunday. Vehicles and an administrative building were set alight and apartment buildings were damaged, he said. Another person was also killed in a separate Russian attack on the Sloviansk community in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, said Vadym Liakh, head of the Sloviansk city military administration. He urged residents not to wait for a mandatory evacuation order but to leave the area. Iran live updates: Saudi Arabia says 2 of its airports were damaged in strikes Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Ukraine’s air force reported that Russia launched 205 drones overnight into Monday, with 172 shot down or suppressed. Russia’s Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that it had struck an electrical substation in the Kharkiv region, in addition to energy and port infrastructure and maritime vessels used by Ukraine's military elsewhere in the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone attack caused a fire on board a commercial vessel that later sank in the Black Sea . Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said. In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy described the attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters. He said the vessel was Turkish-owned and carrying corn. Russia did not immediately comment on the incident. Ukraine has struggled in recent weeks to fend off Russia’s intensified aerial attacks on cities that include ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones .

events.title: Asian shares track Wall Street higher, Treasury yields near multi-decade highs
events.summary: MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 0.2%, while Japan’s Nikkei gained 0.7%. European stock futures climbed 0.5%. SYDNEY – Asian stocks rose on Oct 6 after a tech-fuelled rally lifted the Nasdaq to a record close , with a retreat in oil prices offering further support even as longer-dated Treasury yields hovered near multi-decade highs. The euro languished near 17-month lows after briefly touching US$1.116 overnight, pressured by mounting fiscal concerns in France. Investors dumped French government bonds after an underwhelming budget, while political uncertainty deepened after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election . Brent crude was little changed at US$100 a barrel after losing 1.9% overnight as exports from the Middle East increased and the Group of Seven nations pledged to boost supplies. Nasdaq futures edged up 0.2% and S&P 500 futures rose 0.1%. The Nasdaq notched up a record close overnight, buoyed by softer-than-expected jobs data that dampened expectations for a rate hike from the Federal Reserve in October. Artificial intelligence heavyweight Nvidia climbed 2.1%, reaching a record-high close and boosting its market value to $5.76 trillion. “The rally in the market was tech-led once again, with the marginal easing of interest rate uncertainty along with a slight moderation in geopolitical risk allowing market participants to focus on the extraordinary earnings growth being delivered by AI names,” said Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital.com. The third-quarter earnings season kicks off next week. Goldman Sachs estimated consensus forecasts point to 27% growth in S&P 500 earnings last quarter, with more than half that growth from companies benefiting from AI infrastructure spending. Latin American markets also climbed, led by a rally in Brazilian stocks and the real currency, after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed poll predictions in the first round of the presidential election and advanced to a run-off against leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The relentless climb in Treasury yields continued even as markets scaled back bets for an interest rate rise in October from the Federal Reserve to just 23% from 71% a week ago, after top policymakers stressed the need for more data before tightening again. US 10- and 30-year Treasury yields hit fresh 24-year highs overnight, capping a steady climb since mid-August driven by inflation and debt concerns. An ISM survey showed a measure of prices paid by services businesses for inputs jumped to the highest level in more than four years. The 10-year Treasury yield was steady in Asia at 5.3089%, after climbing 3 basis points overnight to hit 5.3493%, the highest since 2002, while 30-year yields held at 5.6622%, having briefly reached 5.7029% overnight. The sell-off in French bonds calmed a little, with the premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over safer German debt narrowing to 137 basis points on Oct 5. The euro nursed losses at US$1.1215, after falling as much as 0.8% to US$1.116 overnight, its weakest since May 2025. It traded at 177 yen, having been down for seven straight sessions, around the lowest since November 2025. “Deep divisions in France’s parliament raises the risk that the proposed fiscal consolidation is diluted or that the government faces a no-confidence vote,” said Joseph Capurso, head of international economics at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “EUR/USD will likely test support at 1.1109.” That kept the US dollar firm, with the US dollar index at 102.2 after a weekly rise of 0.9%. Spot gold was little changed at US$4,141.31 an ounce. REUTERS

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Firecracker MicroVMs, which started at AWS, seem to be the problem Trump Mobile customers' data dumped - and some never even received their gold device 2 hours ago Microsoft extends the Outlook naughty step with two more file types 4 hours ago Zombie instructions on carefully constructed web pages could trick GitHub Copilot CLI into sharing secrets 6 hours ago Asos app delivers a data leak threat instead of fast fashion 7 hours ago Denmark's ID register spills more people's details than the country has residents 7 hours ago Linux KVM, the hypervisor favoured by hyperscale clouds, apparently has a full VM escape bug. That nasty news came from security researcher Paulos Yibelo, who on X shared a screenshot of a bug bounty award he won for discovering what he described as “Full VM escape zeroday (guest>host root in industry standard hypervisors)!” The bug bounty Yibelo participated in is run by Vercel, a company that provides MicroVMs as sandboxes for AI agents to work inside. The company’s Sandbox uses Firecracker MicroVMs, a technology created by AWS , which relies on Linux KVM – the kernel level hypervisor in Linux. Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch named KVM as the hypervisor identified by Yibelo. “We’ve confirmed a KVM 0day through our Vercel Sandbox bounty program. Affecting the industry’s gold standard solution for Linux virtualization,” he wrote. And that’s all the info that has made it into the public view at this time. The Register can find no chat on relevant mailing lists. We have asked Rauch and Yibelo for additional details. Hopefully, we don’t hear from either of them for days or weeks, for two reasons. One is that guest-host escapes are the nightmare virtualization scenario because they mean whoever runs a guest VM could take over an entire server, and perhaps gain the ability to control other guests. The other is that KVM is astoundingly prevalent: AWS and Google both use it to power their public clouds. Enterprise virtualization players Nutanix, HPE, and Proxmox also rely on KVM. And of course KVM is also in Firecracker, which is open source and could therefore be running in all sorts of places. Whatever Yibelo discovered therefore very much needs a responsible disclosure process, because if hints about the flaw emerge it could allow attackers to do a lot of damage. Once a fix is found, the next question is whether implementing it will require disruption or downtime. It’s possible to hot-patch KVM, and to migrate live VMs from vulnerable hosts to machines running a patched version of Linux. Hopefully those techniques will work. This might be the second nasty bug discovered in KVM this year, after the so-called Januscape flaw. events.title: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates
events.summary: Candidates interviewing for certain teams at OpenAI will now go through a new step in the process, known as the “mission interview.” The company is currently introducing it as a new pilot program, starting with the marketing and human resources teams, OpenAI told Fortune on Monday. The goal is to give job candidates a dedicated space to talk about how they will contribute to OpenAI’s mission, which is “to ensure that artificial general intelligence (AGI) benefits all of humanity.” Specifically, OpenAI wants to gauge how candidates think, including their judgment and ability to weigh tradeoffs—traits that are increasingly critical as artificial intelligence companies work to control technology with great benefits as well as potential dangers. There is no “right” answer, an OpenAI representative said; skepticism and disagreement are welcome, as is intellectual diversity. The person conducting the interview will be from a team separate from whatever role the candidate is applying for. OpenAI is also creating a training program that interested employees can complete to become certified to conduct the interviews, though the program is just starting to ramp up. The evolution in OpenAI’s recruiting process is a marker of the company looking to standardize its evaluations as it matures and balloons in size. The company, which has roughly 8,000 employees worldwide, has 830 open roles as of this writing. By standardizing the process, OpenAI aims to have a consistent measure to evaluate new employees across teams. Many tech companies, including Meta and Amazon , have their own version of a “mission interview,” which is somewhat akin to a test of cultural fit. For example, Amazon employees can be trained as “bar raisers”—interviewers from outside the hiring team, who assess whether a candidate meets Amazon’s companywide “Leadership Principles.” In Anthropic’s version, interviewers reportedly test if candidates are joining the AI lab for its mission or the money, according to Axios. Jobs at leading AI companies are incredibly lucrative, with many positions at OpenAI currently offering salaries of over $300K (and more with stock included). One software engineer with six years of experience reportedly received an offer from OpenAI for $935,000 total compensation, with a $385,000 base, and $2.2 million of restricted stock units (RSUs) vesting over four years, according to anonymous professional network Blind. Anthropic allegedly offered a candidate $620,000 in total compensation, according to another Blind post. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Singapore’s DayOne files for US IPO joining data centre rush
events.summary: DayOne Data Centers is part of a wave of firms in the sector eyeing IPOs as soon as 2026. DayOne Data Centers, headquartered in Singapore, filed for a US IPO to capitalise on strong demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, aiming to raise up to US$5 billion with a US$20 billion valuation. The company reported a net loss of US$81.9 million on US$512 million revenue for the six months ended June 30, expanding rapidly across Asia Pacific and Europe with over 1.5 gigawatts booked since 2022. Backed by major investors like Coatue Management, Hillhouse, SoftBank Vision Fund, and Citadel, DayOne operates in multiple countries and plans to list on Nasdaq under the symbol DODC, amid a wider data centre IPO wave. NEW YORK – DayOne Data Centers filed for a US initial public offering, setting the Singapore-headquartered firm up to capture investors’ resilient demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The data centre operator had a net loss of US$81.9 million (S$104.8 million) o n revenue of US$512 million for the six months ended June 30, compared with a net loss of US$13.5 million on revenue of US$151.5 million in the corresponding period a year earlier, according to its filing on Oct 5 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Once an international affiliate of Chinese data centre operator GDS Holdings, DayOne was known as GDS International before rebranding in 2025. The company filed confidentially in August for a US IPO that may seek to raise as much as US$5 billion at a valuation of about US$20 billion, Bloomberg News has reported. The data centre operator is part of a wave of firms in the sector eyeing IPOs as soon as 2026. Others include Switch, which is seeking a valuation approaching US$50 billion including debt, and London-based Nscale, which could raise as much as US$3 billion, people familiar with the matter have said. DayOne closed a US$4.5 billion Series C funding round in June, led by its biggest shareholders, Coatue Management and Hillhouse, and also including new backers Achi Capital Partners and the Indonesian Investment Authority. Since its inception in 2022, DayOne has secured more than 1.5GW of bookings for capacity in Asia-Pacific and Europe. Along with GDS, which remains an investor, its backers also include SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. DayOne is running or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong, Japan, Finland and Spain, its filing shows. events.title: S’pore beauty salons bank on value-adds, convenience as RTS spells more competition from JB
events.summary: Crystal Lee, CEO of Peachy Skin Bar, recently renovated the salon with pink walls and an open lounge area where customers can enjoy a free drink. SINGAPORE – Lower prices have long drawn Singapore customers to beauty salons across the Causeway, and this is only set to increase when the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link opens in 2027 . With the journey between Woodlands North and Bukit Chagar taking just minutes, the new service could lead to Singapore consumers making 51% more round trips to JB a year, with beauty services listed as one of the top spending categories, a study released in July found. In anticipation of this, some salons in Singapore have opted to improve their in-store experience and take their services directly to clients’ homes, betting that convenience and service quality will help them retain customers. One example is Singapore facial salon Peachy Skin Bar, which offers facial treatments priced between $180 and $500. “Instead of competing purely based on price, I’m finding ways to differentiate my facial business from other competitors in Singapore and Johor Bahru,” said owner Crystal Lee. Her salon in Queen Street, founded in 2019, was recently renovated with pink walls and an open lounge area where customers can enjoy a free drink. “The lounge is so that customers won’t feel trapped in a small room. I wanted my salon to resemble a summer destination where people can come to unwind,” said Lee, adding that her business is focusing on the overall customer experience rather than just the service itself. As a value-add, she has also trained her staff to give customers a shoulder massage between the stages of a facial, rather than leave them alone while waiting for the next step. She noted that even before the RTS came into the picture, competition from JB had always existed, and that building good relationships with her customers has kept them coming back to her salon despite the higher price. Asked if she would consider opening an outlet in JB, Lee said that she prefers to observe the market first. “Opening an outlet in JB would require a lot of money and logistics. I’m not a hasty person, so I prefer to focus on my Singapore outlet for now,” she said. Still, she noted that customers are now more price sensitive and unpredictable. “The RTS intensifies the convenience factor, but we can’t predict how they will behave once it opens. We can only brace ourselves,” she said. Other local beauty businesses are also upping their game by doubling down on the Singapore market. Eyelash salon Perky Lash, which has four salons in Singapore, has operated an outlet in Johor Bahru City Square mall since 2024. “Prices at our JB outlet are 20 to 30 per cent lower than our Singapore outlets,” said founder Jasmin Tay, adding that 80% of its customers are Singaporeans. But rather than opening a second outlet in JB, Perky Lash plans to give its customers here less reason to make the trip across the Causeway. In April, it launched a home visit service here, where staff offer lash services in homes, offices and even hospitals. Jasmin Tay, CEO of Perky Lash, has launched a home visit service in Singapore, where staff offer eye-lash services in homes, offices and even hospitals. “Singaporean customers are very time-starved. Even by opening more outlets, our reach to customers who may not have time to travel to us is limited. With home visits, we hope to broaden our customer base,” said Tay. She added that lashes are a regular-maintenance beauty service rather than a one-off service. “Customers tend to stick to the lash artists they already know and trust,” said Tay. “They value trust and consistency, rather than just the price.” Shiyun Teo, founder of Picasso Hair Studio, which opened in 2014, said that as competition from across the Causeway intensifies, businesses here must give customers compelling reasons beyond price to choose them. Shiyun Teo, founder of Picasso Hair Studio, reckons that convenience and time will play an important role in attracting customers. “We don’t have any immediate plans to open in Johor Bahru, although I wouldn’t completely rule it out in the future,” said Teo. Like Tay, she reckons that convenience and time will play an important role in attracting customers. “Our Novena outlet, for example, is surrounded by condominiums and tuition centres. We have parents who drop their children off for tuition and use that time to get their hair done,” Teo said. “For these customers, maximising their time can sometimes be more important than saving money. “Even with the RTS making JB more accessible, there is still travelling time involved, so I don’t think the decision to cross the Causeway will be purely about comparing prices.” Teo said that choosing a local hair studio gives customers the assurance that their salon and stylist are nearby should any adjustments be needed, saving them another trip across the border.

events.title: Musk is a trillionaire again as SpaceX claws back post-IPO slump
events.summary: Elon Musk's fortune jumped by US$65 billion (S$83.2 billion) on Oct 5 to US$1.04 trillion. Elon Musk's fortune rose by US$65 billion to US$1.04 trillion as SpaceX and Tesla shares increased, making him a trillionaire again for the first time in three months. SpaceX shares gained 13% since October start, Tesla rose 6.7%, driven by optimism and strong quarterly sales from Tesla. Morgan Stanley called SpaceX a cheap play in space and AI sectors, boosting investor confidence and contributing to Musk's wealth recovery after a previous slump. The fortune of the world’s richest person jumped by US$65 billion (S$83.2 billion) on Oct 5 to US$1.04 trillion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as the value of his stakes in SpaceX and Tesla rose. SpaceX shares are up 13% since the start of October while Tesla has gained 6.7%. It marks the first time in three months that the 55-year-old tech mogul’s fortune has required 13 numerals. He became the world’s first trillionaire in June when SpaceX surged in the wake of its record-breaking initial public offering, but quickly lost that crown as shares then slumped on concerns about the company’s sky-high valuation. As at late July, Musk’s US$600 billion-plus wealth decline from its peak exceeded the net worth of anyone who had ever been on Bloomberg’s list of the world’s 500 richest people, other than Musk himself. The latest gains have been fuelled by renewed optimism at both companies. On Oct 5 , analysts at Morgan Stanley called SpaceX one of the cheapest ways to play “the strong optionality” of the space and intelligence sector, adding to a rally in which shares of the space, artificial intelligence and social media company have rebounded 58% from an August low. And last week, Tesla reported better-than-expected sales for the third quarter. Musk’s stake in SpaceX and Tesla makes up more than 98% of his net worth, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index. events.title: Five reasons India's stock market is sinking even when its economy is growing
events.summary: India has one of the world's worst performing major equity markets in 2026 Published 6 October 2026, 00:13 BST India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions. But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks. The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters. Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years. On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research. It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall. Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals. This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too. Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market. India imports over 90% of its crude requirements Persistent energy shocks due to Middle East conflict Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return. "This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins." India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz. While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters. With oil prices rising, inflation is going up and, as a result, interest rates are on the rise globally. The effective yield on US government bonds is above 5%, or at near 25-year highs. These are often considered risk-free investments. As a result, foreign money tends to leave riskier emerging market assets such as Indian equities and chase safer investments like US bonds when interest rates rise. For foreign investors, the problem of muted returns has been compounded by a weaker rupee. In currency-adjusted dollar terms, they have suffered because of the fall in the Indian currency. The Nifty has delivered just 6% annualised dollar returns over the past decade - hardly attractive, especially in comparison with several other competing markets. Indian stocks are still expensive relative to their earnings compared to other emerging markets Indian stocks are cheaper, but still relatively expensive Stock valuations have been another major concern. The market correction over the last two years has reduced the premium that Indian stocks held over their emerging market competitors. "Stocks are cheaper than they have been on average for the last ten years," says Shyamsunder, adding that the premium that Indian shares commanded over other emerging economies has shrunk substantially in the past few years. However, they are still expensive relative to their earnings, especially since companies in countries such as South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from a huge boom in artificial intelligence (AI) which has pushed up their profits. In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story. "Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition.

Now the French multinational is cashing in on its good fortunes to cement its place as a key provider of industrial power and datacenter infrastructure with the $22.6 billion acquisition of American industrial software company PTC. Founded in 1985, PTC made a name for itself developing software for computer-aided design, plus lifecycle management tools for industrial products and applications. The all-cash deal, announced on Monday, positions Schneider Electric to capitalize on the proliferation of datacenters used to train and serve AI models at scale. Since ChatGPT kicked off the AI arms race in late 2022, datacenter design and power requirements have changed considerably. Forty-kilowatt air-cooled racks have given way to 250kW liquid-cooled systems that need much denser power delivery and thermal management systems, all of which need to work together. In light of the growing complexity and supply chain challenges facing datacenter deployments, Schneider has made several strategic acquisitions which expanded its role in bit barn development. In late 2024, not long after Nvidia unveiled its first all-liquid-cooled rack designs, Schneider invested roughly $850 million on a 75 percent stake in Motivair, one of the leading producers of cold plates, rack manifolds, coolant distribution units (CDUs) and rear-door heat exchangers required to support the widespread adoption of liquid-cooled servers. The company is expected to acquire the remainder of Motivair sometime in 2028. As Schneider's role in the datacenter has grown, users of its kit have more products to manage across their lifecycles. Buying PTC expands Schneider's lifecycle management offerings and introduces key design capabilities to its offerings. PTC isn't Schneider's only datacenter-centric acquisition this year. Back in June, the company paid $3.1bn for industrial data operations vendor Cognite. Speaking to investors on Monday, Schneider CEO Olivier Blum suggested that owning PTC and Cognite would enable the company to inject software-defined automation into power systems early in their development, improving their efficiency in the process. Datacenters are one of Schneider's initial targets. "We believe that at the design stage, it is super important that you can help your customer to design both product, machine, processes and energy system. This is where we see CAD engineering as a very critical part of the portfolio," Blum said, according to a transcript of his remarks to investors. events.title: Inside the transgender rights fight injecting chaos into Democrats' midterm efforts
events.summary: An intra-party debate over how best to deflect Republican attacks on transgender issues has Democrats angrily sniping at each other just weeks out from the midterm elections. Why it matters: This is not the position Democrats hoped to be in two years after their 2024 election loss , which many in the party attributed to being outflanked by GOP messaging on trans issues. "People feel you need to respond in some way to some of these attacks because people didn't do it two years ago," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a co-chair of the Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, told Axios. "But you also need to realize what we're winning on right now," Pocan added, saying Democratic candidates need to strike "a balance." "Silence is deadly, and I think we played that out in 2024," said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at the centrist think tank Third Way, citing polling that found most voters believed Democrats "thought there should be no rules in sports, no rules around health care." Driving the news: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) set off a firestorm in her district and on Capitol Hill in September by stating in a direct-to-camera ad that she "voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools." "Parents know what's best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls' sports," Kaptur said in the spot — a response to an ad from Republican Derek Merrin that said she "voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports." Multiple county parties condemned the ad — particularly the reference to transgender girls as "boys" — and urged Kaptur to take it down. One LGBTQ+ group, the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, said in a statement there is "no difference" between Kaptur and Merrin because they are "both united against the LBTQIA+ community." What they're saying: "The ads were deeply offensive to the Equality Caucus and the broader LGBTQ community that we represent," said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the caucus' political arm, Equality PAC. He told Axios: "The Equality Caucus is not going to stand by passively and allow anyone to scapegoat the trans community. It is a red line for us." Equality PAC "is absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time," the group said in a separate statement to Axios, calling Kaptur's language "unacceptable." What we're hearing: Kaptur's colleagues also privately communicated their disgust with the ad to her office, multiple House Democrats familiar with the matter told Axios. The lawmakers predicted there will be in-person conversations with Kaptur when the House returns in November, especially if she wins her election. "Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls' sports stay fair," said Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer. "She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor." Zoom out: It's not just Kaptur. Democratic House candidates Blake Gendebien of New York and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, and Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, have put out ads featuring similar rhetoric. Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) released an ad last week in which he said there are "real concerns about fairness and safety" and that "states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls." That ad, like Kaptur's, raised eyebrows privately among LGBTQ+ House Democrats, though none have called him out publicly for it. The other side: Centrist groups and lawmakers say the party has to be realistic about districts like Kaptur's, which President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024. "Marcy Kaptur and Don Davis are doing the most important work in Democratic politics: winning Trump districts," said Liam Kerr, cofounder of centrist group Welcome PAC. Kerr argued attacks from LGBTQ+ groups will only help swing-district Democrats: "Taking the 20% side of an 80/20 issue may be bad politics, but elevating the big winners repudiating you is even worse advocacy." Between the lines: "Our latest [research] showed that anti-trans attacks take about 8 points off of the Democratic vote if you just let it sit out there," Erickson, the Third Way official, told Axios. "But there are ways to respond that get you back up 10 to 12 to 14 points," she continued. "There are a bunch of different ways to say it ... just being clear that there need to be rules. Not laws, but rules." "When it comes to health care, that parents, not politicians, should be in charge of decisions about their kids' health care." The bottom line: Centrists and LGBTQ+ Democrats alike say a careful balance can and should be struck. Several lawmakers pointed to Senate hopefuls James Talarico and Sherrod Brown as examples for deftly maneuvering on this issue. Erickson said "calling transgender girls 'boys' ... is not respectful" and that candidates "don't have to do it. There's better ways to talk about this."

events.title: Budding rocket scientists put designs to the test in outback competition
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Students launch designs in Australian Universities Rocket Competition at White Cliffs The students design and build their rockets from scratch. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) Domestic and international students take part in the Australian Universities Rocket Competition in outback NSW. Hundreds of competitors travelled to a remote sheep station to launch their designs several kilometres high. Organisers are hoping the competition continues to grow. On a remote sheep station in outback New South Wales, rockets are being launched kilometres into the air. About 20 teams of students have travelled from across Australia, New Zealand and as far away as India to compete in the third Australian Universities Rocket Competition (AURC) at White Cliffs. Jennifer He says students compete to get nearest to different altitude goals. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) The teams are working in partnership with sponsors and companies operating in the aerospace, engineering, defence and university sectors. AURC event director Jennifer He says the teams design and build their rockets from scratch. "They're performing all the verification and analysis on them … some are even making their parts in-house at their universities," she said. "They're developing … their technical skills, but also their organisational [skills], the interpersonal and the way that they connect with each other." Students watch to see if a rocket's parachute successfully deploys. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) University of Queensland student Thomas Molesworth said it was great to see international teams involved in this year's event. "As much as we can model and simulate, there's really no telling how it will perform on the pad," he said. "This is a really good way to apply some of those skills that I've learnt in class to real engineering challenges before moving in the workforce full time. Students from the University of Technology Sydney rocketry team were a bit nervous ahead of the launch. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) Most of the teams spent at least a year designing their rockets. University of Technology Sydney mechanical engineering student Matthew Sutcliffe, 23, is competing for the second time at White Cliffs. "Ever since I was a kid I'd dreamed of working with rockets and space. It's definitely my passion," he said. According to UTS data the team's rocket came within 40 feet (12.2 metres) of the 10,000-feet (3,048m) goal. "All the nerves that were building up to it and just the relief after a perfect flight — it … just made my whole day," he said. More than a dozen rockets were successfully launched. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) Located more than 1,000 kilometres north-west of Sydney, White Cliffs is an ideal location for launches, according to Endeavour Aerospace operations director Liam Grieve. He said clear airspace and being "14 kilometres from anyone" ensured safety. "It is rocket science, at the end of the day, and if anything was to go wrong the area can be contained," Mr Grieve said. "There are 1,000 things that need to go right and if any one of them go wrong then we have a site that needs to be contained and only those here at the site can be exposed." Liam Grieve says holding the competition in an isolated area is crucial for safety. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) Australian Youth Aerospace Association (AYAA) president Myrthe Snoeks said the event had grown considerably since 2019. This is the third onsite event and the second in outback NSW. Ms Snoeks is hoping to see more international teams participate in the future. "Seeing everybody work on these projects, seeing how proud they are when they launch successfully, but also seeing the complexity and growth every year … it's a privilege to witness," she said. events.title: MCP for agent-to-agent comms may be the riskiest protocol you've never heard of
events.summary: The adoption of AI agents in millions of organizations is creating new opportunities for attackers to make them take malicious actions, such as exfiltrating database contents and sensitive business and personal information. In the past five months, Google and four other organizations—with little in common except for their use of AI agents—have acknowledged vulnerabilities that exploit one agent inside a targeted network to spread harmful instructions to other internal agents. The technique is a special form of prompt injection that targets not the LLM but a particular agent, such as one for translation or data analysis. Guardrails inside such agents, if they exist at all, are often lax and will send the instructions to other agents down the chain. Because the latter agent explicitly trusts the first one, it follows the directions. Unexpected and hard to mitigate Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin tested agents from organizations including Google, JP Morgan Chase, Weviate, Rapid7, the French government's interministerial digital directorate, and the US federal government. His proof-of-concept attacks exploit trust gaps in MCP, short for Model Context Protocol . The standard is one way AI apps and agents communicate with each other inside an internal network. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Melbourne Airport's new pick-up and drop-off zones meet passenger approval New passenger pick-up and drop-off zones are now in use at Melbourne Airport. Most of the first travellers to use the new facilities this morning welcomed the new arrangements, saying it was less congested than the previous road network. Melbourne Airport is expanding its international terminal. The first passengers to use Melbourne Airport's new drop-off and pick-up zones have reported a seamless transition to the new arrangements. The airport's departure ramp that was used to drop passengers at the front door of terminals 1, 2 and 3 closed last night after more than 50 years in operation. The new combined drop-off and pick-up area has been built in the multi-level car park at the airport, but with an earlier exit from the Tullamarine Freeway. The new Melbourne Airport drop-off zone is in operation. ( Supplied: Melbourne Airport ) An elevated road travels alongside and then over the old entrance to the airport. The passenger zone, roadway and foot bridge to the airport terminals cost a combined $500 million. The airport said it aimed to reduce traffic congestion outside the terminals' departure areas and featured almost triple the number of bays compared to the forecourt. The passenger zone is connected to the terminals through a bridge. ( ABC News: Stephanie Ferrier ) New zones 'less hectic' than previous ramp There have been concerns about the longer walk to the terminal for elderly travellers and people with mobility issues. But passengers who spoke to the ABC this morning approved of the new arrangement. "Our son managed to find his way really well," said one woman who had just been dropped off for a flight home to New Zealand. This New Zealand traveller says her son had no trouble finding his way to the new drop-off area. ( ABC News ) "So far it's easy, pretty convenient. The last one was a bit hectic, a bit busy," said another traveller. "It's pretty great, lots of room," said another woman who agreed the new zone appeared "less hectic" than the previous facility. Another man said the traffic flowed more easily and he did not mind the longer walk to reach the terminal. "Get our steps in," his travelling companion added. A driver said he felt safer using the new zone, while another said he found it easier to drop off his passengers. Drivers now have to leave the Tullamarine Freeway using the exit to Naarm Way. There was a crash on the freeway this morning, causing delays getting to the airport but it was not known if it was related to the new airport arrangements. Travellers began using the new drop-off and pick-up zones this morning. ( Supplied: Melbourne Airport ) The new zone is designed for passengers taking Qantas, Virgin Australia and international flights. The airport said it had rostered on dozens of extra staff today and the coming weeks to help passengers navigate the new layout. Melbourne Airport CEO Lorie Argus acknowledged the changes posed a challenge for some travellers but she said a lot of work had been done with disability consultants. "We've had a lot of our accessibility groups through to trial the space," Ms Argus said. "People have commented that the walk is longer but we do have dedicated disability bays now that you can book that are right at the front of the hub." events.title: Envision to end operations and stop product development if it can't find partner
events.summary: Envision , a Netherlands-based start-up that made hardware and software tools for the visually impaired , will be stopping product development at the end of the year unless it can find a partner. In a statement posted to the company's website on Monday, founder Karthik Mahadevan and Karthik Kannan said that despite efforts towards a successful business model, the company has been unable to yield profitable results. "We reached the conclusion that we have given it our all and brought Envision as far as we could with our nimble efforts," they wrote. "There’s still so much potential for this product and business to grow, but realising it needs someone who can take it in a new direction, whether that's a new audience or a different business model." Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said they were in talks with a few possible partners who might be able to keep the company going. They were also open to speaking with others who may have ideas as to how to keep it alive. In 2024, Envision's founders spoke with The National about the company's aspirations. Its journey to selling smart glasses for the visually impaired started in 2017, when the start-up's smartphone app, Envision AI, began to gain popularity. The app uses a phone camera to identify and read signs, objects, menus, books or other material in real time, making life easier for visually impaired users. The popularity of the app's free version, according to Mr Kannan at the time, fuelled Envision's desire to improve the user experience based on feedback from customers. “If you're a low-vision person and you have to have a phone in one hand and a cane in the other, that can be cumbersome,” he said. “So we started looking for something that might be sleek and modern-looking to implement.” Part of enhancing the experience, Mr Kannan said, was to take the best aspects of the Envision app and use it in the glasses. Envision's app won a Google Play Award in 2019 in the category of “best accessibility experience”, and Mr Kannan said it could come to an agreement with Google and eventually use the company's largely defunct Google Glass technology for its product. The glasses, priced from $1,899 to $3,499, were introduced in 2020 and underwent various improvements amid the AI boom. In the announcement on Monday, the founders outlined plans to wind down operations and promised there would be a final update, with hopes of keeping the app and some offerings operational for as long as possible "offline”. Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said the ultimate problem was scaling Envision's business model to something sustainable given the competition from Apple and Meta , and the current economy. "On paper, 300 million blind and low-vision people is a big market, but for the majority of them, the problems that come first are ones technology can't solve yet: poverty, lack of basic access, unemployment," Envision’s founders wrote. "That's why even products that are cheap or free struggle to get past that million mark, and paying users are a much much smaller slice of that." In 2024, Envision told The National of the intention to turn the company's focus to Arabic . "As our user base in the Middle East grew and we built up a community of users, we've started to bring a lot more of those efforts in-house,” Mr Kannan said. “As a result, we now have more control over how the AI works when translating documents that are scanned and how it works if there's written text on a blackboard.”

events.title: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base because of threat of Iranian drone attack
events.summary: The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend, the Pentagon said. President Trump said in Monday the threat came from Iran. Why it matters: A U.S. official said the base was under threat of attack by Iran. The latest: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Monday that there are "regular rotations" of U.S. Air Force assets around the world and that the movement of the bombers was not directly tied to the Iranian threat. "We have confidence in the security of all of our bases. All of our bases could be threatened theoretically at any moment and that is why there is so much security built around them," he said. Rubio said the U.S. has been working closely with the British government on an investigation into the threat "and they couldn't be more cooperative." But several hours later, President Trump contradicted Rubio and told reporters the bombers were moved because of a security threat from Iran. "They didn't fly out by accident ... there was a threat. We moved them around a little bit," he said. Trump added that the U.S. knows who was behind the threat and their links to Iran. When asked if Iran planned to launch a drone attack against the base from British soil, Trump said: "If they did they will suffer greatly." Trump was then asked about the attempted terrorist attack on the Fly Dubai flight and said he thinks Iran was responsible. Driving the news: British security forces last week arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel gave the UK intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack. What they're saying: "While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States," the Pentagon said in a statement. It added that the U.S. military bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, "remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States."

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The new vuln, CVE-2026-88779, is a memory overflow bug that leads to denial of service Fortinet sounds the alarm over actively exploited FortiMail zero-day 4 days ago AI agents hacked the hackers, stealing email addresses from security research org 4 days ago Custom malware used in Citrix 0-day attacks targeting govt, banks, professional services 7 days ago Certainties in life: Death, taxes, and critical Citrix vulns under attack 8 days ago ShinyHunters tells The Reg: We hacked the FBI to 'protect our business' 11 days ago The attackers just keep coming after Citrix NetScaler appliances, as both the feds and private security researchers warn that someone found - and has already exploited - yet another Citrix bug before it had a patch. This latest vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-88779 , is a memory overflow bug that leads to denial of service attacks. It only affects NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) service provider or identity provider, used for single sign-on authentication. Late Friday, amid exploitation reports , Citrix confirmed that it was investigating a “newly observed issue related to SAML authentication in customer-managed NetScaler deployments.” By Saturday night, the vendor released a security advisory for NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway with patches, urging vulnerable customers to “install the relevant updated versions as soon as possible.” Citrix also posted a blog about the vulnerability, confirming that it has observed targeted attacks on unmitigated NetScaler deployments that can lead to denial of service. Citrix did not answer our questions about CVE-2026-88779 - including how many instances have been affected and what attackers are doing after exploiting the bug - but urged customers to "quickly apply" the fix to NetScaler instances. "We were recently alerted to a new issue that affects service availability for some NetScaler deployments," a Citrix spokesperson told The Register . "After we were alerted to this issue we immediately developed and published a mitigation while concurrently developing, testing and deploying a fix." On Sunday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed CVE-2026-88779 was under active exploitation and ordered federal agencies to patch the bug by Wednesday. While the new vulnerability is not technically related to the earlier eight CVEs finally disclosed by Citrix on September 27 - weeks after miscreants began abusing two of these security holes ( CVE-2026-88772 and CVE-2026-88771 ) - watchTowr researchers told us they suspect it has been used to purposefully crash machines, making exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 faster. “This vulnerability is incredibly simple to trigger, with a single specially crafted request being all that is needed to knock an appliance offline,” watchTowr’s head of threat intelligence, Jake Knott, told The Register . “Exploitation is already occurring in the wild, and disrupting an authentication gateway can prevent legitimate users from accessing the services behind it.” WatchTowr reproduced the vulnerability on Friday, and Citrix credited the attack-surface management company along with Bishop Fox with helping it address the issue. “Citrix provides an indicator-of-compromise script that teams can run to check exposed appliances for signs of compromise, though a clean result is not definitive proof,” Knott said. “Security teams should prioritize appliances configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server with SAML authentication enabled, and affected organizations should apply the fixed build or Citrix’s interim mitigation if an immediate upgrade is not possible.”® European AI flag bearer Mistral's new open weights model is 'Le Chonk' Oh lawd it is coming ...

events.title: Lawsuit accuses Starbucks of mislabeling 8 'sugar-free' protein drinks
events.summary: Starbucks is facing a consumer lawsuit over claims that the protein drinks labeled as “sugar-free” on its cafe menus may actually contain more sugar than a Reese’s peanut butter cup Starbucks is facing a consumer lawsuit over claims that the protein drinks labeled “sugar-free” on its cafe menus may actually contain more sugar than a Reese’s peanut butter cup. The federal lawsuit filed late Friday in Seattle alleges that eight protein beverages Starbucks sells in the U.S. contain varying amounts of sugar even though the company lists them as sugarless. On Monday, the menu on Starbucks' U.S. website listed a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha with 16 grams of sugar and a 20-ounce (0.6-liter) version of the same drink with 21 grams of sugar. By comparison, one Reese’s cup has 11 grams of sugar. Hagens Berman, a law firm that specializes in class action cases, filed the suit on behalf of three individual consumers who bought Starbucks’ sugar-free protein drinks in California, New York and Washington. “Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, whether that be general health, diabetes and blood glucose levels or other factors, and for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant,” said Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of the Seattle-headquartered firm. The plaintiffs contend that Starbucks' naming and marketing of sugar-free products is “false, deceptive and unlawful” and that the company violated federal labeling regulations. Seattle-based Starbucks said the sugar in its protein drinks comes from the protein-boosted milk it uses. The company said it doesn’t add sugar to the drinks and it uses sugar-free syrup for flavoring. Dutch Bros also offers a lower-sugar version of its caramel-flavored Hopscotch Protein Latte, but it’s advertised as the Hopscotch Zero Sugar Added Protein Latte. The 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced version has 7 grams of sugar and 11 grams of protein. By comparison, a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced Starbucks Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte has 9 grams of sugar and 29 grams of protein. The lawsuit seeks damages on behalf of U.S. consumers who bought the drinks. It also wants the court to order Starbucks to stop using the label “sugar-free” on products that contain sugar.
