events.title: Abu Dhabi’s Eagle Hills to develop residential and tourism projects in Syria
events.summary: Abu Dhabi-based Eagle Hills is working on two major projects in Syria including a residential and tourism development as part of a framework agreement the company has signed with the Syrian government. Total investment in the two projects in Damascus and Latakia has not been disclosed but Syria 's Arab News Agency reported they will create more 40,000 jobs. The agreement was signed on Monday at the People’s Palace in Damascus in the presence of Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara by Eagle Hills and Syria’s ministries of Public Works, and Housing and Tourism. It covers two projects: the Tadamun Towers development in Damascus and the Eco Life tourism project in Latakia. The developments will combine housing, services and employment opportunities, while involving Syrian companies and skilled professionals, Mohamed Alabbar , founder and chairman of Eagle Hills, said during the signing ceremony. “We hope these projects will become communities where people can find suitable homes, good services, job opportunities and a decent life,” he said. He also called on Syrians living inside and outside the country to invest in Syria and take part in its reconstruction, saying domestic expertise would be important to the development of the projects. Mr Alabbar previously said he is looking to invest as much as $18 billion in Syria, with projects worth between $5 billion and $7 billion on the Syrian coast, and up to $11 billion in Damascus and its surroundings. The new projects are also expected to encourage Syrians living both inside and outside the country to invest in Syria and take part in their implementation, Mr Alabbar added. Demand for housing remains strong in Syria as it focuses on rebuilding its economy and attracting more investment. Syria aims to build or rehabilitate two million homes by 2035 to address housing shortages in the country. It plans to fund projects through a mix of government investment, private capital, new partnerships and foreign investment. The country is expected to provide land owned by the General Housing Establishment while private investors will develop projects and infrastructure to help increase housing supply. More than 1.7 million Syrians are estimated to have returned to Syria between December 2024 and April 2026 following the overthrow of Bashar Al Assad's regime nearly two years ago, according to the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR. UAE-based Arada also plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Syria in phases over 10 years. The new project in the west of Damascus will have 11,000 homes, including residential apartments, villas and town houses, branded residences, 500 hotel rooms and 1,000 serviced apartments. Two schools as well as a hospital, offices and retail units will also be built as part of the development. There is strong demand for “good-quality homes” in Syria, driven by residents and foreign citizens living abroad, Ahmed Alkhoshaibi, group chief executive of Arada, told The National . “You have the local current demand, which is very strong for good communities. And you also have Syrians living outside, who want to invest, or have a home or holiday home in the country. So that demand will continue to grow,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said.

events.title: The question you would ask HPE and NVIDIA if nobody was recording
events.summary: There is a question about AI data sovereignty you would ask HPE or NVIDIA if nobody was recording. It is usually specific to your own workload and your own regulator, and it usually ends with whether the sovereign option on the slide survives contact with a procurement team. On Thursday 29 October you can ask it. The Register is hosting a dinner in Washington with HPE and NVIDIA, our editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff in the chair, and nothing said on the record. HPE sends Bharath Ramesh, Head of Product, AI Factory Solutions, and Tracy Mills, Acting Director Federal Systems Integrators & Distinguished Chief Technologist Federal. NVIDIA sends Bert Condensa, Vice President for Enterprise AI Factory Segment Sales. They are there to take questions, and none of them brings a deck. All three spend their working lives at the point where AI infrastructure gets bought, which is where sovereignty requirements are either met or quietly worked around, and the Chatham House Rule means they can say which. That rule is what makes the evening worth the trip. What gets said at a table like this does not get said on a webinar: what a bank had to rebuild, for instance, or which sovereign cloud option somebody paid for and would not buy again. Everyone is there as a peer, the vendors included, and the chair steps in the moment anyone starts to sell. The questions on the table are the practical ones: which options actually hold a boundary, what each costs in capital, capability or elasticity, and whether any of it still holds once the pilot is running for real. It is one table, and places are limited. The seats are for technology, data and risk leaders in healthcare, financial services, research, pharmaceuticals, government and higher education who are making these decisions now. Dinner runs from 6.00pm to 8.30pm at Fiola Mare. Places go by invitation. Request one here. events.title: Bridging Africa's data gap
events.summary: Alexis’s view “Policy without data is like guesswork.” Ghanaian lawmaker Albert Nyakotey Tetteh was making the case for better use of public sector data in infrastructure development when he said that in parliament last month. But his point rings true more broadly: For decades, a lack of data has held back economic development in countries across Africa. Countries reeling from supply chain disruptions, energy shocks, and Western aid cuts are trying to comprehend the scale of the challenges they face in order to reset policies. Gathering relevant data is a vital first step to understanding everything from the value of underground mineral deposits to the money held in pension funds. As a case in point, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention recently told me a health ministry audit in one country revealed half of salaried health staff were “ ghost workers .” However, shrinking budgets throw up a major challenge. In May, South African authorities said the average annual budget allocation for Statistics South Africa — the government department responsible for gathering and publishing official statistics — had fallen by 23% in real terms since 2019 . The knock-on effect is a resource squeeze that has led to surveys being cut. At the same time, questions have been raised about the credibility of its figures. South Africa’s 2022 census missed nearly a third of the population , according to the statistics department’s own follow-up survey. A mismatch on that level distorts how public money is allocated. The continent’s biggest economy, whose statistical analysis is comprehensive compared with most other African nations, is not alone in its challenges. African statistics offices are under mounting funding pressure, with donor-funded surveys cancelled or delayed since Washington ended funding last year for population surveys whose findings were used by governments to collate public health statistics. But there is hope. Artificial intelligence can help by improving the efficiency and accuracy of statistical analysis. The UK’s statistics office recently said it is turning to AI to cut costs and improve data amid “ squeezed finances .” The impact would be felt even more acutely if African officials use this technology to help take the guesswork out of policymaking. Notable An Israeli team of scientists launched a mobile research lab this year that will collect data across east and southern Africa in an attempt to fill huge data gaps in global climate science.

events.title: Euro plummets against US dollar: Has the next financial crisis begun?
events.summary: Euro falls against US dollar: Is a financial crisis looming? The euro has fallen to a 17-month low against the dollar. That will make inflation worse in the EU, where political worries and concern over French debt are already troubling investors. Is a fiscal crisis at hand? The euro hit a 17-month low against the dollar in early trading on Monday, as concerns about eurozone debt, particularly in France, compounded existing investor concerns over global government bond yields and rising oil prices. The euro has been sliding against the dollar for much of 2026, down about 5% since the start of the year. It reached $1.12 (€0.99) on Monday, the lowest level since early 2025. Ricardo Amaro, lead eurozone economist at Oxford Economics, told DW that the general slide can be attributed to a repricing of investor expectations regarding US Federal Reserve policy in terms of higher interest rates in the face of rising global bond yields. However, he said the latest sell-off was prompted in particular by concerns over France, where "investors positioned for higher fiscal risk." The sell-off in French debt gathered pace last week as doubts grow over its long-term viability. French 10-year government bonds — the cost France must pay to borrow money within 10 years of the debt being issued — rose to a 5% yield before easing slightly. France has long had underlying fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron came to office in May 2017, public spending has climbed while he has brought in deep tax cuts. As a result, the country's national debt has increased by well over €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion). France's debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at almost 118%. It consistently posts unbalanced budgets. Its annual budget deficit is now regularly more than 5%, above the 3.4% rate when Macron came to office. For many investors, wider concerns over low eurozone growth levels and surging energy prices have contributed to a renewed focus on France, with many retreating to perceived safer options, such as German government debt. The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week, a closely watched measure of EU financial stability. The resulting pressure on the euro and on other government bond markets, including Italy's, means there are calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent concern over France turning into panic. Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said in a note on Monday that at one point last week, the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" was at hand. "The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot," he said. Ricardo Amaro said the situation presents a challenge for the ECB because it needs to act without making things worse. "Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he added. He expects policymakers to continue monitoring currency developments between the US dollar and the euro, but to stop short of trying to influence the market for now. Uncertainty abounds due to both political and economic pressures. France has been beset by political crises in recent years, where passing annual budgets has become a major test of government stability. Although the 2027 budget has been agreed, with reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, the right-wing National Rally remains well-placed ahead of the 2027 presidential election, in which Marine Le Pen is likely to be the leading candidate. Concerns over French economic policy in the event of Le Pen winning the presidency are spooking investors, similar to how the rise of the far-right AfD in Germany has raised questions over the future direction of the bloc's key economy. Much of the political instability has been driven by voter anger over the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has just called a snap election after measures to deal with the country's housing crisis were voted down in parliament. Amaro says a weakening euro could compound the underlying problem of inflation . "Sharper euro weakness would reinforce the inflationary shock at a time when inflation is already expected to stay high into 2027," he said. A weaker euro would increase the cost of imported goods , particularly those that are priced in US dollars. Global commodities such as oil and gas are priced in dollars, meaning soaring energy prices would likely rise further, as would US imports. With memories of the sovereign debt crisis that afflicted the EU in the early 2010s still fresh, many observers are beginning to wonder if the moves on French debt could be indicative of a new crisis in the eurozone . Some, such as Geoffrey Yu, a senior strategist with BNY, believe such concerns are misplaced. "Comparisons to 2012 are well off the mark," he said.

events.title: Crude oil prices and refinery margins generally increased throughout the third quarter
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: Bloomberg L.P. Note: 3Q26=third quarter of 2026 Petroleum markets in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26) were characterized by increasing prices for crude oil and petroleum products amid persistent conflict in the Middle East. Crude oil prices Crude oil prices steadily climbed in 3Q26 as markets adjusted to renewed military strikes in the Middle East. The front-month futures price of a barrel of Brent crude oil began the quarter at $72 per barrel (b) on July 1, the lowest since February 26, two days before the start of the war. The low prices at the start of the quarter reflected increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz in June following the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). Following the resumption of military strikes on July 7 , crude oil prices increased, with the futures price passing $100/b on July 23 and then trading between $79/b and $98/b until September 8. Daily price volatility in this period generally reflected: Market responses to public statements by U.S., Iranian, and other regional leaders on military plans and the likelihood of a peace deal Flows and disruptions to flows through the Strait of Hormuz Other supply risks and disruptions, such as attacks on oil export infrastructure in Russia Crude oil futures prices passed $100/b again on September 9 following an escalation of military action against energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia, including: U.S. and Iranian attacks on crude oil tankers U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports Attacks on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline Attacks on Saudi Arabian oil tankers around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait Ukraine’s drone attacks on Novorossiysk , one of Russia’s major oil terminals on the Black Sea Prices also increased because some of the measures that had helped to mitigate the price effects of reduced global supplies earlier in the year began to unwind. Since April, reduced crude oil imports to China lowered global oil demand, absorbing some of the shock of reduced supply from the Middle East. In 3Q26, China continued to import far less crude oil than it did before the war. However, China’s 3Q26 crude oil imports were up from May and June, adding some demand back into the market. Additionally, releases from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve slowed significantly in September, limiting additional sources of supply as the disruption has continued. The futures price for Brent crude oil peaked on September 15 at $109/b while spot prices reached as high as $132/b around the same time. Like in April, disruptions of supply— particularly out of Saudi Arabia —put more pressure on Brent crude oil spot prices as buyers struggled to find short-term supply amid the escalating military action. Crude oil prices averaged around $104/b in the final two weeks of the quarter as markets balanced peace discussions with the possibility of a wider scale war. Refinery margins Like in the previous quarter, U.S. refineries ran at unseasonally high levels in 3Q26 with utilization averaging 95%, processing the most crude oil for the third quarter since 2019, when refining capacity was 4% higher. High refinery inputs reflected strong margins for transportation fuels. Motor gasoline , distillate , and jet fuel crack spreads —measures of the refinery margins for these fuels—were all elevated. The quarterly average gasoline crack spread more than doubled the year-ago level despite declining in the second half of the quarter, and the distillate and jet fuel crack spreads almost tripled their year-ago levels as a result of tight global supply. Data source: Bloomberg L.P. Note: The crack spreads reflect the New York Harbor spot prices for RBOB, ultra-low sulfur diesel, and jet fuel minus the Dated Brent spot price. 3Q26=third quarter of 2026 Crack spreads were highest for distillate fuel oil and second highest for jet fuel because the disrupted refining activities in Russia, China, and the Middle East supplied large shares of these fuels to global markets. U.S. distillate fuel supplies have become tight because of high exports to markets in short supply, as well as higher costs for importing regions, such as the U.S. East Coast. As of the week ending September 25, U.S. distillate fuel inventories were 13% below the five-year (2021–2025) average while U.S. gasoline inventories and jet fuel inventories were 7% below and 3% above their five-year averages, respectively. events.title: Scoop: Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen
events.summary: President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. The latest: Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the Camp David meeting in a gaggle with reporters on Monday before heading to Europe. "We constantly are meeting on long-term strategic planning and things of this nature. It is not unusual for us as a team to get together. That was just an opportunity to do it in a setting where there were less distractions," he said. "That is part of the role the National Security Council plays — to bring together different stakeholders to do long-term planning. Six months, nine months, but in many cases five or 10 years down the road. I wouldn't call it routine ... but we had such meetings before," he added. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East. The White House declined to comment. Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind. What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be. "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. "But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well."

events.title: Solar market set for Africa boom, says report
events.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa’s off-grid solar market is due to expand by 450% by 2035, with more than 35% of installations projected to be in Nigeria, according to a new report by global research firm Wood Mackenzie. Across the continent, persistent failures in national grids and growing populations have already created an off-grid “ shadow ” fuel market, predominantly led by diesel generators. However, the recent rise in fuel prices due to the Iran war, alongside the removal of subsidies in Nigeria and a significant drop in solar panel prices in recent decades, are driving the shift to solar. Outside Nigeria, Kenya, and DR Congo are also projected to be major solar power hubs. For more of the continent to reap the benefits of solar power, however, blended funding models and consistent rural electrification policies will be needed to help bridge the power gap, the report warned. — Paige Bruton

events.summary: Three junta-led West African states launched a joint television channel to offer programming in line with their push to de-emphasize Western viewpoints. Tafouk TV, owned by Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, started broadcasting in September, has been praised by Russia’s ambassador in Bamako, and signed a cooperation agreement with the parent company of Moscow’s broadcaster RT to jointly cover events, according to RFI. The three countries, which formed the Alliance of Sahel States in 2023, have simultaneously severed ties with France while strengthening engagements with Russia, particularly defense partnerships against jihadist insurgencies thriving in the semi-arid region. Moscow is also expanding beyond arms and intelligence support; Mali will be one of eight African countries where Moscow plans to build new culture and education centers known as ‘Russia Houses’ in the coming years. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: South Africa and US envoys trade barbs
events.summary: South Africa’s foreign minister Ronald Lamola has publicly questioned whether US ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III should be in the job at all, the latest sign of how little goodwill is left between Pretoria and the Trump administration. The deterioration in ties has simmered for nearly two years, raising fears that Washington may take more economically damaging steps after imposing visa restrictions on unnamed South African officials last month. Lamola’s comments to South Africa’s Sunday Times came after Bozell said Washington had “run out patience” and that the time for dialogue had passed. Lamola said if Bozell is tired of talking, he ought to “get out of the kitchen … you can’t have a diplomat who says time for talking is over.” Pretoria has now lodged two public protests against Bozell in seven months, accusing him of meddling in domestic politics. The Trump administration has pressured Pretoria on race-based policies designed to undo the legacy of apartheid. Priyal Singh, an analyst at the Institute for Security Studies think tank in Johannesburg, told Semafor he expects the sparring to continue at least until the US midterms in November as falsehoods that white South Africans face persecution have found a receptive audience among President Donald Trump’s conservative base. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Budding food scrap pickup services across the US want your coffee grounds and eggshells
events.summary: Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells and carrot tops is a way to reduce the amount of food waste that goes into landfills, where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane DETROIT -- Every Monday, Ricky Blanding drives his Ford Ranger pickup truck around Detroit along a carefully planned route. Blanding hops in and out of the truck, grabbing buckets of food scraps from porches and restaurants, piling those scraps into bins in the truck bed and driving them to a composting site. Blanding is the CEO of Scrap Soils, one of the many budding food waste collection services across the country helping to divert food from landfills and make composting more accessible. It's especially important for those who can't compost at home, who live in cities without municipal curbside pickup or who can't get to a drop-off location. Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells, carrot tops and more reduces the amount of food that goes into dumps where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane. It also ultimately helps create healthy soil for gardeners and urban farmers. Experts say companies like Scrap Soils are an important part of cleaning up the broader food ecosystem. Emily Cassidy, research associate at climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, said composting offers the dual benefits of reducing landfill methane emissions and, once the composting process is complete, returning nutrients to soil. “Because methane has such a big impact on the climate in a short amount of time, the more we can reduce methane, it is like pulling the emergency brake on climate change,” Cassidy said. Beyond mitigating climate change, composting can also improve local food production, she said. “That’s a way that we can see that we’re benefiting the environment, because we’re taking food and then replenishing the ground with those nutrients,” she said. Blanding, a 34-year-old native Detroiter, co-launched Scrap Soils in 2020 to play a local part in solving a statewide food waste problem that mirrors what's happening around the globe . Food waste is a huge source of methane in Michigan landfills, estimates say, and accounts for millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in the state. In Detroit, more than 70 homes and businesses are signed up for Scrap Soils’ weekly pickups. It's an easier way to compost than making space in one's backyard or driving to a city drop-off site. Home pickups start at $15 per month, while businesses pay $60 per month or more, depending on volume. One of those commercial customers is The Grand Porter restaurant in the Southwest neighborhood of Detroit. “We go through a lot of eggs, so mostly egg scraps, eggshells and the cardboard. We put all of our bread scraps, stale bread scraps, in here,” said Lou Hammer, the restaurant's executive chef, pointing to a large bin with bags of food waste inside. “Some tomato tops, some avocado skins. Probably a few other things in there, too.” “It doesn’t take any extra effort,” she said of the pickup service. “This was going to go in a bag anyway. It’s just going to go in a green bag instead.” After completing his nine-hour, more than 100-mile (160-kilometer) weekly route, Blanding drops off the waste at Scrap Soils' partner, Sanctuary Farms in Detroit. There, everything from apple cores to rotted pumpkins to corn husks is composted into a rich soil additive that's available for purchase. “Food waste has not only become the problem,” Blanding said, “but it’s also the solution to so many issues in climate change.” The company ultimately plans to purchase a larger truck, as well as its own property and equipment for composting. It's fundraising to meet a matching grant through the state. Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' That hasn't been without challenges. As Blanding seeks to grow, he's come up against skepticism that a small team with limited resources can make a big impact. Companies like Scrap Soils also face challenges ranging from gaining visibility to getting people to actually sign up and commit. At the same time, emphasizing what can and cannot be composted, and how to do it correctly — such as removing produce stickers before putting a peel in the bucket — is key to its success, too. “The role of a hauler is very important, and education around composting is also very important,” Blanding said. “Being able to continue to get more engagement and more partnership, those things go far in helping us to expand this tiny effort into something that actually can scale,” he added. Despite hurdles, other independent composting programs and companies are expanding. Examples include the Denver Compost Collective , Nashville’s Compost Co.

The decision marks a dramatic reversal, after Ethiopian and Eritrean forces united in fighting the TPLF during the previous conflict. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Games Workshop seeks IT leader to summon the legions in epic saga battling the forces of ERP
events.summary: Games Workshop is on the hunt for a head of IT to guide the organization through its technological saga for the next two years. The UK-based tabletop games retailer and manufacturer of the globally popular Warhammer figures said that under the fixed-term contract, the heroic individual would take overall responsibility for its global IT and customer technology capability, and report to the Chief Operating Officer. “The role has a broad remit spanning our core technology estate, information security, major systems change and the technology behind our customer-facing digital platforms, including warhammer.com,” the job ad said, although sadly it closed for applications over the weekend. “We need someone who can understand what Games Workshop needs now, anticipate what we will need in the future, and make good decisions about how technology supports the long-term success of the business,” it said. Candidates might want to be aware that, if they are lucky enough to be offered the job and they accept the mission, the battle will not be an easy one. The head of IT will take responsibility for core IT environment and information security, advising senior management on technology, security, risk and investment. They will also support the teams to keep “significant technology programs moving, openly tackling the challenges that come with major change, and ensure that we continue to make rapid progress.” The Nottingham-based retailer and manufacturer is in the midst of ERP and supply chain management systems overhauls that were first mobilized years ago and have been beset with delays and over-runs. Back in January 2021, The Register reported that Games Workshop delayed its Microsoft Dynamics-based ERP rollout and appointed a new integrator, having already hoped to go live in 2020. By September that year, it said project issues were impacting the development of new features in online shopping. In January 2022, it added another £500k to the project budget with no end in sight. A year later, it said the business faced ongoing challenges to integrate new IT systems when it was still heavily reliant on working with its legacy tech systems. “Finishing these projects and upgrading our systems continue to be a key area of focus. We are making some progress but it's costing us more time and money – we will remain cost conscious," it told investors. Around four years later, challenges remain ongoing, according to the latest annual report, published in July, for the year ending in May 2026. It said the group’s main financial system is still being supported by a number of legacy ERP applications for which “we have identified control deficiencies in our previous audits.” These still exist, according to a review of IT systems. The report added that the responsibility for delivering IT had moved to its operational manufacturing and supply chain director, under the COO from June, a decision which “helped bring all of the internal departments together.” “Our Systems Improvement Plan (SIP) is on track with very clear milestones for us all to support and deliver,” it added. Games Workshop is famous for the phenomenon of Warhammer 40,000 — also known as WH40K or 40K — thought to be the most popular miniature wargame in the world. Battles are set in the distant future, leaving the technology department to hope the end of its long-running ERP saga comes before that date. ®

events.title: Adnoc signs Thai LNG deal after Iran war disrupts Gulf supply
events.summary: Adnoc has agreed to supply about two million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to Thailand ’s Gulf Development, boosting the country's access to the fuel as the Iran war disrupts supplies from the Middle East. Deliveries under the multi-year sales and purchase agreement are to start in 2027, Adnoc said on Monday. The company did not disclose prices, the length of the contract or where the cargoes will be sourced from. The agreement builds on a first LNG supply deal between the companies signed in 2025. The latest deal comes as Thailand seeks to diversify its LNG supplies after the war sharply curtailed shipments from the Gulf. Natural gas accounts for more than 60 per cent of the country’s power generation, while about 24 per cent of its LNG imports – about 2.2 million tonnes a year – normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz, almost all from Qatar, according to Thailand-based Krungsri Research. State-controlled PTT has been exploring alternative supplies, including from Oman, Mexico and Canada. The regional war has upended a global LNG market that was already heading into a period of tighter seasonal demand. The strait, through which about a fifth of global crude and LNG flowed before the war began in late February, remains largely shut. QatarEnergy declared force majeure in early March, while an Iranian missile strike on the Ras Laffan complex on March 18 knocked out about 17 per cent of Qatar's LNG production capacity. Cargo cancellations to some Asian buyers have since been extended through November, helping push prices in Asia and Europe towards their highest levels since late 2022. Gulf LNG exports remain far below their prewar pace of about three shipments a day. “This agreement builds on our first LNG supply agreement with Gulf Group and reinforces Adnoc’s commitment to ensuring reliable energy supplies to Thailand and our Asian customers,” said Nasser Al Muhairi, acting chief executive of Adnoc downstream industry, marketing and trading. Gulf Development chief executive Sarath Ratanavadi said the agreement would help to build a “diversified, resilient LNG portfolio” and gave the company greater flexibility to meet demand. The supplies will be delivered through Adnoc Trading and its LNG marketing and trading platform , launched in Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM in July. Adnoc is targeting 47 million tonnes a year of marketable LNG beyond 2030 as it expands its portfolio and trading operations.

events.title: From Scan to Treatment Plan, AI Helps Close Breast Cancer’s Deadliest Gaps
events.summary: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among American women — yet the gaps in care are wide. A majority of women over age 40 skip the recommended annual screening. Radiologists are reading more mammograms with fewer colleagues. And when a diagnosis arrives, the tests that inform treatment can take weeks to return results. Companies in the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are building AI applications to support clinicians at each of these friction points, including imaging, risk assessment and treatment planning. About 40 million mammograms are performed in the U.S. each year, but a projected shortfall of tens of thousands of radiologists over the next decade is straining the system’s capacity to read them. At the other end of the care timeline, treatment decisions often hinge on genomic assays sent off to outside labs — assays that take weeks to process, at a moment when speed and certainty matter most. The companies below are addressing both ends of that gap, and everything in between, accelerated by NVIDIA AI infrastructure. Automated Imaging Delivers AI-Powered Insights For women struggling to find time or a nearby location for breast cancer screening, access is a practical barrier that translates into missed diagnoses. NVIDIA Inception startup iSono Health was built around simplifying this imaging workflow. The company’s FDA-cleared ATUSA platform — a wearable, automated 3D quantitative ultrasound system — captures a standardized breast volume in approximately two minutes per breast, compared with up to 45 minutes for a conventional handheld ultrasound. The system’s AI, trained on thousands of full-breast scans comprising over 1.5 million ultrasound frames, automates image acquisition. It uses NVIDIA GPU acceleration and open source medical imaging technology to deliver a 3D scan that the company says is 28% more sensitive than a handheld 2D ultrasound. Handheld ultrasound depends on whoever holds the probe, so a woman’s scans typically can’t be compared from one year to the next. ATUSA captures the whole breast the same way every time, creating a repeatable view of breast tissue that could help clinicians analyze how a patient’s tissue changes across successive scans, while also reducing operator errors and variability. ATUSA is commercially available through partner clinics across California, Texas, Georgia, Tennessee and Washington D.C., with new sites coming online regularly. “Getting the scan closer to the patient is the first breakthrough,” said Neda Razavi, CEO of iSono Health. “Our vision is to make that scan increasingly informative: helping clinicians see what is there, understand what has changed and make more informed decisions.” iSono Health has developed AI capabilities for lesion detection, 3D segmentation and lesion classification. It next plans to extend its AI pipeline into multimodal diagnostic intelligence spanning 3D ultrasound, mammography, MRI and clinical information. The company has a multicenter clinical study with 3,200 patients underway to further validate the platform’s performance, with lead research sites at UC Davis and Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Finding Cancers, Cutting False Alarms Another NVIDIA Inception company, Whiterabbit.ai, develops AI technology for breast cancer screening. Its FDA-cleared WRDensity software automatically assesses breast density from mammograms and has been used in the care of hundreds of thousands of patients. The company has also developed WRRisk, a clinical decision support software for estimating patients’ long-term risk of developing breast cancer — and is researching a new generation of AI for mammography that could help radiologists detect more cancers while automating the screening of mammograms that are negative for breast cancer. The goal is to reduce the burden on a strained radiologist workforce, accelerate results and reduce avoidable callbacks for patients, and lower downstream healthcare costs. “Every day, breast radiologists face a needle-in-a-haystack problem, trying to find roughly one cancer in every 200 mammograms,” said Jason Su, cofounder and chief technology officer of Whiterabbit.ai. “We hope AI can be a powerful sidekick to radiologists, helping to clear away the hay so they can focus their expertise where it matters most.” Whiterabbit trains its AI models on a cluster of NVIDIA GPUs housed at Washington University in St. Louis, supplemented by additional GPU capacity in the cloud. Inference runs on NVIDIA GPUs deployed directly in the clinic. Predicting Which Treatments Will Work Once a patient is diagnosed with breast cancer, the next question is what to do about it — and the answer depends on predicting how the cancer will respond to treatment. Today, these predictions are limited in scope and accuracy, and often require a separate tissue biopsy with a two- to four-week wait. Ataraxis AI is building clinical intelligence that predicts patient outcomes and response to different therapies using digital data, including pathology slides that are already part of the standard patient workup. “The tools oncologists rely on today to guide therapy decisions were largely trained once, fifteen years ago, and never updated. Our models get stronger every time we acquire more clinical trial data,” said Joseph Cappadona, member of technical staff at Ataraxis AI. “But as we scale our models, the bigger shift is being able to answer more questions to help oncologists personalize therapy across all cancers.” Ataraxis’s AI models analyze digital pathology slides and standard clinical variables to predict treatment response and recurrence risk. One model predicts whether presurgical chemotherapy is likely to shrink a patient’s tumor to the point of response before the operating room. After surgery, another model estimates a patient’s five-year recurrence risk and the likely benefit of chemotherapy as a next step. Both models have been validated across more than 10 institutions and multiple clinical trials, and are in active clinical use. They run on NVIDIA GPUs on premises, in an offsite data center and in the cloud — using PyTorch accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA throughout. Providing Tumor Insights With 3D Visualization Another NVIDIA Inception company, SimBioSys , joined NVIDIA on a recent panel marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month. The company builds AI-powered precision medicine technology that creates accurate 3D models of breast tumors, veins and other soft tissue, delivering important insights to help guide surgeries and influence treatment plans. It has also built a tool to estimate the risk of breast cancer recurrence based on 3D volumetric data from a patient’s breast MRI, tumor pathology and clinical data. “We’re building a platform that now allows us to take multimodal data — imaging exams, pathology results, genomic testing when applicable and other biological inputs — and, using AI, bring that all together,” said Stacey Stevens, CEO of SimBioSys, at the event.

events.title: Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO prospectus leaked this week, and boy was it filled with interesting details. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or YouTube. You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live For starters there's the fact a third of it is all about existential AI risks, then there's the fact that, despite some impressive revenue growth the company still has yet to turn a profit. Combine that with massive capex predictions, and you have an IPO with massive valuation, yet a long, hard road toward anything resembling earnings. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg editor in chief Matt Rosoff, and enterprise IT reporter Lindsay Clark on this week's episode of The Kettle where they discuss the revelations, what they mean for the state of the AI industry, and just how much distraction from its actual problems Anthropic can eke out by keeping that doomsday narrative front and center. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:04) Hi everyone, and welcome to another episode of The Register's Kettle podcast. With me to talk about the revelations are our editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff and enterprise IT reporter Lindsay Clark who brought us news of this whole mess. Thank you both for joining me. Lindsay Clark (00:36) Thank you. Matt Rosoff (00:37) Thanks for having us. Brandon (00:38) Yeah. So Lindsay, I know we didn't break this story. This was, I believe, a Financial Times exclusive, but what was reported about those IPO docs, in the story you wrote and just how apocalyptically optimistic is this whole thing? Lindsay Clark (00:53) Well we have this scenario where a company, Anthropic, is trying to sell itself by telling people that there's an existential risk to its technology, which I think is a bit of a weird way to go about it. But nonetheless, that's in the prospectus according to the Financial Times. And they also offer some insight into the numbers that are going around. Anthropic is still massively loss-making as far as we know. Brandon (01:22) There was what, I think you said, $8 billion loss on $4.6 billion of [revenue] or something? Lindsay Clark (01:28) That's right, and it says it plans to spend $500 billion or so on cloud computing over the next few years. So I don't know what you make of those numbers, but it's hard to get them to add up in my head. Brandon (01:40) I mean it's interesting just how it's still not a profitable company. But Matt and I were discussing earlier, I was saying that I think it's interesting that Anthropic is pushed ahead with this IPO despite OpenAI pausing it, because I feel like Anthropic has long had this reputation as sort of being the more safety-conscious, the more conservative AI company. But here they are with OpenAI kind of saying, Well, we're gonna pump the brakes on our IPO until we can make sure our models are safe, but Anthropic is plowing ahead. And Matt, you had an interesting take on that and it was more to the financial end, right? So what were you saying to me about that earlier? Matt Rosoff (02:21) I think that if you probably were to look at OpenAI's numbers, they would be even worse than Anthropic's. Now there was a report that they had actually turned profitable on an adjusted basis [in] Q2 this year, but that's if you strip out all of the training costs. So I guess if it's just inference alone, without the training costs and without certain other costs, they have decent margins. So maybe there is a path to profitability. Now it looks as if their operating loss last year was almost double their revenue. So if their revenue continues to increase at the rate that it is, which is, it seems like it's going up 4x, 12x per year, something like that, depending on the period you're looking at. If they can't get the expenses under control, the business doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense. Nonetheless, I think they are growing faster because they were earlier to enterprise and they have become more essential to more companies than OpenAI did. And I think OpenAI is still sort of adjusting its business model and maybe not growing at quite the same rate. So that's my suspicion is that those numbers would look even worse. Brandon (04:01) Yeah, so the safety argument is probably just some spackle slapped on top of the bad financials to try to kinda hide it, I guess. If what you're saying is correct. Matt Rosoff (04:12) That's my speculation. It doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense to say, well, we're so worried about this amazing thing that we've built that we don't want to show you our books and we're not gonna go public yet until we have that all figured out. That seems like a strange argument to make. Brandon (04:31) Yeah, I would have to agree with that. So speaking of economic impact, Lindsay, you were talking a bit more in your story about some of the broader sort of economic scope of the AI industry. And I'm curious, could you go more into some of the numbers you discussed in your story? Lindsay Clark (04:51) Yeah, sure. So it was a few months ago, I think in August, ING. Well, I'll go back a bit. So in 2025, there was an economist, Jason Furman, who estimated that 92% of the US GDP growth in the second half of 2025 was down to AI investment. events.title: Qatar’s luxury market attracts 34,000 visitors
events.summary: Many Gulf events have been postponed or canceled because of the war, but Qatar’s annual bonanza of bling was lively last week. More than 34,000 people attended the six-day Doha Jewellery & Watches Exhibition, and many — unlike this reporter — weren’t lookie-loos. Doha’s exhibition center was transformed into a gallery of coveted gems and timepieces, with the cars at the valet reflecting the wealth of the clientele inside. Shoppers were reluctant to talk, but several said they attend every year because exhibitors (there were more than 50 representing 500 brands) bring in inventory that isn’t usually available in Qatar. One jeweler said sales in a single week were like Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day, and Christmas all rolled into one. For those seeking iced-out Pateks, or more modest trappings, the exhibition returns in late April. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Abu Dhabi's XRG invests in Argentina's LNG expansion
events.summary: Abu Dhabi’s XRG is backing Argentina’s bid to become a major liquefied natural gas exporter. ADNOC’s international arm agreed in June to take a 32% stake in three Argentine gas blocks . They will feed the country’s first LNG export terminal, designed to produce 12 million tons a year in its initial phase. “ No country or company secures its energy future alone ,” Executive Chairman Sultan Al Jaber said in Paris last week. At a time when exports from their home markets have been severely constrained, such international investments are only increasing in importance, helping Gulf producers meet customer demand and benefit from higher prices. This year, QatarEnergy took a stake in Golden Pass LNG in Texas, Saudi Aramco acquired an interest in the nearby Port Arthur LNG terminal, and XRG has bought into LNG projects in Texas and Mozambique. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Gulf SWFs on track for major investments despite war
events.summary: Gulf sovereign wealth funds are on track for one of their most active years of dealmaking ever, even as war disrupts businesses and economic growth. Regional funds are forecast to invest $136 billion by year-end , making 2026 their second-busiest on record, according to consultancy Global SWF. Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala leads with $26.2 billion invested so far this year. Nearly half of Gulf sovereign fund investment went to the US, showing that American assets remain attractive despite the debate about the future of Gulf states’ relationship with their main strategic ally. Gulf funds are major backers of the $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Kuwait’s and Qatar’s funds may also be called on to transfer money to their government budgets to help prop up state finances, hit by the decline in oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, Global SWF said. That won’t stop the funds from expanding rapidly in coming years, with Gulf funds set to control $8.8 trillion by 2030, up from $6.1 trillion. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes
events.summary: As of Oct. 1, 2026, states must pay more to run SNAP. AP Photo/Allison Dinner The number of people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is falling fast. The program formerly known as food stamps helped roughly 42 million Americans put food on the table in 2025. As of June 2026, the most recent data available, the number of people enrolled in the program in the whole country had declined by almost 13% to 36.4 million . Among those no longer getting benefits are an estimated 1.5 million children . What explains this decline? President Donald Trump says a strong economy has driven down demand for the program. It’s possible that some people have left the program because their incomes rose. But the enrollment decline has a lot to do with the big tax-and-spending package the president signed into law in July 2025 . States are struggling to keep up For example, the law caused some immigrants residing legally in the country, such as refugees and those seeking asylum, to no longer be eligible for SNAP benefits. In addition, more people enrolled in SNAP now may only get up to three months of benefits if they don’t work, engage in training programs or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. These work requirements previously applied only to adults up to the age of 54; that cutoff is rising to 64. Another change is that parents of older children ages 14-17 are now expected to meet these work requirements . All states are phasing in these restrictions, but the number of people getting SNAP benefits is falling much faster in some states than others. That includes Arizona, where enrollment has fallen by almost half , along with Louisiana and Illinois , where it’s down by about one-fifth. And now, states must pay more to run SNAP , which is federally funded but state-administered. In my research on the history of SNAP, I’ve found that changes in the way states run their programs have a big impact on who can get help. States are struggling to adapt to new federal policies. As additional changes roll out, more families may lose access to SNAP. Covering more of the administrative costs As of Oct. 1, 2026, states have to pay 75% of all administrative costs, which include paying staff who manage the enrollment process and maintaining the program’s computer systems. Previously, states paid 50% of those costs. The federal government estimates that states and local governments will pay roughly US$17 billion more in administrative costs over the next five years. In the 2027 fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, California – with the largest population of any state – will be responsible for paying roughly $670 million more to run the program. Wyoming, with the smallest number of residents, will pay about $3 million more . Costs will be shifted to local governments in nine of the 10 states where SNAP is administered by counties. Looming changes tied to ‘payment error rates’ State agencies and some state legislatures are imposing stricter rules and requiring applicants to provide more paperwork documenting their income, expenses and the number of people in their household. Caseworkers in states such as Arizona have reportedly been overwhelmed with the paperwork. Those seeking help have spent hours trying to get through on phone lines and have faced monthslong delays. States are taking these steps to get ready for another change that will roll out in October 2027. At that point, many states will also have to cover up to 15% of the costs of benefits for the first time since the program began in the 1960s. This cost is much larger than the administrative costs and could be staggering for many states . How much a state pays will be based on its “payment error rate.” These error rates measure how much in benefits are paid above or below what families are actually entitled to based on their household size, income and expenses. It is calculated based on an in-depth review of a small sample of a state’s benefits payments each year. These inaccurate payments are generally a result of mistakes on the part of the applicant or their caseworker – they rarely are the result of fraud. The payment error rate includes benefits paid to ineligible participants. It does not include payments never made to applicants who were eligible for benefits but wrongly denied them or incorrectly dropped from the program. Supporters of SNAP argue that this makes states err on the side of denying benefits. Range of rates States with an error rate less than 6% won’t face new costs for benefits. But only nine states had rates that low in 2025. States with an error rate between 6% and 8% will be responsible for 5% of the costs of their residents’ SNAP benefits. States with an error rate between 8% and 10% will have to cover 10%. States with error rates over 10% will have to cover 15%. There’s a weird twist: If a state has an error rate over 13.32% , it won’t have to pay part of the cost of residents’ SNAP benefits for up to two years as they would have had it been in the 6% to 13.32% range. Farm bill politics could play a role To reduce their error rates, states need to invest in more staff, training, technology and better application and verification procedures. But states had little time to do all that. The states’ share of costs slated to kick in as of October 2027 is based on the error rates in the fiscal year that ended in September 2026. Organizations representing state and local governments and social workers are pushing for an across-the board two-year delay. What’s more, legislation known as the “ farm bill ,” which sets policies for agriculture, conservation and food-related assistance like SNAP, is now ensnared in the dispute. Democrats, whose support is needed to pass the legislation in the Senate, would like to see most of the new SNAP changes repealed. Congress aims to pass a farm bill roughly every five years, but the most recent one, which was finalized in 2018, has expired . Short of rolling back all the SNAP policy changes, many Democrats have refused to vote for the farm bill unless it includes a two-year delay for all states in shouldering part of the cost of SNAP benefits. If the Democratic Party holds a majority in one or both chambers of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections, their leverage could increase in these negotiations. The Republican Party’s version of the farm bill now pending in the Senate includes a one-year delay in the benefits-funding changes. But it would increase the states’ burden even more than the policy planned for October 2027. That’s a nonstarter for Democrats. What states can do about all this Meanwhile, there are many signs that a large share of the people who have lost their SNAP benefits are struggling to feed their families. More people, for example, are seeking help from food pantries and banks , which fear they will not be able to keep up with growing demand. It’s hard to predict what might happen next. events.title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
events.summary: By teaching entrepreneurship, colleges can better prepare students for a fast-changing job market and technological disruption. Igor Golovniov/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their unemployment rate hit 5.7% , compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s one of the worst rates in the past 20 years. Meanwhile, roughly 4 in 10 graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic. As an educator for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate? What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok attained that threshold in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly. Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers. I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit. 3 core lessons The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences develop the capabilities students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers. Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech. Making adaptability a core skill: Students need to learn how to be nimble . This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world. To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator . The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape. Understanding customer value: Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech . Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level. Emphasizing fundamentals: Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate. Students in startup training have to deal with uncertainty, resource constraints and customer interaction, all of which will make them more nimble in their careers. David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images The many paths toward entrepreneurship Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value. But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course. That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback. More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, such as Cornell and the University of Washington . At Georgia Tech, we have a playbook that we have developed through our experiences that follows the following principles: Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum: One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out. Build a pathway to business creation: Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, including MIT , Rice University and the University of Texas . But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a learn/make/launch/scale pathway that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them. Offer real venture experience: A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch.

events.title: Hungary’s former foreign minister grilled over ties to China's BYD automaker while in office
events.summary: Péter Szijjártó, Hungary’s former foreign minister, is appearing before a parliamentary committee to answer questions about his dealings with Chinese automaker BYD while in office BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungary’s former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó appeared before a parliamentary committee on Monday to answer questions about his dealings with Chinese automaker BYD while still in office. He left politics in July to take up an executive position with the company. Szijjártó, who served as Hungary's foreign minister for 12 years under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán before an election defeat in April, announced in July that he would resign his seat in Hungary’s parliament to take the job at the world’s top electric carmaker . The announcement prompted accusations of a conflict of interest, and criticism of his central role in facilitating substantial government subsidies for the company while in office. In addition to securing the deal allowing BYD to open its first European factory near the southern Hungarian city of Szeged, Szijjártó also announced in 2025 that the company would locate its European headquarters and a research and development center in Budapest, and receive 20 billion forints ($63.7 million) in government assistance. Upon arriving at the closed-door National Security Committee hearing on Monday, Szijjártó told reporters that there had been “serious misunderstandings” related to BYD’s investment in Hungary. He made no mention of his new position at the company, which he earlier described as an “executive responsible for the group’s external relations and the development of new business lines.” “I consider it a great success that this factory came to Hungary,” Szijjártó said on Monday. “I would also like to point out that the proposed and awarded government subsidies for the construction of the BYD factory in Szeged have remained well within the framework of the usual subsidies for investments of this magnitude.” Iran live updates: Saudi Arabia says 2 of its airports were damaged in strikes Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, told lawmakers in July that Szijjártó had helped BYD “with hundreds of billions (of forints) in public money, diplomatic support and state infrastructure,” and that an investigation would be launched to “examine all the decisions, negotiations and state commitments” made by Szijjártó related to the BYD investment. While in office working under Orbán, Szijjártó concluded numerous foreign investment deals with Chinese companies to open factories in Hungary, largely related to battery production for the electric vehicle industry. Orbán’s government hoped the investments would make Hungary a global hub of lithium-ion battery manufacturing, yet decreased demand and other market pressures have so far prevented those investments from paying high dividends. Since taking office in May, Magyar’s government has promised increased regulation and tighter oversight of the battery production sector following some workplace accidents and findings at several plants that showed contamination levels over legal limits. events.title: Average five-year fixed mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
events.summary: Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer. Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year. In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets has increased expectations of a base rate rise . Meanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level. There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages . Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”. She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.” The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property. Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning There are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last week reporting that annual price growth had halved in September . Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability. He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”

events.title: Washington has picked a side in Ethiopia's new war
events.summary: There is new cause for alarm in the Horn of Africa. A week after a coalition of seven opposition groups announced an alliance to overthrow the government of Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, fighting has broken out across several regions of the country of 130 million people. Led by the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front, the militias of Ethiopia’s largest regions of Amhara and Oromia have also pledged their support. Early battles have taken place along a critical commercial route leading east to the port of Djibouti, while drone strikes were carried out around the army’s main airbase near the capital, Addis Ababa. The choice of economic and political targets reflects the reality that even though the Tigrayans are weaker militarily than in their previous war that ended in 2022, they can still create asymmetric pressure on the government. Ethiopia’s army is now quickly regrouping and is pushing the TPLF back into Tigray, where government forces have retaken the regional airport and now occupy the capital, Mekelle. As the conflict moves into urban areas, the risk of displacement and civilian casualties grows. And in a region already suffering from aid shortages, and anticipating even greater food insecurity from this year’s El Nino, humanitarians are rightly nervous about a potential catastrophic fallout. But the Tigrayans and their “Alliance for Survival” allies believe they have an ace up their sleeves. A coalition of neighboring states, led by Egypt and including Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia have reportedly been working in the background to support the Prime Minister’s armed opponents. Abiy’s announcement of building three new hydroelectric dams on the Nile, along with his threatening claims on the Eritrean port of Assab, and his army’s support for the Rapid Support Forces militia next door in Sudan have made him no friends across the region. All would like to see his ambitions contained. With a fully internationalized conflict already raging in neighboring Sudan and long-time foe Eritrea poised to enter the fight on the side of the Tigrayans, the risk that Ethiopia’s conflict converges with existing regional instability and animosities is high. The fallout from a regional war on US priorities from counterterrorism to Red Sea security would be disastrous, which raises the question why isn’t the Trump Administration doing more to stop it? On Oct. 4, the State Department urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to “exercise maximum restraint,” though curiously did not address the current fighting by Ethiopia’s internal armed groups. But back in June, the State Department sanctioned a group of Tigrayan officials for “undermining resolution to the crisis in Tigray” and last week the US ambassador in Addis blamed Tigrayans for their “poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive.” None of this suggests an even-handed approach this time around that would enable Washington to mediate an end to the violence as it did in 2022 to end the last Tigray war. This time, Washington has picked a side. Rubio’s newfound prioritization of commercial diplomacy , reflected in the announcement last week of the sale of $5 billion in Boeing aircraft to Ethiopia’s national airline, speaks to Washington’s focus on economic returns over peacemaking. But that view is shortsighted. Ethiopia’s double-digit economic growth and large infrastructure plans are vulnerable to the threat of nationwide war and regional meddling. The African Union has called for calm , but only Washington has the political leverage to manage a regional crisis. With Red Sea instability occupying more of Washington’s strategic focus, it would do well to prioritize peacemaking and ensure that Ethiopia’s economic potential is not undone by a descent into a region-wide conflict.
