events.title: Democratic-controlled Senate would confirm ‘very few’ Trump nominees
events.summary: The News The winner of Senate control would snatch one of the biggest tangible prizes of the midterms: control over President Donald Trump’s nominees. If Democrats are in charge, don’t expect many of Trump’s picks to move at all. “If the nominees are as crappy as his present ones, very few of them are going to get through. If he sends us a new [Defense Secretary Pete] Hegseth, I bet he wouldn’t pass the Senate,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told Semafor in a pre-election interview. “It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.” Democrats are favored to take the House, which would limit big bipartisan breakthroughs on legislation next year. But if Republicans can hold the Senate, they’d at least retain the ability to confirm Trump nominees — most notably, lifetime judicial appointments. Schumer’s comments confirm that Democratic control of the Senate under Trump would turn the battle to confirm Senate nominees into trench warfare, with committee chairmen able to bottle up Trump’s picks easily and Schumer able to simply not put them on the floor. Perhaps a handful of judges would be confirmed, but Cabinet secretaries would face long slogs. There’s also little hope that a Democratic majority would confirm a Supreme Court nominee — should a vacancy arise — after then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s blockade of Merrick Garland during the Obama years. “A Democrat-controlled Senate will without any question block every single one of President Trump’s nominees. This includes every cabinet member and every judge who is committed to upholding the Constitution,” said Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo. “[Schumer is] not going to change his playbook of obstruction and opposition.” Know More It’s been more than a decade since the president’s party lost control of the Senate during a midterm election. After the 2014 red wave, Senate Republicans gave former President Barack Obama few lower-level judges, blocked a Supreme Court seat from being filled, and even blocked his attorney general nominee, Loretta Lynch, from confirmation until the Senate passed a human trafficking bill. There’s no way around a judicial nominee blockade, but Trump can lean on acting officials in the executive branch. If Republicans do lose Senate control, look for the GOP to use its blunt confirmation tools — including confirming large tranches of nominees — in November and December to accomplish as much as they can before Schumer takes control again. There are currently 27 judicial vacancies at the district level and 10 nominees to fill those, mostly in Republican states. There are also a handful of nominees ready to be confirmed to federal appeals courts. If Republicans hold the chamber, they will probably prioritize judicial appointments for the next two years.

events.title: Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what
events.summary: There has been much chilly weather in the sunny meadowlands of AI futures. Fortunately, to use an indecently inappropriate adverb, the rest of the world isn’t really looking, being too busy chewing its nails over the very many other intimations of disaster. Sure, rebel swarms of attack agents breaking out of the labs isn’t a good look. OpenAI delaying its IPO and a new model launch likewise. All these things soak up whatever bandwidth the news media have to AI right now. Putting them in a bigger context, that of promises made and not kept, problems known but not fixed, the observable risk-reward ratios as models develop, we may at last start having a sense of what sort of crisis awaits. Actual crises are frequently triggered by crises in confidence, themselves caused when frameworks of assumption stop standing up to reality and wishful thinking. Thus, the assumption to date is that models will get more powerful and infrastructure more capable, in a way that justifies — demands — massive capex. The economics of giant infrastructure investment when you can’t buy what you need is a great bet in free markets that presupposes that freedom, and yeah, about that. A bigger problem is the idea that more powerful AI is always better. It frequently is, but that’s not good enough, When frontier models have to be kept in LLM jail for uncontrollable dishonesty, not so much. Here, the bigger context is that we’ve known that at heart LLM probability space is entirely relative. There is no ground truth there. Nobody has fixed hallucinations, and now we see the fascinating phenomenon of a machine that doesn’t understand truth but can deliberately lie. If more powerful models are better at that, scratch one assumption. Another huge assumption is that even at the current level of model reliability, agentic architectures are ready to be useful. Those who show all the caution of a chronic gambler on a winning "streak" are as ready to get the brakes slammed on as their opposites. The principal contender for the one true proof of concept that agentic AI is a dangerous fount of unexpected consequence is Meta’s new Muse. It is aimed at low-information credulous users and its star turn is, of course, shopping. The AI use case that’s five years away, and always has been. It’s Meta, so of course it soaks up all the information about you, your online activities and the people you talk to as much as it can. It will soon have ultracute animated Tamagotchi-style pets you can wear around your neck to improve your status as a Meta monitoring post. And we did say it was Meta, so has all the attention to security and careful design you may expect. Which is why it’s already been caught sending people’s physical addresses to strangers, and why when researcher Jonny at neuromatch.social went poking around its infrastructure — each instance runs permanently on its own Linux VM — they found just a ton of fun. Headline party tricks hard-coded. What looks like attempts to train off Claude. And yes, you can get it to run your own things on that VM deep within Meta, which Jonny points out is a botnet paradise waiting to happen. This banger of a bad ‘un is being given away to Meta users, who pretty much define a vulnerable target audience for tech that may not be totally trustworthy. Meta, of course, is dead against AI safety regulation. Place your bets on the headlines to follow. In any case, the upside of using agents as demoed in every keynote is either so trivial and trite — book me a restaurant! — or so catastrophic if it fails — organize my family vacation! — that consumer agents are a bust. It’s just that Meta may be bringing a lot of accelerant to that particular fire. There are other fires, of course, many known about since everything kicked off. Model collapse due to training on data contaminated with output? Still a thing, still no fix a "better" AI might provide. And that habit AI has of retailing everything and paying for nothing, choking off its own training data supply chain and a huge chunk of commerce and culture with it? Very much still a thing. Where AI does make consistent progress is in domain-specific tasks. Science, engineering, mathematics, and coding, if you match a model with enough reinforcement learning with humans who know how to manage them, there are startling results. You don’t get much innovation, not much newness, which is the true driver of progress. Better than humans is highly contextual. Computers have been better at chess for decades, but there isn’t a better chess. Horses run faster than humans, and that’s been useful for four millennia, but we got to peak horses quite some time ago. So the question is, have we reached peak AI, where the cost of future developments don’t match the risk they won’t work well enough to justify? If ChatGPT already writes a perfectly good business letter in a couple of seconds, there is no meaningful improvement to be had for users. Most AI is profoundly annoying, in ways that have nothing to do with the models and everything to do with perverted UX in an attempt to justify growth. That is both unsustainable and a tacit admission that AI hasn’t solved its use case problem. If we are at or near peak AI, is that the crisis that bursts that goddam bubble? Certainly a readjustment, as all bets on the continuous uptick curve are off. AI as it stands is useful enough to power a big industry sector, just in ways that are and remain at odds to how it is marketed and its future fantasies. Trust in AI Max may be shaken, but there's still room for lots of improvement. That slowdown that everyone who isn’t a miscreant is calling for may happen organically, if we escape the smoking-is-good-for-you mentality of the Metans and the Muskovites. That’s still a gamble we shouldn't be taking, but the odds may be better than we thought. ®

events.title: Non-oil sectors in UAE and Saudi Arabia maintain strong growth trajectory despite Iran war
events.summary: The non-oil private sectors of the UAE and Saudi Arabia maintained their expansion trajectory in September, as the Arab world’s two largest economies shook off the effects of the Iran war . The seasonally adjusted Riyad Bank purchasing managers’ index – a benchmark gauge of the kingdom’s non-oil economy – rose to 55.3 in September, from 53.8 in August, well above the neutral 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. The rate of improvement in the non-oil sector business activity last month was the strongest since February and marked the sixth consecutive month of improvements in business conditions. The acceleration last month was largely driven by a marked rise in new order growth, although it masked the softening in the rate of output growth. New orders hit levels closer to the index’s long-run average, suggesting that demand in the kingdom has recovered well after a slowdown in the middle of 2026. Businesses surveyed also referred to gradual improvements in the market that led to increased client numbers and higher spending. “The acceleration was primarily demand-led. New orders increased at their fastest pace since February,” said Naif Alghaith, chief economist at Riyad Bank. The September reading of the PMI index was broadly consistent with the “wider picture of the Saudi economy”, which was driven by domestic consumption, investment activity, government and PIF-related projects. “The strong improvement in new orders provides a positive forward-looking signal for activity in the coming months,” Mr Alghaith said. While the recovery was predominantly driven by the domestic market in September, new orders from foreign customers have now dropped for seven months running. Companies surveyed pointed to the effects of supply chain disruption amid the regional conflict that in some cases led to shipping delays. Gulf states including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, Opec’s biggest oil producer, have faced attacks during the war, which is now in its seventh month. The tourism and leisure, retail, aviation and properties sectors across the Gulf took a hit as Iran attacked civilian infrastructure and regional energy installations during the early days of the conflict. Gulf economies have bounced back gradually, although Iran continues to attack commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, while Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports are under a "maritime blockade" from Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthi rebels. Demand drives UAE Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years in response to higher input costs. Meanwhile, business activity increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand both purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index in September remained stable at 55.3 recorded in August, well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. The latest PMI reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, said David Owen, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. “Businesses saw customer demand improve, not just in local markets but abroad as well, with new export business rising at the strongest rate in nearly two years,” he added. The improvement in the UAE’s business conditions was mainly driven by a “rapid monthly rise in output”, with the fastest rate of growth since February, before the outbreak of the war. Stronger demand conditions also supported a marked increase in new orders, although the pace of expansion eased from the seven-month high posted in August. The overall new order numbers were also supported by an increase in new business from abroad, which expanded for the third consecutive month and at the sharpest pace since November 2024, PMI data showed. However, as the demand strengthened, companies raised their output prices at the steepest rate since May 2011, which was among the fastest since the survey began. "While the economic picture looks more robust now, selling charges also rose markedly, suggesting that firms are taking the opportunity to boost their margins following a period of strong input cost pressures,” Mr Owen said. “With oil markets remaining volatile, and shipping routes still constrained, input costs and selling charges may remain elevated." Dubai momentum Non-oil private sector business activity in Dubai, one of the biggest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Dubai PMI posted 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, signalling a “solid improvement”, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026 so far. The boost to Dubai’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven a "sharp and accelerated increase in output”, the fastest so far this year. New orders also rose markedly, supported by the strongest expansion in new business from abroad for two years, the PMI survey data showed. Although employment in the emirate increased in September, the backlog of work still increased at a sharp pace. “The rate of output price inflation quickened to the fastest since January 2014 as companies passed on higher input costs to customers,” the survey found.

events.title: HKTDC’s Belt and Road Summit drives momentum
events.summary: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The 11th Belt and Road Summit, which took place in Wan Chai on 9-10 September, brought together more than 6,200 top officials, business leaders and senior professionals from 70-plus B&R countries and regions to explore opportunities for further cooperation and partnerships. Co-organised by the HKSAR Government and the Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC), the signature event gave attendees the chance to promote cross-regional trade and industry collaboration, as well as to accelerate new initiatives and achieve concrete outcomes. Underlining these intentions, the Summit’s broad theme this year was “Advancing High-Quality Development‧Embarking on a New Journey”. Significant results were achieved not just in showcasing over 300 investment projects, arranging more than 800 meetings between potential dealmakers, and facilitating the signing of more than 60 memoranda of understanding (MOUs) and other agreements. Equally notable was the diversity of sectors involved, ranging from finance and professional services to manufacturing and construction; the presence of organisations from the ASEAN bloc, Central Asia and the Middle East, and the interest shown in what Hong Kong can offer nowadays as both a “super connector” and a “super value-adder”. The two-day agenda featured a series of keynote addresses from high-profile speakers plus plenary sessions and informative panel discussions. This allowed participants to share their expertise on policy issues, navigating risk, and creating opportunities for enterprises to expand into international markets at a time of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical uncertainties. There was also an emphasis on innovation, enhancing trade and investment resilience, and helping to transform initial connections into tangible results and lasting ties. For instance, in his opening remarks, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu noted the importance of a proactive approach to advancing regional exchanges and opening new markets. The former highlighted the immense possibilities in trade, transport, industry, technology, capital investment and human resources that came with reviving the ancient Silk Road in a modern format and establishing comprehensive strategic links. Cosse said it made sense then because the B&R pillars of infrastructure, connectivity, trade facilitation and financial integration aligned with Uruguay’s long-term belief in multilateral cooperation and free trade. And today that commitment to enhancing capital flows and developing joint projects with Hong Kong and other partners in Asia remains as strong as ever. Besides formal plenary sessions and high-powered debates, this year’s Summit also introduced new thematic zones to spotlight Hong Kong’s ability to support the practical needs of enterprises in different sectors. For instance, the “GoGlobal Connect Zone” showed how the city’s professional services expertise has helped Chinese Mainland companies plan for expansion and connect with international markets. There were also roundtable discussions and a one-stop exchange and matchmaking platform to assist with answers and general advice. Separately, the Central Asia Zone featured eight exhibitors from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, showcasing the rapid development and investment opportunities in Central Asia. And the Middle East Zone gave attendees a much fuller understanding of the potential for business and investment in the six countries, covering Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE. Saleumxay Kommasith, the Deputy Prime Minister of Laos, used his special address to illustrate Belt and Road cooperation in practice. He highlighted the impact of the Laos-China Railway, which opened in 2021. Since then, it has carried more than 70 million passengers and transported over 90 million metric tonnes of freight.

events.title: The Agentic AI Super Cycle
events.summary: The biggest technology revolutions of the past were driven by steam engines in the 1700s, railroads in the 1800s, electricity, cars, phones, planes, computers, and the internet in the 1900s. Now we are at the dawn of the Agentic AI revolution, which will be the biggest of them all. A few years ago, Goldman Sachs predicted Generative AI would increase global GDP by about 7% over 10 years. McKinsey had a roughly similar projection. Today, more than half of USA GDP growth is due to AI infrastructure investment. Agentic AI is much more powerful and more economically impactful than generative AI (and any previous industrial revolution) and requires much more compute investment for broad adoption. More than half of GDP in advanced economies is labor, with more than half of that labor being cognitive work that can be made much more productive with agentic AI. So far, coding is the early adopter, with most coders now using agentic AI to generate and validate most code. That makes the coder more of an architect and manager. What’s astounding is that this happened in less than 2 years. Frontier models are now used extensively to generate code for the next frontier model. But how quickly will other fields extensively adopt Agentic AI, and will supply chain constraints be overcome to meet the demand? Recently, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, called for a pacing of the development of frontier models to ensure everyone is building in the right controls and safeguards. AI leaders agree these controls are important. “We’ll make AI that is incredibly safe,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO. Any pacing of model development won’t slow the pace of investment. Dario noted safeguards will involve more training. Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, noted on CNBC recently, “even if we stop today, the amount of intelligence that’s available in the world is massive,” and “there is so much opportunity to drive growth with good ROI (return on investment).” Data center AI CapEx (capital expenditure) will reach ~$1 trillion this year, and is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030 (Source: Jensen Huang, Goldman Sachs Technology Conference). By comparison, world GDP is expected to be $123 trillion this year. AI is expected to go from ~1% to ~3%. Of the world’s top 10 highest market capitalization companies, 8 are major AI players: Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, TSMC, SpaceX, Meta, Broadcom. Collectively they make up almost 20% of the total market cap of the world’s publicly traded companies. Only a couple of these AI companies were in the top 10 a decade ago. Anthropic is expected to join the top 10 market capitalization club later this year. Massive companies like Nvidia are projecting 70% growth in revenues next year at huge scale. It’s natural to think this can’t keep going. But maybe it can. The key factors are: If agentic AI has high ROI; If it has a huge TAM (Total Addressable Market), and If it continues to become more powerful and less costly for years to come. If all those conditions are met, then we are in the biggest supercycle of our lives — and of history. The AI leader companies will get much bigger along with the US and world economies. There will be losers, there will be pauses/plateaus/consolidation, but this is a 10+ year Super 2 Cycle. Data center AI investment offers very attractive ROI The hyperscalers, Anthropic, and OpenAI are ramping AI CapEx because they see rapid demand growth, strong ROI, and because they don’t want to fall behind competition. This is a gold rush. Morgan Stanley in July concluded the major hyperscalers had paths to 25% to 50% ROIC (return on invested capital) for GenAI. These are very attractive returns. Dave Patterson, distinguished engineer and fellow at Google, said at the recent AI Infra Summit that Google recovers its cash outlay for a TPU in 1 year, and in 2 years for its custom Axion CPU. At Goldman Sachs Tech Conference, Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, said TPUs paid back twice as fast as GPUs, so even GPUs recover their investment in 2 years. This is a fantastic ROI, although he might be leaving out land and building costs. The reason this isn’t increasing near-term profits already is because Google keeps increasing CapEx spend faster than revenue growth. Amazon senior vice president Peter DeSantis talked at AI Infra Summit about how the company builds the data center and the racks in parallel with building the Trainiums. This accelerates cash recovery, enabling Trainium shipments from the end of the production line to the data center to be in operation (and making money) in a couple months. He contrasted this to most companies that build the chips, then the trays, then the racks, then the rows, then install. That keeps cash tied up much longer before revenue generation. New Street forecasts that hyperscaler negative cash flow will bottom in 2028 at 20% of revenues, but then rapidly turns to a positive free cash flow of 10% of revenues by 2030. AI cloud revenue grows almost 10× from 2026 to 2030! And AI cloud revenue by 2030 exceeds non-AI. TSMC builds >90% of all AI compute devices (GPUs and custom XPUs like TPU and Trainium). TSMC is an extremely well-run company that does its homework thoroughly. events.title: Extreme Environments Push Chips To Their Breaking Point
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Orbital data centers, military/aerospace vehicles, HPC experiments, quantum, and advanced manufacturing equipment are all putting pressure on chips to withstand extreme environments. Conditions include any combination of thermal and mechanical shock, radiation, high speeds, noise, vibration, pressure, and humidity. Advanced 4D modeling, simulation, AI/LLM-based design exploration, and physical lab tools are all needed to ensure complex chips and systems can survive. Chips that were once qualified against a limited set of operating conditions are now being designed for environments where multiple stresses hit at once. Radiation, thermal shock, vibration, pressure, noise, and cryogenic temperatures are colliding in applications ranging from orbital data centers and defense systems to particle physics, quantum computing, and advanced manufacturing. That is changing how chips are designed and qualified. AI-enabled design tools, machine learning, and language models can explore more design options earlier, but virtual models still have to be checked against physical behavior. For extreme-environment electronics, the challenge is not just predicting failure modes, but reproducing enough of the real operating environment to trust the prediction. Space is becoming one of the clearest pressure points. The growth of satellite constellations, orbital data centers, space probes, surface explorers, and military space systems is increasing demand for radiation-hardened designs, including at newer process nodes where performance and power benefits must be balanced against survivability. That demand is already showing up in the design ecosystem. “We have seen a major uptick in activity for rad-hard fab processes, particularly in the new process nodes to support orbital data centers,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys . “A lot of this is owing to the Golden Dome (multi-layered U.S. missile defense initiative). The next frontier for the next battlefield is space, and so you’re seeing the investment now accelerate, and we’re going to see a lot more rad-hard designs added.” Beyond national security, governments and nations are competing for global leadership in emerging technologies. For example, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) is working with Morgan State University, Northrop Grumman, and Project Omega on the DARPA-funded Rads to Watts program, which aims to convert Cold War-era radioactive decay into high-density nuclear micro-power radiovoltaic systems for extreme environments, including space, remote sensing, undersea infrastructure, and defense applications. [1] Radioisotopes such as Strontium-90 will be converted directly into electricity to operate for decades without refueling or battery replacement. Researchers achieve this by combining ultra-thin semiconductor layers with high-energy, beta-emitting isotopes. Simulation, characterization, and survivability analysis are essential to ensure these systems can operate in harsh environments. Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory is working with Siemens on a project titled Accelerating eXtreme Environment Specs-to-Silicon (AXESS) that uses LLMs and smaller surrogate models to speed up design exploration, then integrate and co-optimize all stages of chip development for quantum computing, fusion energy, and particle physics. [2] Fig. 1: A Fermilab engineer holds a custom circuit board designed to measure chip performance in cryogenic environments. Source : JJ Starr/Fermilab Each extreme-environment application presents a unique set of physical stressors that the hardware device must account for. “Particle accelerators and research accelerators are a particularly challenging environment because the doses are ridiculously high, and you need the equipment to do its thing while it’s getting damaged by the radiation,” said Hugh Barnaby, leader of extreme environment reliability in the U.S. Department of Defense’s ME Commons SWAP Hub at Arizona State University. “That extends to the medical equipment that’s used in proton therapies for cancer, which uses high-energy electrons. And in semiconductor manufacturing, lithography causes radiation damage. They’re using X-rays now for some of the really advanced technology, like backside power delivery. They have the power distribution on the backside of the chip. They used to use a wafer-analysis technique called LADA (laser-assisted device alteration), but now they can’t because the power is on the backside. They can’t use the lights. So they’re considering X-ray-assisted device alteration lasers (XADA). The problem is, they’re worried about the X-rays causing damage to the material.” Barnaby and one of his students, Jereme Neuendank, found that strange things happen to semiconductors at very low temperatures. [3] “If you combine that with radiation, it gets even weirder,” said Barnaby. ” We had some good theories with models backing them up, and we’re still doing a lot of work in that area.” Lab tools are evolving to study the effects of multiple stressors at once. ASU researchers developed the Rigel DSTAT, which has three rods collectively containing 9,000 Curies (Ci) of radioactive material to simulate the radiation environments found in space and nuclear applications. It also contains a tiny cryostat, which enables devices to be exposed to really saturated, extremely cold temperatures by evacuating a chamber and then filling it with either liquid nitrogen or argon, whose temperatures are about the same. “Then we can do radiation testing at liquid nitrogen, which is 77 Kelvin,” said Barnaby. Fig. 2: This illustrated setup shows how ASU’s extreme environments lab would test radiation and extreme cold together to mimic space. Illustration by Sophia Franz. Source : ASU The tool was ideal for a company designing readout ICs for satellites that would need to withstand cold, radiation, ionizing-dose threats, and low-frequency noise. In particular, random telegraph noise has emerged as one of the biggest reliability problems today, especially in analog/mixed-signal electronics. And that noise problem is exacerbated in the cold. “You want the cold to reduce the noise that comes off of the diodes that are creating the currents, the light detectors,” Barnaby noted. “They like the cold there. But when you’re doing the CMOS, to do the readout of those signals, the random telegraph noise signal does not, at best, improve with cold temperature. We’re still studying that physics.” The applications for these kinds of lab tools are growing. “We have talked to people about doing research in thermal energy exploration,” he explained. “We’ve also been getting into advanced packaging, which means extending into a pretty wide array of reliability issues such as pressure, humidity, high tempe

events.title: Buyer missed one option and got 1% of the cable they needed
events.summary: Every Monday morning The Register kicks off proceedings by asking the same question – “Who, Me?” – the title of the reader-contributed column in which you share your tales of the occasions on which you didn’t quite nail the brief yet somehow found career relief. This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Terry” who told us that in the 1970s he worked for a defense-related company. “I needed 100 meters of RG8 50 ohm coax cable, so ordered it from an ‘accredited’ supplier,” he wrote. “What I didn’t notice was that there was an option for ‘partial delivery’." Terry’s order duly arrived, all one meter of it – plus paperwork explaining that the other 99 meters would be along presently, thanks to the partial delivery option. “Needless to say, the one meter was not enough to span the distance between the two laboratories I was trying to link with an RF connection,” Terry wrote. Offering the partial delivery option cost the supplier their accreditation. Terry later learned that a junior employee at the cable supplier was sacked over the matter, after admitting he thought sending one meter of cable was a jolly jape. “I did not think it was a joke at the time,” Terry wrote. Have you made a procurement error that ended up costing you, or your supplier? If so, don’t short-change your fellow readers! Instead, click here to share your story with Who, Me? Our mailbag is a little short on stories, so contributions of any length are very welcome. ®

events.title: Trump proposal could make it easier to suspend or expel Head Start students
events.summary: The Trump administration has proposed changes to Head Start regulations that would remove rules against suspending and expelling preschoolers It was sometime around Xavier Rogers' second birthday that his mom and Early Head Start teachers noticed a shift in his demeanor. Xavier, usually a happy baby, now mostly wanted to play alone and would sometimes bite and hit other kids in his class. Instead of removing Xavier from his class, his Chicago-area preschool gave the family extra support from a social-emotional and mental healthcare team. “With these supports in place, I feel like he has grown tremendously,” said Xavier's mom, Joanna Isitt, a Head Start teacher herself. Now 4, “he’s become much, much more aware of himself and how he feels and how others may feel.” He's less likely to resort to negative behaviors, and he even encourages her to join him in breathing exercises, saying, “OK, Mama, smell the flowers, blow the candles.” The protections and support Isitt and her son received are part of longstanding Head Start regulations, but they could soon disappear under the Trump administration’s proposed rule change for the 61-year-old early childhood education program. The proposal would eliminate federal guidelines that keep kids who exhibit behaviors like Xavier’s from being removed from Head Start programs. Instead of receiving the help he needed to self-regulate, the little boy could have been told to leave, and his mother could have been left scrambling for alternative care. AP has partnered with The 74 , an education-focused nonprofit news outlet, to cover the impact of the Trump administration's proposed changes to Head Start. The family lives in Illinois, which has its own regulations against imposing exclusionary discipline such as suspensions and expulsions on preschoolers. But some other states, such as South Carolina and Florida, do not. The updated Head Start rules would ask providers to make their own discipline policies by following state and local licensing requirements. Advocates and experts fear Head Start students and families in these places could experience a more punitive reality if the proposed changes take effect. Suspensions and expulsions are associated with negative outcomes, including lower educational achievement, decreased likelihood of graduating high school and depression. “If the state of Florida doesn’t have standards related to suspension and expulsion, and that’s what the administration wants us to go by … I think as a country we should all be very concerned that we’re taking our most vulnerable children and families and potentially putting them in an environment where they’re going to have no protections,” said Wanda Minick, executive director of the Florida Head Start Association. Only 14 states and Washington, D.C., have laws or policies that align with Head Start’s rules around exclusionary discipline, according to a recent analysis by the Children’s Equity Project at Arizona State University. Of those, researchers said, only around half the laws appear to apply to all children under 5, the population served by Head Start. And in only one, Minnesota, do the regulations explicitly include Head Start programs. That means that in 70% of states, Head Start students would be left with fewer guardrails should the rule change pass. Many of the states with flexible rules or no laws end up removing the most preschoolers from their classrooms, while states with tighter regulations suspend far fewer, according to an analysis of 2023-24 federal data by The 74 and The Associated Press. The data captures suspensions for pre-kindergartners who are enrolled in public school districts. South Carolina reported suspending 604 public preschoolers a total of 1,181 times that year, while Minnesota reported zero students suspended. Florida reported expelling 466 public preschoolers, more than any other state. Ultimately, the data shows, some Head Start students would remain shielded from expulsion and suspension, but some would not — simply depending on where they live. The public may comment on the rule change through Oct. 6. Iran live updates: Saudi Arabia says 2 of its airports were damaged in strikes Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' The Trump administration is attempting to roll back these discipline safeguards along with many of the tools that prevent behaviors from escalating in the first place, advocates said. These include lower adult-to-child ratios, a required number of monthly mental health consultations, timely developmental screenings and staff breaks. In this environment, “if they were to make it permissible to either reject kids or throw them out, I think a lot of teachers would, because they’re just feeling so much strain,” said Joel Ryan, executive director of the Washington State Association of Head Start.

events.title: Lao man deported by the US to Eswatini is released after more than a year in prison
events.summary: A Lao man deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has been released after more than a year in prison CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said. Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program. Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago. Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said. Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane. “He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything," Nguyen said. “He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition.” He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos. An Eswatini government spokesperson didn’t immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh’s release. Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said. Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations. Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far. Iran live updates: Saudi Arabia says 2 of its airports were damaged in strikes Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent. The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back. Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn’t give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December. The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held. events.title: Saudi Aramco cuts Asia crude prices to six-year low amid recovery as oil flows rebound
events.summary: Saudi Aramco has cut prices for its flagship crude grade sold to Asian buyers to a six-year low, as the world’s largest oil exporter competes for market share amid a recovery in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned Saudi oil company will sell Arab Light crude to Asian customers at a discount of $5 a barrel below the regional benchmark for November, widening the discount from $2 a barrel in October, according to a Bloomberg survey. Traders and refiners polled by Bloomberg had expected Aramco to raise prices by $5 a barrel for November. The price reduction signals that Saudi Arabia may be seeking to boost sales to Asia as oil flows from the Middle East recover after months of disruption linked to the Iran war. Aramco raised its November crude prices for Europe by $3 a barrel, while leaving prices for the US unchanged from October, Bloomberg reported. Although attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue, the volume of oil passing through the waterway has increased over the past few months. Saudi Arabia sold almost 100 million barrels of oil to Asian buyers in mid-September, helping to avert a looming supply crunch. The kingdom has also restored much of the crude flow through its East-West pipeline after suffering damage in an attack. The recovery has helped increase oil exports from the Middle East, with JPMorgan estimating last week that shipments had reached 98 per cent of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. The pipeline allows Saudi Arabia to transport crude from its eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, providing an alternative export route that bypasses the strait. Aramco’s official selling prices apply to crude supplied under long-term contracts to refiners, who would typically collect their shipments from Ras Tanura on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast. Ras Tanura hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports, with cargoes typically heading to markets in Europe and Asia, including China, Japan and South Korea. But continued risks to shipping through the strait have prompted many customers to avoid the route. Aramco has asked Asian refiners to submit nominations for the volumes they intend to collect in November from ports inside the Arabian Gulf, as well as from Yanbu on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Opening the taps on diesel reserves is a risky gamble for Europe
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has bounced Europe into a risky gamble. On Friday, under threat of a US ban on diesel exports, the Group of Seven major economies agreed to release emergency petroleum stocks. Mr Trump may be looking just to elections in a month, but London, Paris and Berlin risk burning their remaining reserves. Opening the taps is meant to alleviate the crisis in diesel caused by the US-Iran war. The G7 countries collectively will provide 100 million barrels over four months, split between crude and refined products, and front-loaded with diesel. In return, they have all agreed not to impose restrictions on oil exports – for now. The Gulf shuttle scheme, guarded by US ships and aviation, appears to have succeeded in restoring crude oil flows to near prewar levels. This comes at a heavy cost in death and injury of mariners, damage to vessels, and hiring and guarding the vessels. Escorting refined product shipments is harder: they are more varied, travel in smaller ships and are usually more flammable than crude. Before the war, the Arab countries within the Gulf exported about 5.5 million barrels daily of refined products, particularly diesel, jet fuel and heavy fuel oil. That plunged to below 2 million barrels per day when the US began its attack, and has recovered to 3 million bpd or so. Iran added another 900,000 bpd of net exports of refined products and natural gas liquids. This has now fallen to near-zero by sea, and perhaps minor amounts going overland by lorry or rail. Europe and Japan hold large stocks of petroleum products, especially diesel and petrol, while the US’s strategic petroleum reserve is almost entirely crude oil. The US has marketed about 130 million barrels, taking its crude stocks down to the lowest levels since the early 1980s. It looks doubtful that it can provide much more without causing permanent damage to the artificial salt caverns that hold the oil. Though this drawdown has helped keep crude prices hovering at relatively moderate levels, that is not the locus of the current crisis – Brent crude closed the week at $102 per barrel, while wholesale diesel in New York is going for $200. If half the proposed release consists of diesel, it amounts to about 400,000 bpd over four months, replacing about a third of the exports lost this year. That would be helpful, but far from a full or permanent solution. There is also the oddity that European stocks are not owned by their governments, unlike in the US. Instead, oil companies are mandated to hold more than normal commercial levels. Approval for a release does not necessarily mean that all that diesel comes on the market. Despite the tight conditions, commercial product stocks at the crucial Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub actually rose last month, and are not down much since May, unlike in the US where they have plummeted. Hard hit from a diesel ban The proposed prohibition of American diesel exports would have hit Europe hard. The UK and EU import about 270,000 bpd of diesel from the US, a third of their total imports, though this jumped to 420,000 bpd during the worst of the crunch this summer. It would have hurt other nations too, and would quickly have rebounded on the US as refiners would have cut back runs. The US still imports significant amounts of petrol – a politically more visible and sensitive fuel – and might well have faced retaliatory bans. Should the Europeans have resisted the demand, or called Mr Trump’s bluff? On the one hand, they worried about a difficult winter. If he had just forbidden sales specifically to Europe, the fuel would have been shuffled around through other countries to end up there anyway. So, to have a real impact, he would have had to impose a blanket ban. Strategic stocks are made to be used in emergencies. While the US had already emptied much of the SPR in 2022 and hardly refilled it since, European stocks are well above legal minimum levels, and have been rebuilt since 2022. Solidarity between the G7 and the members of the International Energy Agency is fundamental for collective management of energy shocks. On the other hand, the European countries did not start this war, they are not combatants, and they do not control it. If they burn through their reserves over the next four months, they had better be sure a resolution to the crisis is coming soon. The hazy thinking coming out of the White House and the Pentagon about war aims and strategy does not inspire such confidence. Polls suggest the Republicans will suffer a drubbing in November’s midterm elections. After that, Mr Trump will find it hard to advance any of his domestic agenda. Many expect he will back down in Iran, perhaps after launching one final thunderclap so he can go home claiming a victory. That itself runs the risk that Tehran miscalculates, and decides to respond in kind rather than absorbing the blow. But it is at least as likely that, unable to achieve much at home, he will escalate. In turn, if the Iranians had not realised it already, all the headlines inform them that refineries are an Achilles heel. The Ukrainian campaign against Russia tells the same tale. Refineries in Israel and in all the Gulf states except Oman were damaged earlier this year. Saudi refineries in Jazan and Yanbu have been attacked from Yemen over the past month, and on Saturday, there were reports of a fire and smoke at a refinery in Riyadh. Europe wants to avoid the worst cases of a US diesel export ban on the one hand, and running short in the middle of a flare-up of the conflict in midwinter. The way it structures its strategic stocks gives it a way out. It can appear to have conceded to Mr Trump’s demands for a big release. But if its companies do not actually want to sell much of their stocks, that is not the governments’ fault, and will not become apparent for some weeks anyway. By then, the US elections will be over and the next moves by Washington and Tehran may be clearer.

events.title: The Live Conversation: Education Beyond the Checklist
events.summary: The International Schools Festival puts the spotlight on new approaches to education and how best to go about the application process Over 1,700 parents, students and educators attended the International Schools Festival – Hong Kong Island 2026. Held at Hong Kong Ocean Park Marriott Hotel on September 19, it featured 46 schools and education advisers, and offered families guidance on admissions, curricula, university applications and future education planning. Across five parent talks and 10 school-led information sessions, speakers returned to one central message: education should not be driven by fear or the pursuit of a perfect résumé. Whether choosing a primary school or planning for university, families should focus on well-being, curiosity and adaptability. A new approach to admissions At the morning panel session entitled, “Rethinking the Admissions Journey,” school leaders challenged the idea that primary admissions should be treated as a test children must be trained to pass. Instead of rehearsed answers, they said schools want to see curiosity, confidence, emotional readiness and a child’s natural ability to communicate and engage with others. At English Schools Foundation’s (ESF) Kennedy School, principal Brenda Cook said they do not look for one fixed type of applicant profile.

events.title: Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder?
events.summary: In Focus Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder? Temu is quickly losing its shine in the face of a wave of global regulation. Can the platform reinvent itself? In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot. “Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig. The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience. That expense paid off: Temu’s downloads jumped 45 per cent on the day of the Super Bowl campaign compared with a day earlier, according to a report by trade outlet ModernRetail, citing Sensor Tower data.

events.title: Serb separatist Dodik declares victory in Bosnia vote as ethnic tensions and EU hopes collide
events.summary: Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in Bosnia's election, which was influenced by economic pressures, EU membership prospects, and ethnic tensions SARAJEVO, Bosnia-Herzegovina -- Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia on Sunday that was shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union, and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992-95 war . Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that have sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia. Formerly the president of the country's Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war. With nearly 90% of votes counted, Dodik's ally Zeljka Cvijanovic of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats had more than 55% of votes to take one of the three seats in the country's tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by around 30 percentage points. Speaking at a news conference late Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a “vast majority” in Republika Srpska's assembly, and credited U.S. President Donald Trump's “magnificent victory” in 2024 and Russian President Vladimir Putin's support for the election win. “No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said. "We will not give up, but continue for our people ... I cannot believe that we smashed it like this.” Around 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country's multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament, and heads of institutions for the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs. With over 94% of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipovic of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegovic, by fewer than three percentage points. Both Filipovic and Becirovic declared victory in their races late Sunday before all votes were counted. Bosnia's Central Election Commission said that 1,432,269 votes were cast in total, a turnout of 42% that was down by around 8% from Bosnia's last election in 2022. Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a U.S.-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war. Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia's national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country. Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' At his party’s final election rally Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska’s administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia “is dead.” “It is an impossible country. It doesn’t make any sense,” Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian Ambassador Igor Khalabukov. Such political and ethnic divisions — in which the country's Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines — have blocked Bosnia's progress toward joining the EU despite the bloc's efforts to encourage the country's divided leaders to work together for reform. Dragan Bursac, an analyst, said that despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he “is still in command. He is everywhere.” “It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them,” Bursac said. One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades after the war that started in 1992, after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions. Bosnia’s wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladic , who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes. Bosnian Serbs view Mladic as a hero despite his conviction by a U.N. court over the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995, and other atrocities.

events.title: Marc Elias’ Democracy Docket sees Trump 2.0 success
events.summary: The News One of the Democratic Party’s most prolific lawyers also is becoming one of its most prolific posters. Marc Elias has argued dozens of cases around mail-in balloting and election access across the country and in front of the Supreme Court over the last decade. But he has also moonlighted as an election law content creator and advisor for Democracy Docket, a digital media company he founded in 2020 to focus on redistricting, gerrymandering, and voting access. What began as a hobby to help explain complex redistricting cases more effectively has grown into a serious media operation. Last month, Democracy Docket surpassed 500,000 free email subscribers, the company first told Semafor, including 70,000 subscribers paying $10 a month or $120 per year. The company also has a YouTube channel with more than 800,000 subscribers, a following that has grown significantly in recent months (the account has added half a million subscribers on the platform since January 2025). “In this era where so many political disputes, so many public controversies really wind up in court, and oftentimes the court arguments frame the public debate — I think lawyers have an obligation to speak directly and plainly in language that everyone, non-lawyers and lawyers alike, can understand,” he said. “That is something I’ve tried to do, particularly in the area of voting and elections, but really more broadly, in the area of democracy.” Elias told Semafor that he founded the outlet for a fairly prosaic reason: He’d maxed out the number of people he could send emails to on a private email listserv that he’d previously used to send election and redistricting law updates to a few hundred Democratic policymakers, executives, and officials across the country. The timing turned out to be convenient: COVID-19 lockdowns prompted a wave of court cases around mail-in balloting, an issue which Elias knew well and was, at times, directly involved in. Democracy Docket began posting public legal documents before many news outlets, gaining email subscribers and direct online traffic through Twitter and Facebook. Elias told Semafor that his readership is a mix of DC insiders, #Resistance liberals who watch Elias’ interviews on MS NOW, and legal and political professionals interested in keeping up with the ins and outs of election laws and voting access issues. While Elias told Semafor he dedicates just a few days a month to the management side, he acknowledged Democracy Docket has become a profitable enterprise. Asked how much money the company brought in each year, Elias declined to elaborate but said that the vast majority of the company’s revenue came from basic subscriptions, with a small but growing VIP tier of supporters paying $500 a year. Those projections would likely put the company in the ballpark of $9 million to $11 million in annual revenue. Max’s view Democracy Docket is part of a wave of new digital news outlets founded in the Trump era that have surged during the Republican president’s second term. While liberal and left-of-center audiences channeled their interest (and horror) with Trump during his first term by tuning into MSNBC, CNN, The New York Times, and The Washington Post, this go around, shares of those audiences have seemed to abandon traditional outlets for more ideological new media outlets positioned against traditional media. Outlets like Zeteo, The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and More Perfect Union have added millions of readers, listeners, and YouTube subscribers, even as cable news viewership continues to slide. Some of the movement appears to be ideological: Elias told me that some of the best days of membership for the site have come in the wake of blow-ups at major news outlets like CBS News, which he argues shows viewers were upset with what they saw as media owners’ capitulation to Donald Trump. But perhaps more interesting, Democracy Docket’s real innovation is in the continued erosion of the wall between real political players and the media that cover them. The proximity between Elias’ legal work and journalistic output is likely a bit too close for those who prefer a more traditional separation of church and state, though Elias insists that he’s fairly hands-off when it comes to the newsroom’s coverage. He said that he has occasionally disagreed with Democracy Docket’s stories and opinions. “Sometimes you’ll see they report it one way and then I write an opinion piece and I don’t correct them in my opinion piece, I just like say ‘this is what I think about the case, and if you want to know what I think the outcome of the case is, you know, become a premium member,’” he said. Notable Older outlets like the Guardian and The Atlantic have similarly benefited from increased left-of-center interest by explicitly positioning themselves as checks on the current administration — and even on some of their less-aggressive peers.

events.title: CEO’s podcast sparks tensions atop The Atlantic
events.summary: The Scoop Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson was talking about the media business on Vox’s podcast last month when host Peter Kafka asked him: How was the magazine’s editor-in-chief, Jeffrey Goldberg, feeling about the growing success of Thompson’s personal podcast? “We make a lot of money on the stuff I do,” he said. “Jeff likes when we make money.” Thompson’s response ricocheted around The Atlantic’s newsroom. Thompson’s podcast, , has emerged as a source of tension between the magazine’s business and editorial teams. Journalists have complained that the lucrative and high-profile show is not subject to The Atlantic’s editorial rules, input, or oversight — yet a casual listener could easily take it for an Atlantic editorial product. Thompson’s show is made by the magazine’s business side, and — like any number of contemporary podcasts — features interviews with technologists and business leaders, interspersed with sponsored content. When the podcast launched in 2024, the newsroom raised no objections; The Atlantic has featured a robust paid content arm for years through its creative marketing studio and custom events business. But as the show’s profile has risen in recent months, the podcast has caused increasing consternation internally. Thompson, despite his commercial role, is a well-known former tech reporter and former editor-in-chief of Wired. Last year, when he published a well-received memoir of his family and time as an elite long-distance runner, The Atlantic ran an excerpt . On , he has booked and interviewed top-tier guests, including OpenAI founder Sam Altman — leading staff to complain that the CEO’s bookings are, intentionally or not, undercutting the newsroom’s own efforts. According to four people familiar with the situation, the podcast has been a particular source of friction between Thompson and Goldberg. Goldberg, who also has a close relationship with Atlantic owner Laurene Powell Jobs, does not report to the CEO and instead reports directly to the Atlantic’s board of directors. (Goldberg had formally reported to Thompson’s predecessor, Bob Cohn.) Dissolving Lines The traditional separation between news outlets’ editorial and business halves has been facing pressure from both sides of that line. Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner’s podcast has drawn world leaders, cultural figures, and executives. Axios CEO Jim VandeHei regularly writes columns and occasionally breaks news on the company’s site, in addition to steering its business. The growth of independent media in the Substack era has also created a generation of journalists who run both the business and editorial arms of their own small media outlets. In this media environment, Thompson’s sponsored podcast is hardly an outlier. But it’s the latest instance in which Thompson’s attempts to nudge the newsroom on the business side have run up against a more skeptical and traditionalist editorial staff. Deepening the tension are differing views about the substance of the AI story. Thompson inked a content-licensing deal between The Atlantic and OpenAI in 2024, angering newsroom staffers, some of whom view the frontier AI labs as having stolen journalists’ work for training. The publication’s editorial union publicly expressed skepticism of the deal and the publication’s policies around AI. The magazine’s tech editor published an op-ed saying publishers like The Atlantic were making a “ devil’s bargain .” In an August 2024 letter first reported by Semafor, editorial staff said OpenAI was hallucinating Atlantic stories and linking to aggregation of the publication’s reporting. And while The Atlantic has published largely skeptical coverage of major AI companies and their products’ impact on society, Thompson’s tone, in his podcasts and LinkedIn posts, has been more optimistic. The View From The Atlantic The Atlantic declined to comment. But one senior company source stressed that there are clear disclaimers demarcating content made by the business side of the company, even if the content itself can feel journalistic in tone — perhaps unsurprising in the case of , as Thompson is a former journalist. Max’s view The Atlantic is one of the clear media success stories of the second Trump term, fueled by Signalgate and other critical reporting and commentary on the Trump administration, a successful events business, and shrewd moves to capitalize on the public stumbles of its DC neighbor, The Washington Post. The 168-year-old magazine’s breakout journalism, its digital success, and a bit of good timing have given both Goldberg and Thompson plenty to brag about on the media podcast circuit. But strains at the top of the organization over its brand and direction reflect many premium news outlets’ dilemmas about survival and profit in a post-traffic, AI-ascendant media age. Marketers have infinite options for buying ads, meaning publishers no longer have the leverage they did when they controlled much of their own distribution. Meanwhile, independent journalists are developing direct relationships with advertisers and marketers, creating more fluidity between the editorial and business sides of their brands. Still, the old boundaries existed for a reason. Fragmentation has allowed many powerful figures to get their message across by circumventing traditional media outlets whose questions many CEOs and politicians don’t want to answer. It’s not surprising that Altman was willing to sit down with The Atlantic’s CEO on a sponsored business-side podcast, but not with the magazine’s tech journalists. Room for Disagreement Readers and audiences understand that when someone runs or owns a news outlet, they have the right to make it publish their opinions and thoughts, Kafka told Thompson. “It’s not against the law, but it’s also a little creepy.”

events.title: AI nonprofit will spend $10 million on journalism
events.summary: The Scoop A Silicon Valley nonprofit close to the AI safety movement is pledging $10 million by the end of 2027 to fund mainstream and independent coverage of artificial intelligence. The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism plans to announce that it is launching an institutional grantmaking fund, which executive director Cillian Crosson said will provide grants to newsrooms and other ambitious AI reporting projects. The first recipient of the grant is , NPR’s new video podcast from former hosts Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, which is receiving a $480,000 grant from the organization. Tarbell is also separately backing NPR’s “Power and Influence” desk, giving the public media outlet $250,000 to help expand its coverage of how AI intersects with politics, money, and power. “We think that having resources at newsrooms is an important part of ensuring strong coverage,” Crosson told Semafor. The new fund will “increase our support but it also allows us to more easily support a more diverse range of perspectives.” The organization, which is backed by groups including the deep-pocketed nonprofit Coefficient Giving , said it plans to fund investigative teams, AI verticals at national outlets, and other large-scale initiatives in new and legacy media. In particular, the organization is focused on expanding reporting and on frontier companies and the ways that AI companies and aligned political action groups are influencing American politics and tech regulations. It’s a significant expansion from the organization’s previous commitments, which have totaled $400,000 over four years. Tarbell’s previous grants focused on backing early-career journalists inside established newsrooms, offering media organizations reporting grants ranging from $1,000 to $20,000 to work on individual stories on AI. With increased monetary backing, the organization said it planned to issue grants between $50,000 and $500,000, but could make multimillion-dollar grants for the right projects. Funding and AI safety In recent years, Tarbell fellows have fanned out across several major news outlets, breaking stories that have often exposed reckless or aggressive actions by AI companies and frontier labs. Though Tarbell offers funding with no formal strings attached, it has drawn criticism from some in the AI industry and on the political right who see it as fueling what they view as exaggerated safety concerns. The subjects of some of Tarbell’s journalism, including OpenAI, have complained about the reporting and financial support from some organizations aligned with effective altruism, a loose philosophical movement whose concerns include an AI-driven apocalypse. As Semafor previously reported , cash-strapped news organizations have balanced concerns about optics of outside groups funding journalism with the much-needed financial support and aggressive journalists who have broken legitimate stories about AI and safety concerns. Semafor has not found instances where Tarbell interfered directly in any stories, and the organization is quick to point out that not all of the projects it backs are AI skeptics or strong AI safety proponents. In a telephone interview last week, Crosson reminded Semafor that the organization has two editorial firewalls: One between itself and its backers, and another between Tarbell and the media organizations it supports. It discloses its donors over $10,000, its fellows maintain complete autonomy over their reporting, and the organization asks news outlets it partners with to disclose when it has provided funding to support a journalist or project. In an interview with Semafor, Roose noted that Newton had worked with Tarbell at Platformer in recent years, and found the organization to be a strong supporter of independent journalism, and did not interfere or insert itself into any editorial content. “Their funding has been very useful in helping us get started,” Roose said. “It was a way for us to de-risk going out on our own. We’re feeling quite good about it and we’re grateful.”

events.title: Basel III applicable in almost all member jurisdictions by 2027
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) Three quarters of the Basel Committee’s 27 member jurisdictions have now published regulations implementing the full set of Basel III standards. Almost all member jurisdictions have publicly announced that banks must apply Basel III by April 2027 or earlier. The Committee will continue to closely monitor and assess the full and consistent implementation of Basel III standards. Member jurisdictions of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision made further progress in implementing the Basel III reforms, according to the Committee’s latest progress update , published today. The update and monitoring dashboard set out the jurisdictional adoption status of the Basel III standards as of end-September 2026 and show where the standards are already implemented by banks. They cover the final elements of Basel III published by the Committee in December 2017 and the finalised minimum capital requirements for market risk of January 2019. The implementation date for these reforms was 1 January 2023, as announced by the Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS) – the Basel Committee’s oversight body – in March 2020 . As of 30 September 2026, three quarter of the member jurisdictions have published their rules adopting the final Basel III, ie all standards with an implementation date of 1 January 2023. The revised credit risk and operational risk standards, as well as the output floor, are already effective in around 85% of the member jurisdictions. Looking ahead, almost all member jurisdictions have publicly announced that banks must apply Basel III by April 2027 or earlier. The monitoring dashboard provides the implementation history of Basel standards by member jurisdictions, including the publication and implementation dates of their domestic regulations. At the 9 March 2026 meeting of the GHOS, members welcomed the implementation progress and reaffirmed their expectation of full and consistent implementation of the Basel III framework by all member jurisdictions as soon as possible. The series of shocks to financial markets over the past few years and recent market developments have highlighted the importance of having a prudent global regulatory framework in place and a regulatory level playing field. The GHOS tasked the Committee with continuing to monitor and assess the full and consistent implementation of Basel III.
